prompt_html:
A group of 16 distinct people will be partitioned into 4 indistinguishable 4-person committees. Within each committee, two different members will be appointed: one as chairperson and one as secretary.

The number of different assignments can be written as 3rM, where r and M are positive integers and M is not divisible by 3. What is r?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Because the question requires different chairperson and secretary holders, give each temporarily numbered committee four slots: chair, secretary, ordinary member 1 and ordinary member 2. There are 16! placements. Every final assignment has exactly 4!(2!)^4 such representations, so N = 16!/[4!(2!)^4]. The exponent of 3 in 16! is floor(16/3) + floor(16/9) = 5 + 1 = 6. The denominator contributes exactly one factor of 3, from 4!. Hence r = 6 - 1 = 5, giving A.
skill_search: Permutations and assignments to distinct positions Uniform overcount correction in arrangements Prime exponents in products and factorials

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Temporarily label the committees and order their two ordinary members. Correct the resulting permutation count for these artificial distinctions, obtaining N = 16!/[4!(2!)^4]. Then count the factors of 3 in this quotient without evaluating the factorials.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Because the question requires different chairperson and secretary holders, give each temporarily numbered committee four slots: chair, secretary, ordinary member 1 and ordinary member 2. There are 16! placements. Every final assignment has exactly 4!(2!)^4 such representations, so N = 16!/[4!(2!)^4]. The exponent of 3 in 16! is floor(16/3) + floor(16/9) = 5 + 1 = 6. The denominator contributes exactly one factor of 3, from 4!. Hence r = 6 - 1 = 5, giving A.
domain_case_checks: The 16 people are distinct, and the four committees are disjoint, nonempty groups of four.
The question explicitly assigns chairperson and secretary to different members of each committee. The two offices are distinguishable; the other two members have no distinguished positions.

Every assignment has exactly 4! committee labellings and independently 2! orderings of the ordinary members in each committee. The division therefore removes a uniform multiplicity without losing or adding assignments.
The factor 9 in 16! contributes two factors of 3. There is no contribution from a multiple of 27 because 27 > 16.

The factorial quotient is a positive integer by its counting interpretation. Subtracting denominator prime exponents is therefore valid, and the resulting r = 5 leaves a positive integer M not divisible by 3.

useful_alternatives.method: Partition first, then assign the offices.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: There are 16!/[(4!)^4 4!] partitions into four indistinguishable groups of four. Each group has 4 × 3 = 12 ordered choices of chairperson and secretary. Thus N = 16! × 12^4/[(4!)^4 4!], whose exponent of 3 is 6 + 4 - 4 - 1 = 5.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for separating committee membership from office assignment and checking why internal member permutations and whole-committee permutations require different corrections.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Assigning 16 distinct people to 16 distinguishable temporary slots gives 16! arrangements; assigning two different people to the labelled offices gives 4 × 3 choices.
skills.learning_objective: Count assignments to distinguishable positions using successive available choices, while respecting the prohibition on assigning one person to two positions.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Each actual assignment has 4!(2!)^4 temporary representations, arising from committee labels and ordinary-member orders.
skills.learning_objective: Identify artificial labels and orders, prove their representation multiplicity is constant, and divide by that multiplicity without identifying distinct offices.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The requested r is v_3(N), calculated as floor(16/3) + floor(16/9) - v_3(4!) = 5.
skills.learning_objective: Determine the exact exponent of a prime in a factorial quotient, including additional contributions from higher powers of the prime.

prompt_html: A team of students is going to compete against a team of teachers in a trivia contest. The total number of students and teachers is 15. Ash, a cousin of one of the students, wants to join the contest. If Ash plays with the students, the average age on that team will increase from 12 to 14. If Ash plays with the teachers, the average age on that team will decrease from 55 to 52. How old is Ash?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: The student equation gives a=14(s+1)-12s=2s+14. The teacher equation gives a=52(t+1)-55t=52-3t. Since t=15-s, equating the expressions for a gives 2s+14=52-3(15-s)=7+3s, so s=7 and t=8. Hence a=2(7)+14=28. Indeed, (12·7+28)/8=14 and (55·8+28)/9=52, so the answer is A.
skill_search: Arithmetic mean, count and total Update an arithmetic mean after membership changes Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Eliminate choices using a valid necessary condition

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Let s and t be the original numbers of students and teachers, and let a be Ash's age. Convert each average into a total: 12s+a=14(s+1), 55t+a=52(t+1), and s+t=15. Rearrange the first two equations and solve the resulting linear system.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The student equation gives a=14(s+1)-12s=2s+14. The teacher equation gives a=52(t+1)-55t=52-3t. Since t=15-s, equating the expressions for a gives 2s+14=52-3(15-s)=7+3s, so s=7 and t=8. Hence a=2(7)+14=28. Indeed, (12·7+28)/8=14 and (55·8+28)/9=52, so the answer is A.
domain_case_checks: The original student and teacher teams must both be nonempty because their original average ages are specified; hence s,t are positive integers with s+t=15.
After Ash joins, the denominators are s+1 and t+1, both positive. Thus converting each mean equation into a total equation is reversible.
All subsequent rearrangements and substitutions are reversible linear operations, giving a unique real solution.
The solution s=7, t=8 consists of positive integers and satisfies the stated total of 15.
The resulting age 28 satisfies both original average conditions, so no extraneous solution has been introduced.
There are no empty-team or zero-denominator degenerate cases compatible with the question.

useful_alternatives.method: Use parity and congruences to eliminate options, then verify feasibility.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Since a=14+2s, Ash's age must be even. Since a=52-3t, it must be congruent to 1 modulo 3. Of the offered values, only 28 has both properties. Back-substitution gives s=7 and t=8, so it is genuinely feasible rather than merely the only surviving option.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful in this multiple-choice setting when integer group sizes make modular conditions especially restrictive.

skills.learning_objective: Convert exactly between an arithmetic mean, the number of observations, and their total.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The equations a=2s+14, a=52-3t, and s+t=15 are solved simultaneously.
skills.learning_objective: Solve a linear system created from several verbal constraints and verify its consistency.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The team sizes are required to be positive integers, and all mean denominators are checked to be nonzero.
skills.learning_objective: Retain positivity, integrality, and nonzero-denominator restrictions while solving a word problem.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The values s=7, t=8, and a=28 are substituted into both original average statements.
skills.learning_objective: Verify a proposed solution against every original numerical and domain condition.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The alternative method uses that a is even and a≡1 (mod 3) to eliminate options.
skills.learning_objective: Extract divisibility and residue conditions from integer equations and apply them to candidate values.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Necessary parity and modulo-3 conditions eliminate all options except 28 before feasibility is checked.

prompt_html:
Consider the following statements about the polynomial \(p(x)\), where \(a<b\):

I \(p(a) \le p(b)\)

II \(p'(a) \le p'(b)\)

III \(p''(a) \le p''(b)\)

Which of these statements is a necessary condition for \(p(x)\) to be increasing for \(a \le x \le b\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: If p is increasing and a<b, then p(a)≤p(b), so I is necessary. For II and III, take a=0, b=1 and p(x)=4x−x^3. On [0,1], p'(x)=4−3x^2≥1>0, so p is strictly increasing. However, p'(0)=4>1=p'(1), and p''(0)=0>−6=p''(1). Thus this admissible polynomial violates both II and III, proving that neither is necessary. The answer is B.
skill_search: Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Definitions of interval monotonicity Construct a legal counterexample Polynomial differentiation Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Derivative sign tests for monotonicity Separate example checking from a universal proof

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Prove I directly from the definition of increasing. Refute the necessity of II and III with one increasing cubic, checking its derivative sign throughout the interval and then comparing its endpoint derivatives.
audited_reference.concise_proof: If p is increasing and a<b, then p(a)≤p(b), so I is necessary. For II and III, take a=0, b=1 and p(x)=4x−x^3. On [0,1], p'(x)=4−3x^2≥1>0, so p is strictly increasing. However, p'(0)=4>1=p'(1), and p''(0)=0>−6=p''(1). Thus this admissible polynomial violates both II and III, proving that neither is necessary. The answer is B.
domain_case_checks: The inequalities concern real values on the nondegenerate interval [a,b], with a<b. Polynomials are continuous and differentiable throughout this interval.
If increasing means strictly increasing, then p(a)<p(b), which still implies I. If it means nondecreasing, equality is allowed; constant polynomials are included. The answer is unchanged.
The case a=b is excluded. In that degenerate case, all three endpoint comparisons would be equalities.
No particular endpoints or polynomial degree are prescribed, so the cubic on [0,1] is a legal counterexample. Its increase is verified on the whole interval, not merely at the endpoints.
The test p'>0 is used as a sufficient condition for strict increase, not as a reversible characterization: a strictly increasing function can have zero derivative at some points.

skills.evidence_in_solution: A necessary condition C must satisfy: p increasing on [a,b] implies C.
skills.learning_objective: Translate a necessary-condition question into the correct implication without reversing it.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Applying the definition of increasing to the ordered endpoints a<b proves p(a)≤p(b).
skills.learning_objective: Apply the ordered-input definition of monotonicity, including the distinction between strict and nonstrict comparisons.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The polynomial 4x−x^3 is increasing on [0,1] but violates both derivative endpoint comparisons.
skills.learning_objective: Refute necessity using a witness that satisfies the entire premise and violates the proposed condition.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Differentiating p(x)=4x−x^3 gives p'(x)=4−3x^2 and p''(x)=−6x.
skills.learning_objective: Compute first and second derivatives of a polynomial accurately.

skills.evidence_in_solution: For 0≤x≤1, x^2≤1, so multiplying by −3 reverses the inequality and gives 4−3x^2≥1.
skills.learning_objective: Establish a bound valid throughout an interval, preserving inequality direction.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The bound p'(x)≥1>0 proves that the counterexample is strictly increasing, despite its falling derivative values.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish the sign of a derivative from whether that derivative itself increases.

skills.evidence_in_solution: I receives a universal proof; II and III are each refuted by one counterexample. Examples satisfying a condition would not prove its necessity.
skills.learning_objective: Explain the different evidential roles of a universal argument and a single counterexample.

shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose p(x)=4x−x^3 on [0,1] to refute both derivative conditions at once.
conditions_checked: The polynomial and endpoints are not fixed numerically, so this is an admissible choice.
The bound p'(x)≥1 proves increase throughout the interval.
Both II and III fail in the same example.
The example refutes necessity; it is not being used to prove a universal claim.

prompt_html: For a positive integer \(n\), let \(A(n)\) be the area between \(y=x^2+3x-1\) and \(y=x^2+3\lfloor x\rfloor-1\) from \(x=1\) to \(x=n\). Which formula equals \(A(n)\) for every positive integer \(n\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let \(f(x)=x^2+3x-1\) and \(g(x)=x^2+3\lfloor x\rfloor-1\). Then \(f(x)-g(x)=3(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)\ge 0\). For each integer \(k=1,\ldots,n-1\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor=k\) on \([k,k+1)\), so the corresponding area is \(\int_k^{k+1}3(x-k)\,dx=3/2\). Values at the integer endpoints do not affect the integral. Hence the total area is \((n-1)(3/2)=\frac32(n-1)\), also giving zero when \(n=1\).

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Subtract the two graph ordinates, note that the difference is nonnegative, and split \([1,n]\) into the \(n-1\) unit intervals on which the floor function is constant. Each interval contributes \(3/2\).
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let \(f(x)=x^2+3x-1\) and \(g(x)=x^2+3\lfloor x\rfloor-1\). Then \(f(x)-g(x)=3(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)\ge 0\). Hence the total area is \((n-1)(3/2)=\frac32(n-1)\), also giving zero when \(n=1\).

When \(n=1\), the interval is degenerate and the area is zero; the empty-sum interpretation of the formula gives the same result.
For every real \(x\), \(0\le x-\lfloor x\rfloor<1\). Thus the first graph is never below the second, and the area equals the integral of their signed difference without further sign cases.
The floor function changes value at integers, but altering finitely many endpoint values does not change the definite integral.

Cancelling the common terms and splitting the integral are exact equality transformations. No squaring, division by a possibly zero quantity, or other non-reversible operation is used, so no extraneous solutions arise.

prompt_html: If \(x^3 + a x^2 - b x - c = 0\) has roots \(r, -s, -t\), then \(x^3 - a x^2 - b x + c = 0\) has roots:
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: P(-x)=-x^3+ax^2+bx-c, so Q(x)=-P(-x). For every u, Q(-u)=-P(u), hence Q(-u)=0 if and only if P(u)=0. Therefore the roots r,-s,-t become -r,s,t. The input change is invertible and the outside multiplier is nonzero, so this accounts for every root, with multiplicity.
skill_search: Transform polynomial zeros by affine substitution Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Factorisation and algebraic expansion Domain restrictions and reversible operations Sum and product of polynomial roots Substitute or independently check a proposed result Construct a legal counterexample Separate example checking from a universal proof

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Call the original polynomial P(x) and the second polynomial Q(x). Compute Q(x)=-P(-x), then negate each original root.
audited_reference.concise_proof: P(-x)=-x^3+ax^2+bx-c, so Q(x)=-P(-x). For every u, Q(-u)=-P(u), hence Q(-u)=0 if and only if P(u)=0. Therefore the roots r,-s,-t become -r,s,t. The input change is invertible and the outside multiplier is nonzero, so this accounts for every root, with multiplicity.
domain_case_checks: These are polynomials, so there are no denominator or radical restrictions. The identity works over both the real and complex numbers.
No positivity or distinctness assumption on r,s,t is needed. In particular, the main question does not state that r,s,t>0.
Both polynomials remain genuine monic cubics even if some or all of a,b,c vanish. Replacing x by -x and multiplying by -1 are reversible; neither introduces extraneous roots.
A zero root remains zero. If P(x)=(x-u)^m H(x), with H(u)≠0, then Q(x)=(-1)^(m+1)(x+u)^m H(-x), so the root -u has the same multiplicity m.
Root order is irrelevant. Special values, such as all three roots being zero, can make offered lists coincide; C is the list guaranteed for arbitrary admissible coefficients.

prompt_html:
Find the maximum value of

\[ 4^{\sin x} - 4 \times 2^{\sin x} + \frac{17}{4} \]

for real \(x\).
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let \(t=2^{\sin x}\). Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\) and the exponential with base 2 is increasing, \(\tfrac12\leq t\leq2\). Thus \[4^{\sin x}-4\cdot2^{\sin x}+\frac{17}{4}=t^2-4t+\frac{17}{4}=(2-t)^2+\frac14\leq\left(\frac32\right)^2+\frac14=\frac52.\] Equality holds when \(t=\tfrac12\), equivalently \(\sin x=-1\), which is attained. Therefore the maximum is \(\tfrac52\), option B.
skill_search: Allowed sine and cosine values Laws of real exponentials Monotonicity and interval images of real exponentials Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Quadratic extrema on a closed interval Recover exponents using injectivity Periodicity and endpoint inclusion Substitute or independently check a proposed result Complete the square and locate a quadratic vertex

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Set t = 2^{sin x}, retain its exact range [1/2, 2], and complete the square in the resulting quadratic. Bound the square on this interval and check that equality is attainable.
audited_reference.concise_proof:
Let \(t=2^{\sin x}\). Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\) and the exponential with base 2 is increasing, \(\tfrac12\leq t\leq2\). Thus
\[4^{\sin x}-4\cdot2^{\sin x}+\frac{17}{4}=t^2-4t+\frac{17}{4}=(2-t)^2+\frac14\leq\left(\frac32\right)^2+\frac14=\frac52.\]
Equality holds when \(t=\tfrac12\), equivalently \(\sin x=-1\), which is attained. Therefore the maximum is \(\tfrac52\), option B.
domain_case_checks: Both exponential bases are positive, so the original expression is defined for every real x.
The exact attainable range of t = 2^{sin x} is the closed interval [1/2, 2]. Unbounded x does not make sin x or t unbounded.

The identities 4^{sin x} = (2^{sin x})² and t² − 4t + 17/4 = (t − 2)² + 1/4 are exact. The substitution is not one-to-one in x, but it preserves the attainable expression values when its range is retained.
The inequality is squared only after establishing 0 ≤ 2 − t ≤ 3/2. Squaring is reversible on these nonnegative quantities, including its equality condition; no extraneous candidate is introduced.
The maximum is attained precisely at x = −π/2 + 2πk, k ∈ Z. The other endpoint t = 2 gives the minimum 1/4, attained at x = π/2 + 2πk.

useful_alternatives.method: Factor the gap from the candidate maximum.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: For q(t) = t² − 4t + 17/4, we have 5/2 − q(t) = (t − 1/2)(7/2 − t). On [1/2, 2], the first factor is nonnegative and the second is strictly positive. Hence q(t) ≤ 5/2, with equality exactly at t = 1/2.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: When an endpoint suggests a candidate extremum and an exact algebraic certificate of its global optimality is wanted.

\[ (\cos\theta) x - (\sin\theta) y = 2 \\ (\sin\theta) x + (\cos\theta) y = 1 \]

are solvable

options.label: A
options.html: for all values of \(\theta\) in the range \(0 \le \theta < 2\pi\);

options.label: B
options.html: except for one value of \(\theta\) in the range \(0 \le \theta < 2\pi\);

answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Write c = cosθ and s = sinθ. The coefficient determinant is c²+s² = 1 ≠ 0 for every real θ. Explicitly, x = 2c+s and y = c−2s give cx−sy = 2(c²+s²) = 2 and sx+cy = c²+s² = 1. Thus every permitted θ has a unique real solution, proving A independently of the options.
skill_search: Determinants and solvability of two-variable linear systems Pythagorean trigonometric identity Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result Separate example checking from a universal proof

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Compute the coefficient determinant: Δ = cosθ·cosθ − (−sinθ)sinθ = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. A nonzero determinant guarantees a unique solution, so there are no exceptional angles.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Write c = cosθ and s = sinθ. The coefficient determinant is c²+s² = 1 ≠ 0 for every real θ. Explicitly, x = 2c+s and y = c−2s give cx−sy = 2(c²+s²) = 2 and sx+cy = c²+s² = 1. Thus every permitted θ has a unique real solution, proving A independently of the options.
domain_case_checks: θ is real with 0 ≤ θ < 2π; x and y are unrestricted real unknowns. Sine, cosine and the displayed solution are defined throughout this domain.
A zero individual coefficient causes no failure. At θ = 0, π/2, π and 3π/2, the respective solutions are (2,1), (1,−2), (−2,−1) and (−1,2).
The determinant is always 1, so no singular or inconsistent parameter case remains to investigate. This does not rely on the generally false claim that every zero-determinant system is inconsistent.

The paired combinations c×(first equation)+s×(second equation) and −s×(first equation)+c×(second equation) are reversible: their transformation matrix has determinant c²+s² = 1. No division by sinθ or cosθ is needed, and substitution confirms that no extraneous solutions arise.
The endpoint θ = 0 is included and works. The endpoint 2π is excluded as stated; including it would not create an exception.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: With c = cosθ and s = sinθ, c×(first equation)+s×(second equation) gives (c²+s²)x = 2c+s. Similarly, −s×(first equation)+c×(second equation) gives (c²+s²)y = c−2s. Since c²+s² = 1, these give the solution directly; substitution verifies both original equations.

prompt_html: For all real \(x\), which expression is equal to \(1-\cos^2 x\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: For every real \(x\), \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\). Hence \(1-\cos^2 x=\sin^2 x\), so the correct option is B.

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use the Pythagorean identity \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\). Subtracting \(\cos^2 x\) from both sides, which is reversible for every real \(x\), gives \(1-\cos^2 x=\sin^2 x\).
audited_reference.concise_proof: For every real \(x\), \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\). Hence \(1-\cos^2 x=\sin^2 x\), so the correct option is B.

prompt_html: For how much of the interval \(0\le x\le2\pi\) is \(\cos x<0\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: On the unit circle, \(\cos x<0\) exactly in quadrants II and III, so the solution set in \([0,2\pi]\) is \((\pi/2,3\pi/2)\). Its length is \(3\pi/2-\pi/2=\pi\), while the full interval has length \(2\pi\). Hence the required proportion is \(\pi/(2\pi)=1/2\), giving option B.
skill_search: Recover all angles and signs in an interval Interval length and proportion Construct a legal counterexample

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use the unit circle: \(\cos x\) is the horizontal coordinate, so it is negative exactly on the left half of the circle. Thus \(\pi/2<x<3\pi/2\). Find this interval's length and divide by the length \(2\pi\) of the full interval.
audited_reference.concise_proof: On the unit circle, \(\cos x<0\) exactly in quadrants II and III, so the solution set in \([0,2\pi]\) is \((\pi/2,3\pi/2)\). Its length is \(3\pi/2-\pi/2=\pi\), while the full interval has length \(2\pi\). Hence the required proportion is \(\pi/(2\pi)=1/2\), giving option B.
domain_case_checks: The variable is real and restricted to the nondegenerate interval \([0,2\pi]\), whose length is \(2\pi>0\).
At \(x=\pi/2\) and \(x=3\pi/2\), \(\cos x=0\), so these points are excluded by the strict inequality. Excluding finitely many endpoints does not change interval length.
At the ambient endpoints, \(\cos 0=\cos 2\pi=1\), so neither endpoint satisfies the inequality.
The characterization \(\cos x<0\iff \pi/2<x<3\pi/2\) on the stated interval is an equivalence. No squaring or other nonreversible operation is used, so there are no extraneous solutions.
Dividing by \(2\pi\) is valid because it is positive and nonzero.

prompt_html: How many solutions does \(\tan x=0\) have in \(0\le x<2\pi\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: For tan x to be defined, cos x≠0. On this domain, tan x=0 iff sin x=0; multiplying by the nonzero denominator is reversible. Thus x=kπ. Since 0≤kπ<2π, the only integers are k=0 and k=1, giving x=0 and x=π. Hence there are 2 solutions.
skill_search: Basic trigonometric equations on an interval Domain restrictions and reversible operations Periodicity and endpoint inclusion Tangent quotient identity

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use tan x=sin x/cos x. On the domain cos x≠0, tan x=0 is equivalent to sin x=0, so x=kπ for an integer k. Restricting to 0≤x<2π gives k=0,1.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For tan x to be defined, cos x≠0. On this domain, tan x=0 iff sin x=0; multiplying by the nonzero denominator is reversible. Thus x=kπ. Since 0≤kπ<2π, the only integers are k=0 and k=1, giving x=0 and x=π. Hence there are 2 solutions.
domain_case_checks: Tangent is defined only when cos x≠0; in particular, x=π/2 and x=3π/2 are not solutions because tan x is undefined there.
The step sin x/cos x=0 ⇔ sin x=0 is reversible only after imposing cos x≠0.
For x=kπ, cos x=(-1)^k≠0, so every candidate from the zero family is in the domain of tangent.
The interval includes x=0 but excludes x=2π, so the coterminal endpoint 2π is not counted.
The two admitted solutions, 0 and π, are distinct; there are no parameter or degenerate cases.

prompt_html:
Find the positive difference between the two real values of \(x\) for which

\[(\log_2x)^4+12\left(\log_2\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\right)^2-2^6=0.\]
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: The domain is x>0. Setting t=(log₂x)²≥0 gives t²+12t−64=(t−4)(t+16)=0. Thus t=4, since t=−16 is impossible. Hence log₂x=±2, giving exactly x=4 and x=1/4. Both satisfy the original equation because 16+48−64=0. Their positive difference is 4−1/4=15/4, so C is correct.
skill_search: Domain restrictions and reversible operations Real logarithm product, quotient and power laws Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Signs of real quantities and squares Factorisation and algebraic expansion Solving quadratics and checking roots Logarithm–exponential inverse correspondence Laws of real exponentials Substitute or independently check a proposed result Existential possibility and admissible witness construction

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use log₂(1/x)=−log₂x for x>0. Treat the equation as a quadratic in t=(log₂x)²≥0, factor, reject the inadmissible negative value of t, and reverse both the square and the logarithm before subtracting the x-values.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The domain is x>0. Setting t=(log₂x)²≥0 gives t²+12t−64=(t−4)(t+16)=0. Thus t=4, since t=−16 is impossible. Hence log₂x=±2, giving exactly x=4 and x=1/4. Both satisfy the original equation because 16+48−64=0. Their positive difference is 4−1/4=15/4, so C is correct.
domain_case_checks: Both real logarithms are defined exactly when x>0. Their fixed base 2 is positive and different from 1.
The identity log₂(1/x)=−log₂x and the subsequent factorisation preserve equivalence throughout the domain. No division by log₂x is used.
The substitution t=(log₂x)² has range [0,∞), so the algebraic candidate t=−16 yields no real x.
The squared-logarithm substitution is many-to-one. Reversing t=4 requires both logarithm values +2 and −2; the negative logarithm gives the positive solution x=1/4 and must not be discarded.

The boundary t=0 corresponds to x=1, which gives −64 in the original equation and is not a solution. For each of the two admissible logarithm values, the inverse-logarithm relation gives exactly one positive x.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The distinct positive values x=4 and x=1/4 each give 16+48−64=0. Since the question states that there are two real values, these two witnesses identify them. Without that stated count, two successful substitutions alone would not prove completeness.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: As an independent check when simple candidate roots are noticed. The factorisation is preferable when proving the root count rather than taking it from the wording.

prompt_html:
For real \(x\), let \(P\) be \(x=0\), and let \(Q\) be \(2^x=1\).

Which statement is correct?

options.label: B
options.html: \(P\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(Q\).

options.label: C
options.html: \(P\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(Q\).

options.label: D
options.html: \(P\) is neither necessary nor sufficient for \(Q\).

answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: If x=0, then 2^x=2^0=1, so P⇒Q. Conversely, if 2^x=1=2^0, injectivity of the real exponential with base 2 gives x=0, so Q⇒P. Thus P is both necessary and sufficient for Q.
skill_search: Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Recover exponents using injectivity Laws of real exponentials Domain restrictions and reversible operations Distinguish converse from original statement

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Check both implications. Substitution of x=0 proves sufficiency; rewriting 1 as 2^0 and using exponential injectivity proves necessity.
audited_reference.concise_proof: If x=0, then 2^x=2^0=1, so P⇒Q. Conversely, if 2^x=1=2^0, injectivity of the real exponential with base 2 gives x=0, so Q⇒P. Thus P is both necessary and sufficient for Q.
domain_case_checks: The domain is all real x. The base 2 is positive and differs from 1, so 2^x is defined for every permitted x and is injective.
The value x=0 is permitted and satisfies both statements.
Injectivity excludes every nonzero real x, including negative and nonintegral values; no further cases are needed.
Rewriting 1 as 2^0 and then equating exponents are reversible here. No solutions are lost or introduced.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Use 2^0=1 both to verify P⇒Q and to rewrite the equation in Q.

prompt_html:
The lines given by the following equations are perpendicular.

\((1+\sqrt{3})y=px+5\) and \(y=(2-\sqrt{3})x+8\)

What is the value of \(p\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let r=√3. Since 1+r and 2−r are nonzero, both slopes are finite: m₁=p/(1+r) and m₂=2−r. As (2−r)(2+r)=1, perpendicularity requires m₁=−1/m₂=−(2+r). Hence p=−(1+r)(2+r)=−(5+3r), so p=−5−3√3.
skill_search: Extract the slope from a line equation Perpendicularity from line slopes Solve one-variable linear equations Exact surd and rational arithmetic Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Read the two finite slopes. The first line has slope p/(1+√3), while the second has slope 2-√3. Since (2-√3)(2+√3)=1, the slope perpendicular to 2-√3 is −(2+√3). Equating slopes gives p/(1+√3)=−(2+√3), so p=−(1+√3)(2+√3)=−5−3√3.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let r=√3. Since 1+r and 2−r are nonzero, both slopes are finite: m₁=p/(1+r) and m₂=2−r. As (2−r)(2+r)=1, perpendicularity requires m₁=−1/m₂=−(2+r). Hence p=−(1+r)(2+r)=−(5+3r), so p=−5−3√3.
domain_case_checks: √3 is the positive real square root of 3, so 1+√3 is nonzero.
The identity (2−√3)(2+√3)=1 shows that 2−√3 is nonzero.
Both lines are nonvertical for every real p, so the finite-slope perpendicularity criterion m₁m₂=−1 applies.
Multiplication or division by 1+√3 and 2−√3 is reversible because these quantities are nonzero.
The resulting equation is linear in p and has one real solution; there are no additional parameter cases.
The constants 5 and 8 affect only the intercepts, not perpendicularity.

useful_alternatives.method: Use the slope-product equation directly.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Set [p/(1+√3)](2−√3)=−1. Since the factors divided by are nonzero, p=−(1+√3)/(2−√3). Multiplying numerator and denominator by 2+√3 gives p=−(1+√3)(2+√3)=−5−3√3.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the negative-reciprocal slope is not immediately recognized.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The equation (1+√3)y=px+5 is converted to slope-intercept form, giving slope p/(1+√3).
skills.learning_objective: Extract the slope of a nonvertical line from an equation while dividing every term by the y-coefficient.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The slopes are required to be negative reciprocals, equivalently to have product −1.
skills.learning_objective: Use m₁m₂=−1 for two finite-slope perpendicular lines and recognize the vertical-horizontal exception.

skills.learning_objective: Use conjugates to simplify reciprocals involving quadratic surds and expand the result exactly.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The quantities 1+√3 and 2−√3 are checked to be nonzero before division and cancellation.
skills.learning_objective: Check that all divisors are nonzero before claiming algebraic equivalence.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The obtained value makes the first slope −(2+√3), whose product with the second slope is −1.

prompt_html: How many integer values of \(x\) satisfy \(|x^2-9|\leq 7\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Because 7 ≥ 0, |x²-9| ≤ 7 is equivalent to -7 ≤ x²-9 ≤ 7. Adding 9 throughout, a reversible operation, gives 2 ≤ x² ≤ 16. Thus √2 ≤ |x| ≤ 4. Since |x| is an integer, |x| ∈ {2,3,4}, giving x = ±2, ±3, ±4. Hence there are 6 values, so the correct option is D.
skill_search: Domain restrictions and reversible operations Absolute values and square roots of squares Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Integer points in bounded intervals Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Rewrite the absolute-value inequality reversibly as -7 ≤ x² - 9 ≤ 7, then add 9 to obtain 2 ≤ x² ≤ 16. Since x is an integer, |x| is an integer and must be 2, 3 or 4. Each nonzero magnitude gives two values of x, so the total is 3 × 2 = 6.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Because 7 ≥ 0, |x²-9| ≤ 7 is equivalent to -7 ≤ x²-9 ≤ 7. Adding 9 throughout, a reversible operation, gives 2 ≤ x² ≤ 16. Thus √2 ≤ |x| ≤ 4. Since |x| is an integer, |x| ∈ {2,3,4}, giving x = ±2, ±3, ±4. Hence there are 6 values, so the correct option is D.
domain_case_checks: The stated domain is x ∈ ℤ; the expression |x²-9| is defined for every such x.
The equivalence |u| ≤ 7 ⇔ -7 ≤ u ≤ 7 is valid because 7 is nonnegative.
Adding 9 to all three parts of the compound inequality is reversible and preserves both inequality directions.
The lower equality x² = 2 has no integer solution; the smallest permitted integer magnitude is therefore 2.
The upper endpoints x = ±4 satisfy equality: |16-9| = 7.
The nearby excluded values fail: x = ±1 gives 8 and x = 0 gives 9.
Every permitted magnitude is nonzero, so its positive and negative values are distinct; there is no zero degeneracy.

useful_alternatives.method: Count a containing interval and subtract the failures.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: From x² ≤ 16, the possible integers are -4 through 4, giving 9 values. The condition x² ≥ 2 removes exactly -1, 0 and 1, leaving 9-3=6.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the outer square bound produces a short consecutive interval of integers.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The solution retains the integer domain and checks when the absolute-value equivalence and later transformations are reversible.
skills.learning_objective: Preserve the stated integer domain and state the conditions under which an inequality transformation is equivalent.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The absolute-value inequality is converted to -7 ≤ x²-9 ≤ 7, and both signs corresponding to each nonzero magnitude are recovered.
skills.learning_objective: Convert |u| ≤ a into a two-sided inequality for a ≥ 0 and retain both positive and negative solutions.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Adding 9 throughout gives 2 ≤ x² ≤ 16, with inclusive endpoints preserved.

prompt_html: If \([X]\) is the smallest integer greater than or equal to \(X\), what is the value of \([ -2.2 ] + [ 3 ] + [ 5.2 ]\)?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Since −3 < −2.2 ≤ −2, 2 < 3 ≤ 3, and 5 < 5.2 ≤ 6, the three ceilings are −2, 3 and 6. Their sum is −2+3+6=7.

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use the ceiling characterization: ⌈x⌉ is the unique integer n satisfying n−1 < x ≤ n. Thus ⌈−2.2⌉=−2, ⌈3⌉=3 and ⌈5.2⌉=6, so the sum is 7.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Since −3 < −2.2 ≤ −2, 2 < 3 ≤ 3, and 5 < 5.2 ≤ 6, the three ceilings are −2, 3 and 6. Their sum is −2+3+6=7.
domain_case_checks: The ceiling function is defined for every real number, so all three inputs are valid.
For the negative input, −2—not −3—is the smallest integer at least −2.2.
The exact integer input is an equality case: ⌈3⌉=3, not 4.
For 5.2, the least integer no smaller than it is 6.
No equation-solving transformation is used, so reversibility and extraneous solutions do not arise.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Move from each input in the positive direction to the first integer encountered. This gives −2, 3 and 6.

prompt_html: John, Mary, and Joe played a game of marbles. At the end of the game, John had 15 marbles more than Mary, but only one-third of what Joe had. If each player initially had 20 marbles, what was the total number of marbles with John after the game?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: The three players initially had 3×20=60 marbles in total. If John finished with x marbles, Mary finished with x-15 and Joe with 3x. Conservation gives x+(x-15)+3x=60, hence x=15. The corresponding counts are John 15, Mary 0 and Joe 45, which satisfy every condition. Therefore the answer is B.
skill_search: Model verbal linear relationships Solve a one-variable linear equation Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Let John's final number be x. Then Mary has x-15 and Joe has 3x. Assuming the game only redistributed the original 60 marbles, x+(x-15)+3x=60, so 5x=75 and x=15.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The three players initially had 3×20=60 marbles in total. If John finished with x marbles, Mary finished with x-15 and Joe with 3x. Conservation gives x+(x-15)+3x=60, hence x=15. The corresponding counts are John 15, Mary 0 and Joe 45, which satisfy every condition. Therefore the answer is B.
domain_case_checks: Final marble counts must be nonnegative integers.
The phrase “John had one-third of what Joe had” gives x=Joe/3, equivalently Joe=3x. Multiplication by 3 is reversible because 3 is nonzero.
Adding 15 and dividing by 5 when solving 5x-15=60 are reversible operations, so no extraneous solution is introduced.
The solution places Mary at the boundary value 0. This is permitted because the question does not require every player to retain a positive number of marbles.
The coefficient 5 is nonzero, so the linear equation has exactly one real solution, which is also an admissible integer.

prompt_html: To gain entry for the Bachelor's programs in different colleges, students need to appear for the AST entrance test. Of all students who register for the test, only 80% appear for the test. Of these students, only 75% clear the test and gain entry into a college of his/her liking. By what percentage is the number of students who do not appear for the test after registering less than the number of students who clear the test?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let \(T>0\) students register. Then \(T/5\) do not appear, while \((3/4)(4T/5)=3T/5\) clear. Therefore the required percentage is \[\frac{3T/5-T/5}{3T/5}\times100\%=\frac23\times100\%=66\tfrac23\%.\] Cancelling \(T\) is reversible because \(T>0\). Hence the exact answer is option D.
skill_search: Proportions of wholes and nested subsets Relative percentage comparison Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Normalize the number registered to 100, which is valid because all relevant counts scale proportionally. Then 80 appear, so 20 do not appear. Of the 80 who appear, \(75\%=60\) clear. Thus the number not appearing is less than the number clearing by \(60-20=40\), measured relative to 60: \(40/60\times100\%=66\tfrac{2}{3}\%\).
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let \(T>0\) students register. Then \(T/5\) do not appear, while \((3/4)(4T/5)=3T/5\) clear. Therefore the required percentage is \[\frac{3T/5-T/5}{3T/5}\times100\%=\frac23\times100\%=66\tfrac23\%.\] Cancelling \(T\) is reversible because \(T>0\). Hence the exact answer is option D.
domain_case_checks: The registered total must be positive; if it were zero, the requested relative percentage would have denominator zero and be undefined.
The number clearing is \(3T/5>0\), so division by it is valid.
If student counts are required to be integers and the stated percentages are exact, a positive total divisible by 5 suffices; the result is independent of the chosen compatible total.
There is no equality case: \(T/5<3T/5\) for every \(T>0\). No equation-solving step introduces extraneous values.
The exact percentage is 66⅔%, which equals the revised option D. Its recurring decimal is 66.666…%; no rounding or truncation is needed.

useful_alternatives.method: Use proportions directly.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Non-attenders form \(1/5\) of the total and clearers form \((3/4)(4/5)=3/5\). Their ratio is therefore \(1:3\), so the shortfall is two of the three clearer-parts, namely \(2/3=66\tfrac23\%\).
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when an unspecified total makes a ratio calculation more natural than introducing 100 students.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The solution applies 75% to the 80% who appear, obtaining \((0.75)(0.80)=0.60\) of all registrants.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the reference group for each stated proportion and correctly compose proportions of nested subsets.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The relative shortfall is calculated as \((60-20)/60\), using the number who clear as the reference quantity.
skills.learning_objective: Calculate how many percent one nonnegative quantity is less than another, using the larger comparison quantity as the denominator.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The total is taken to satisfy \(T>0\), ensuring that the number clearing is nonzero and that cancellation and division are valid.
skills.learning_objective: Check that reference quantities and cancelled factors are nonzero before division.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The result is independently checked using 100 registrants and compared with every offered option.
skills.learning_objective: Verify a percentage result using a convenient compatible total and the original wording.

shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose 100 registrants, giving whole-number counts of 80 attendees, 20 non-attendees and 60 clearers.
conditions_checked: The total is unspecified and may be normalized because every count is proportional to it.
A total of 100 is positive and compatible with the exact percentages.
Scale invariance, rather than one isolated example, justifies the general conclusion.
shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: Normalize to 100 and calculate the relative shortfall.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: It avoids writing and later cancelling a variable T.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is a minor notational convenience and is itself the standard ordinary percentage method, not a material shortcut.

prompt_html:
Find the maximum value of the function
\[\text{f}(x) = \frac{1}{4^{x} + 4^{-x} - 2\left(2^{x} + 2^{-x}\right) + 8}.\]
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let D(x) be the denominator. Since 4^x = (2^x)^2, we have D(x) = 6 + (2^x − 1)^2 + (2^(−x) − 1)^2 ≥ 6 for every real x. Thus f(x) ≤ 1/6. Equality holds precisely when both squares vanish, which is equivalent to x = 0. Since f(0) = 1/6, the maximum is 1/6, option B.
skill_search: Laws of real exponentials Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares Domain restrictions and reversible operations Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Recover exponents using injectivity Substitute or independently check a proposed result Sharp bounds and attainment for global extrema Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Reciprocal exponential substitution

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Complete two squares in the denominator. Use their nonnegativity to obtain a positive lower bound, take reciprocals, and check when equality is attained.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let D(x) be the denominator. Since 4^x = (2^x)^2, we have D(x) = 6 + (2^x − 1)^2 + (2^(−x) − 1)^2 ≥ 6 for every real x. Thus f(x) ≤ 1/6. Equality holds precisely when both squares vanish, which is equivalent to x = 0. Since f(0) = 1/6, the maximum is 1/6, option B.
domain_case_checks: For every real x, the exponential terms are defined and positive. The identity D(x) ≥ 6 proves that the denominator never vanishes, so the real domain of f is all of R.
Completing the squares is an identity, hence reversible. Since D(x) > 0, the passage D(x) ≥ 6 ⇔ 1/D(x) ≤ 1/6 is also reversible, with the inequality reversed.
Equality in the bound requires both nonnegative squares to be zero. The equation 2^x = 1 has the unique real solution x = 0 because base 2 is injective.
The bound holds for every real x, so no cases are omitted. As x tends to either infinity, D(x) tends to infinity and f(x) tends to 0; these ends cannot give a larger value.
In the alternative substitution t = 2^x + 2^(−x), one must retain t ≥ 2. The unconstrained quadratic vertex t = 1 is inadmissible; the boundary t = 2 is attained at x = 0.
No equation is squared in the main proof, so no extraneous roots are introduced.

useful_alternatives.method: Use the sum of reciprocal exponentials as a constrained substitution.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Set t = 2^x + 2^(−x). Then t − 2 = (2^x − 1)^2/2^x ≥ 0. Also t^2 = 4^x + 4^(−x) + 2, so D = t^2 − 2t + 6 = (t − 1)^2 + 5. Since t ≥ 2, D ≥ 6, with equality at x = 0.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when an expression is polynomial in a sum of reciprocal exponentials. It also explains why 1/5 is tempting but invalid here. Directly completing two squares is shorter for this particular denominator.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Rewrites 4^(±x) as (2^(±x))^2 and uses 2^(−x) = 1/2^x.
skills.learning_objective: Recognize compatible exponential bases and rewrite their powers into an algebraic form.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Rewrites the denominator exactly as 6 + (2^x − 1)^2 + (2^(−x) − 1)^2.
skills.learning_objective: Complete squares while preserving every coefficient and constant.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Both squares are nonnegative, and their sum is zero only when both are zero.
skills.learning_objective: Use nonnegative squares to prove bounds and identify their equality conditions.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The exponential terms exist for all real x, and D ≥ 6 excludes denominator zeros.
skills.learning_objective: Establish the domain of a reciprocal expression before applying reciprocal inequalities.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses D ≥ 6 > 0 to obtain 1/D ≤ 1/6.
skills.learning_objective: Reverse inequalities correctly when taking positive reciprocals or multiplying by a negative number.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The equality condition 2^x = 1 forces x = 0.
skills.learning_objective: Recover the unique exponent from an exponential equality with a valid injective base.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Substitution into the original expression confirms D(0) = 6 and f(0) = 1/6.
skills.learning_objective: Verify that an equality candidate is admissible and attains the claimed value.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Combines the universal upper bound f(x) ≤ 1/6 with its attainment at x = 0.
skills.learning_objective: Prove a global optimum by establishing a bound for every admissible input and checking an equality witness.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The alternative method introduces t = 2^x + 2^(−x) and retains the restriction t ≥ 2.
skills.learning_objective: Carry the attainable range of a substituted variable into the transformed optimization problem.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The product 2^x·2^(−x) = 1 makes the denominator quadratic in t = 2^x + 2^(−x).
skills.learning_objective: Exploit reciprocal exponential terms to reduce an expression to a constrained algebraic problem.

shortcut_assessments.method_here: Use the legal choice x = 0 as a witness attaining the upper bound, after proving that bound globally.
conditions_checked: At x = 0 the original denominator is 6, so the input is admissible.
The example establishes attainment, not the universal upper bound.

shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: None; checking attainment is part of the ordinary proof.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful witness construction, but not a material shortcut.

shortcut_assessments.method_here: Establish the global denominator bound D ≥ 6 by nonnegative squares, reverse the positive reciprocal inequality, and verify equality.

prompt_html:
A sequence of real numbers \((a_n)\) is defined by \(a_1 = 2\) and the recurrence
\[a_{n+1}(a_n - 1) = \frac{1}{2}a_n^2 - a_n + \frac{1}{2} \qquad (n \geq 1).\]
Find the value of
\[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n + 1).\]
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: The recurrence is a_{n+1}(a_n-1)=(a_n-1)^2/2. Since a_1=2, a_2=1/2. If a_n<1, cancellation is valid and gives a_{n+1}=(a_n-1)/2<0<1. Thus induction shows that a_n≠1 for every n, so the reduced recurrence holds throughout. Setting b_n=a_n+1 gives b_1=3 and b_{n+1}=b_n/2. Therefore S_N=Σ_{n=1}^N b_n=6(1-2^{-N}), which tends to 6. Hence the answer is D.
skill_search: Factorisation and algebraic expansion Domain restrictions and reversible operations Signs of real quantities and squares Translate and evaluate a recurrence Mathematical induction Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Geometric progression and multiplicative indexing Finite and infinite geometric sums Telescoping sums and endpoint limits

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Factor the right-hand side, prove that a_n=1 is never reached, and cancel a_n-1. Then set b_n=a_n+1: the requested summands form a geometric progression with first term 3 and ratio 1/2.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The recurrence is a_{n+1}(a_n-1)=(a_n-1)^2/2. Since a_1=2, a_2=1/2. If a_n<1, cancellation is valid and gives a_{n+1}=(a_n-1)/2<0<1. Thus induction shows that a_n≠1 for every n, so the reduced recurrence holds throughout. Setting b_n=a_n+1 gives b_1=3 and b_{n+1}=b_n/2. Therefore S_N=Σ_{n=1}^N b_n=6(1-2^{-N}), which tends to 6. Hence the answer is D.
domain_case_checks: Indices begin at n=1. The first summand is a_1+1=3, and b_n=3(1/2)^{n-1} involves n-1 transitions.
If a_n=1, the original recurrence becomes 0=0 and does not determine a_{n+1}. This exceptional state must not be cancelled away. It is unreachable: a_1=2, a_2=1/2, and a_n<1 implies a_{n+1}<1.
Consequently, division by a_n-1 is reversible at every actual term, and the initial condition determines a unique sequence. The shift b_n=a_n+1 is also reversible, with inverse a_n=b_n-1.
The formula gives a_n=-1+3(1/2)^{n-1}>-1 at every finite index. The allowed fixed point -1 is approached but never attained; each summand a_n+1 remains positive.

The infinite geometric sum is justified because |1/2|<1. Its value is the limit of finite partial sums, not the limit of the individual summands. Splitting it into the separately divergent series Σa_n and Σ1 would not justify an answer.

useful_alternatives.method: Telescope the recurrence.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: After the same cancellation check, a_n+1=2(a_n-a_{n+1}). Hence S_N=2(a_1-a_{N+1}). Using a_{N+1}=-1+3·2^{-N} gives S_N=6(1-2^{-N}) and limit 6.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for seeing how a recurrence can turn a series into endpoint terms, or for obtaining the finite partial sum without recalling the geometric-sum formula.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Recognises a_n^2/2-a_n+1/2 as (a_n-1)^2/2.
skills.learning_objective: Recognise a scaled perfect square and expose a common factor in a recurrence.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Separates the exceptional state a_n=1 before dividing by a_n-1.
skills.learning_objective: Justify cancellation in an implicit recurrence by proving that the cancelled factor never vanishes.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses a_n<1 to obtain (a_n-1)/2<0<1.
skills.learning_objective: Use the sign of a recurrence expression to exclude a future exceptional value.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Computes a_2=1/2 and obtains a_{n+1}=(a_n-1)/2 on the justified domain.
skills.learning_objective: Translate an implicit recurrence into an explicit update while retaining its initial condition and valid indices.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Proves a_n<1 for every n≥2 from the base case a_2=1/2 and the preserved inequality.
skills.learning_objective: Prove that a recurrence preserves a property at all later indices rather than relying on a few computed terms.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Introduces b_n=a_n+1, exactly the expression being summed, and obtains b_{n+1}=b_n/2.
skills.learning_objective: Shift the sequence to remove an additive constant, updating both the recurrence and initial term.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Derives b_n=3(1/2)^{n-1} from b_1=3 and b_{n+1}=b_n/2.
skills.learning_objective: Obtain an exact geometric term formula with the correct initial value and transition count.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Evaluates S_N=6(1-2^{-N}) and uses |1/2|<1 to take its limit.
skills.learning_objective: Evaluate a convergent geometric series through its partial sums, distinguishing the series value from the summand limit.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses a_n+1=2(a_n-a_{n+1}) to reduce S_N to 2(a_1-a_{N+1}).
skills.learning_objective: Cancel consecutive differences in a finite sum and retain the correct endpoint indices before taking a limit.

shortcut_assessments.method_here: Derive b_{n+1}=b_n/2 for b_n=a_n+1, then use the exact geometric rule and its partial sums.
conditions_checked: The cancelled factor is proved nonzero at every actual term.
The initial value is b_1=3, so the nth term uses n-1 transitions.
The ratio is 1/2, and its absolute value is less than 1.
shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: Safely factor the recurrence and sum the shifted geometric series.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: None relative to the baseline; the repeated-rule method is the baseline.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful recognition of structure, but not a material shortcut.

subtopic: Optimization of trig expression via substitution
prompt_html:
Find the maximum value of
\[f(x) = \frac{2\sin^2 x + 10\cos x - 14}{\cos^2 x + 3\cos x - 10}\]
where \(x\) is a real number.
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let c = cos x ∈ [−1,1]. Then f(x) = [−2(c−2)(c−3)]/[(c−2)(c+5)]. Neither denominator factor vanishes on this interval, so cancellation gives f(x) = 2(3−c)/(c+5). Now 0 < 2(3−c) ≤ 8 and c+5 ≥ 4, hence f(x) ≤ 8/4 = 2. Equality holds when c = −1, which is attained at x = π. Therefore the maximum is 2, option D.
skill_search: Pythagorean trigonometric identity Allowed sine and cosine values Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares Domain restrictions and reversible operations Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Certify a global extremum with a sharp bound Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Put c = cos x ∈ [−1,1], replace sin²x by 1−c², factor and legally cancel the common factor. Bound the resulting positive numerator above and denominator below, then check that both bounds are attained together.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let c = cos x ∈ [−1,1]. Then f(x) = [−2(c−2)(c−3)]/[(c−2)(c+5)]. Neither denominator factor vanishes on this interval, so cancellation gives f(x) = 2(3−c)/(c+5). Now 0 < 2(3−c) ≤ 8 and c+5 ≥ 4, hence f(x) ≤ 8/4 = 2. Equality holds when c = −1, which is attained at x = π. Therefore the maximum is 2, option D.
domain_case_checks: The image of cosine for real x is exactly [−1,1]. Replacing x by c = cos x preserves the set of attainable function values, although the substitution is not one-to-one.
The original denominator is (c−2)(c+5). Its zeros, 2 and −5, are outside [−1,1], so the original function is defined for every real x.
Cancelling c−2 is reversible on the permitted interval because c−2 is never zero there. No admissible value is removed or introduced.
The reduced denominator lies in [4,6] and is strictly positive. Thus numerator and denominator bounds can be used with the stated inequality directions.
The upper numerator bound and lower denominator bound occur together at c = −1. At x = π, the original denominator is −12 and f(π) = 2, so this is an attained maximum, not merely a supremum.
The corresponding lower bound is f(x) ≥ 4/6 = 2/3, attained at c = 1. The uniform bounds cover every interior value as well as both endpoints.

useful_alternatives.method: Rewrite the reduced fraction as a positive reciprocal plus a constant.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: After valid cancellation, f(x) = −2 + 16/(c+5). Since 4 ≤ c+5 ≤ 6, it follows that 2/3 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2. This also shows that the expression decreases as c increases.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for making the direction of change explicit and avoiding confusion between the maximum and minimum. The monotonicity is in c, not globally in x.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses sin²x = 1−cos²x to express the numerator entirely in cosine.
skills.learning_objective: Use the Pythagorean identity to reduce a mixed sine–cosine expression to one trigonometric variable.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Restricts c = cos x to [−1,1] and recognises that both endpoints are attainable.
skills.learning_objective: Carry the exact cosine range into an algebraic optimisation and check endpoint attainability.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Introduces c = cos x without treating c as an unrestricted real variable.
skills.learning_objective: Replace a trigonometric expression by an algebraic variable while preserving precisely the attainable values.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Factors −2c²+10c−12 as −2(c−2)(c−3) and c²+3c−10 as (c−2)(c+5).
skills.learning_objective: Factor paired quadratics while retaining scalar factors and identifying a common factor.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Establishes c−2 < 0, c+5 > 0 and 2(3−c) > 0 throughout the permitted interval.
skills.learning_objective: Use interval information to determine signs before cancellation or fraction comparisons.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Rejects the denominator zeros c = 2 and c = −5 as unattainable and justifies cancelling c−2.
skills.learning_objective: Check original and cancelled denominator factors against the feasible domain before simplifying.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses the positive numerator and denominator bounds to obtain f ≤ 8/4 and f ≥ 4/6.
skills.learning_objective: Bound a positive ratio in the correct directions and identify when equality in the component bounds is compatible.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Combines the uniform bound f(x) ≤ 2 with the admissible equality point x = π.
skills.learning_objective: Prove a global maximum by establishing both a domain-wide upper bound and an input attaining it.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Checks f(π) directly in the original expression, including its nonzero denominator.
skills.learning_objective: Verify a proposed extremising input against the original expression rather than only its simplified form.

conditions_checked: x = π is admissible and the original denominator is −12.
This example proves that the value 2 occurs, not that all values are at most 2.

prompt_html: Given curve \(y= -\frac{1}{3}x^3+a^2x+a\), has a local minimum in the second quadrant, find the possible values of \(a\).

options.label: G
options.html: There are no possible values of \(a\).

answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Write f(x)=-x³/3+a²x+a. Then f'(x)=a²-x² and f''(x)=-2x. A second-quadrant local minimum must have x<0, f'(x)=0 and f(x)>0. At a stationary point, a²=x², so f(x)=a+2x³/3. Since x<0, positivity of f(x) forces a>0. Thus x=-a, and f(-a)=a(1-2a²/3)>0 is equivalent to 0<a<√(3/2). Conversely, every a in this interval gives x=-a<0, f(-a)>0 and f''(-a)=2a>0, so it does give a second-quadrant local minimum.
skill_search: Cartesian quadrant membership Differentiate polynomials with constant parameters Stationary points and local extrema of polynomials Signs of real quantities and squares Factorisation and algebraic expansion Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Domain restrictions and reversible operations Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Absolute values and square roots of squares Substitute or independently check a proposed result Construct a legal counterexample Existential possibility and admissible witness construction

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Differentiate and impose both second-quadrant conditions. At a stationary point, use a²=x² to simplify the ordinate and establish a>0 before selecting x=-a and solving the height inequality.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Write f(x)=-x³/3+a²x+a. Then f'(x)=a²-x² and f''(x)=-2x. A second-quadrant local minimum must have x<0, f'(x)=0 and f(x)>0. At a stationary point, a²=x², so f(x)=a+2x³/3. Since x<0, positivity of f(x) forces a>0. Thus x=-a, and f(-a)=a(1-2a²/3)>0 is equivalent to 0<a<√(3/2). Conversely, every a in this interval gives x=-a<0, f(-a)>0 and f''(-a)=2a>0, so it does give a second-quadrant local minimum.
domain_case_checks: The parameter a and coordinate x are real. The polynomial is differentiable everywhere, so every local minimum must be stationary.
The second quadrant requires both x<0 and y>0; points on either axis are excluded.
When a=0, the curve is y=-x³/3. It is strictly decreasing and has a stationary inflection at the origin, not a local minimum.
For a<0, the local minimum is at x=-|a| and has ordinate a-(2/3)|a|³<0. It cannot lie in the second quadrant.
At a=√(3/2), the minimum has ordinate zero and lies on the negative x-axis. For larger positive a, its ordinate is negative.
Division by a occurs only after proving a>0. On that domain, division by a and replacing a²<3/2 by a<√(3/2) are reversible. No extraneous solutions are introduced.

useful_alternatives.method: Use absolute values and a first-derivative sign chart.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: For a≠0, the stationary points are x=±|a|. The derivative a²-x² changes from negative to positive at -|a|, so this is the local minimum. Its ordinate is a-(2/3)|a|³, which is positive exactly when a>0 and a²<3/2. For a=0, the derivative has no sign change.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the learner is unsure which of x=±a is the minimum as a changes sign, or wants classification without the second-derivative test.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The minimum must satisfy x<0 and y>0, with both axes excluded.
skills.learning_objective: Translate Cartesian quadrant membership into both required strict coordinate inequalities.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Differentiation gives f'(x)=a²-x² and f''(x)=-2x, treating a as constant.
skills.learning_objective: Differentiate a polynomial with a constant parameter, including its second derivative.

prompt_html: Let \(P\) be a property of a real number \(x\). Each of the following is a statement about all real values of \(x\). Exactly one of the following statements is true. Which one is it?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: For c = 1 or 2 and real x, x² ≥ c² is equivalent to ¬(|x| < c). Thus ¬P(x) ⇒ x² ≥ c² has the equivalent contrapositive |x| < c ⇒ P(x), giving E ⇔ A and F ⇔ B. Also, G means P(x) ⇒ x² < 1, which is equivalent to C. Every statement except D therefore has a distinct equivalent partner and cannot be uniquely true. Hence D is true. The premise is consistent: take P(x) to mean x = 1. Then D holds for every real x; A, B, E and F fail at x = 0, while C and G fail at x = 1. This example checks consistency, rather than replacing the uniqueness argument.
skill_search: Absolute values and square roots of squares Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Negate and reverse to form a contrapositive Compare option implications and incompatibility Separate example checking from a universal proof Construct a legal counterexample Existential possibility and admissible witness construction

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Rewrite the squared inequalities using absolute values. Contraposition gives A ⇔ E and B ⇔ F, while interpreting “only if” gives C ⇔ G. A member of any of these pairs cannot be the sole true statement. The explicit exactly-one-true premise therefore forces D.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For c = 1 or 2 and real x, x² ≥ c² is equivalent to ¬(|x| < c). Thus ¬P(x) ⇒ x² ≥ c² has the equivalent contrapositive |x| < c ⇒ P(x), giving E ⇔ A and F ⇔ B. Also, G means P(x) ⇒ x² < 1, which is equivalent to C. Every statement except D therefore has a distinct equivalent partner and cannot be uniquely true. Hence D is true. The premise is consistent: take P(x) to mean x = 1. Then D holds for every real x; A, B, E and F fail at x = 0, while C and G fail at x = 1. This example checks consistency, rather than replacing the uniqueness argument.
domain_case_checks: All statements concern the same fixed property P over all real x. Exactly one complete universal statement is true; this is not a claim that exactly one conditional holds at each individual x.
For c > 0, x² < c² ⇔ |x| < c and x² ≥ c² ⇔ |x| ≥ c. These transformations are reversible because √(x²) = |x| and both magnitudes are nonnegative.
Equality is retained correctly: x = ±1 satisfies x² ≥ 1, not x² < 1; x = ±2 satisfies x² ≥ 4, not x² < 4. D permits P to hold at x = ±1 but forbids it at x = ±2.
Contraposition is an equivalence; taking the converse or merely negating both sides is not.

Vacuous truth does not create an exceptional answer. If P is always false, C, D and G are all true. If P is always true, A, B, E and F are all true. Both constant properties violate the exactly-one premise.
The property P(x) ⇔ x = 1 is an admissible consistency witness. No continuity, positivity or other restriction on P is stated.

prompt_html:
Let
\[W = \int_0^1 4^{\sqrt{x}}\,dx, \qquad X = \int_1^2 2^{\sqrt{x-1}}\,dx, \qquad Y = \int_0^{1/2} 2\cdot 2^{2x}\,dx, \qquad Z = \int_{-1}^1 \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{(x+1)/2}\,dx.\]
Which of the following gives \(W\), \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) in order from smallest to largest?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Using t=x−1 for X, t=2x for Y and t=(x+1)/2 for Z gives \[W=\int_0^1 2^{2\sqrt t}\,dt,\quad X=\int_0^1 2^{\sqrt t}\,dt,\quad Y=\int_0^1 2^t\,dt,\quad Z=\int_0^1 2^{t/2}\,dt.\] For every 0<t<1, we have t/2<t<√t<2√t: in particular, t²<t implies t<√t since both quantities are nonnegative. As 2^u is strictly increasing, the normalized integrands satisfy the corresponding strict order. They are continuous, so integrating gives Z<Y<X<W, which is A.
skill_search: Translate the variable and integral limits Laws of real exponentials Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Monotonicity of real exponential functions Pointwise comparison of definite integrals Domain restrictions and reversible operations

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use affine substitutions to put every integral on [0,1], rewrite all integrands with base 2, and compare their exponents pointwise. No antiderivatives are needed.
audited_reference.concise_proof:
Using t=x−1 for X, t=2x for Y and t=(x+1)/2 for Z gives
\[W=\int_0^1 2^{2\sqrt t}\,dt,\quad X=\int_0^1 2^{\sqrt t}\,dt,\quad Y=\int_0^1 2^t\,dt,\quad Z=\int_0^1 2^{t/2}\,dt.\]
For every 0<t<1, we have t/2<t<√t<2√t: in particular, t²<t implies t<√t since both quantities are nonnegative. As 2^u is strictly increasing, the normalized integrands satisfy the corresponding strict order. They are continuous, so integrating gives Z<Y<X<W, which is A.
domain_case_checks: All original integrands are real and continuous on their closed intervals. For W, x≥0; for X, x−1≥0. Every exponential base is positive.

The substitutions are increasing bijections onto [0,1]. Their differentials are dx=dt for X, dx=dt/2 for Y and dx=2dt for Z. Thus the prefactors in Y and Z cancel exactly, and the transformations are reversible.
The comparison t<√t is made only for 0<t<1. Squaring or taking square roots preserves this comparison because both sides are nonnegative; no extraneous roots are introduced.

At t=0, all normalized integrands equal 1. At t=1, their values in the order Z,Y,X,W are √2,2,2,4. The endpoint equality between X and Y does not prevent strict integral inequality because their integrands differ strictly throughout (0,1).

skills.evidence_in_solution: The changes t=x−1, t=2x and t=(x+1)/2 put X, Y and Z on [0,1], with the differential factors included.
skills.learning_objective: Normalize shifted and scaled definite integrals to a common interval, updating bounds, integrands and differentials together.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The identities 4^{√t}=2^{2√t} and (√2)^t=2^{t/2} express all four integrands using base 2.
skills.learning_objective: Use power-of-a-power laws with positive bases to express exponentials in a common base.

skills.evidence_in_solution: For 0<t<1, the proof establishes t/2<t<√t<2√t, using t²<t and nonnegativity.
skills.learning_objective: Compare a number in (0,1) with its square root while preserving the sign conditions needed for squaring.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Since 2>1, the strict ordering of the four exponents gives the same strict ordering of their exponential values.
skills.learning_objective: Determine whether exponential inequalities preserve or reverse exponent order from the value of the base.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The normalized continuous integrands are strictly ordered on (0,1), so their definite integrals are strictly ordered despite endpoint equalities.
skills.learning_objective: Deduce strict integral inequalities from a global pointwise comparison and justify the strictness.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The square-root domains are valid, the affine substitutions are reversible, and nonnegativity validates the square-root comparison.
skills.learning_objective: Check real domains and reversibility before transforming expressions or comparing their values.

solution_html: By the power rule and linearity, \[ \int_{-1}^{1}\sum_{k=1}^{11}kx^{k-1}\,dx =\sum_{k=1}^{11}[x^k]_{-1}^{1} =\sum_{k=1}^{11}\bigl(1-(-1)^k\bigr). \] This summand is \(2\) when \(k\) is odd and \(0\) when \(k\) is even. Since \(1,3,5,7,9,11\) are the six odd indices, the value is \(6\cdot2=12\).
skill_search: Integrate powers and evaluate endpoints Split and combine definite integrals Signs of real quantities and squares Odd/even integrals on a symmetric interval

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Write the integrand as \(\sum_{k=1}^{11}kx^{k-1}\). An antiderivative is \(F(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{11}x^k\), so the integral is \(\sum_{k=1}^{11}(1-(-1)^k)\). The six odd values of \(k\) contribute \(2\) each and the even values contribute \(0\), giving \(12\).
audited_reference.concise_proof:
By the power rule and linearity,
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}\sum_{k=1}^{11}kx^{k-1}\,dx
=\sum_{k=1}^{11}[x^k]_{-1}^{1}
=\sum_{k=1}^{11}\bigl(1-(-1)^k\bigr).
\]
This summand is \(2\) when \(k\) is odd and \(0\) when \(k\) is even. Since \(1,3,5,7,9,11\) are the six odd indices, the value is \(6\cdot2=12\).
domain_case_checks: The displayed expression is a finite polynomial, so it is continuous and integrable throughout \([-1,1]\).
The ellipsis is interpreted as the stated pattern \(kx^{k-1}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,11\), consistently with the first terms and the final term \(11x^{10}\).
The power rule is valid for every exponent \(k-1\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\}\); no logarithmic or singular case occurs.
Both endpoints are included when evaluating \(F(1)-F(-1)\). No non-reversible operation is used and there are no extraneous solutions or parameter cases.

The odd powers \(2x,4x^3,6x^5,8x^7,10x^9\) integrate to zero on \([-1,1]\). For \(j=0,\ldots,5\),
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}(2j+1)x^{2j}\,dx=2.
\]
Thus the six remaining terms total \(12\).

prompt_html:
Three players \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) take turns throwing a fair six-sided die in the order \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(\ldots\) until one of them wins. The win conditions on a player's own throw are:
\[\begin{aligned} &A \text{ wins if } A \text{ throws a } 6, \\ &B \text{ wins if } B \text{ throws a } 5 \text{ or a } 6, \\ &C \text{ wins if } C \text{ throws a } 4, 5 \text{ or } 6. \end{aligned}\]
If a player throws and does not win, play passes to the next player. What is the probability that \(B\) is the first to win?
answer_verification_basis: independent reviewed content for this testing release
solution_html: Let P be the probability that B eventually wins. In the first round, B wins with probability b=(5/6)(2/6)=5/18. All three players fail with probability q=(5/6)(4/6)(3/6)=5/18. After three failures, independent future throws give exactly the original game again. Wins by A or C contribute zero to B's probability, so P=b+qP. Hence (13/18)P=5/18 and P=5/13. Also, the probability of no winner after n complete rounds is q^n, which tends to zero, so the game terminates with probability 1.
skill_search: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity Condition on the correct event and denominator Independent trials and path probabilities Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities First-step and restart probability equations Equivalence-preserving solution of a linear equation Geometric sums and convergence Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Group play into rounds beginning with A. Compute the probability that B wins during a round and the probability that all three players fail, then use a restart equation for B's eventual winning probability.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let P be the probability that B eventually wins. In the first round, B wins with probability b=(5/6)(2/6)=5/18. All three players fail with probability q=(5/6)(4/6)(3/6)=5/18. After three failures, independent future throws give exactly the original game again. Wins by A or C contribute zero to B's probability, so P=b+qP. Hence (13/18)P=5/18 and P=5/13. Also, the probability of no winner after n complete rounds is q^n, which tends to zero, so the game terminates with probability 1.
domain_case_checks: Use the standard model of independent throws, each with six equally likely faces.
For B to win in a round, A must first fail. No condition on C's throw is needed, because play stops immediately when B wins.
A restart requires all three players to fail, not merely A and B. The first-round outcomes A wins, B wins, C wins, and all fail are disjoint and exhaustive.
Here q=5/18 lies strictly between 0 and 1. Arbitrarily long play is possible, but infinite play has probability zero.
The rearrangement and division are reversible because 1-q=13/18 is nonzero. The resulting probability 5/13 lies in [0,1], and sequential stopping makes ties impossible.

useful_alternatives.method: Sum a geometric series over the winning round.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: For n≥0, the probability that n whole rounds fail and B wins in round n+1 is q^n b. These events are mutually exclusive, so P=b(1+q+q^2+...)=b/(1-q)=5/13, with b=q=5/18 and |q|<1.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: When geometric series are familiar, or when the distribution of the round in which B wins is also wanted.

useful_alternatives.method: Condition a round on producing a winner.
useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The single-round winning masses for A, B and C are 3/18, 5/18 and 5/18. Failed rounds regenerate the same independent state, so the winner of the first decisive round has these masses normalized by their sum 13/18. Thus B's probability is (5/18)/(13/18)=5/13.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: When finding all three winning probabilities together, or explaining why B and C have equal eventual chances despite different per-throw success probabilities.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Among six equally likely faces, the numbers of winning and failing faces are respectively (1,5) for A, (2,4) for B, and (3,3) for C.
skills.learning_objective: Convert each player's specified winning faces into correct per-throw win and failure probabilities.

skills.evidence_in_solution: B's success probability conditional on reaching its throw is 1/3, whereas B's first-round winning probability from the initial state is 5/18. The decisive-round alternative normalizes by 13/18.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish a probability conditional on a turn being reached from a probability measured from the start of the game.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Independent throws give b=(5/6)(2/6), q=(5/6)(4/6)(3/6), and probability q^n for n failed rounds.
skills.learning_objective: Multiply the probabilities along a specified sequence of independent outcomes and justify why past failures do not change future throw probabilities.

skills.evidence_in_solution: Partitioning the first round into the three possible winners and complete failure gives P=b+qP.
