subtopic: Intersections of absolute-value cubic and absolute-value linear
prompt_html: Let \(p\) be a real number, and let \(n\) denote the number of points of intersection of the curves \(y = |x^3 - p^3|\) and \(y = p^3 |x - 1|\). \(n\) cannot take which of the following values?
solution_html:
For \(p<0\), the left side \(|x^3-p^3|\) is nonnegative and the right side \(p^3|x-1|\) is nonpositive. Equality would require \(x=p\) and \(x=1\), impossible; hence \(n=0\). For \(p=0\), only \(x=0\) works, giving \(n=1\).

For \(p>0\), put \(q=p^3>0\). Equality of the two magnitudes is equivalent to either

\[x^3-q=q(x-1)\quad\text{or}\quad x^3-q=-q(x-1).\]

The first gives \(x(x^2-q)=0\), with three distinct roots \(0,\sqrt q,-\sqrt q\). The second gives \(F(x)=x^3+qx-2q=0\). Since \(F^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+q>0\) and its limits at the two infinities have opposite signs, it has exactly one real root.

A root is shared by the two equations only if \(2q(x-1)=0\), hence \(x=1\), which requires \(q=1\). Thus \(p=1\) gives three distinct intersections, and every other positive \(p\) gives four.

The complete attainable set is \(\{0,1,3,4\}\), witnessed by \(p=-1,0,1,2\) respectively. The impossible value is 2, answer E.

prompt_html: Let \(y = t^{\sin 2x} - 2 \, t^{-\sin 2x}\), where \(t \gt 0\) and \(x\) is real. For what values of \(t\), is the product between the maximum value of \(y\) and the minimum value of \(y\) positive.
solution_html:
Let \(u=t^{\sin 2x}\). Then \(y=u-2/u\).

For \(u\gt 0\), the expression \(u-\frac{2}{u}\) increases as \(u\) increases, because
\[\frac{d}{du}\left(u-\frac{2}{u}\right)=1+\frac{2}{u^2}\gt 0.\]
Case 1: \(t\geq 1\).

Since \(-1\leq \sin 2x\leq 1\), we have \(\frac{1}{t}\leq u\leq t\). Hence the maximum value of \(y\) is \(t-\frac{2}{t}\), and the minimum value of \(y\) is \(\frac{1}{t}-2t\).

Since \(t\geq 1\), we have \(\frac{1}{t}-2t\lt 0\). Therefore the product is positive exactly when \(t-\frac{2}{t}\lt 0\). Multiplying by \(t\gt 0\) gives \(t^2\lt 2\), so \(t\lt \sqrt{2}\). In this case, we get \(1\leq t\lt \sqrt{2}\).

Case 2: \(0\lt t\leq 1\).

Now \(t\leq u\leq \frac{1}{t}\). Hence the maximum value of \(y\) is \(\frac{1}{t}-2t\), and the minimum value of \(y\) is \(t-\frac{2}{t}\).

Since \(0\lt t\leq 1\), we have \(t-\frac{2}{t}\lt 0\). Therefore the product is positive exactly when \(\frac{1}{t}-2t\lt 0\). Multiplying by \(t\gt 0\) gives \(1-2t^2\lt 0\), so \(t\gt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). In this case, we get \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lt t\leq 1\).

Combining the two cases gives
\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lt t\lt \sqrt{2}.\]

prompt_html:
The following is an attempted proof of the conjecture:

if \(\sin\theta \gt \cos\theta\), then \(\sin\theta \gt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Suppose \(\sin\theta \gt \cos\theta\).

Then \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta \gt 0\). (I)

Squaring the positive quantity \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\) gives \((\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \gt 0\), which expands using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) to \(1 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \gt 0\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta \lt \frac{1}{2}\). (II)

From (II), \((\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \lt 2\), hence \(|\sin\theta + \cos\theta| \lt \sqrt{2}\), so in particular \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta \gt -\sqrt{2}\). (III)

Adding the inequalities (I) \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta \gt 0\) and (III) \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta \gt -\sqrt{2}\) gives \(2\sin\theta \gt -\sqrt{2}\), so \(\sin\theta \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\); squaring this inequality yields \(\sin^2\theta \gt \frac{1}{2}\). (IV)

Since \(\sin^2\theta \gt \frac{1}{2}\) means \(|\sin\theta| \gt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), and \(\sin\theta \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) rules out \(\sin\theta \lt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), we conclude \(\sin\theta \gt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). (V)

Which one of the following is the case?

options.html: The proof is incorrect, and the first error occurs in line (I).
options.label: B

options.html: The proof is incorrect, and the first error occurs in line (II).
options.label: C

options.html: The proof is incorrect, and the first error occurs in line (III).
options.label: D

options.html: The proof is incorrect, and the first error occurs in line (IV).
options.label: E

options.html: The proof is incorrect, and the first error occurs in line (V).
options.label: F

solution_html:
The conjecture is false. Counterexample: \(\theta = \frac{5\pi}{6}\) gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\sin\theta \gt \cos\theta\) holds, but \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \lt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Lines (I)--(III) are valid.

(I) is just a rearrangement of the hypothesis.

(II) Since \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta \gt 0\), squaring preserves positivity: \((\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \gt 0\). Expanding and using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) correctly gives \(1 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \gt 0\), hence \(\sin\theta\cos\theta \lt \frac{1}{2}\).

(III) \((\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = \sin^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), and using (II) this is less than \(1 + 1 = 2\), so \(|\sin\theta + \cos\theta| \lt \sqrt{2}\), hence \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta \gt -\sqrt{2}\).

The error is in line (IV). Adding the inequalities is fine and correctly yields \(\sin\theta \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). The fallacy is the next step: squaring is order-preserving on non-negative numbers; with a negative lower bound, this inequality alone does not justify comparing the squares in the same direction. From \(\sin\theta \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) one cannot conclude \(\sin^2\theta \gt \frac{1}{2}\); for example \(\sin\theta = 0\) satisfies \(\sin\theta \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) but \(\sin^2\theta = 0 \lt \frac{1}{2}\). Indeed at the counterexample \(\theta = \frac{5\pi}{6}\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \gt -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) but \(\sin^2\theta = \frac{1}{4} \lt \frac{1}{2}\), so (IV) fails.

So (IV) is the first error, and the proof is incorrect.

subtopic: Systems with exponentials and logs (change of variables)
prompt_html:
Let \(k\) be a real constant. Consider the simultaneous equations
\[k \cdot 2^x + \log_2 y + \log_2 z = 3,\]
\[2^x + k \log_2 y + \log_2 z = 2,\]
\[2^x + \log_2 y + \log_2 z = k,\]
in real unknowns \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), subject to \(y \gt 1\) and \(z \gt 0\).

Which of the following is the necessary and sufficient condition on \(k\) for the system to have a real-valued solution set \(\{x,y,z\}\)?
solution_html:
Let \(X = 2^x\), \(Y = \log_2 y\), \(Z = \log_2 z\). The constraints translate to \(X \gt 0\), \(Y \gt 0\) (since \(y \gt 1\)), and \(Z \in \mathbb{R}\) (since \(z \gt 0\)). The system becomes
\[kX + Y + Z = 3, \quad X + kY + Z = 2, \quad X + Y + Z = k.\]
Subtract the third equation from the first: \((k-1)X = 3 - k\), so \(X = \frac{3-k}{k-1}\) (requires \(k \neq 1\)).

Subtract the third from the second: \((k-1)Y = 2 - k\), so \(Y = \frac{2-k}{k-1}\).

Then \(Z = k - X - Y\) is automatically a real number.

Positivity of \(X\):
\[\frac{3-k}{k-1} \gt 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad 1 \lt k \lt 3.\]
Positivity of \(Y\):
\[\frac{2-k}{k-1} \gt 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad 1 \lt k \lt 2.\]
Both must be true, therefore: \(1 \lt k \lt 2\).

At \(k=1\), the first subtracted equation is \(0=2\), so there is no solution. Conversely, whenever \(1<k<2\), the displayed \(X,Y\) are positive and \(Z=k-X-Y\) is real. Taking \(x=\log_2X\), \(y=2^Y\), and \(z=2^Z\) gives real unknowns with \(y>1,z>0\) satisfying all three original equations. This proves sufficiency as well as necessity.

prompt_html: Let \(n\) be an integer. Which of the following is a necessary but not sufficient condition for which \(n^3 + 5n\) is divisible by \(12\)?

options.html: \(n\) is \(1\) more than a multiple of \(4\).
options.label: A

options.html: \(n\) is \(2\) more than a multiple of \(4\).
options.label: G

solution_html:
Modulo 3, n³+5n≡n³−n=n(n−1)(n+1), which is divisible by 3 for every integer n.

Modulo 4, n³+5n≡n³+n. For n≡0,1,2,3 the residues are respectively 0,2,2,2. Therefore 12 divides n³+5n exactly when 4 divides n.

Every multiple of 4 is even, but n=2 is even and gives 18, not divisible by 12. Thus being even is necessary but not sufficient, option C.

Answer: C.

Within the guaranteed single-correct-answer format, n=4 rejects A, B, D, F and G, while n=2 proves C is not sufficient. If E were necessary but not sufficient, E would imply C is necessary, and the n=2 example would make C necessary but not sufficient too, contradicting uniqueness. prompt_html:
For each positive integer \(k\), let \(F(k)\) be the sum of all real solutions \(x\) of
\[\sin(2^k x)=\frac{1}{2}\]
in the interval \(0\leq x\leq \frac{2\pi}{2^k}\). Find
\[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}F(k).\]
solution_html:
For \(k = 1\), there are exactly two solutions:
\[\frac{\pi}{6}\times \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{5\pi}{6}\times\frac{1}{2}.\]
For \(k = 2\), because of the domain restriction, there are also exactly two solutions:
\[\frac{\pi}{6}\times \frac{1}{2^2} \text{ and } \frac{5\pi}{6}\times\frac{1}{2^2}.\]
Similarly for \(k=3\), because of the domain restriction, there are also exactly two solutions:
\[\frac{\pi}{6}\times \frac{1}{2^3} \text{ and } \frac{5\pi}{6}\times\frac{1}{2^3}.\]
The same pattern continues.

Therefore: \(F(1) = \pi\times\frac{1}{2}\), \(F(2) = \pi\times\frac{1}{2^2}\) and \(F(3) = \pi\times\frac{1}{2^3}\). They form a geometric sequence with first term \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), common ratio \(1/2\). Thus
\[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}F(k) = \frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}} = \pi.\]

The series begins at k=1 and has ratio 1/2, so its sum is (π/2)/(1-1/2)=π.

prompt_html:
A set \(X\) of positive integers, with \(|X| \geq 3\), is called cross-linked if and only if for every number \(x\) in \(X\) there exist two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(X\), both different from \(x\), and a prime \(p\), such that \(p\) divides each of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Let \(Y\) be a set of positive integers with \(|Y| \geq 3\).

Which of the following statements is equivalent to \(Y\) being not cross-linked?

options.html: For every number \(x\) in \(Y\), and for every two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\), there is no prime which divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).
options.label: A

options.html: For every number \(x\) in \(Y\) there exist two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\), both different from \(x\), such that no prime divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).
options.label: B

options.html: There exists a number \(x\) in \(Y\), and there exist two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\), such that no prime divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).
options.label: C

options.html: There exists a number \(x\) in \(Y\) such that for every two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\), there is no prime which divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).
options.label: D

options.html: There exists a number \(x\) in \(Y\) such that for every two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\), there is a prime which divides \(x\) but divides neither \(y\) nor \(z\).
options.label: E

options.html: There exists a number \(x\) in \(Y\) such that for every prime \(p\) which divides \(x\), \(p\) divides neither of any two distinct numbers \(y\), \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\).
options.label: F

options.html: For every number \(x\) in \(Y\) there exist two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\), both different from \(x\), and a prime \(p\), such that \(p\) divides \(x\) but \(p\) does not divide \(y\) and \(p\) does not divide \(z\).
options.label: G

solution_html:
A good way to approach this question is to simply write down the negation of cross-linked.

Start outwards. \(Y\) is cross-linked requires some property \(p_1\) to be true for every \(x\) in \(Y\). Therefore the negation is that there exists an \(x\) in \(Y\) for which this property \(p_1\) is false.

The property \(p_1\): there exist distinct \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\), different from \(x\), for which some property \(p_2\) is true. Therefore not having the property \(p_1\), or the negation of \(p_1\), is: there does not exist such \(y\) and \(z\) with property \(p_2\). Another way of writing the same idea: if you examine every pair of possible \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\), then none of them have property \(p_2\).

The property \(p_2\): there exists a prime \(p\) that divides \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). Not having property \(p_2\), or the negation of \(p_2\): for every prime \(p\), \(p\) does not divide all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), or equivalently, no prime \(p\) divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Altogether, a valid negation is:

There exists a number \(x\) in \(Y\) such that for every two distinct numbers \(y\) and \(z\) in \(Y\) with \(y \neq x\) and \(z \neq x\), there is no prime which divides all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

This is option D.

This is exactly D: for some x no allowed pair forms a triple with a common prime divisor. The final negation says at least one of the three divisibility assertions fails. It does not require a prime divisor of x that divides neither other number. For example Y={6,10,15} is not cross-linked because its only triple has gcd 1, although every member shares some prime factor with another member.

prompt_html:
Find the units digit of
\[7^{7^{7^{7^7}}}.\]
You may find it useful to consider the remainder of odd powers of 7 when divided by 4.
solution_html:
The units digits of 7¹,7²,7³,7⁴ are 7,9,3,1. Since 7⁴≡1 mod 10, multiplication proves this cycle repeats for all positive powers.

Let E be the exponent on the outermost 7. It is 7 raised to an odd positive integer. Since 7≡−1 mod 4, E≡−1≡3 mod 4.

The third position of the units cycle is 3, so the answer is C.

Answer: C.

prompt_html:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be polynomials. Consider the following four statements.

I: If \(f'(x) \geq g'(x)\) for all \(x \geq 0\) and \(f(0) \geq g(0)\), then \(f(x) \geq g(x)\) for all \(x \geq 0\).

II: If \(f(x) \geq g(x)\) for all \(x \geq 0\), then \(\int_0^x t\,f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \geq \int_0^x t\,g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for all \(x \geq 0\).

III: If \(\int_0^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \geq \int_0^x g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for all \(x \geq 0\), then \(f(x) \geq g(x)\) for all \(x \geq 0\).

IV: If \(\int_0^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \geq \int_0^x g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for all \(x \geq 0\), then \(\int_0^x t^2\,f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \geq \int_0^x t^2\,g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for all \(x \geq 0\).

Which of the statements are true?
solution_html:
Let \(h=f-g\). Statement I is true: \(h(x)=h(0)+\int_0^x h'(t)\,dt\geq0\) for \(x\geq0\). Statement II is true because pointwise \(h(t)\geq0\) implies \(t h(t)\geq0\) on that interval.

For III and IV take \(g=0\) and \(f(t)=3t^2-4t+1\). Then \[\int_0^x f(t)\,dt=x(x-1)^2\geq0\quad(x\geq0),\] so their antecedent holds for every permitted upper limit.

Nevertheless \(f(1/2)=-1/4<0\), disproving III. Also \[\int_0^1 t^2 f(t)\,dt=\frac35-1+\frac13=-\frac1{15}<0,\] disproving IV. Thus I and II only are true, option F.

prompt_html: A circle has centre \(A=(6,7)\). Two tangents from the point \(B=(1,2)\) touch the circle at \(P\) and \(Q\). Given that length \(BP=2\sqrt{10}\), find the sum of the gradients of the tangent lines \(BP\) and \(BQ\).
solution_html:
Translate everything by the vector \((-1,-2)\). This does not change any gradients, so we can work in the transformed universe which has much nicer numbers!

The point \(B=(1,2)\) becomes \(O=(0,0)\), and the centre \(A=(6,7)\) becomes \(C=(5,5)\).

Let the radius of the circle be \(r\). Since \(OP=2\sqrt{10}\) and \(OC=\sqrt{5^2+5^2}=5\sqrt{2}\), the right triangle \(OCP\) gives
\[OC^2=OP^2+r^2.\]
So \(50=40+r^2\), hence \(r^2=10\). The transformed circle is
\[(x-5)^2+(y-5)^2=10.\]
A tangent line through the origin has equation \(y=mx\). Substitute the tangent equation into the circle equation:
\[(x-5)^2+(mx-5)^2=10.\]
The expanded quadratic is
\[(m^2+1)x^2-10(m+1)x+40=0.\]
For the line to be a tangent, this quadratic must have exactly one solution for \(x\), so its discriminant must be \(0\):
\[[-10(m+1)]^2-4(m^2+1)(40)=0.\]
So
\[100(m+1)^2-160(m^2+1)=0.\]
Dividing by \(20\) gives
\[5(m+1)^2-8(m^2+1)=0.\]
Expanding,
\[5m^2+10m+5-8m^2-8=0,\]
so
\[3m^2-10m+3=0.\]
The two tangent lines have gradients equal to the two roots of this quadratic. Therefore the sum of the gradients is \(\frac{10}{3}\).

Altenative geometrical method

It is possible to find the answer to this geometrically. Work with the transformed version of the problem, centre \((5,5)\), two tangents both passing \(O\). Let \(P\) be the lower of the two points, drop a perpendicular vertical line from \(P\) to the \(x\)-axis, let \(X\) be the point where it cross the \(x\)-axis. Let \(PX=a\) and \(OX=b\). By symmetry, we can draw a horizontal line from \(Q\) to the \(y\)-axis, call the point of intersection \(Y\), and then \(QY=a\) and \(OY=b\). The sum of gradients is then just
\[\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab} = \frac{(2\sqrt{10})^2}{ab}.\]
Therefore, it is enough to find \(ab\).

Next observe that crucially, if we construct a right angled triangle with \(XC\) being the hypotenuse, by drawning two lines, one horizontal one vertical, then this triangle is similar to \(OXP\), by scale factor \(1/2\), which we get by comparing the lengths of their hypotenuses. Thus its other sides are \(a/2\) and \(b/2\). Next bring these together into the isosceles right-angled triangle with hypotenuse \(OC\), so that we deduce:
\[b/2+a=5 \text{ and } b-a/2=5.\]
From which we find \(b=6\) and \(a=2\), hence
\[\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab} = \frac{(2\sqrt{10})^2}{12}=\frac{10}{3}.\]

prompt_html: A safe is protected by a 6-character password that uses each of the letters \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\), \(e\), \(f\) exactly once. After each attempt the safe reports only the number of positions in which the attempted string agrees with the password (it does not say which positions). The following three attempts have already been made: \(abcdef\) gave 0 correct positions, \(feadbc\) gave 0 correct positions, and \(fbdcae\) gave 3 correct positions. A player now plays optimally, choosing each subsequent attempt with full knowledge of all responses received so far. What is the smallest number \(N\) such that the player is guaranteed to be able to identify the password after at most \(N\) further attempts (regardless of what the password actually is)?
solution_html:
Throughout, write a candidate password as \(\pi_1\pi_2\pi_3\pi_4\pi_5\pi_6\), a permutation of \(\{a, b, c, d, e, f\}\).

Step 1: Position constraints from the first two attempts.

Each attempt giving \(0\) correct positions tells us, for every position \(i\), that the letter placed there is not \(\pi_i\). The attempt \(abcdef\) rules out \(\pi_1 = a\), \(\pi_2 = b\), \(\pi_3 = c\), \(\pi_4 = d\), \(\pi_5 = e\), \(\pi_6 = f\). The attempt \(feadbc\) rules out \(\pi_1 = f\), \(\pi_2 = e\), \(\pi_3 = a\), \(\pi_4 = d\), \(\pi_5 = b\), \(\pi_6 = c\). Combining,
\[\pi_1 otin \{a, f\}, \quad \pi_2 otin \{b, e\}, \quad \pi_3 otin \{a, c\}, \quad \pi_4 eq d, \quad \pi_5 otin \{b, e\}, \quad \pi_6 otin \{c, f\}.\]

Step 2: Combine with the third attempt.

The attempt \(fbdcae\) has \(3\) correct positions, so exactly \(3\) of the six claims
\[\pi_1 = f, \quad \pi_2 = b, \quad \pi_3 = d, \quad \pi_4 = c, \quad \pi_5 = a, \quad \pi_6 = e\]
hold. But \(\pi_1 = f\) and \(\pi_2 = b\) are already ruled out by Step 1, so both must be false. Exactly \(3\) of the remaining \(4\) claims must therefore hold; equivalently, exactly one of them fails.

Step 3: Enumerate the candidates.

For each choice of "false claim", the other three letters are pinned and we fill in the remaining three positions using the unused letters, subject to the Step 1 constraints.

Case A, \(\pi_6 eq e\): pin \(\pi_3 = d\), \(\pi_4 = c\), \(\pi_5 = a\). Letters \(\{b, e, f\}\) remain for positions \(\{1, 2, 6\}\). The constraint \(\pi_2 otin \{b, e\}\) forces \(\pi_2 = f\); then \(\pi_6 otin \{c, e, f\}\) forces \(\pi_6 = b\), leaving \(\pi_1 = e\). Candidate: \(efdcab\).

Case B, \(\pi_5 eq a\): pin \(\pi_3 = d\), \(\pi_4 = c\), \(\pi_6 = e\). Letters \(\{a, b, f\}\) remain. Then \(\pi_1 otin \{a, f\}\) forces \(\pi_1 = b\); \(\pi_5 otin \{a, b, e\}\) forces \(\pi_5 = f\), leaving \(\pi_2 = a\). Candidate: \(badcfe\).

Case C, \(\pi_4 eq c\): pin \(\pi_3 = d\), \(\pi_5 = a\), \(\pi_6 = e\). Letters \(\{b, c, f\}\) remain for \(\{1, 2, 4\}\) with \(\pi_1 \in \{b, c\}\), \(\pi_2 \in \{c, f\}\), \(\pi_4 \in \{b, f\}\). Two valid assignments: \(bcdfae\) and \(cfdbae\).

Case D, \(\pi_3 eq d\): pin \(\pi_4 = c\), \(\pi_5 = a\), \(\pi_6 = e\). Letters \(\{b, d, f\}\) remain for \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) with \(\pi_1 \in \{b, d\}\), \(\pi_2 \in \{d, f\}\), \(\pi_3 \in \{b, f\}\). Two valid assignments: \(bdfcae\) and \(dfbcae\).

So the candidate set has six elements:
\[\{badcfe, \; bcdfae, \; bdfcae, \; cfdbae, \; dfbcae, \; efdcab\}.\]

Step 4: One further attempt cannot guarantee identification.

First observe that any two of the six remaining candidates agree in at least two positions. Now consider any one further attempt. If two candidates agree in a certain position, then that position contributes the same amount to both of their response scores: either the attempt matches both of them there, or it matches neither of them there. Since any two candidates agree in at least 2 positions, they can differ in at most 4 positions. Therefore, under any single attempt, the response scores of any two candidates can differ by at most \(4\).

So the range of the six possible response scores is at most \(4\), implies at least two of them will have to respond with the same response, and therefore it is not possible to determine the password with a single further attempt, and hence \(N\geq 2\).

Step 5: Two further attempts suffice.

We now show that two further attempts are enough.

The high-level idea is to choose a test attempt that splits the six candidates into useful response groups. A good test should not be too similar to many candidates, otherwise many candidates may give the same high response. For example, a test with \(bfdcae\) that gives all six candidates the same response of \(4\) would be poor. But it should also not be too far away from all candidates, because if all candidates returned \(0\), we would learn nothing as well.

So the aim is to choose a test whose responses divide the candidates into manageable buckets. There are many possible attempts that can work; we only need to exhibit one valid strategy.

For attempt \(4\), we could for example try \(abcfde\). The six candidates give responses
\[badcfe o 1, \quad bcdfae o 2, \quad bdfcae o 1, \quad cfdbae o 1, \quad dfbcae o 1, \quad efdcab o 0.\]
A response of \(0\) identifies the password as \(efdcab\); a response of \(2\) identifies it as \(bcdfae\). If the response is \(1\), the candidate set narrows to \(\{badcfe, bdfcae, cfdbae, dfbcae\}\).

In that case, for attempt \(5\), try \(baecdf\). The four remaining candidates give
\[badcfe o 3, \quad bdfcae o 2, \quad cfdbae o 0, \quad dfbcae o 1,\]
all distinct, so the password is identified.

Hence two further attempts always suffice, and combining with Step 4, \(N = 2\). The answer is B.

prompt_html: How many distinct real solutions does \(4^x + 6^x = 9^x\) have?
solution_html:
Compare the graphs of \(y=4^x+6^x\) and \(y=9^x\). There is a solution between \(1\) and \(2\), since
\[4^1+6^1\gt 9^1\]
but
\[4^2+6^2\lt 9^2.\]
After this crossing, \(9^x\) grows faster than both \(4^x\) and \(6^x\), so once \(9^x\) has overtaken \(4^x+6^x\), it cannot be caught again. This suggests that there is exactly one real solution.

Remark: This question belongs to a well-known class of problems. The usual version is more demanding and asks for the value of \(x\). This is how it is done.

Divide through by \(9^x\):
\[\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^x+\left(\frac{6}{9}\right)^x=1, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2x}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^x=1.\]
Let \(u=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^x\). Then \(u\gt 0\) and
\[u^2+u-1=0,\]
whose only positive root is
\[u=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}.\]
Since \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^x\) takes every positive value exactly once, there is exactly one real solution.

prompt_html:
A line \(l\) with positive gradient is a common tangent to the circles \(x^2+y^2=4\) and \((x-9)^2+y^2=25\), such that the two circles lie on the same side of \(l\).

Find the gradient of \(l\).
solution_html:
Let \(O=(0,0)\) be the centre of \(x^2+y^2=4\), and let \(O_2=(9,0)\) be the centre of \((x-9)^2+y^2=25\).

Since \(l\) is tangent to both circles, \(OP\) and \(O_2Q\) are perpendicular to \(l\). Their lengths are the radii of the circles, so \(OP=2\) and \(O_2Q=5\).

Draw \(OR\) parallel to \(l\), and draw \(O_2R\) perpendicular to \(OR\), as in the diagram. Then \(O_2R\) represents the difference between the perpendicular distances from the two centres to the tangent line, so
\[O_2R=5-2=3.\]
Let \(OR=a\). Since \(OR\perp O_2R\), triangle \(OO_2R\) is right-angled at \(R\). Also \(OO_2=9\), because the centres are \((0,0)\) and \((9,0)\).

By Pythagoras,
\[a^2+3^2=9^2.\]
So
\[a^2=72,\]
hence
\[a=6\sqrt{2}.\]

Now let \(\theta\) be the angle that \(l\) makes with the positive \(x\)-axis. Since \(OR\) is parallel to \(l\), the gradient of \(l\) is \(\tan\theta\). In triangle \(OO_2R\),
\[\tan\theta=\frac{O_2R}{OR}=\frac{3}{6\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\]
Therefore the gradient of \(l\) is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\).

Remark: If you are not aware of the fact that the gradient of \(l\) is \(\tan\theta\), you can use a different approach. Drop a perpendicular from \(R\) down to \(OO_2\), call the point of intersection \(X\), then \(ORX\) and \(ORO_2\) are similar triangles. The required gradient is
\[\frac{XR}{OX} = \frac{O_2R}{OR}.\]

prompt_html:
What is the smallest positive value of \(k\) for which the line \(x = k\) is a line of symmetry of both of the curves
\[y = \sin\!\left(2x - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad y = \cos\!\left(3x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)?\]
solution_html:
A vertical symmetry line of a sine or cosine curve passes through a maximum or minimum.

For the first curve,

\[\sin\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\pm1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2x-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi,\]

so its vertical symmetry lines are

\[x=\frac{5\pi}{12}+\frac{n\pi}{2},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.\]

For the second curve,

\[\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\pm1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad3x+\frac{\pi}{4}=m\pi,\]

so its vertical symmetry lines are

\[x=-\frac{\pi}{12}+\frac{m\pi}{3},\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.\]

For a common symmetry line,

\[\frac{5\pi}{12}+\frac{n\pi}{2}=-\frac{\pi}{12}+\frac{m\pi}{3}.\]

Multiplying by \(12/\pi\) gives \(3(n+1)=2m\). Hence \(n=2t+1\) and \(m=3t+3\) for some integer \(t\). Therefore

\[x=\frac{11\pi}{12}+t\pi.\]

The smallest positive value occurs at \(t=0\), giving \(\displaystyle k=\frac{11\pi}{12}\). Hence the answer is E.

For cosine the analogous difference is−2sin(3k+π/4)sin3t, so k=mπ/3−π/12,m∈Z. Equating the families gives5+6n=4m−1, hence3(n+1)=2m. Therefore n is odd: n=2j−1,m=3j, and common axes have k=jπ−π/12. The smallest positive occurs atj=1, namely11π/12.

subtopic: Stationary points and number of real roots
prompt_html: The function \(f\) is defined for all real \(x\) by \[f(x) = \frac{1}{4}x^4 - \frac{1}{3}k x^3 - k^2 x^2 + k,\] where \(k\) is a real constant. Given that the equation \(f(x) = 0\) has four distinct real roots, what are the possible values of \(k\)?
solution_html:
Differentiate: \(f'(x)=x^3-kx^2-2k^2x=x(x+k)(x-2k)\).

If \(k=0\), then \(f(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^4\), so \(f(x)=0\) does not have four distinct real roots.

Now suppose \(k \neq 0\). The stationary points occur at \(x=-k\), \(x=0\), and \(x=2k\). They are minimum, maximum and minimum respectively. For 4 distinct roots, we must have the minimums below \(x\)-axis and maximum above \(x\)-axis.

Start with maximum at \(x=0\), \(f(0) = k\), so we must have \(k\gt 0\).

Next, both local minima must be below the \(x\)-axis.

At \(x=-k\),
\[f(-k)=\frac{1}{4}k^4+\frac{1}{3}k^4-k^4+k=k-\frac{5}{12}k^4,\]
and hence
\[k-\frac{5}{12}k^4\lt 0.\]
Since \(k\gt 0\), this gives
\[k^3\gt \frac{12}{5}.\]
At \(x=2k\),
\[f(2k)=4k^4-\frac{8}{3}k^4-4k^4+k=k-\frac{8}{3}k^4.\]
So
\[k-\frac{8}{3}k^4\lt 0.\]
Since \(k\gt 0\), this gives
\[k^3\gt \frac{3}{8}.\]
Combining these conditions, we need
\[k^3\gt \frac{12}{5}.\]
Therefore
\[k\gt \sqrt[3]{\frac{12}{5}}.\]

Ifk≠0, the three stationary points are−k,0,2k; x=0 is the central local maximum, since f′ changes from positive to negative there. Its value isk. Four distinct real zeros require this maximum to be positive, so k>0. For k>0 the stationary points are ordered−k<0<2k. Their values are f(−k)=k−5k⁴/12, f(0)=k, f(2k)=k−8k⁴/3. prompt_html:
A sequence is defined by \(a_0 = \frac{1}{2}\), and \(a_n = 2\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}a_r\) for \(n\geq 1\). Evaluate
\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{a_r+a_{r+1}}.\]
solution_html:
The sequence \((a_n)\) is a geometric sequence in disguise! To see this, let
\[S_n=\sum_{r=0}^n a_r.\]
For \(n\geq 1\), we have
\[a_n=2\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}a_r=2S_{n-1}.\]
Therefore
\[S_n=S_{n-1}+a_n=S_{n-1}+2S_{n-1}=3S_{n-1}.\]
Since \(S_0=a_0=\frac{1}{2}\), it follows that \(S_n\) is a geometric sequence:
\[S_n=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^n.\]
For \(n\geq 1\),
\[a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^n-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^{n-1}=3^{n-1}\]
is also a geometric sequence!

Now for sequence of the summation, for \(r\geq 1\),
\[\frac{1}{a_r+a_{r+1}}=\frac{1}{3^{r-1}+3^r}=\frac{1}{4\cdot 3^{r-1}},\]
is also geometric, with \(a=1/4\) and common ratio \(= 1/3\), hence
\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{a_r+a_{r+1}} =\frac{1/4}{1-1/3}= \frac{3}{8}.\]

subtopic: Level sets of tan(x) — circles in polar coords
prompt_html:
The set of points satisfying
\[\tan(x^2+y^2)=1, \qquad x^2+y^2 \lt k\pi,\]
is made up of finitely many separate closed curves. For each separate closed curve, consider the region enclosed by that curve.

Given that the sum of the areas of these regions is \(30\pi^2\), find the smallest possible integer value of \(k\).
solution_html:
Treating \(x^2+y^2\) as a single unknown, solving gives:
\[x^2+y^2 = \frac{\pi}{4}+n\pi \geq 0.\]
This is a circle for \(n=0,1,2,...\) on the right-hand side.

Since \(x^2+y^2\lt k\pi\), we need
\[\frac{\pi}{4}+n\pi\lt k\pi.\]
Dividing by \(\pi\) gives
\[n+\frac{1}{4}\lt k.\]
If \(k\) is a positive integer, then this means
\[n=0,1,2,\ldots,k-1.\]
So there are \(k\) circles. The area enclosed by each circle is \(\pi r^2\), so the sum of the areas is
\[\pi\sum_{n=0}^{k-1}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+n\pi\right).\]
This is the sum of an arithmetic sequence, therefore it is
\[\pi^2\left(\frac{k}{4}+\frac{k(k-1)}{2}\right).\]
Equate to \(30\pi^2\), so
\[\frac{k}{4}+\frac{k(k-1)}{2}=30\quad\iff\quad (2k+15)(k-8)=0.\]
Since \(k\) is positive,
\[k=8.\]
The smallest integer value of \(k\) is \(8\).

prompt_html:
A rectangle has its sides parallel to the coordinate axes and lies entirely within the region enclosed by \(y=2|x-4|\) and \(y=x+6\).

What is the maximum possible area of the rectangle?

You may assume that the rectangle with maximum possible area has its bottom edge meeting both arms of the graph \(y=2|x-4|\).
solution_html:
Use the permitted assumption that the maximizing rectangle's bottom edge meets both arms. If its bottom height is \(b\), its bottom corners are \((4-b/2,b)\) and \((4+b/2,b)\), so its width is \(b\). The increasing upper line has its smallest height over this span at the left end, namely \(10-b/2\). Thus its greatest feasible height is \(10-3b/2\), with \(0\leq b\leq20/3\).

Every point of this rectangle lies above the V-graph and below the line: the V-graph is at most \(b\) over the chosen span, while the line is at least the chosen top height. Its area satisfies

\[A=b\left(10-\frac{3b}{2}\right)=\frac{50}{3}-\frac32\left(b-\frac{10}{3}\right)^2\leq\frac{50}{3}.\]

Equality holds at \(b=10/3\), giving width \(10/3\), height \(5\), and top height \(25/3\). This is a feasible rectangle. Hence the maximum possible area is \(\frac{50}{3}\), answer F.

prompt_html:
A positive integer \(k\) is chosen uniformly at random from \(1,2,3,\ldots,8\).

For each non-negative integer \(n\), define
\[a_n=(2k+1)\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}\left(\frac{k-4}{4}\right)^r.\]
Let
\[S=a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots.\]
What is the probability that \(S\) converges to a finite value and \(S\gt 8\)?
solution_html:
By the binomial theorem,
\[\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}\left(\frac{k-4}{4}\right)^r = \left(1+\frac{k-4}{4}\right)^n = \left(\frac{k}{4}\right)^n.\]
So \(a_n=(2k+1)\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)^n\), and hence
\[S=(2k+1)\left(1+\frac{k}{4}+\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)^2+\cdots\right).\]
This converges when \(\frac{k}{4}\lt 1\), so \(k\lt 4\). Since \(k\) is a positive integer, the possible values are \(k=1,2,3\).

For these values,
\[S=\frac{2k+1}{1-\frac{k}{4}}=\frac{4(2k+1)}{4-k}.\]
We need \(S\gt 8\), so
\[\frac{4(2k+1)}{4-k}\gt 8.\]
Since \(k\lt 4\), we can multiply by \(4-k\) without changing the inequality. This gives \(4(2k+1)\gt 8(4-k)\), so \(8k+4\gt 32-8k\), hence \(16k\gt 28\). Therefore \(k\gt \frac{7}{4}\).

Among \(k=1,2,3\), this gives \(k=2,3\). Therefore there are \(2\) successful values out of \(8\), so the required probability is \(\frac14\). The answer is B.
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.concise_proof: By the binomial theorem, a_n=(2k+1)[1+(k−4)/4]^n=(2k+1)(k/4)^n for every nonnegative integer n, includinga₀=2k+1. Since2k+1>0, the infinite series converges exactly when|k/4|<1. Among the eight allowed integers this meansk=1,2,3. For the convergent cases, S=(2k+1)/(1−k/4)=4(2k+1)/(4−k). The values for k=1,2,3 are4,10,28 respectively. ThereforeS>8 precisely for k=2,3. Uniform selection from all eight possible k gives probability2/8=1/4.

prompt_html: A triangle \(ABC\) has \(AB=x\), \(BC=2\), and \(\angle BAC=30^\circ\). Find the range of values of \(x\) for which there are two non-congruent possible triangles satisfying these conditions, and in both triangles \(\angle ABC\) is acute.
solution_html:
Let \(\angle ACB=C\). By the sine rule:
\[\frac{2}{\sin 30^\circ}=\frac{x}{\sin C}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \sin C=\frac{x}{4}.\]
For there to be two non-congruent possible triangles, \(\sin C=\frac{x}{4}\) must give two possible values of \(C\).

Let the smaller possible value of \(C\) be \(\theta\), where \(0^\circ\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). Then the two possible values of \(C\) are \(\theta\) and \(180^\circ-\theta\).

For the triangle with \(C=\theta\), where \(0^\circ\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\), we must have:
\[0\lt \sin \theta \lt 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0\lt \frac{x}{4}\lt 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x\lt 4.\]
For the triangle with \(C=180^\circ-\theta\), to ensure the triangle is valid, we need the angle at \(B\) to be positive:
\[B=180^\circ-30^\circ-(180^\circ-\theta)=\theta-30^\circ\gt 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta\gt 30^\circ.\]
Since \(\sin\theta=\frac{x}{4}\), this gives
\[\frac{x}{4}\gt \frac{1}{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\gt 2.\]
Therefore, together \(2\lt x\lt 4\).

Now impose the condition that \(\angle ABC\) is acute in both triangles.

If \(C=180^\circ-\theta\), then \(B=\theta-30^\circ\), which is automatically acute when \(30^\circ\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\).

If \(C=\theta\), then
\[B=180^\circ-30^\circ-\theta=150^\circ-\theta.\]
For this to be acute, we need
\[150^\circ-\theta\lt 90^\circ,\]
so \(\theta\gt 60^\circ\). Since \(\sin\theta=\frac{x}{4}\), this gives
\[\frac{x}{4}\gt \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x\gt 2\sqrt{3}.\]
Combining this with previous conditions on \(x\), we obtain
\[2\sqrt{3}\lt x\lt 4.\]

Their B angles are150°−α andα−30° respectively. Both are positive exactly whenα>30°, while distinctness requiresα<90°. For both B angles to be acute,150°−α<90° requiresα>60°. The other B=α−30° is automatically less than60° whenα<90°, and is positive. Thus60°<α<90°, equivalent to2√3<x<4 because sine increases on[0°,90°].

prompt_html:
The function \(f\) is defined by
\[f(x)=\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right), \qquad -1\lt x\lt 1.\]
Solve
\[f(x)=4f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right).\]
It may be helpful to first find constants \(a\) and \(b\) such that, for \(u,v\in(-1,1)\),
\[f\left(\frac{u+v}{1+uv}\right)=af(u)+bf(v).\]
solution_html:
First lets find \(a\) and \(b\). We have
\[f\left(\frac{u+v}{1+uv}\right)=\ln\left(\frac{1+\frac{u+v}{1+uv}}{1-\frac{u+v}{1+uv}}\right)=\ln\left(\frac{(1+u)(1+v)}{(1-u)(1-v)}\right).\]
So
\[f\left(\frac{u+v}{1+uv}\right)=\ln\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)+\ln\left(\frac{1+v}{1-v}\right)=f(u)+f(v).\]
Therefore \(a=1\) and \(b=1\).

Now apply this identity with \(u=v=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\):
\[2f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)+ f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=f\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1+\frac{1}{2}}\right) =f\left(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right).\]
Apply it again,
\[4f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) =2f\left(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right) =f\left(\frac{2\cdot \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}}{1+\left(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)^2}\right)=f\left(\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{17}\right).\]
Therefore
\[f(x)=f\left(\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{17}\right).\]
Since \(f\) is one-one on \(-1\lt x\lt 1\),
\[x=\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{17}.\]
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Prove the logarithmic addition identity and apply the double-argument transformation twice.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For u,v in (-1,1), put w=(u+v)/(1+uv). Since 1+uv>0 and 1±w=(1±u)(1±v)/(1+uv)>0, w is in (-1,1). Moreover (1+w)/(1-w)=[(1+u)/(1-u)][(1+v)/(1-v)], so logarithm laws give f(w)=f(u)+f(v): a=b=1. Starting with t=1/sqrt(2), let s=2t/(1+t^2)=2sqrt(2)/3, so f(s)=2f(t). Double once more: x=2s/(1+s^2)=12sqrt(2)/17, hence f(x)=4f(t). The map x to (1+x)/(1-x) is strictly increasing on (-1,1), as is ln, so f is injective and this solution is unique.

prompt_html:
Six sealed black bags are labelled \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\), \(T\) and \(U\). Each bag contains the same number of balls. This number is a non-zero whole number from \(3\) to \(8\) inclusive.

Each bag has a label with a statement written on it. The statement may be true or false.

Bag \(P\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is a multiple of \(3\)."

Bag \(Q\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is even."

Bag \(R\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is prime."

Bag \(S\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is at most \(4\)."

Bag \(T\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is at least \(7\)."

Bag \(U\) has a label which says: "The number of balls in this bag is a perfect square."

Given that exactly one of the six statements is true, which bag has the true statement on its label?
solution_html:
Let \(n\) be the number of balls in each bag. We simply check which labels would be true for each possible value of \(n\).
\[\begin{array}{c|c} n & \text{True labels} \\ 3 & P,\ R,\ S \\ 4 & Q,\ S,\ U \\ 5 & R \\ 6 & P,\ Q \\ 7 & R,\ T \\ 8 & Q,\ T \\ \end{array}\]
Only \(n=5\) gives exactly one true statement, where \(R\) is true, so the answer is \(R\).

prompt_html:
In a TMUA-style question, students are asked to determine which, if any, of the five statements \(1,2,3,4,5\) are true. They must then identify the correct option from the list provided in the question.

Assume that a competent student can always correctly determine the truth value of any statement they choose to check.

A teacher is designing such a question and wants to choose the option set that maximises the smallest number of checks a lucky student might need to determine the correct option. Equivalently, the teacher wants to maximise the fewest checks after which it is possible for the student to know the correct option.

Which of the following four candidate option sets best achieves the teacher's aim?

Option Set I
\[\begin{array}{l} \text{A:}\qquad \text{only statement } 1 \text{ is true} \\ \text{B:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,2,3 \text{ are true} \\ \text{C:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,2,4 \text{ are true} \\ \text{D:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,4,5 \text{ are true} \\ \text{E:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,5 \text{ are true} \end{array}\]
Option Set II
\[\begin{array}{l} \text{A:}\qquad \text{only statement } 1 \text{ is true} \\ \text{B:}\qquad \text{only statement } 2 \text{ is true} \\ \text{C:}\qquad \text{only statement } 3 \text{ is true} \\ \text{D:}\qquad \text{only statement } 4 \text{ is true} \\ \text{E:}\qquad \text{only statement } 5 \text{ is true} \end{array}\]
Option Set III
\[\begin{array}{l} \text{A:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,2 \text{ are true} \\ \text{B:}\qquad \text{only statements } 2,3 \text{ are true} \\ \text{C:}\qquad \text{only statements } 3,4 \text{ are true} \\ \text{D:}\qquad \text{only statements } 4,5 \text{ are true} \\ \text{E:}\qquad \text{no statements are true} \end{array}\]
Option Set IV
\[\begin{array}{l} \text{A:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,2 \text{ are true} \\ \text{B:}\qquad \text{only statements } 2,3 \text{ are true} \\ \text{C:}\qquad \text{only statements } 3,4 \text{ are true} \\ \text{D:}\qquad \text{only statements } 4,5 \text{ are true} \\ \text{E:}\qquad \text{only statements } 1,5 \text{ are true} \end{array}\]
solution_html:
For each option set, we look for the smallest number of statement checks that could identify an option in the luckiest case.

If one statement check can uniquely identify an option, then the smallest possible number of checks for that option set is \(1\).

For Option Set I, statement \(3\) is true only in option B. So if a student checks statement \(3\) and finds it true, they immediately know the answer is B. Therefore the lucky minimum is \(1\).

For Option Set II, each option says exactly one different statement is true. So if the student checks the true statement, they immediately know the answer. Therefore the lucky minimum is \(1\).

For Option Set III, statement \(1\) is true only in option A, and statement \(5\) is true only in option D. So one lucky check is enough. Therefore the lucky minimum is \(1\).

For Option Set IV, each statement appears in exactly two options. For example, statement \(1\) is true in A and E, statement \(2\) is true in A and B, and so on. Therefore no single statement check can ever identify the correct option. Therefore the minimum number of checks is greater than 1, and this is our best choice!

It can be shown that the lucky minimum for Option Set IV is \(2\), though this detail is not required to deduce the answer to the question.

prompt_html:
A student makes the following claim:

If \(f\) is a real-valued function such that, for some constant \(a\), \(\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=a\) for all real values of \(x\), then there exists a constant \(k\) such that \(f(x)=kx+a\) for all real values of \(x\).

Examine their claim above, and determine which of the following is true?

options.html: \(f(x)=2x+1\) is a counterexample to the claim.
options.label: B

options.html: \(f(x)=\sin x\) is a counterexample to the claim.
options.label: C

options.html: \(f(x)=\tan x\) is a counterexample to the claim.
options.label: D

options.html: \(f(x)=\cos x\) is a counterexample to the claim.
options.label: E

options.html: \(f(x)=-x\) is a counterexample to the claim.
options.label: F

solution_html:
A counterexample must satisfy the assumption of the if, but fail the then conclusion.

For (C), if \(f(x)=\sin x\), then
\[\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=\frac{\sin x+\sin(-x)}{2}=0.\]
So the assumption is true with \(a=0\). However, \(\sin x\) is cleary not of the form \(kx+0\), so (C) is a counterexample, and this statement is correct, so it is the answer.

For completeness, let's check the rest.

For (B), if \(f(x)=2x+1\), then
\[\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=\frac{(2x+1)+(-2x+1)}{2}=1.\]
So the assumption is true with \(a=1\). However, \(f(x)=2x+1\) is of the form \(kx+a\), with \(k=2\) and \(a=1\). So (B) is not a counterexample.

For (D), \(f(x)=\tan x\) is not defined for all real values of \(x\), for example at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\). Therefore it does not satisfy the assumption of the claim, so it is not a counterexample.

For (E), if \(f(x)=\cos x\), then
\[\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=\frac{\cos x+\cos x}{2}=\cos x.\]
This is not constant, so the assumption is false. Hence (E) is not a counterexample.

For (F), if \(f(x)=-x\), then
\[\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=\frac{-x+x}{2}=0.\]
So the assumption is true with \(a=0\). However, \(f(x)=-x\) is of the form \(kx+a\), with \(k=-1\) and \(a=0\). So (F) is not a counterexample.

prompt_html:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be non-zero real numbers with \(x \neq y\).

Which one of the following statements is both necessary and sufficient for \(x \lt y\)?
solution_html:
Here are some general facts to note.

If \(n\) is odd, then \(a\lt b\) is equivalent to \(a^{1/n}\lt b^{1/n}\), since taking an odd \(n\)th root preserves the inequality.

However, if \(n\) is even, then \(a\lt b\) is not equivalent to \(a^n\lt b^n\), since raising both sides to an even power does not preserve the inequality in general.

Apply the first result to our \(x\lt y\), we can see that \(x^{1/5} \lt y^{1/5}\) is definitely equivalent, and given there is only one equivalent statement, this must be it.

Remark: It is possible to rule out each of the distractors with a single numerical counterexample.

For A, take \(x=-1\) and \(y=1\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[y^{-1/3}=1 \quad \text{and} \quad x^{-1/3}=-1,\]
so \(y^{-1/3}\lt x^{-1/3}\) is false.

For B, take \(x=1\) and \(y=2\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[2^{1/5}\lt 1^{1/5}\]
is false.

For C, take \(x=-8\) and \(y=-1\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[x^{2/3}=4 \quad \text{and} \quad y^{2/3}=1,\]
so \(x^{2/3}\lt y^{2/3}\) is false.

For D, take \(x=1\) and \(y=8\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[y^{2/3}=4 \quad \text{and} \quad x^{2/3}=1,\]
so \(y^{2/3}\lt x^{2/3}\) is false.

For E, take \(x=-8\) and \(y=-1\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[|x|^{1/3}=2 \quad \text{and} \quad |y|^{1/3}=1,\]
so \(|x|^{1/3}\lt |y|^{1/3}\) is false.

For F, take \(x=1\) and \(y=8\). Then \(x\lt y\), but
\[x^{-1/3}=1 \quad \text{and} \quad y^{-1/3}=\frac{1}{2},\]
so \(x^{-1/3}\lt y^{-1/3}\) is false.

prompt_html:
For which of the following is it a necessary but not sufficient condition that
\[2x^3-3px^2+p=0\]
has exactly one real root?
solution_html:
Let \(f(x)=2x^3-3px^2+p\), then \(f'(x)=6x^2-6px=6x(x-p)\). So the stationary points are at \(x=0\) and \(x=p\).

Their corresponding values are \(f(0)=p\) and \(f(p)=2p^3-3p^3+p=p-p^3=p(1-p^2)\).

First consider \(p\neq 0\). For the cubic to have exactly one real root, the two stationary values must have the same sign. If either stationary value is zero, then the cubic has a repeated root and another real root. So we need
\[f(0)f(p)=p\cdot p(1-p^2)\gt 0.\]
This gives
\[p^2(1-p^2)\gt 0.\]
Since \(p^2\gt 0\), we need
\[1-p^2\gt 0.\]
Hence
\[-1\lt p\lt 0\qquad\text{or}\qquad 0\lt p\lt 1.\]
Now we check \(p=0\) separately. In this case, \(f(x)=2x^3\), which has exactly one real root, namely \(x=0\).

Therefore, the necessary and sufficient condition is \(-1\lt p\lt 1\).

Option A is necessary and sufficient, so it is not the answer.

Option B is necessary because \(-1\lt p\lt 1\) implies \(-1\leq p\leq 1\), but the converse is not true. Therefore, it is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

So, Option B is the correct answer.

Remark: Since we are looking for a necessary but not sufficient condition, and there should be only one correct option, we can immediately rule out A because A implies B. If A were the solution, then B would also be a solution, but there can be only one solution. In the same way, we can immediately rule out C and D. However, in reality, these eliminations do not make it any quicker to deduce the correct option for this question!

prompt_html:
Determine the total number of ordered pairs of positive integers \((x,y)\) satisfying
\[\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{9}.\]
solution_html:
Clearing denominators gives \(9(x+y)=xy\), so \(xy-9x-9y=0\).

Now, crucially, notice that we want to factorise this in some way so that we can enumerate the possible values of \(x\) and \(y\). This can be done by adding a constant to both sides. If \(x=9\), for example, then the \(xy\) and \(9y\) terms cancel, leaving \(-81\). Hence the correct constant to add is \(81\), which completes the factorisation, as this makes \((x-9)\) a factor:
\[xy-9x-9y+81=81 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x-9)(y-9)=81.\]

Also, since \(1/y\gt 0\), we have \(1/x\lt 1/9\), so \(x\gt 9\). Similarly, \(y\gt 9\). Therefore, both \(x-9\) and \(y-9\) must be positive divisors of \(81\).

Each positive divisor \(d\) of \(81\) gives exactly one solution
\[x=9+d,\qquad y=9+\frac{81}{d},\]
and both values are automatically positive integers.

Since
\[81=3^4,\]
the number of positive divisors of \(81\) is
\[4+1=5.\]
Therefore, there are \(5\) ordered pairs.

prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=x^3-px^2-p^2x+k\) where \(k\) is a real constant. Suppose that \(p\) and \(q\) are real numbers satisfying \(-3\leq p\leq 3\) and \(-3\leq q\leq 3\).

The function \(f\) has non-negative gradient at \(x=q\).

Find the area of the region of all possible points \((p,q)\) in the \(p\)-\(q\) plane.
solution_html:
We have \(f'(x)=3x^2-2px-p^2\). Since \(f\) has non-negative gradient at \(x=q\), we need
\[3q^2-2pq-p^2\geq 0.\]
Notice that \(p\) is a root, so \((q-p)\) is a factor, and factorising gives
\[3q^2-2pq-p^2=(3q+p)(q-p).\]
So we need
\[(3q+p)(q-p)\geq 0.\]
Therefore \(q-p\geq 0\) and \(3q+p\geq 0\), or \(q-p\leq 0\) and \(3q+p\leq 0\). See the diagram below.

The regions are congruent when split at \(p=0\), so we can just work out the right side, and then double the area.

The entire right half of the square is a rectangle of area \(3\times 6=18\).

The unshaded region between the two lines is a triangle. Its vertical side lies on \(p=3\), between \((3,-1)\) and \((3,3)\), so its base has length \(4\). Its perpendicular height is \(3\). Hence its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\times4\times3=6\).

Therefore, the shaded area for \(p\geq0\) is \(18-6=12\), and the total area of the region is twice this value, namely \(24\).

prompt_html:
Let \(ABCD\) be a convex quadrilateral, with its vertices labelled in order. A quadrilateral is called a rhombus if all four of its sides are equal in length.

Which of the following statements, taken individually, are sufficient to guarantee that \(ABCD\) is a rhombus?

1. \(AB=AD\), and the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) intersect at right angles.

2. \(AB=CD\), and the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) divide \(ABCD\) into four similar triangles.

3. The diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) divide \(ABCD\) into four similar triangles.

4. The diagonal \(AC\) divides \(ABCD\) into two triangles, and the diagonal \(BD\) divides \(ABCD\) into two triangles, with all four of these triangles having the same area.

5. \(AB=BC=CD\), and the triangles \(ABC\) and \(BCD\) are congruent.
solution_html:
Statement 1 is not sufficient. For example, take
\[A=(1,0),\quad B=(0,1),\quad C=(-2,0),\quad D=(0,-1).\]
Then the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) are perpendicular, and \(AB=AD=\sqrt{2}\). However, \(BC=CD=\sqrt{5}\), so \(ABCD\) is not a rhombus.

Statement 2 is sufficient, although this is quite hard to see!

Let the diagonals meet at \(O\), and write
\[OA=a,\quad OB=b,\quad OC=c,\quad OD=d.\]
Since the four triangles \(AOB\), \(BOC\), \(COD\) and \(DOA\) are all similar, the triangles \(AOB\) and \(BOC\) are similar. The angles \(\angle AOB\) and \(\angle BOC\) are supplementary.

If two similar non-degenerate triangles have supplementary angles at \(O\), those angles must both be \(90^\circ\). Indeed, if the supplementary angles were distinct, similarity would force both angles into the same triangle; their sum is already \(180^\circ\), leaving no positive third angle. This is impossible for a nondegenerate triangle. Hence the diagonals are perpendicular.

So the four small triangles are similar right-angled triangles.

Now compare triangles \(AOB\) and \(COD\). They are similar right-angled triangles. Also, statement 2 gives \(AB=CD\), which are their hypotenuses. Therefore the two triangles are congruent.

Hence either \(a=c\) and \(b=d\), or \(a=d\) and \(b=c\).

If \(a=c\) and \(b=d\), then
\[AB=BC=CD=DA=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.\]
So \(ABCD\) is a rhombus.

If \(a=d\) and \(b=c\), then triangle \(BOC\) has equal perpendicular sides. Since all four small triangles are similar, all four are isosceles right-angled triangles. Hence again all four sides of \(ABCD\) are equal.

So statement 2 is sufficient.

Statement 3 is a weaker version of 2, and is not sufficient. For example, take
\[A=(1,0),\quad B=(0,2),\quad C=(-4,0),\quad D=(0,-2).\]
The diagonals divide the quadrilateral into four right-angled triangles with side ratio \(1:2\), so the four triangles are similar. However, the side lengths of \(ABCD\) are
\[\sqrt{5},\quad \sqrt{20},\quad \sqrt{20},\quad \sqrt{5},\]
so it is not a rhombus.

Statement 4 is not sufficient. A non-square rectangle satisfies statement 4, since each diagonal divides the rectangle into two triangles of equal area. However, a non-square rectangle is not a rhombus.

Statement 5 is not sufficient. For example, take
\[A=\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),\quad B=(0,0),\quad C=(1,0),\quad D=\left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).\]
These points form a convex quadrilateral in the order \(A,B,C,D\). Also \(AB=BC=CD=1\), while \(AC=BD=\sqrt{3}\), so triangles \(ABC\) and \(BCD\) are congruent by SSS. However,
\[AD=2,\]
so \(ABCD\) is not a rhombus.

Therefore the only sufficient statement is statement 2.

prompt_html:
Find the area of the region in the \((x,y)\)-plane consisting of all points satisfying both
\[|x| + |y| \leq 2 \quad \text{and} \quad |x-1| + |y| \leq 2.\]
solution_html:
The inequality \(|x|+|y|\leq 2\) describes a diamond centred at \((0,0)\), while \(|x-1|+|y|\leq 2\) describes an identical diamond centred at \((1,0)\).

Sketch out the two diamonds, then you will see that their common region is also a diamond. Its leftmost and rightmost vertices are \((-1,0)\) and \((2,0)\), so its horizontal diagonal has length \(3\).

Its upper and lower vertices are
\[\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}\right) \quad\text{and}\quad \left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right),\]
so its vertical diagonal also has length \(3\).

Therefore, the area of the common region is
\[\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 3=\frac{9}{2}.\]

audited_reference.concise_proof: The two inequalities are equivalent to max(|x|,|x−1|)+|y|≤2. For every real x, max(|x|,|x−1|)=|x−1/2|+1/2, as verified by cases x≤1/2 and x≥1/2. Thus the region is |x−1/2|+|y|≤3/2. Its vertices are (−1,0),(1/2,3/2),(2,0),(1/2,−3/2). The perpendicular diagonals both have length 3, so the area is (1/2)·3·3=9/2.

prompt_html:
Find the value of
\[\sum_{r=1}^{100} \frac{1}{\sqrt{r} + \sqrt{r-1}}.\]
solution_html:
Rationalising each term gives
\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r-1}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r-1}} \times \frac{\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1}}{\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1}} =\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1}.\]
Therefore,
\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{r=1}^{100}\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r-1}} &=\sum_{r=1}^{100}\left(\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1}\right)\\ &=\sqrt{100}-\sqrt{0}\\ &=10. \end{aligned}\]

prompt_html:
The two curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in the \(xy\)-plane have equations
\[x^2+y^2-2y-12=0 \,\, \text{ and }\,\,x^2+y^2-2x-4y=0.\]
Let \(P\) be a point on \(C_1\) and \(Q\) be a point on \(C_2\). What is the least possible value of the length of \(PQ\)?
solution_html:
\(C_1\): \(x^2+(y-1)^2=13\), so its centre is \(A=(0,1)\) and its radius is \(\sqrt{13}\).

\(C_2\): \((x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=5\), so its centre is \(B=(1,2)\) and its radius is \(\sqrt{5}\).

Now \(AB=\sqrt{2}\). The circles intersect if \(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5}\gt \sqrt{13}\). Since
\[(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5})^2=7+2\sqrt{10}\gt 13,\]
the circles intersect.

Hence we may choose \(P=Q\) at an intersection point, so the least possible value of \(PQ\) is 0. Therefore the least possible distance is attained at an intersection point.

Alternatively, subtracting the two equations gives \(2x+2y-12=0\), so \(y=6-x\). Substituting this into either equation gives
\[x^2-5x+6=0,\]
which has two distinct real roots. Hence the circles intersect, so the least possible value of \(PQ\) is \(0\).

prompt_html:
Let \(x\) be any real number. Find the minimum value of
\[4^{\sin^2 x} - 5 \cdot 2^{\sin^2 x} + 7.\]
solution_html:
Another completing the square question with a twist!

Let \(u = 2^{\sin^2 x}\). Since \(\sin^2 x\) takes every value in \([0,1]\) (and only those values) as \(x\) varies over \(\mathbb{R}\), \(u\) ranges over \([2^0, 2^1] = [1, 2]\).

Note that \(4^{\sin^2 x} = (2^{\sin^2 x})^2 = u^2\), so the expression becomes
\[g(u) = u^2 - 5u + 7 = \left(u - \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{4}.\]
The minimum of \(g\) is \(\frac{3}{4}\) if \(u\) is allowed to be \(\frac{5}{2}\), it is not! As \(u\) varies between 1 to 2, given the shape of \(g(u)\), the minimum is clearly at \(u=2\):
\[g(2) = 4 - 10 + 7 = 1.\]

prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=-x^3+kx^2+3\), where \(k\) is a real constant. Suppose that \(f(x)=0\) has exactly \(3\) distinct real roots.

Which of the following equations must also have exactly \(3\) distinct real roots?

I \(\quad -f(x)+a=0\), where \(a\) is an arbitrary real constant

II \(\quad 5-2f(2-3x)=0\)

III \(\quad f(-|x|)-3=0\)
solution_html:
We have \(f'(x)=x(2k-3x)\), so the stationary points are at \(x=0\) and \(x=\frac{2k}{3}\).

Since \(f(0)=3\gt 0\) and \(f(x)=0\) has three distinct real roots, \(x=0\) must be the local maximum and the other stationary point must be a local minimum below the \(x\)-axis. Hence \(\frac{2k}{3}\lt 0\), so \(k\lt 0\).

Equation I need not have three distinct real roots, since \(a\) can be chosen sufficiently large that both stationary values of \(-f(x)+a\) are positive, giving only one real root.

For II, let \(u=2-3x\). Then
\[5-2f(2-3x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(u)=\frac{5}{2}.\]
The local maximum value is \(3\) and the local minimum value is negative. Since \(0\lt \frac{5}{2}\lt 3\), the line \(y=\frac{5}{2}\) intersects the graph three times. As \(u=2-3x\) is one-to-one, II has three distinct real roots.

For III,
\[f(-|x|)-3=|x|^3+kx^2=x^2(|x|+k).\]
Since \(k\lt 0\), the equation has the three distinct roots \(x=0\), \(x=k\) and \(x=-k\).

Therefore, II and III only must have exactly three distinct real roots.

prompt_html:
The graph of \(y = \sin x\) is transformed by the following five operations, applied in the order given:

I\(\quad\,\) a reflection in the line \(y = -3\);

II\(\quad\) a stretch by scale factor \(2\) parallel to the \(x\)-axis;

III\(\quad\) a translation of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) in the negative \(x\)-direction.

IV\(\quad\) a reflection in the line \(x = 0\);

V\(\quad\) a reflection in the line \(x=\frac{4\pi}{3}\).

Which of the following is the equation of the resulting curve?
solution_html:
The reflection in the line \(y=-3\) affects only the \(y\)-coordinate, while transformations II to V affect only the \(x\)-coordinate. We may therefore apply transformation I last.

Starting with \(y=\sin x\), the stretch and translation give
\[y=\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right).\]
Reflecting in \(x=0\) gives
\[y=\sin\left(-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right).\]
The lines of symmetry of this curve satisfy
\[-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi,\]
so \(x=-\frac{2\pi}{3}-2n\pi\). The least positive value is \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\), so reflection in \(x=\frac{4\pi}{3}\) leaves the curve unchanged.

Finally, reflection in \(y=-3\) changes \(y\) to \(-6-y\), giving
\[y=-6-\sin\left(-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right) =-6+\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\pi}{6}\right).\]

The vertical midline is-6, excluding A,D,E. At x=pi/3 the final ordinate is-6, while B gives-6+sqrt(2)/2 and therefore differs.

subtopic: Trig equation from infinite geometric series
prompt_html:
The equation
\[\cos x + \cos^3 x + \cos^5 x + \cos^7 x + \ldots = \tan x\]
has how many solutions for \(0 \leq x \lt 2\pi\)?
solution_html:
The left-hand side is a geometric series with first term \(\cos x\) and common ratio \(\cos^2 x\). It converges for \(\cos^2 x \lt 1\), so we must exclude \(x = 0\) and \(x = \pi\), where \(\cos^2 x=1\). The right-hand side \(\tan x\) is not defined for \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \frac{3\pi}{2}\), so we also exclude these \(x\).

When the series converges, its sum to infinity is
\[\frac{\cos x}{1 - \cos^2 x} = \frac{\cos x}{\sin^2 x}.\]
Substitute into the equation, we get
\[\frac{\cos x}{\sin^2 x} = \tan x \quad \iff\quad \frac{\cos x}{\sin^2 x} =\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}.\]
Multiplying both sides by \(\sin^2 x \cdot \cos x\), which is nonzero as we precisely excluded the values of \(x\) for which they are zero, simplify, eventually gives
\[\sin^3 x + \sin^2 x - 1 = 0\]
Let \(u=\sin x\). Since \(-1\leq u\leq 1\), we need to count the solutions of \(u^3=1-u^2\) in this interval. For \(-1\leq u\leq 0\), we have \(u^3\leq 0\) and \(1-u^2\geq 0\), so there are no solutions. For \(0\leq u\leq 1\), the function \(u^3\) is strictly increasing from \(0\) to \(1\), while \(1-u^2\) is strictly decreasing from \(1\) to \(0\). Hence they intersect exactly once, at some \(u=k\) with \(0\lt k\lt 1\). The equation \(\sin x=k\) has exactly two solutions for \(0\leq x\lt 2\pi\), so the original equation has \(2\) solutions.

audited_reference.concise_proof: The series has first term c=cos x and ratio c^2. It converges when|c|<1; at c=1 or-1 its nonzero terms do not tend to zero. Tangent also requires c!=0. Thus admissible solutions have both sin x and cos x nonzero, and the sum is c/(1-c^2)=cos x/sin^2 x. Equating this to sin x/cos x and multiplying by the nonzero denominators gives cos^2 x=sin^3 x. Put s=sin x. Since cos^2 x>0 at a legal solution, s>0, and since cosine is nonzero, s<1. The equation becomes s^3+s^2-1=0 on(0,1). This polynomial is continuous, has values-1 and 1 at 0 and 1, and derivative 3s^2+2s>0 on(0,1). It therefore has exactly one root s0 in(0,1). Every sine value strictly between 0 and 1 has exactly two preimages in 0<=x<2pi, one in each upper quadrant. Both have nonzero sine and cosine and satisfy the original convergent-series equation. Hence there are exactly two solutions, option C.

prompt_html:
The circle \(C\) is inscribed in the triangle bounded by the three lines
\[y=0,\qquad y=\sqrt3x,\qquad x+y=\sqrt{1}+\sqrt2+\sqrt3.\]
You may find \(\tan 22.5^\circ=\sqrt2-1\) useful.

Which of the following is the equation of \(C\)?
solution_html:
The centre of an inscribed circle is the intersection of the internal angle bisectors.

At the origin, the angle between \(y=0\) and \(y=\sqrt3x\) is \(60^\circ\). Its internal angle bisector therefore makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the positive \(x\)-axis, so

\[y=x\tan30^\circ=\frac{x}{\sqrt3}.\]

The line \(x+y=1+\sqrt2+\sqrt3\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \((1+\sqrt2+\sqrt3,0)\). At that vertex, the internal angle bisector has gradient \(-\tan22.5^\circ=1-\sqrt2\), so its equation is

\[y=(\sqrt2-1)(1+\sqrt2+\sqrt3-x).\]

Intersecting the two angle bisectors gives

\[\frac{x}{\sqrt3}=(\sqrt2-1)(1+\sqrt2+\sqrt3-x).\]

Substitution shows that \(x=\sqrt3\), and then \(y=1\). Thus the centre is \((\sqrt3,1)\).

Because the circle is tangent to \(y=0\), its radius is \(1\). Therefore

\[(x-\sqrt3)^2+(y-1)^2=1.\]

Hence the answer is A.

The centre is strictly inside all three half-planes, each side is at distance 1, and the radius-one disk is contained in their intersection. prompt_html:
Let \(f\) be a real-valued function such that
\[\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1\]
and \(f(x)=f(x+1)\) for all real \(x\).

Find
\[\sum_{r=1}^{100}\int_0^r f(r^r x)\,dx.\]
solution_html:
Remark: The functions \(f(x), f(4x), f(27x), f(256x),\ldots\) do not look especially friendly. You may wonder how much the coefficients of \(x\) inside \(f\) matter. It turns out that they do not matter at all!

For any positive integer \(k\), the graph of \(y=f(kx)\) is obtained from the graph of \(y=f(x)\) by a horizontal stretch with scale factor \(\frac{1}{k}\).

Since \(f\) has period \(1\), the function \(f(kx)\) completes \(k\) periods on the interval \([0,1]\). Each compressed period has integral
\[\frac{1}{k}\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=\frac{1}{k}.\]
Therefore,
\[\int_0^1 f(kx)\,dx=k\cdot\frac{1}{k}=1.\]
For each \(r\), the number \(r^r\) is a positive integer, so
\[\int_0^1 f(r^r x)\,dx=1.\]
Also, since \(r^r\) is an integer,
\[f(r^r(x+1))=f(r^r x+r^r)=f(r^r x),\]
so \(f(r^r x)\) has period \(1\).

Hence the interval \([0,r]\) consists of \(r\) intervals of length \(1\), each contributing an integral of \(1\). Therefore,
\[\int_0^r f(r^r x)\,dx=r.\]
Thus the required sum is
\[\sum_{r=1}^{100}r =1+2+3+\cdots+100 = \frac{100\cdot101}{2} =5050.\]

prompt_html:
A real number \(x\) satisfies
\[x^2-3x+1=0.\]
For each non-negative integer \(n\), define
\[p_n=x^n+\frac{1}{x^n}.\]
Find the value of \(p_6\).

You may find it helpful to consider a recurrence relation of the form \(p_n=3p_{n-1}+kp_{n-2}\) for some constant \(k\).
solution_html:
Since \(x^2-3x+1=0\) and \(x\neq 0\), dividing by \(x\) gives
\[x+\frac{1}{x}=3.\]
For \(n\geq 2\),
\[\begin{aligned} 3p_{n-1} &=\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)\left(x^{n-1}+\frac{1}{x^{n-1}}\right)\\ &=x^n+x^{n-2}+\frac{1}{x^{n-2}}+\frac{1}{x^n}\\ &=p_n+p_{n-2}. \end{aligned}\]
Therefore,
\[p_n=3p_{n-1}-p_{n-2},\]
so \(k=-1\).

The initial values are \(p_0=2\) and \(p_1=x+\frac{1}{x}=3\).

We can now apply the recurrence repeatedly:
\[\begin{aligned} p_2&=3p_1-p_0=3(3)-2=7,\\ p_3&=3p_2-p_1=3(7)-3=18,\\ p_4&=3p_3-p_2=3(18)-7=47,\\ p_5&=3p_4-p_3=3(47)-18=123,\\ p_6&=3p_5-p_4=3(123)-47=322. \end{aligned}\]
Hence
\[p_6=322.\]

Alternatively, \(x+1/x=3\) gives \(p_3=(x+1/x)^3-3(x+1/x)=18\), and then \(p_6=p_3^2-2=322\). The recurrence is useful but is not required.

subtopic: Integration of step functions / floor function
prompt_html:
Let \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) denote the greatest integer less than or equal to \(x\).

Find the value of
\[\int_{100}^1\log_{10}\left(\frac{\lfloor 2x\rfloor}{\lfloor 2x\rfloor+1}\right)\,dx.\]
solution_html:
Reversing the limits changes the sign of the integral:
\[\int_{100}^1\log_{10}\left(\frac{\lfloor 2x\rfloor}{\lfloor 2x\rfloor+1}\right)\,dx=-\int_1^{100}\log_{10}\left(\frac{\lfloor 2x\rfloor}{\lfloor 2x\rfloor+1}\right)\,dx.\]

For \(\frac{k}{2}\leq x\lt\frac{k+1}{2}\), we have \(\lfloor2x\rfloor=k\). On \([1,100)\), the values of \(\lfloor2x\rfloor\) are \(2,3,\ldots,199\), each on an interval of length \(\frac12\). Therefore
\[\int_1^{100}\log_{10}\left(\frac{\lfloor 2x\rfloor}{\lfloor 2x\rfloor+1}\right)\,dx=\frac12\sum_{k=2}^{199}\log_{10}\left(\frac{k}{k+1}\right).\]

The isolated endpoint \(x=100\), where the floor is 200, does not change the integral. Using the logarithm laws and the telescoping product,
\[\frac12\log_{10}\left(\frac23\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac45\cdots\frac{199}{200}\right)=\frac12\log_{10}\left(\frac1{100}\right)=-1.\]

Hence the original integral is \(-(-1)=1\), so the answer is F.

prompt_html: In how many ways can \(8\) identical balls be placed into \(3\) distinct boxes so that no box contains more than \(4\) balls?
solution_html:
For now, let us simplify the problem and remove the restriction that no box may contain more than \(4\) balls. What is the total number of ways to distribute the balls? How do we count them?

Imagine the \(8\) balls laid out in a row. To split them into \(3\) groups, we can add \(2\) dividers to divide the row of \(8\) balls into \(3\) groups. Therefore, we can think of the problem as having \(10\) positions, of which we need to choose \(2\) for the dividers, with the rest occupied by the balls. Note that if we choose positions \(1\) and \(2\) for the dividers, then the distribution of balls is \(0,0,8\), which is allowed in the unrestricted problem. Therefore, the total number is given by \(10\) choose \(2\):
\[\binom{10}{2}=45.\]
Now let us subtract the cases in which a box has \(5\) or more balls, to bring back our restriction. Suppose the first box contains at least \(5\) balls. Place \(5\) balls in that box first, leaving \(3\) balls to distribute freely among the three boxes, including the box with \(5\) balls. So now we need to place \(2\) dividers among a row of \(3\) balls. This is the same problem, but with fewer balls, so the total number of ways of doing this is
\[\binom{5}{2}=10.\]
There are \(3\) choices for the box containing at least \(5\) balls, so that gives \(10\times 3=30\) ways. Also, no distribution has two such boxes, since that would require at least \(10\) balls.

Therefore, the required number of ways is \(45-30=15\).

Alternatively, we can enumerate them in an orderly way, writing the numbers of balls in the three boxes as a three-digit numbers, in ascending order:
\[044,\ 134,\ 143,\ 224,\ 233,\ 242,\ 314,\ 323,\ 332,\ 341,\ 404,\ 413,\ 422,\ 431,\ 440.\]
Here, for example, \(134\) means that the three boxes contain \(1\), \(3\) and \(4\) balls respectively. The initial zero in \(044\) means that the first box is empty.

Now count, there are 15 of them.

prompt_html:
Find all values of \(k\) such that the equation
\[\int_0^y \left(x+1-k-|x-1|+|x-k|\right)\,dx=0\]
has exactly three distinct solutions for \(y\), where \(k\gt 1\) and \(y\geq 0\).
solution_html:
Let

\[f(x)=x+1-k-|x-1|+|x-k|.\]

Since \(k\gt1\), resolving the modulus signs gives

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}x,&0\leq x\lt1,\\2-x,&1\leq x\lt k,\\x+2-2k,&x\geq k.\end{cases}\]

Write \(F(y)=\int_0^y f(x)\,dx\). For \(0\leq y\leq1\),

\[F(y)=\frac{y^2}{2},\]

so \(y=0\) is the only root in this interval.

For \(1\leq y\leq k\),

\[F(y)=\frac12+\int_1^y(2-x)\,dx=2y-1-\frac{y^2}{2}.\]

The roots of this expression are \(2\pm\sqrt2\). Only \(2+\sqrt2\) can lie in the interval \(1\leq y\leq k\).

For \(y\geq k\), put \(t=y-k\geq0\). Then

\[F(k+t)=F(k)+(2-k)t+\frac{t^2}{2},\]

where \(F(k)=2k-1-\frac{k^2}{2}\). The discriminant of this quadratic in \(t\) is

\[\Delta=2(k-1)(k-3).\]

If \(1\lt k\lt3\), then \(\Delta\lt0\), so there are no further roots. If \(k=3\), there is one repeated root, giving only two distinct solutions altogether.

If \(3\lt k\lt2+\sqrt2\), the middle branch has no root, while the final quadratic has two positive roots. Together with \(y=0\), this gives exactly three distinct solutions.

If \(k\geq2+\sqrt2\), the middle branch contributes the root \(y=2+\sqrt2\) (at \(y=k\) when equality holds), and the final branch contributes exactly one additional root. Again there are exactly three distinct solutions.

Therefore the required condition is \(k\gt3\), so the answer is B.

Thus F(y)=integral_0^y h is y^2/2 on [0,1], 1-(y-2)^2/2 on [1,k], and 1-(k-2)^2+(y-(2k-2))^2/2 for y>=k. For 1<k<=2, h is nonnegative and F(y)>0 for every y>0, so only y=0 is a solution. For k>2, F increases from 0 to 1 at y=2, decreases to its minimum 1-(k-2)^2 at y=2k-2, then increases without bound. Exactly two additional distinct positive zeros occur precisely when this minimum is negative, that is k>3. At k=3 the minimum is zero and supplies only one additional distinct root y=4, giving two roots total. For 2<k<3 there are no additional roots. The complete condition for three distinct roots is therefore k>3.

prompt_html:
A TMUA question asks candidates to identify which one of the conditions below is a sufficient but not necessary condition for some statement \(P\), concerning a real number \(x\), to hold.

Friedrich Gauss, sitting the exam, noticed to his delight that the examiner has designed the question poorly, and the correct option can be deduced without knowing or examining \(P\) in the slightest!

Which is the correct option?
solution_html:
Let a condition be called correct if it is sufficient but not necessary for \(P\).

Suppose condition \(Q\) is correct, and condition \(R\) implies \(Q\). Then
\[R \implies Q \implies P,\]
so \(R\) is also sufficient for \(P\).

Also, since \(Q\) is not necessary for \(P\), there is some value of \(x\) for which \(P\) is true but \(Q\) is false. Since \(R \implies Q\), this same value also makes \(R\) false. Hence \(R\) is also not necessary for \(P\).

Therefore, if one option is implied by another option, the weaker option cannot be the unique correct answer.

Now rewrite the options:
\[|x-2|\lt 2 \iff 0\lt x\lt 4,\]
\[x^2-5x+6\lt 0 \iff (x-2)(x-3)\lt 0 \iff 2\lt x\lt 3,\]
\[\log(x-2) \text{ is defined} \iff x\gt 2,\]
\[|x-2|\lt 1 \iff 1\lt x\lt 3.\]
The condition \(2\lt x\lt 3\) implies each of the following:
\[0\lt x\lt 4,\qquad x\gt 2,\qquad 1\lt x\lt 3,\qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.\]
So if any of those four conditions were correct, then \(2\lt x\lt 3\) would also be correct. That would give more than one correct option, which is impossible.

Hence all the other options are eliminated, and the only possible correct option is B.

The option sets are A=(0,4), B=(2,3), C=(2,∞), D=(1,3), E=R. These follow respectively from absolute-value bounds, (x−2)(x−3)<0, the positive logarithm argument, and the unrestricted real domain. prompt_html:
The real numbers \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are such that exactly two of the following six statements are true.

Which two statements are true?

I. \(a\leq c\)

II. \(a\leq |c|\)

III. \(a\gt 0\)

IV. \(a\leq 0\)

V. \(b\gt |c|\)

VI. \(c\lt |a|\)
solution_html:
Statements III and IV are opposites. For any real value of \(a\), exactly one of
\[a\gt 0\]
and
\[a\leq 0\]
is true.

Since exactly two statements are true altogether, exactly one of statements I, II, V and VI must be true.

Now statement I cannot be the only true statement among I, II, V and VI. If
\[a\leq c,\]
then since \(c\leq |c|\) for every real \(c\), we also have
\[a\leq |c|.\]
So I being true would force II to be true.

Statement II also cannot be the only true statement among I, II, V and VI. If VI is false, then
\[c\geq |a|.\]
Since \(|a|\geq a\), this gives
\[c\geq a,\]
so
\[a\leq c.\]
Thus I would be true.

Statement V also cannot be the only true statement among I, II, V and VI. If II is false, then
\[a\gt |c|.\]
So \(a\gt 0\), and hence \(|a|=a\). Also \(|c|\geq c\), so
\[|a|=a\gt |c|\geq c.\]
Therefore
\[c\lt |a|,\]
so VI would be true.

Therefore the only statement among I, II, V and VI that can be the single true one is VI.

So VI is true, and I, II and V are false. Since II is false,
\[a\gt |c|.\]
This implies \(a\gt 0\), so statement III is true and statement IV is false.

Hence the two true statements are III and VI.

Therefore the correct answer is
\[\textbf{(D)}\ \text{III and VI}.\]

This is possible. For example, take
\[a=2,\quad b=0,\quad c=1.\]
Then
\[a\leq c\]
is false,
\[a\leq |c|\]
is false,
\[a\gt 0\]
is true,
\[a\leq 0\]
is false,
\[b\gt |c|\]
is false, and
\[c\lt |a|\]
is true.

If I held, II would also hold since c≤|c|, producing at least I,II,III true. Thus I is false, so c<a. As a>0, |a|=a and VI is true. These are the required two, III and VI; II and V must be false. prompt_html:
It is given that the equation
\[(x+p)^{1/2} + (x-p)^{1/4} = p\]
has at least one real solution for \(x\), where \(p\) is a real constant.

What is the complete set of possible values of \(p\)?
solution_html:
For the even roots to be real, we need
\[x+p\geq 0\]
and
\[x-p\geq 0.\]
Also, the left-hand side is non-negative, so we must have
\[p\geq 0.\]

Since \(p\geq 0\), the domain condition becomes
\[x\geq p.\]

Let
\[t=(x-p)^{1/4}.\]
Then \(t\geq 0\) and
\[x=p+t^4.\]
Substituting into the equation gives
\[\sqrt{x+p}+(x-p)^{1/4}=p,\]
so
\[\sqrt{2p+t^4}+t=p.\]

For fixed \(p\), the expression
\[\sqrt{2p+t^4}+t\]
is continuous, strictly increasing and unbounded above for \(t\geq 0\). Therefore its minimum value occurs at \(t=0\), giving
\[\sqrt{2p}.\]
So the equation has a solution if and only if
\[p\geq \sqrt{2p}.\]

If \(p=0\), this is true.

If \(p\gt 0\), squaring gives
\[p^2\geq 2p.\]
Dividing by \(p\gt 0\) gives
\[p\geq 2.\]

Therefore the complete set of possible values of \(p\) is
\[p=0\quad\text{or}\quad p\geq2.\]
The answer is C.

subtopic: Averages and medians with distinct integers
prompt_html:
Eight distinct integers are split into two sets of four. The first set has mean \(10\) and median \(9\). The second set has mean \(13\) and median \(11\).

What is the smallest possible value of the range of the set of all eight integers?
solution_html:
Let the first set be \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) with \(a\lt b\le c\lt d\). Mean \(10\) gives \(a+b+c+d=40\); median \(9\) gives \(b+c=18\), so \(a+d=22\). Distinctness with \(b+c=18\) and \(b\lt c\) forces \(b\le 8\) and \(c\ge 10\), hence \(a\le 7\) and \(d\ge 15\).

Let the second set be \(\{e,f,g,h\}\) with \(e\lt f\le g\lt h\). Mean \(13\) gives \(e+f+g+h=52\); median \(11\) gives \(f+g=22\), so \(e+h=30\). Distinctness forces \(f\le 10\) and \(g\ge 12\), hence \(e\le 10\) and \(h\ge 20\).

Lower bound on the maximum. Suppose \(h=20\). Then \(e=10\), and \(e\le f\le 10\) with \(f\) integer forces \(f=10=e\), contradicting distinctness. So \(h\ge 21\).

Upper bound on the minimum. The overall minimum is at most \(a\le 7\).

Hence range \(\ge h-a\ge 21-7=14\). We sharpen this: if \(a=7\), then \(b+c=18\) with \(7\lt b\lt c\) and \(b\le 8\) forces \((b,c)=(8,10)\), so set \(1=\{7,8,10,15\}\). With \(h=21\), we need \(e=9\) (since \(e\ne 7,8,10\) and \(e\le 10\)), then \(f+g=22\) with \(9\lt f\lt g\lt 21\), \(f\le 10\) forces \(f=10\) (taken) or \(f=9=e\). No valid configuration, so range \(14\) is unattainable.

Construction for range 15. Take set \(1=\{6,7,11,16\}\): sum \(40\), median \(\frac{7+11}{2}=9\). Take set \(2=\{9,10,12,21\}\): sum \(52\), median \(\frac{10+12}{2}=11\). The eight values \(\{6,7,9,10,11,12,16,21\}\) are distinct, and the range is \(21-6=15\).

Answer: C.

prompt_html:
Consider the three integrals

\[P = \int_{-2}^{4} (x-1)\,|x-1|\, dx, \qquad Q = \int_{0}^{4} |x-3|\,(x-1)\, dx, \qquad R = \int_{-2}^{2} x\,|x-1|\, dx.\]

Which of the following lists \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) in order from smallest to largest?
solution_html:
We calculate each integral separately.

First,
\[P=\int_{-2}^{4}(x-1)|x-1|\,dx.\]
Let \(u=x-1\). Then the limits become \(-3\) and \(3\), so
\[P=\int_{-3}^{3}u|u|\,du.\]
The function \(u|u|\) is odd, so its integral over \([-3,3]\) is \(0\). Hence
\[P=0.\]

Next,
\[Q=\int_0^4 |x-3|(x-1)\,dx.\]
We split at \(x=3\):
\[Q=\int_0^3 (3-x)(x-1)\,dx+\int_3^4 (x-3)(x-1)\,dx.\]
Now
\[(3-x)(x-1)=-x^2+4x-3,\]
so
\[\int_0^3 (-x^2+4x-3)\,dx = \left[-\frac{x^3}{3}+2x^2-3x\right]_0^3=0.\]
Also
\[(x-3)(x-1)=x^2-4x+3,\]
so
\[\int_3^4 (x^2-4x+3)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+3x\right]_3^4 = \frac43.\]
Thus
\[Q=\frac43.\]

Finally,
\[R=\int_{-2}^{2}x|x-1|\,dx.\]
We split at \(x=1\):
\[R=\int_{-2}^{1}x(1-x)\,dx+\int_1^2 x(x-1)\,dx.\]
So
\[R=\int_{-2}^{1}(x-x^2)\,dx+\int_1^2(x^2-x)\,dx.\]
Hence
\[R=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{1} + \left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^2.\]
This gives
\[R=-\frac92+\frac56=-\frac{11}{3}.\]

Therefore
\[R=-\frac{11}{3},\qquad P=0,\qquad Q=\frac43.\]
So the order from smallest to largest is
\[R<P<Q.\]
The answer is E.

Alternative method

For each of the integrals, sketch the graphs of the integrand to infer signed area that is associated with each integral. For example, \(x|x-1|\) is just \(x(x-1)\) for \(x\geq 1\) and \(x(1-x)\) for \(x\lt 1\).
