subtopic: A reversible condition for a right angle in a kite
prompt_html: In convex kite \(ABCD\), \(AB=AD\) and \(CB=CD\). Its diagonals meet internally at \(O\), where \(AO=p\), \(OC=q\) and \(BO=DO=r\), with \(p,q,r>0\). Which condition is necessary and sufficient for \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\)?
solution_html:
The line through the equal-distance points \(A\) and \(C\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(BD\). Thus the diagonals are perpendicular and \(AB^2=p^2+r^2\), \(BC^2=q^2+r^2\), while \(AC=p+q\).

By Pythagoras and its converse, \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\) holds exactly when \(AB^2+BC^2=AC^2\). Substitution gives \(p^2+q^2+2r^2=(p+q)^2\), equivalent to \(r^2=pq\). Every step is reversible, establishing both necessity and sufficiency.

Put O=(0,0), A=(0,p), C=(0,−q), B=(−r,0), D=(r,0). The vectors from B are BA=(r,p) and BC=(r,−q). Their dot product is r²−pq. A right angle at B is equivalent to zero dot product, hence exactly r²=pq, with both necessity and sufficiency established.

subtopic: An intersection ratio is not an area ratio
prompt_html: \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram. Point \(P\) lies on \(AB\) and point \(Q\) lies on \(AD\), with \(AP:PB=2:1\) and \(AQ:QD=3:1\). Lines \(DP\) and \(BQ\) meet at \(X\). What fraction of the area of \(ABCD\) is the area of triangle \(APX\)?
solution_html:
An invertible affine change of coordinates preserves ratios of areas and division ratios, so take \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(1,0)\) and \(D=(0,1)\). Then \(P=(2/3,0)\) and \(Q=(0,3/4)\).

The lines have equations \(DP:\ y=1-3x/2\) and \(BQ:\ y=3(1-x)/4\). Equating them gives \(x=1/3\), then \(y=1/2\). Thus the height of \(X\) above \(AB\) is half the parallelogram height.

The area ratio is \(\tfrac12\cdot(2/3)\cdot(1/2)=1/6\). This result is independent of the original side lengths and angle.

prompt_html: From \(O\), point \(A\) is \(10\text{ km}\) away on a bearing of \(060^\circ\), while point \(B\) is \(10\sqrt3\text{ km}\) away on a bearing of \(150^\circ\). Which pair gives \(AB\) and the bearing of \(B\) from \(A\)?

subtopic: Two conditions can express the same restriction
prompt_html:
\(ABCD\) is a parallelogram. Consider:

I. \(ABCD\) is cyclic.

II. Its diagonals are perpendicular.

III. Two adjacent sides are equal.

Which pairs of conditions are sufficient to guarantee that \(ABCD\) is a square?
solution_html:
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. If it is cyclic, they are also supplementary, so all angles are right angles: I makes it a rectangle.

If its side vectors are \(u,v\), perpendicular diagonals give \((u+v)\cdot(u-v)=|u|^2-|v|^2=0\). Thus II makes the adjacent side lengths equal, giving a rhombus. III directly gives the same rhombus condition.

Combining I with either II or III gives a rectangle with equal adjacent sides, hence a square. But II and III together can hold in a non-square rhombus, so that pair is insufficient. Exactly the two pairs listed in D work.

subtopic: The farthest point is on the major arc
prompt_html: A circle has radius \(4\). Chord \(AB\) has length \(4\sqrt3\). Point \(P\) varies along the major arc \(AB\). What is the greatest possible area of triangle \(APB\)?
solution_html:
Let \(M\) be the chord midpoint and \(O\) the centre. Since \(AM=2\sqrt3\), \(OM=\sqrt{4^2-(2\sqrt3)^2}=2\). The base \(AB\) is fixed, so maximising the triangle area is the same as maximising the perpendicular distance from \(P\) to the chord.

On the major arc, the farthest point is the end of the perpendicular diameter opposite the chord. Its distance from the chord is \(4+2=6\). Therefore the greatest area is \(\tfrac12(4\sqrt3)(6)=12\sqrt3\), and it is attained at that point.

subtopic: Cubic graphs - modulus and root counts
prompt_html:
Let \(k\geq0\). For which values of \(k\) does the equation

\[|x^3-3x-1|=k\]

have exactly three distinct real solutions?
solution_html:
For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), the derivative \(3(x^2-1)\) gives a local maximum 2 at \(x=-1\) and minimum -2 at \(x=1\). A level strictly between -2 and 2 meets the cubic three times; a level equal to either extreme meets it twice; a level outside meets it once.

For \(k>0\), count the disjoint levels \(f(x)=1+k\) and \(f(x)=1-k\). The totals are 6 for \(0<k<1\), 5 at 1, 4 for \(1<k<3\), 3 at 3, and 2 for \(k>3\).

At \(k=0\), the two levels coincide at 1, so there are three roots, not six. Therefore \(k=0\) or 3.

The number N(y) of distinct roots of g(x)=y is 3 for -3<y<1, 2 at y=-3 or 1, and 1 outside [-3,1]. For k=0, |g|=0 is just g=0, giving 3 roots. For k>0, the levels ±k are disjoint: the total is 6 for 0<k<1, 5 for k=1, 4 for 1<k<3, 3 for k=3, and 2 for k>3. Exactly k=0 and k=3 work.

prompt_html:
What is the coefficient of \(x^7\) in the expansion of

\[(1+x)^{10}(1-x)^7?\]
solution_html:
Pair seven factors to obtain \[(1+x)^{10}(1-x)^7=(1-x^2)^7(1+x)^3.\]

The first factor has only even powers. To obtain degree 7, the degree pairs can only be \((6,1)\) and \((4,3)\). Hence the coefficient is

\[(-1)^3\binom73\cdot3+(-1)^2\binom72\cdot1=-105+21=-84.\]

The constant and quadratic terms in the cubic factor cannot contribute, because they would require an odd power in the other factor.

prompt_html:
Bag A contains 4 red and 2 blue balls. Bag B contains 2 red and 4 blue balls. One bag is selected with probability \(1/2\) for each bag.

Three balls are drawn in order from the selected bag, without replacement.

Given that the first two balls are both red, what is the probability that the third ball is blue?
solution_html:
Let \(RR\) mean that the first two balls are red. Summing the two bag branches gives

\[P(RR)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac46\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac26\cdot\tfrac15=\tfrac7{30}.\]

The probability of red, red, then blue is

\[P(RRB)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac46\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac24+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac26\cdot\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac44=\tfrac2{15}.\]

Hence \(P(\text{third blue}\mid RR)=(2/15)/(7/30)=4/7\). The bags were equally likely before the observations, not afterwards.

\[n^2-1\text{ is divisible by }24.\]

Which of the following is sufficient but not necessary for this condition?

options.html: \(n\) and 6 have no common factor greater than 1.
options.label: C

solution_html:
For odd \(n\), the consecutive even numbers \(n-1,n+1\) include a multiple of 4, so their product is divisible by 8. If \(n\) is not divisible by 3, one of these neighbours is divisible by 3. Thus being odd and not divisible by 3 guarantees divisibility by 24.

Conversely an even \(n\) makes \(n^2-1\) odd, while a multiple of 3 makes it indivisible by 3. Therefore option C is necessary and sufficient, rather than the requested type.

A prime greater than 3 satisfies both conditions, so E is sufficient. It is not necessary: \(n=25\) is composite and \(25^2-1=624=24\cdot26\). A fails at 3; B and D fail at 4. E is the unique answer.
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Characterize divisibility by24 as coprimality with6, then distinguish sufficiency from necessity for each offered condition.
audited_reference.concise_proof: If24 divides n²−1, then n must be odd, since even n gives an odd n²−1. Also3 cannot divide n, since that would give n²−1≡−1 mod3. Conversely, for odd n the consecutive even numbers n−1,n+1 have product divisible by8; if3 does not divide n, one of n−1,n+1 is divisible by3. Since8 and3 are coprime,24 divides their product. Thus the condition is equivalent to gcd(n,6)=1. Every prime greater than3 is odd and not divisible by3, so E is sufficient. It is not necessary: n=25 gives n²−1=624=24·26 but is composite. A fails at n=3; B fails at n=2; D fails at n=4. C is necessary as well as sufficient, so does not meet the requested strictly sufficient-but-not-necessary description.

Sufficient but not necessary requires both a universal forward implication and a legal converse counterexample.

prompt_html:
For a real number \(k\), let \(S(k)\) be the statement:

There exists a real number \(a\) such that, for every real number \(x\), \[x^2-2ax+2a+k>0.\]

For which values of \(k\) is the negation of \(S(k)\) true?
solution_html:
Complete the square in \(x\) and then in \(a\):

\[x^2-2ax+2a+k=(x-a)^2+k+1-(a-1)^2.\]

For a fixed \(a\), its minimum over all real \(x\) occurs at \(x=a\), and is \(k+1-(a-1)^2\). Some choice of \(a\) makes this strictly positive exactly when \(k+1>0\): the best choice is \(a=1\).

Thus \(S(k)\) holds exactly when \(k>-1\); its negation holds for \(k\leq-1\). Equivalently, for every \(a\) there then exists \(x\) with the expression at most 0: choose \(x=a\).
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Complete the square in x and then in the parameter a; negate the quantified existence statement with its strict boundary.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The expression equals (x−a)²+k+1−(a−1)². For fixed a its minimum over all real x is k+1−(a−1)², attained at x=a. Thus it is strictly positive for every x exactly when k+1>(a−1)². There exists such an a exactly when k+1>0: necessity follows from (a−1)²≥0, and sufficiency follows by choosing a=1. Hence S(k) is true exactly for k>−1. Its negation is “for every real a there exists a real x with x²−2ax+2a+k≤0.” It holds exactly for k≤−1. Indeed at x=a the value is k+1−(a−1)²≤0 for every a. Therefore C is correct.

prompt_html:
What is the largest positive integer \(d\) such that

\[n^5-5n^3+4n\]

is divisible by \(d\) for every positive integer \(n\)?
solution_html:
Factor the expression:

\[n^5-5n^3+4n=n(n^2-1)(n^2-4)=(n-2)(n-1)n(n+1)(n+2).\]

For \(n\geq3\), five consecutive integers include a multiple of 5, a multiple of 3, and a multiple of 4 together with another even integer. The product is therefore divisible by \(5\cdot3\cdot8=120\). For \(n=1,2\), the expression is 0, also divisible by 120.

At \(n=3\) the expression equals exactly 120, so any integer dividing every value must divide 120. Hence 120 is the largest possible.

audited_reference.concise_proof: n⁵−5n³+4n=n(n²−1)(n²−4)=(n−2)(n−1)n(n+1)(n+2). For n≥3 these are five consecutive positive integers: one is divisible by5, one by3, and their even factors together supply at least2³ (there is a multiple of4 and another even term). Thus the product is divisible by120. For n=1,2 it is0 and is also divisible by120. At n=3 the value is1·2·3·4·5=120. Any positive integer dividing the expression for every n must therefore divide120 and cannot exceed it. Since120 works universally, it is the largest possible d.

prompt_html:
A real number \(a_n\) is defined for every integer \(n\), including negative integers and zero. It is known that \(a_0=0\), and that for every integer \(n\):

  • If \(a_n=0\), then \(a_{n+4}=0\).
  • If \(a_{n+6}=0\), then \(a_n=0\).

Which statement must be true?
solution_html:
From a zero at index \(j\), the first rule produces a zero at \(j+4\). Put \(n=j-6\) in the second rule to get a zero at \(j-6\). The permitted moves are therefore \(+4\) and \(-6\).

They combine to give \(+2=4+4-6\) and \(-2=4-6\). Starting at index 0, repetition reaches every even integer in both directions. Thus \(a_{2n}=0\) always.

Odd indices are not determined. A sequence with all even terms 0 and odd terms \(a_n=n^2+1\) satisfies both implications but makes A, C and E false. The all-zero sequence satisfies both rules but makes B false. Only D is forced.

audited_reference.concise_proof: If a_m=0, the first implication gives a_{m+4}=0. The second, used with n=m-6, gives a_{m-6}=0. Composing +4,+4,-6 yields +2, while +4,-6 yields -2. Starting from a₀=0 and iterating ±2 proves every even index has value zero, including negative indices. No odd zero is forced: the assignment a_even=0 and a_odd=1 satisfies all implications and refutes A and E. B is refuted by the all-zero sequence. C is refuted by setting a_even=0, a₁=1, a₃=2 and all other odd values 1; every odd value is nonzero, so the zero implications impose no relation between them. Thus only D must hold.

prompt_html:
A five-digit number is formed using five different digits chosen from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The number is even, and the digits 1 and 2 are not adjacent.

How many such numbers are possible?
solution_html:
The last digit is 2, 4 or 6. For each last digit there are \(6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=360\) arrangements of the first four positions before the adjacency restriction.

If the last digit is 2, the bad arrangements have 1 immediately before it. There are \(5\cdot4\cdot3=60\), leaving 300.

If the last digit is 4 or 6, both forbidden adjacent digits must lie in the first four positions. Choose their two companions from the other four available digits in \(4\cdot3/2=6\) ways; arrange these two digits and the block 12/21 in \(3!=6\) ways, and choose the block order in 2 ways. This excludes 72 from each case, leaving 288 each.

Total: \(300+288+288=876\).
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Count all even five-digit arrangements, then subtract disjoint adjacency violations classified by the final digit.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The final digit is2,4 or6. For each choice, the preceding four positions are an ordered selection of four of the remaining six digits, giving6·5·4·3=360. There are1080 even numbers before the adjacency restriction. For a forbidden number ending in2, adjacency forces the preceding digit to be1. The other three positions can be filled in5·4·3=60 ways. For a forbidden number ending in4 or6, the adjacent pair1,2 lies entirely in the first four positions. Choose its other two digits from the four available ones in C(4,2)=6 ways; arrange the three objects (the block and two digits) in3!=6 ways and orient the block in2 ways, giving72 for each final digit. The forbidden total is60+72+72=204, so the allowed count is1080−204=876. Numbers omitting1 or2 remain correctly included in the unrestricted total and never enter the forbidden count.

An even last digit2 must be handled differently because it occupies one member of the forbidden adjacent pair.
The condition does not require both1 and2 to appear.

prompt_html:
A continuous function \(f\) satisfies \(f(2-x)=f(x)\) for every real \(x\). It is given that

\[\int_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,dx=9,\qquad \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx=4.\]

\[\int_{-1}^{3}\bigl[3f(x-1)-2f(x+1)\bigr]\,dx.\]

Translating the first graph changes its interval to \([-2,2]\); translating the second changes its interval to \([0,4]\). Reflection in \(x=1\) maps these intervals to one another, so both signed integrals are 11. The answer is \(3(11)-2(11)=11\).

Substituting u=x−1 and v=x+1 in the requested expression gives3∫₋₂²f−2∫₀⁴f. The first integral is9+2=11 and the second2+9=11, hence the result is33−22=11.

prompt_html:
A continuous function \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)+f(4-x)=6\) for every real \(x\). It is also known that

\[\int_0^4x^2f(x)\,dx=40.\]

What is \(\int_0^4xf(x)\,dx\)?

Let \(J_r=\int_0^4x^rf(x)\,dx\). Reflecting the unweighted integral gives \(2J_0=24\), hence \(J_0=12\). Reflect the entire graph \(x^2f(x)\) about \(x=2\):

\[J_2=\int_0^4(4-x)^2[6-f(x)]\,dx=128-16J_0+8J_1-J_2.\]

Since \(J_2=40\), this gives \(80=128-192+8J_1\), so \(J_1=18\).

Reflection gives K=∫₀⁴u²f(4−u)du=∫₀⁴u²(6−f(u))du=6·64/3−40=88. Expanding the weight instead gives K=16A−8B+C=232−8B. Therefore232−8B=88 and B=18.

The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(t)=1-|t|\) when \(|t|\le1\), and \(f(t)=0\) when \(|t|>1\). Find

prompt_html:
A continuous function \(f\) satisfies \(f(-x)=f(x)\) and \(f(2-x)=-f(x)\) for every real \(x\). Given that \(\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=3\), find

\[\int_{-2}^{5}f(2x-1)\,dx.\]
solution_html:
Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) in the second identity gives \(f(x+2)=-f(x)\), hence \(f(x+4)=f(x)\). Adjacent intervals of length 2 cancel, so every length-4 interval has integral zero. Horizontal compression gives

\[\int_{-2}^{5}f(2x-1)\,dx=\frac12\int_{-5}^{9}f(u)\,du=\frac12\int_7^9f(u)\,du.\]

Shift the remaining interval back by 8: it becomes \([-1,1]\), with integral \(2(3)=6\) by evenness. The answer is 3.

Thus the total is(1/2)(3+3)=3.

prompt_html:
A continuous even function \(f\) satisfies \(f(x+1)-f(x)=2x+1\) for every real \(x\). It is given that \(\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=2\). Find

\[\int_0^3xf(x)\,dx.\]
solution_html:
Set \(h(x)=f(x)-x^2\). Then \(h\) is even and has period 1, while \(H=\int_0^1h=2-1/3=5/3\). The identities imply \(h(1-x)=h(x)\); reflecting the weighted graph on \([0,1]\) therefore gives \(\int_0^1xh(x)\,dx=H/2\). On \([j,j+1]\), translation and periodicity give \(\int_j^{j+1}xh(x)\,dx=(j+1/2)H\). Summing for \(j=0,1,2\) gives \(\int_0^3xh=9H/2=15/2\). Thus

\[\int_0^3xf(x)\,dx=\int_0^3x^3\,dx+\frac{15}2=\frac{81}4+\frac{30}4=\frac{111}4.\]

subtopic: Sufficiency of integral data and counterexamples
prompt_html:
A continuous function \(f\) is even and \(\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=1\). Which integrals have a numerical value uniquely determined by this information?

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{I}:&\quad\int_{-1}^1(x+1)f(x)\,dx\\\mathrm{II}:&\quad\int_{-1}^1f(x^2)\,dx\\\mathrm{III}:&\quad\int_0^1f(x-\tfrac12)\,dx\end{aligned}\]
solution_html: In I, \(xf(x)\) is odd, so its symmetric integral is zero, and \(\int_{-1}^1f=2\). Thus I is always 2. For II and III compare the two allowed functions \(f(x)=1\) and \(f(x)=3x^2\). Each is even and integrates to 1 on \([0,1]\). In II they give 2 and \(6/5\), respectively. In III they give 1 and \(1/4\). Thus neither II nor III is determined, and only I qualifies.

subtopic: Shifted polynomial integrals and root counts
prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=5x^4-15x^2+4\). For a fixed real number \(k\), consider

\[\int_{-1}^{1}f(x-a)\,dx=k.\]

What is the complete range of \(k\) for which this equation has exactly four distinct real solutions for \(a\)?
solution_html: Expand only the even powers of \(x\), because the odd terms integrate to zero on \([-1,1]\). The integral simplifies to \(10a^4-10a^2\). Put \(u=a^2\ge0\). Four distinct values of \(a\) require two distinct positive roots of \(u^2-u-k/10=0\). Their sum is 1, so both are positive exactly when their product \(-k/10\) is positive, provided the roots are real and distinct. Hence \(k<0\) and \(1+2k/5>0\), giving \(-5/2<k<0\). At the lower endpoint there are only two values of \(a\); at zero there are three.

subtopic: Necessary and sufficient conditions for integral cancellation
prompt_html:
Let \(f\) be continuous on the real numbers. Consider the property

\[P:\quad\int_a^{a+2}f(x)\,dx=0\quad\text{for every real }a.\]

Each identity below is required for every real \(x\).

I. \(f(-x)=-f(x)\) and \(f(x+2)=f(x)\).

II. \(f(-x)=f(x)\) and \(f(x+2)=f(x)\).

III. \(f(x+1)=-f(x)\).

Which conditions are each sufficient, but not necessary, for \(P\)?
solution_html:
I is sufficient: oddness gives zero integral on \([-1,1]\), and a period of 2 makes every length-2 integral equal to that one. II fails for \(f(x)=1\). III is sufficient because its two consecutive length-1 integrals cancel.

To show I and III are not necessary, define \(f(x)=1-4|x|\) on \([-1/2,1/2]\) and repeat this graph with period 1. Its endpoint values agree, so it is continuous. Each period has zero signed area (two positive triangles cancel two negative triangles), hence \(P\) holds. Yet \(f(0)=1\), so it is not odd, and \(f(x+1)=f(x)\), not \(-f(x)\). Thus I and III are sufficient but not necessary.

subtopic: Range with excluded inputs after cancellation
prompt_html:
For real \(x\ne1\), define

\[f(x)=\frac{4^x-6\cdot2^x+8}{2^x-2},\qquad g(x)=\frac1{f(x)^2+6f(x)+10}.\]

What is the exact range of \(g\)?
solution_html: Put \(t=2^x\), so \(t>0\) and \(t\ne2\). Factorisation gives \(f=t-4\), hence \(g=1/((t-1)^2+1)\). The maximum 1 is attained at \(t=1\); zero is never attained. The output \(1/2\) needs \(t=0\) or \(t=2\), both forbidden. Every other \(v\in(0,1]\) is attained by \(t=1+\sqrt{1/v-1}\), which is positive and is not 2. Thus only \(1/2\) is missing from \((0,1]\).

subtopic: Composite quadratic root counting on a restricted domain
prompt_html: The function \(f\) is defined for all real numbers by \(f(x)=x^2-4x+1\). For which values of \(k\) do \(y=f(f(x))\) and \(y=k\) have exactly three distinct intersections in the region \(x\ge0\)?
solution_html: Completing squares gives \(f(f(x))=((x-2)^2-5)^2-3\). For \(k\ge-3\), put \(s=\sqrt{k+3}\). The two possibilities are \((x-2)^2=5+s\) and \((x-2)^2=5-s\). For \(s>0\), the first gives just one nonnegative x, since \(\sqrt{5+s}>2\). The second gives two distinct nonnegative x-values exactly when \(0<5-s\le4\), or \(1\le s<5\). Thus \(-2\le k<22\). At \(s=0\) the branches coincide, and \(k<-3\) is impossible.

For x≥0, a value u>4 has one preimage x=2+√u;0<u≤4 has two preimages2±√u;u=0 has one preimage2;u<0 has none. For k<−3 there are no solutions. For k≥−3 let s=√(k+3). The candidate values are u=5+s and u=5−s. If s=0 they coincide at5, giving one x. For s>0 the upper branch always gives one x. subtopic: Universal inequalities in a bounded region
prompt_html: The region \(R\) consists of all points satisfying \(x^2-2x<y<4-x^2\). Find the complete set of real values of \(m\) for which every point in \(R\) satisfies \(y>mx-2\).
solution_html:
The region exists only for \(-1<x<2\). All its points lie strictly above \(mx-2\) exactly when \(Q(x)=x^2-(m+2)x+2\ge0\) throughout that interval. As \(x\) approaches \(-1\), this requires \(m+5\ge0\). At \(x=\sqrt2\), it requires \(4-(m+2)\sqrt2\ge0\), hence \(m\le2\sqrt2-2\).

Conversely, for \(m\ge-5\) and \(-1<x<0\), \(Q(x)\ge(x+1)(x+2)>0\). For \(m\le2\sqrt2-2\) and \(0\le x<2\), \(Q(x)\ge(x-\sqrt2)^2\ge0\). These prove sufficiency. Both parameter endpoints are included, because the region excludes its lower boundary.

audited_reference.concise_proof: The two parabolas leave a nonempty vertical interval exactly when x^2-2x<4-x^2, or -1<x<2. For each such x, every y strictly above the lower parabola satisfies y>mx-2 exactly when q_m(x)=x^2-(m+2)x+2>=0. If q_m(x)<0, choose y between the lower curve and the smaller of the line and upper curve to obtain a counterexample. Necessity: approaching x=-1 from the right requires q_m(-1)=m+5>=0, hence m>=-5; otherwise continuity gives failing interior x. Also x=sqrt(2) is interior, and q_m(sqrt(2))>=0 yields m<=2sqrt(2)-2. For sufficiency, suppose -5<=m<=2sqrt(2)-2. When -1<x<0, q_m(x)>=q_(-5)(x)=(x+1)(x+2)>0. When 0<=x<2, q_m(x)>=q_(2sqrt(2)-2)(x)=(x-sqrt(2))^2>=0. Thus both parameter endpoints are included, and every point in R satisfies the strict line inequality.

subtopic: Reflection identities and periodic zero counting
prompt_html: A continuous function \(f\), defined on the real numbers, satisfies \(f(2-x)=f(x)\) and \(f(8-x)=f(x)\) for every real \(x\). In \([1,4]\), its only zeros are \(x=2\) and \(x=3\). How many distinct solutions of \(f(x^2+1)=0\) lie in \([-5,5]\)?
solution_html:
Composing the two reflections gives \(f(x+6)=f(x)\). Reflection about \(x=4\) maps the zeros 2 and 3 to 6 and 5. Hence the zeros on \([1,7)\) are exactly \(2,3,5,6\), and all zeros are their translates by multiples of 6.

The input \(t=x^2+1\) ranges over \([1,26]\). Its zero values are \(2,3,5,6,8,9,11,12,14,15,17,18,20,21,23,24,26\): 17 in total. Each exceeds 1, so each gives two distinct inputs \(x=\pm\sqrt{t-1}\). Both endpoints \(x=\pm5\) are allowed. The total is 34.

prompt_html: Let \(k\ge0\). For which values of \(k\) do \(y=|x^2-4|\) and \(y=k|x-3|\) have exactly two distinct intersections?

Exactly two total roots therefore require the first discriminant negative: \(k^2-12k+16<0\), or \(6-2\sqrt5<k<6+2\sqrt5\). Include \(k=0\) separately.

subtopic: Preimage counts through a cubic composition
prompt_html: Let \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) and let \(a\) be a real constant. Find the complete set of values of \(a\) for which \(y=f(f(x)+a)\) crosses or touches the x-axis at exactly seven distinct points.
solution_html:
The outer zeros are \(0,\pm\sqrt3\), so count solutions of \(f(x)=-a\), \(f(x)=-a+\sqrt3\), and \(f(x)=-a-\sqrt3\). Their root sets are disjoint. Since \(f'(x)=3(x^2-1)\), the stationary heights are \(2\) and \(-2\). A level \(t\) has three preimages if \(|t|<2\), two if \(|t|=2\), and one otherwise.

By odd symmetry the total depends on \(A=|a|\). As \(A\) increases, the three levels pass the stationary heights at \(2-\sqrt3,2,2+\sqrt3\). The counts on the successive open ranges are \(9,7,5,3\), with counts \(8,6,4\) at the three boundaries. Exactly seven occurs for \(2-\sqrt3<|a|<2\).

prompt_html:
For which values of the real constant \(k\) does the equation

\[\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x-4)=\log_2(5x+k)\]

have exactly two distinct real solutions?
solution_html:
The original logarithms require \(x>4\) and \(5x+k>0\). Combining the logarithms gives

\[(x-1)(x-4)=5x+k,\qquad x^2-10x+4-k=0.\]

The candidate roots are \(x=5\pm\sqrt{21+k}\). For two distinct real roots, \(k>-21\). Both are greater than \(4\) exactly when the smaller root is:

\[5-\sqrt{21+k}>4,\qquad \sqrt{21+k}<1,\qquad k<-20.\]

At either retained root, \(5x+k=(x-1)(x-4)>0\), so the final logarithm is also defined. Thus the required interval is \(\boxed{-21<k<-20}\).

At \(k=-21\) there is only one distinct root. At \(k=-20\), the candidate \(x=4\) is invalid.

prompt_html:
The solution set of

\[\log_{1/2}\!\left(\log_2(x^2-5x+6)\right)>-1\]

is a union of two open intervals. What is the sum of their lengths?

Write \(q=x^2-5x+6\). The argument of the outer logarithm must be positive. Since its base is less than \(1\),

\[0<\log_2q<2,\qquad 1<q<4.\]

Complete the square: \(q=(x-\tfrac52)^2-\tfrac14\). Consequently,

\[\frac{\sqrt5}{2}<\left|x-\frac52\right|<\frac{\sqrt{17}}2.\]

The intervals are

\[\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{17}}2,\frac{5-\sqrt5}2\right),\quad \left(\frac{5+\sqrt5}2,\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}2\right).\]

Each has length \((\sqrt{17}-\sqrt5)/2\). Their total length is therefore \(\boxed{\sqrt{17}-\sqrt5}\).

prompt_html:
Evaluate

\[\log_2 31+\sum_{r=2}^{31}\log_2\!\left(1-\frac1{r^2}\right).\]
solution_html:
All logarithm arguments are positive. Combine the sum into a single logarithm, and factor each term:

\[1-\frac1{r^2}=\frac{r-1}{r}\,\frac{r+1}{r}.\]

The first product is \((1/2)(2/3)\cdots(30/31)=1/31\). The second is \((3/2)(4/3)\cdots(32/31)=32/2=16\).

\[\prod_{r=2}^{31}\left(1-\frac1{r^2}\right)=\frac{16}{31}.\]

Hence the expression is

\[\log_2 31+\log_2\frac{16}{31}=\log_2 16=\boxed4.\]

subtopic: Exact range of exponential rational functions
prompt_html:
For real \(x\), define

\[f(x)=\frac{4^x-6\cdot2^x+13}{4^x-4\cdot2^x+5}.\]

What is the greatest value of \(f(x)\)?
solution_html:
Put \(t=2^x>0\). The denominator is \((t-2)^2+1>0\). If the value of the fraction is \(y\), then

\[(y-1)t^2+(6-4y)t+5y-13=0.\]

For \(y\ne1\), this quadratic must have a real root. Its discriminant is

\[(6-4y)^2-4(y-1)(5y-13)=4\bigl(5-(y-3)^2\bigr).\]

Therefore \(y\le3+\sqrt5\). The exceptional case \(y=1\) cannot exceed this bound.

At \(y=3+\sqrt5\), the quadratic has its repeated root \(t=4-\sqrt5>0\). This is allowed, at \(x=\log_2(4-\sqrt5)\). Thus the bound is attained and the greatest value is \(\boxed{3+\sqrt5}\).

prompt_html:
How many ordered pairs of positive integers \((m,n)\) satisfy

\[\log_2m+\log_2n=\log_2(m+n)+3\]

and also have \(m+n\) equal to a perfect square?
solution_html:
Combine the logarithms to obtain \(mn=8(m+n)\), hence

\[(m-8)(n-8)=64.\]

Also, \(n(m-8)=8m>0\), so \(m>8\); similarly \(n>8\). We therefore need only positive factor pairs of \(64\).

\(m-8,\ n-8\) (either order)\(m+n\)Square?
\(1,64\)\(81\)Yes
\(2,32\)\(50\)No
\(4,16\)\(36\)Yes
\(8,8\)\(32\)No

The valid ordered pairs are \((9,72),(72,9),(12,24),(24,12)\). The answer is \(\boxed4\).

prompt_html:
The real numbers \(a,b,c\) are greater than \(1\), with

\[c=ab^2,\qquad \log_a b+\log_b c=5.\]

There are two possible values of \(\log_a c\). What is their positive difference?
solution_html:
Put \(p=\log_a b>0\) and \(q=\log_b c>0\). By definition, \(b=a^p\) and \(c=b^q=a^{pq}\). On the other hand,

\[c=ab^2=a^{1+2p}.\]

Since \(a>1\), equal powers give \(pq=1+2p\). Together with \(p+q=5\), this gives

\[p(5-p)=1+2p,\qquad p^2-3p+1=0.\]

Thus \(p=(3\pm\sqrt5)/2\). Both values are positive, and so are the corresponding values of \(q\). Each can be realised by choosing any \(a>1\) and putting \(b=a^p\).

\[\log_a c=1+2p=4\pm\sqrt5.\]

The positive difference is \(\boxed{2\sqrt5}\). No change-of-base formula is needed.

prompt_html:
What is the complete set of real values of \(x\) satisfying

\[\log_x(x^2-3x+2)>1?\]
solution_html:
The base requires \(x>0\) and \(x\ne1\). The argument \((x-1)(x-2)\) must be positive. Together these give \(0<x<1\) or \(x>2\).

For \(0<x<1\): the logarithm is decreasing, and \(1=\log_x x\). Thus

\[x^2-3x+2<x,\qquad x^2-4x+2<0.\]

Intersecting \(2-\sqrt2<x<2+\sqrt2\) with this domain gives \(2-\sqrt2<x<1\).

For \(x>2\): the base exceeds \(1\), so instead we require \(x^2-4x+2>0\). This gives \(x>2+\sqrt2\).

The complete answer is \(\boxed{2-\sqrt2<x<1\text{ or }x>2+\sqrt2}\). All displayed endpoints are excluded.

subtopic: Global logarithm domains with a parameter
prompt_html:
For a real constant \(a\), let

\[f_a(x)=\log_2\!\left(4^x-2a\cdot2^x+a+2\right).\]

Which condition on \(a\) is necessary and sufficient for \(f_a(x)\) to be defined for every real \(x\)?
solution_html:
Put \(t=2^x\). The requirement is

\[t^2-2at+a+2>0\qquad\text{for every }t>0.\]

If \(a\le0\): the first two terms are positive for \(t>0\), and the limit as \(t\) approaches \(0\) from above is \(a+2\). The requirement holds exactly when \(a\ge-2\). In particular, at \(a=-2\) the expression is \(t^2+4t>0\), so this endpoint is included.

If \(a>0\): the minimum occurs at the allowed value \(t=a\), and equals \(a+2-a^2\). Therefore

\[a+2-a^2>0,\qquad (a-2)(a+1)<0,\]

which gives \(0<a<2\) in this case. At \(a=2\), the argument vanishes when \(t=2\), so the logarithm is undefined.

Combining the cases gives \(\boxed{-2\le a<2}\).

prompt_html:
A sequence of positive real numbers is defined by

\[a_1=16,\qquad a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2a_n}\quad(n\ge1).\]

Let \(P_n=a_1a_2\cdots a_n\). What is the smallest positive integer \(n\) for which

\[P_n>2^{\,n+6-3/32}?\]
solution_html:
Set \(b_n=\log_2a_n\). Then \(b_1=4\) and \(b_{n+1}=(1+b_n)/2\). Subtract the fixed value \(1\):

\[b_{n+1}-1=\frac{b_n-1}{2},\qquad b_n=1+\frac3{2^{n-1}}.\]

The logarithm of the product is the sum of these terms:

\[\log_2P_n=n+3\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1{2^{n-1}}\right) =n+6(1-2^{-n}).\]

Since base \(2\) is increasing, the stated inequality is equivalent to

\[6\cdot2^{-n}<\frac3{32},\qquad 2^n>64.\]

At \(n=6\) there is equality, which is not sufficient. The smallest allowed integer is \(\boxed7\).

subtopic: Range of a composite trigonometric exponential
prompt_html:
For real \(\theta\), define

\[f(\theta)=\log_{1/2}\!\left(4^{\sin\theta}-3\cdot2^{\sin\theta}+3\right).\]

Which option gives the complete range of \(f\)?
solution_html:
As \(-1\le\sin\theta\le1\), the substitution \(t=2^{\sin\theta}\) takes every value in \([1/2,2]\). The logarithm argument is

\[t^2-3t+3=\left(t-\frac32\right)^2+\frac34.\]

The minimum \(3/4\) occurs at \(t=3/2\), inside the interval. For the maximum, check the endpoints: the values are \(7/4\) at \(t=1/2\) and \(1\) at \(t=2\). The argument therefore takes every value in \([3/4,7/4]\).

The base \(1/2\) reverses this order. From \((1/2)^z=2^{-z}\), the identity \(\log_{1/2}u=-\log_2u\) follows directly. Hence

\[\boxed{\log_2\frac47\le f\le\log_2\frac43}.\]

Both endpoints are attained; the logarithm argument is always positive.

prompt_html:
What is the length of the curve consisting of all real points \((x,y)\) satisfying

\[\log_2(y+\sqrt3\,x)+\log_2(y-\sqrt3\,x)=\log_2(16-4x^2)?\]
solution_html:
Combining the logarithms and equating their arguments gives

\[(y+\sqrt3x)(y-\sqrt3x)=16-4x^2,\qquad x^2+y^2=16.\]

This is a circle of radius \(4\), but the original equation also requires

\[y+\sqrt3x>0,\qquad y-\sqrt3x>0,\]

or \(y>\sqrt3|x|\). On the circle this is the upper arc between the rays at angles \(\pi/3\) and \(2\pi/3\). Its central angle is \(\pi/3\).

The third logarithm is defined throughout this open arc, since \(16-4x^2=y^2-3x^2>0\). Thus no additional points are lost.

\[\text{Arc length}=4\times\frac\pi3=\boxed{\frac{4\pi}{3}}.\]

Excluding the two endpoints does not change the arc length.

subtopic: Equivalence and preserving numbers of roots
prompt_html:
Fix a real number \(a>1\). Consider the equation \(a^x=2x+1\).

Which of the following equations must have the same number of distinct real solutions as this equation, for every such \(a\)?

I \(\log_a(2x+1)=x\)
II \(a^{2x}=(2x+1)^2\)
III \(a^{x^3-1}=2x^3-1\)
solution_html:
I: By the definition of a logarithm, this is equivalent to \(a^x=2x+1\). Every original solution already has \(2x+1>0\). The solution sets are identical.

II: Taking the positive square root gives \(a^x=|2x+1|\). This retains the original solutions and also admits the branch

\[a^x=-2x-1\qquad(x<-1/2).\]

On that interval, the left side is strictly increasing from \(0\), and the right side is strictly decreasing from arbitrarily large positive values to \(0\). By continuity they meet exactly once. So II adds one solution.

III: Put \(t=x^3-1\). This is a one-to-one correspondence from the real numbers onto the real numbers. The equation becomes \(a^t=2t+1\), so its number of solutions is unchanged.

The correct selection is \(\boxed{\text{I and III only}}\).
answer_verification_basis: Saved mathematical audit and applied corrections

audited_reference.ordinary_method:
Every solution of the original equation has 2x+1>0. Taking a logarithm is therefore reversible, and the domain of I enforces the same condition. I has exactly the original solutions.
For III, t=x³-1 is a bijection R→R. Its equation becomes a^t=2t+1, so each original solution has exactly one transformed preimage.
For II, equality of squares allows both a^x=2x+1 and a^x=-(2x+1). The second branch lies at x<-1/2. Its function K(x)=a^x+2x+1 is continuous and strictly increasing, tends to -∞ as x→-∞, and is positive at -1/2. It has exactly one root on that negative branch.
The original equation has finitely many roots: a^x-2x-1 is strictly convex, so it has at most two zeros. II therefore has exactly one extra distinct solution and cannot have the same count.

subtopic: Modulus of a logarithm and piecewise equations
prompt_html:
What is the product of all positive real solutions of

\[\log_2\!\left((x-2)^2\right)=\left|\log_2x\right|?\]
solution_html:
The domain is \(x>0\), with \(x\ne2\).

For \(x\ge1\): the right side is \(\log_2x\), so \((x-2)^2=x\). Thus

\[x^2-5x+4=(x-1)(x-4)=0,\]

giving the valid solutions \(x=1,4\).

For \(0<x<1\): the right side is \(\log_2(1/x)\). Therefore

\[x(x-2)^2=1,\qquad (x-1)(x^2-3x+1)=0.\]

Only \(x=(3-\sqrt5)/2\) lies in this interval. The root \(1\) belongs to the previous case; \((3+\sqrt5)/2>1\) is not valid in this case.

\[\text{Product}=1\cdot4\cdot\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}=\boxed{6-2\sqrt5}.\]

prompt_html:
Consider all real ordered pairs \((x,y)\) satisfying

\[(2^x+2^y)(2^{-x}+2^{-y})=\frac92,\qquad x^2+y^2=5.\]

What is the sum of \(2^{x+y}\) over all these ordered pairs?
solution_html:
Expand the first equation to obtain

\[2+2^{x-y}+2^{y-x}=\frac92.\]

For \(t=2^{x-y}>0\), this is \(t+1/t=5/2\), so \(t=2\) or \(1/2\). Hence \(x-y=1\) or \(-1\).

Now

\[(x+y)^2=2(x^2+y^2)-(x-y)^2=10-1=9,\]

so \(x+y=3\) or \(-3\). Each sign of the sum combines with each sign of the difference to give a unique pair. The four pairs are \((2,1),(1,2),(-1,-2),(-2,-1)\).

\[\text{Required sum}=2\cdot2^3+2\cdot2^{-3}=16+\frac14=\boxed{\frac{65}{4}}.\]

prompt_html:
Let \(\alpha=2-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(\beta=2+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).

What is the complete solution set of

\[\left(x^2-4x+\frac{17}{4}\right)^{x^2-6x+8}<1?\]
solution_html:
The base \(B=(x-2)^2+1/4\) is positive for every real \(x\). Write the exponent as \(E=(x-2)(x-4)\).

For \(B^E<1\), there are exactly two possibilities: \(0<B<1\) with \(E>0\), or \(B>1\) with \(E<0\).

First possibility: \(B<1\) means \(\alpha<x<\beta\). The exponent is positive for \(x<2\) or \(x>4\). Their intersection is \(\alpha<x<2\).

Second possibility: \(B>1\) means \(x<\alpha\) or \(x>\beta\). The exponent is negative for \(2<x<4\). Their intersection is \(\beta<x<4\).

At \(x=\alpha,\beta\), the base is \(1\); at \(x=2,4\), the exponent is \(0\). Each gives value \(1\), so every endpoint is excluded.

\[\boxed{\alpha<x<2\text{ or }\beta<x<4}.\]

subtopic: Radical equations and parameter root counts
prompt_html:
For which real values of \(a\) does the equation

\[\sqrt{x+a}=x-1\]

have exactly one real solution, with that solution strictly between \(1\) and \(3\)?
solution_html:
The original equation requires \(x\geq1\). Squaring gives \(x^2-3x+1-a=0\), with roots \(x=(3\pm\sqrt{5+4a})/2\). Every root of this quadratic with \(x\geq1\) satisfies the original equation, since then \(x+a=(x-1)^2\).

At \(a=-5/4\) there is one distinct root, \(x=3/2\). If \(-5/4<a\leq-1\), both roots are admissible, including \(x=1\) at \(a=-1\). If \(a>-1\), only the larger root is admissible. It is less than \(3\) exactly when \(a<1\).

Hence the answer is the isolated value \(a=-5/4\), together with \(-1<a<1\). The endpoints \(a=-1\) and \(a=1\) fail for different reasons: two solutions, and a solution equal to \(3\), respectively.

audited_reference.concise_proof: The equation implies x−1≥0, hence x≥1. Squaring then gives a=x²−3x+1=(x−3/2)²−5/4. Conversely if x≥1 and this identity holds, then x+a=(x−1)²≥0 and its principal square root is x−1; thus the transformed equation is equivalent on x≥1. On x≥1 the quadratic decreases from −1 at x=1 to its minimum −5/4 at x=3/2, then increases strictly to infinity. Therefore a<−5/4 gives no roots; a=−5/4 gives exactly one root x=3/2; −5/4<a<−1 gives two roots in (1,2); a=−1 gives the two roots 1 and 2; and a>−1 gives exactly one admissible root on x>2. The isolated root x=3/2 lies strictly between 1 and 3. On the unique-root branch a>−1, the quadratic is strictly increasing for x>2 and equals 1 at x=3, so its root is below 3 exactly when a<1. Hence the full answer is a=−5/4 or −1<a<1. At a=1 the only admissible root is x=3 and fails strictness.

prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=x^2-4x\) and suppose \(-4<a<0\).

The curves \(y=f(|x|)\) and \(y=f(x-a)\) enclose a region of area \(3\).

What is the sum of the squares of all possible values of \(a\)?
solution_html:
The difference \(f(|x|)-f(x-a)\) is \((2a+8)x-a(a+4)\) for \(x<0\) and \(2ax-a(a+4)\) for \(x\geq0\). The common \(x^2\) terms cancel.

The intersections are \(x=a/2<0\) and \(x=(a+4)/2>0\). Between them the difference is positive. Its graph is a triangle of base \(2\) and height \(-a(a+4)\). Thus the enclosed area is \(-a(a+4)\).

Setting this equal to \(3\) gives \((a+1)(a+3)=0\). Both values lie in \((-4,0)\), so the required sum is \((-1)^2+(-3)^2=10\). Piecewise integration of the same linear difference gives the identical area.

prompt_html:
For a real parameter \(a\), consider:

P: For every \(x\in[0,1]\), there is a \(y\in[0,1]\) such that \((x-y)^2<a\).

Q: There is a \(y\in[0,1]\) such that, for every \(x\in[0,1]\), \((x-y)^2<a\).

For which values of \(a\) is P true and Q false?
solution_html:
P is true exactly when \(a>0\): choose \(y=x\). For \(a\leq0\), a nonnegative square can never be strictly smaller than \(a\).

For a fixed \(y\), the largest value of \((x-y)^2\) on \([0,1]\) is \(\max(y^2,(1-y)^2)\). Its least possible value over \(y\in[0,1]\) is \(1/4\), attained at \(y=1/2\).

Because the required comparison is strict and the endpoints are included, Q is true exactly when \(a>1/4\). Therefore P is true and Q false exactly for \(0<a\leq1/4\).

subtopic: Circle existence and strict quadrant containment
prompt_html:
For real \(a,b,c\), consider

\[x^2+y^2+2ax+2by+c=0\]

Which condition is necessary and sufficient for this equation to describe a nondegenerate circle whose entire circumference lies in the open first quadrant \(x>0\), \(y>0\)?
solution_html:
Completing the square gives centre \((-a,-b)\) and squared radius \(R^2=a^2+b^2-c\). A nondegenerate circle requires \(R>0\). Its circumference lies strictly in the first quadrant exactly when \(-a>R\) and \(-b>R\).

Thus \(a<0\), \(b<0\), \(0<R^2<a^2\) and \(0<R^2<b^2\). Substituting for \(R^2\) gives \(c>b^2\), \(c>a^2\) and \(c<a^2+b^2\), which combine to the stated condition.

Equality at the lower bound permits tangency to an axis, which the open quadrant excludes. Equality at the upper bound gives a point rather than a nondegenerate circle. A larger value gives no real circle.

On the circumference the minimum x-coordinate is −a−r and the minimum y-coordinate is −b−r, both attained at axial extreme points. Entire containment in x>0,y>0 is equivalent to −a>r and −b>r. These conditions force a<0,b<0 and, with those signs established, are equivalent to r²<min(a²,b²). Substituting r² gives a²+b²−c<min(a²,b²), or c>max(a²,b²). Together the necessary and sufficient conditions are a<0,b<0,max(a²,b²)<c<a²+b². Conversely these conditions give 0<r<min(−a,−b), hence all circumference coordinates are strictly positive. For explicit option checks, a=b=−1,c=1 gives a nondegenerate circle of radius 1 touching both axes, refuting the inclusive lower bound. With a=b=−1,c=1/2 its radius is √(3/2)>1, so it crosses the axes despite c>0. Taking a=b=−1,c=3/2 gives a valid contained circle, showing the stated strict interval is feasible.

subtopic: Closure under transformations and minimal finite sets
prompt_html:
A nonempty finite set \(S\) consists of real numbers other than \(0\) and \(1\).

For every \(x\in S\), both \(1-x\) and \(1/x\) also belong to \(S\).

What is the least possible number of elements of \(S\)?
solution_html:
The set \(\{-1,1/2,2\}\) satisfies both closure conditions, so three elements are possible. A one-element set would require simultaneously \(x=1-x\) and \(x=1/x\), which is impossible.

Suppose there were two distinct elements \(x,y\). The map \(z\mapsto1-z\) must permute them. It cannot fix both, since its only fixed point is \(1/2\), so it swaps them and \(x+y=1\).

Likewise \(z\mapsto1/z\) must permute the set. Its only allowed real fixed point is \(-1\); it cannot fix both distinct elements, so it must swap them and \(xy=1\). But two real numbers with sum \(1\) and product \(1\) would solve \(t^2-t+1=0\), whose discriminant is negative. Thus two are impossible and the minimum is three.

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Force representatives in three disjoint real intervals, then exhibit a closed three-element set.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Any nonempty closed set contains a negative number: if a chosen x<0 this is immediate; if x>1 then 1-x<0 is in the set; if 0<x<1 then 1/x>1 and 1-1/x<0 are in the set. Let a<0 be such an element. Closure gives 1-a>1 and then 1/(1-a)∈(0,1). These three elements lie in disjoint intervals and are therefore distinct, proving |S|≥3. The set {-1,2,1/2} is closed: 1-x swaps -1 and 2 and fixes 1/2, while reciprocal fixes -1 and swaps 2 and 1/2. It excludes 0 and 1, so the lower bound is attained.

prompt_html: Which one of the following is a simplification of \(\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2-2x}\) where \(x\ne 2\) and \(x\ne 0\)?
solution_html:
Factorise numerator and denominator:

\[\frac{x^2-4}{x^2-2x}=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x(x-2)}\]

Cancel \((x-2)\) (valid since \(x\ne 2\)):

\[=\frac{x+2}{x}\]

Answer: D.

At the permitted value x=4, the original expression is 3/2, whereas A, B, C and E give 0, 1/2, 1/2 and 6/5 respectively, so none of them is an identity on the stated domain.

prompt_html:
To attract more customers, a distributor provides a 20% discount on the listed price while still making a 10% profit.

If the distributor procured the product for $120, what should be the listed price of the product?
solution_html:
A 10% profit on $120 gives a selling price of

\[120\times 1.1 = 132.\]

If the listed price is \(x\), then after a 20% discount the selling price is \(0.8x\).

So

\[0.8x=132 \Rightarrow x=165.\]

Hence, the correct answer is D.

audited_reference.concise_proof: A 10% profit on the $120 cost requires a selling price S = 120 × 1.10 = $132. A 20% discount on listed price L gives S = 0.80L. Therefore L = 132/0.80 = $165. Since 0.80 is nonzero, this solution is unique. Checking forward, 80% of $165 is $132, which exceeds the cost by $12, exactly 10% of $120.

Prices must be positive. The result satisfies L = 165 > S = 132 > 120, consistent with a discount followed by a positive profit.
Division by the fixed positive multiplier 0.80 is defined and reversible, so the equation has exactly one real solution and introduces no extraneous solutions.

prompt_html:
Michael runs a book shop. For every customer who buys four books, he sells the first book at the listed price, but gives a 10% discount on each of the other three books.

Assuming each book is priced at $60, what is the net amount, in dollars, paid by a customer who buys four books?
solution_html:
The first book costs $60.

Each of the other three books gets 10% off, so each costs

\[60-0.1(60)=54.\]

Total amount paid:

\[60+3(54)=60+162=222.\]

Hence, the correct answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Percentage change multipliers and reverse percentages Deterministic category counts and weighted totals Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Find the discounted unit price, 60×0.90 = 54 dollars. Add the price of one full-price book and three discounted books: 60 + 3×54 = 222 dollars. Check that the saving from $240 is $18, matching three $6 discounts.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Each discounted book costs 60×(1−10/100) = 54 dollars. Exactly three books receive this discount, while the first costs 60 dollars. Therefore the total is 60 + 3×54 = 222 dollars. Only option D equals this amount.
domain_case_checks: The customer buys exactly four books: one at full price and three at discounted prices. These groups account for all four books exactly once.
Each percentage discount has the individual book's listed price of $60 as its base. The discounts are independent, not successive reductions applied to a running total.
All listed prices are equal, so which particular book is designated first does not affect the total.
The full-price total is $240, and the saving is exactly 3×$6 = $18. The resulting $222 is positive and lies strictly between $216, the cost if all four books were discounted, and $240.
All amounts are exact whole-dollar amounts. No rounding is needed, and there is no varying parameter or additional quantity case to investigate.

prompt_html:
In a laboratory experiment, a concentrated mixture containing 80% of a chemical is processed in a special container.

40% of the mixture is removed. The container is then filled back to full capacity with water.

What percentage of the final mixture is the chemical?
solution_html:
Assume the container initially holds 100 ml.

Then the chemical is

\[80\text{ ml}.\]

Removing 40% of the mixture leaves 60% of the chemical:

\[0.6\times 80 = 48\text{ ml}.\]

Water is then added back to restore the total volume to 100 ml, so the chemical remains 48 ml in 100 ml total.

Therefore the final percentage is 48%.

Hence, the correct answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Constituent conservation in homogeneous dilution Percentage change multipliers and reverse percentages Part-to-whole fractions and complements Aggregate rates through total quantities Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Removing 40% of a homogeneous mixture leaves 60% of its original chemical. Since refilling with pure water restores the original total but adds no chemical, multiply the original concentration by the retained fraction: 80%×0.60=48%.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let the original full quantity be V>0. Initially it contains 0.80V of chemical. Removing 40% of a homogeneous mixture removes 40% of its chemical, leaving 0.60×0.80V=0.48V. Refilling with water adds no chemical and restores the total quantity to V. The final chemical percentage is therefore (0.48V/V)×100%=48%, which is option D.
domain_case_checks: The requested quantity is the chemical percentage after refilling, not the amount removed or the concentration immediately after withdrawal.
The ordinary mixture interpretation is homogeneous, representative withdrawal: removing 40% of the mixture removes 40% of each constituent. No selective separation or chemical reaction is stated.
The phrase 'filled back to full capacity' indicates that the final total equals the original full total. Water contributes no chemical.
Bookkeeping uses one consistent additive measure of mixture amount, as in the usual ideal-mixture model. The numerical capacity and its units cancel.
The capacity V must be positive, so division by V is valid. Mixture amounts need not be integers.
The given percentages are fixed exact values, so 48% is exact and requires no rounding. There is no variable endpoint or root-selection case to resolve.

skills.definition: For a homogeneous mixture, model withdrawal of a fraction of the mixture as withdrawal of the same fraction of each constituent, and model addition of a constituent-free diluent as leaving that constituent's amount unchanged while updating the total mixture amount.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 retains 60% of the original chemical and then adds no chemical during refill. M2 treats the retained portion as still 80% chemical and the added water as 0% chemical.
skills.learning_objective: Track a constituent through proportional withdrawal and addition of pure diluent, keeping constituent amount distinct from concentration.
skills.name: Constituent conservation in homogeneous dilution

skills.definition: Identify the original quantity serving as the percentage base; represent an increase or decrease of r% by multiplication by 1+r/100 or 1-r/100 respectively; and recover an unknown original or changed quantity by reversing a nonzero multiplier.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Removing 40% gives the retained multiplier 1−0.40=0.60; M1 applies it to the chemical amount and M2 uses it for the retained mixture quantity.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the percentage base and calculate a retained amount using the correct decrease multiplier.
skills.name: Percentage change multipliers and reverse percentages

skills.definition: Express the size of a specified part as a fraction of a positive whole, and obtain the remaining fraction by subtracting from one while retaining the same reference whole.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The final chemical amount 0.48V is divided by the restored total V. The remaining original water fraction is also checked against the same reference whole.
skills.learning_objective: Use the final total mixture as the reference whole when calculating the chemical fraction.
skills.name: Part-to-whole fractions and complements

skills.definition: For several contributions measured with common numerator and denominator units, compute the overall rate as the sum of the numerator quantities divided by the sum of the denominator quantities. Derive the relevant weights or inputs first; do not average component rates unless those weights justify it. Common positive scaling of every contribution leaves the aggregate ratio unchanged.

skills.learning_objective: Combine two concentration contributions through total chemical and total mixture amounts rather than an unweighted average of concentrations.
skills.name: Aggregate rates through total quantities

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The water account gives 0.12V+0.40V=0.52V, confirming a complementary chemical fraction of 0.48. Every original option is compared with the exact result.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The retained portion has amount 0.60V and concentration 0.80; the added water has amount 0.40V and concentration 0. Their total chemical amount is 0.80(0.60V)+0(0.40V), and their combined amount is V, giving concentration 0.48.
limitations: The weights must be the actual mixture amounts; averaging 80% and 0% equally would be invalid.
This is not shorter than M1 and uses the same ideal homogeneous-mixture assumptions.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: Multiply the initial concentration by the retained fraction, with the final total restored.
conditions_checked: No numerical capacity is fixed by the question.

For any V>0, the final fraction is (0.80×0.60V)/V=0.48, proving scale independence.

prompt_html: How many 3-member teams can be formed out of 6 individuals, provided that one specific individual must be in the team?
solution_html:
Fix the required individual in the team. Then choose the remaining 2 members from the other 5 people:

\[\binom{5}{2}=10.\]

Hence, the correct answer is B.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Count fixed-size unordered subsets Division by uniform representation multiplicity Count a finite set through its complement

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Include the specified individual, leaving two members to choose from the other five. Since teams are unordered, use C(5,2) = 5×4/2 = 10. The denominator 2 removes the two orders of each chosen pair.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Include the specified individual first. Every permitted team then corresponds uniquely to an unordered pair chosen from the other five individuals. There are C(5,2) = 5×4/2 = 10 such pairs: the division by 2 accounts for the two orders of each pair. Thus there are exactly 10 teams, which is option B.
domain_case_checks: The six individuals are distinct, and a team contains three distinct people; nobody can occupy two membership places.
The compulsory individual is fixed in advance. There is no factor of 6 for choosing that person.
Including the compulsory individual leaves five available people and two remaining membership places. The selection is feasible because 0 ≤ 2 ≤ 5.
No roles or ordering are specified within a team. Reversing the order of the two chosen teammates does not create a different team.

Removing the compulsory individual from any valid team produces exactly one pair from the other five people; adding that individual to any such pair produces a valid team. This proves completeness and absence of duplication.
For the complement method, all three-person teams split exhaustively and disjointly into those containing the compulsory individual and those omitting that individual.
The answer is an exact integer count of teams. No approximation, rounding, or continuous endpoint analysis is needed.

skills.definition: For n distinct objects and an integer r with 0≤r≤n, count unordered r-element selections using C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n−r)!), adjusting the pool and quota for forced or excluded objects and including the endpoint cases r=0 and r=n.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 includes the compulsory individual and chooses two additional members from five. M2 counts all triples and the triples omitting the compulsory person using binomial coefficients.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the free selection pool and required number of additional members, then use a binomial coefficient without counting different orders separately.
skills.name: Count fixed-size unordered subsets

skills.definition: When a finite set of representations maps onto the intended objects and every object has exactly k representations, with k a positive integer, count the objects by dividing the number of representations by k. Justify coverage, constant multiplicity and which representations describe the same object.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The ordered choices of the two freely selected teammates number 5×4. Each valid team has exactly two such representations, obtained by reversing those teammates.
skills.learning_objective: Identify a constant representation multiplicity and divide by it exactly once.
skills.name: Division by uniform representation multiplicity

skills.definition: For an admissible subset A of a finite universe U, use |A|=|U|−|U\A| after identifying all forbidden elements, avoiding omissions and duplicate subtraction.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 subtracts the C(5,3) teams omitting the compulsory person from the C(6,3) unrestricted teams.
skills.learning_objective: Count a constrained finite set by subtracting an exhaustively identified forbidden subset from an easy total.
skills.name: Count a finite set through its complement

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: There are C(6,3) = 20 unrestricted teams. Exactly C(5,3) = 10 omit the compulsory individual. These forbidden teams form the complete complement of the valid teams, so the required count is 20−10 = 10.
limitations: It requires two combination counts and a subtraction, so it is longer than the direct reduced-pool method here.
Subtracting only some teams that omit the compulsory individual would not establish the count.
useful_alternatives.method: Count all three-person teams and subtract those omitting the specified individual.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the unrestricted universe and its forbidden subset are easier to count than the valid configurations directly, or as a check on the direct method.

prompt_html:
A box contains 30 balls, of which 8 are black, 10 are green, and 12 are yellow.

If two balls are drawn at random, what is the probability that the two balls drawn are not both green?
solution_html:
The probability of not getting both green balls is

\[1-P(\text{both green}).\]

The number of ways to choose 2 green balls from 10 is

\[\binom{10}{2}=45,\]

and the total number of ways to choose any 2 balls from 30 is

\[\binom{30}{2}=435.\]

So

\[P(\text{both green})=\frac{45}{435}=\frac{3}{29}.\]

Hence, the required probability is

\[1-\frac{3}{29}=\frac{26}{29}.\]

So the correct answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Model finite random-experiment events Negate conjunctions and disjunctions correctly Update counts for sampling without replacement Condition on the correct event and denominator Favourable-over-total probability ratio Multiplication rule for sequential probability Probability through a complementary event Exact surd and rational arithmetic Add probabilities of mutually exclusive events

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the complement of “both green”. With two distinct balls selected, P(both green)=(10/30)(9/29)=3/29. Subtract this from 1 to obtain 26/29. This is already the shortest clear ordinary method; a longer direct enumeration is not needed as a baseline.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Drawing two balls means selecting two distinct balls from the box, without returning a ball between selections. The probability that both are green is (10/30)(9/29)=3/29. “Not both green” is the complementary event, so its probability is 1−3/29=26/29. This is option D.
domain_case_checks: The stated counts are positive integers and sum to 8+10+12=30. There are enough balls for a two-ball selection.

Use the ordinary meaning of drawing two balls from the box: a sample of two distinct balls. Drawing simultaneously or successively without returning the first ball gives the same event probability. A with-replacement experiment would require a different sampling instruction.
The first-green event has probability 10/30>0, so conditioning on it is valid. After that event, there are 9 green balls among 29 remaining balls; both probability denominators are positive.
The draws are not independent: the conditional second-green probability 9/29 differs from the initial green proportion 10/30.
The requested event includes zero green balls and exactly one green ball. Its only excluded case is two green balls, so complementing that case is exhaustive and introduces no overlap.
The 8 black and 12 yellow balls may be grouped as 20 non-green balls because the event distinguishes only green from non-green.
Both 3/29 and 26/29 lie strictly between 0 and 1. No approximation or rounding is required.

skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 identifies the event as all patterns except GG; T1 partitions it into first non-green, or first green followed by non-green.

prompt_html:
The numbers of defects in eight of the nine batches of batteries are 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 3, 7, 8.

If the median defects per batch for all nine batches equals the arithmetic mean defects per batch for all nine batches, which of the following could be the number of defects in the ninth batch?
solution_html:
Arrange the eight known values in ascending order:

\[2,3,3,4,5,6,7,8.\]

Let the ninth value be \(x\).

The total of the eight known values is

\[2+4+6+5+3+3+7+8=38.\]

If \(x=2,3,\) or \(4\), then the median of the nine values is 4, so the mean would also have to be 4. That would require

\[\frac{38+x}{9}=4 \Rightarrow 38+x=36,\]

which is impossible.

If \(x=7\), then the ordered list becomes

\[2,3,3,4,5,6,7,7,8,\]

so the median is 5. The mean is then

\[\frac{38+7}{9}=\frac{45}{9}=5.\]

Thus the condition is satisfied when \(x=7\).

Hence, the correct answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Median from ordered positions and frequencies Arithmetic mean and recovery of a total Update an arithmetic mean after membership changes Substitute or independently check a proposed result Existential possibility and admissible witness construction Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Solve one-variable linear equations

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Sort the known counts as 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and find their total, 38. For each of the first three options, the added count is at most 4, so the median is 4; each resulting total exceeds 36, so its mean exceeds 4. For the remaining option, insert 7: the fifth value is 5 and the total is 45, giving mean 5. This grouped option check is shorter than solving an unrestricted parameter problem.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The eight known counts sum to 38 and, in order, are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Adding any of 2, 3 or 4 makes the fifth ordered value 4. Their respective totals are 40, 41 and 42, all greater than 9×4=36, so none has mean 4. Adding 7 gives 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, whose median is 5 and whose mean is (38+7)/9=5. Thus exactly option D works.
domain_case_checks: The missing count x is a nonnegative integer because defects are counted. No upper bound on a batch's defect count is supplied or needed. Repeated counts are permitted.
All nine batches contribute equally to the arithmetic mean, so its denominator is 9, not 8. The known total is 38.
The median of nine counts is their fifth ordered value. It is neither the fifth value in the printed order nor the average of the middle two values of the original eight-count list.
For every integer x with 0≤x≤4, the fifth ordered value is 4, including x=0 and x=4. For every integer x≥5, it is 5, including x=5.

These two cases exhaust the count domain: there is no integer strictly between 4 and 5. Equality of mean and median gives x=-2 in the first case, which is inadmissible, and x=7 in the second case, which is admissible. Thus 7 is also the only solution over all nonnegative integer counts, not merely the only listed solution.
Multiplication by the positive constant 9 preserves equivalence. All calculations are exact; no approximation or rounding is required.
Every original option is checked independently. Selection does not rely on assuming that the question must have exactly one correct option.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The completed nine-count list uses its fifth ordered value. Insertion of a count at most 4 gives median 4; insertion of a count at least 5 gives median 5.

prompt_html:
The heights of seven students are shown below.

Student 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
Height 4 ft 3 in 4 ft 6 in 4 ft 9 in 4 ft 9 in 5 ft 0 in 5 ft 9 in 5 ft 9 in

What is the range of the heights of the seven students, in inches?
solution_html:
The greatest height is \(5\) ft \(9\) in:

\[ 5(12)+9=69\text{ inches}. \]

The smallest height is \(4\) ft \(3\) in:

\[ 4(12)+3=51\text{ inches}. \]

Therefore

\[ 69-51=18\text{ inches}. \]

The correct answer is C.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Model constraints from mean, median and range Exact unit conversion by cancellation

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Read the minimum and maximum heights, subtract them directly in mixed units, and convert the difference: (5 − 4) × 12 + (9 − 3) = 18 inches. Only the two extrema need arithmetic.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The shortest height is 4 ft 3 in and the tallest is 5 ft 9 in. Their difference is 1 ft 6 in, which equals 12 + 6 = 18 inches. Thus the range is 18 inches, option C.
domain_case_checks: The task concerns the seven fixed heights in the table and asks for their statistical range, expressed in inches.
Every listed height is at least 4 ft 3 in and at most 5 ft 9 in, and both endpoint heights occur. These are therefore the actual minimum and maximum, not merely bounds.
Students 6 and 7 share the maximum height. Repetition does not change the maximum value or the range.
The inch components satisfy 0 ≤ inches < 12. Since 9 ≥ 3, subtracting the mixed measurements requires no borrowing: the difference is 1 ft 6 in.
Using maximum minus minimum gives a nonnegative difference. The exact conversion 1 ft = 12 in produces an exact answer; no approximation or rounding is needed.

skills.definition: For a nonempty finite list of real data, order its entries and translate an arithmetic mean into a total, a median into the appropriate central entry or central-pair average, and a range into maximum minus minimum, respecting multiplicities and stated restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The range component of this registered skill is used: all seven entries are checked to identify the minimum 4 ft 3 in and maximum 5 ft 9 in, and their difference is requested. Mean and median are not needed here.
skills.learning_objective: Translate mean, median and range statements into constraints on an ordered finite list.
skills.name: Model constraints from mean, median and range

skills.definition: Convert a measured quantity by multiplying by an exact conversion ratio equal to one, orienting the ratio so the source unit cancels and the required target unit remains.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 converts the one-foot component using 1 ft × (12 in/ft) = 12 in, then adds 6 in. M2 converts the endpoint heights to 51 in and 69 in before subtraction.
skills.learning_objective: Orient and apply an exact conversion factor so that the original units cancel.
skills.name: Exact unit conversion by cancellation

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Express the two extrema in one unit first: minimum = 4 × 12 + 3 = 51 inches and maximum = 5 × 12 + 9 = 69 inches. Their difference is 18 inches. This normalizes units before subtraction rather than subtracting mixed measurements first.
limitations: It uses slightly larger intermediate numbers than M1.
It does not bypass the meaning of range or exact unit conversion.
Converting every table entry is unnecessary.
useful_alternatives.method: Convert the endpoint heights to inches before subtracting.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when a learner prefers a single unit throughout, or when mixed-unit subtraction would otherwise require borrowing.

prompt_html: According to the histogram below, what is the modal score for 71 students?
solution_html:
The mode is the score that occurs most frequently.

From the histogram, the greatest frequency is 12 students, and this occurs at score 5.

So the modal score is 5.

Hence, the correct answer is B.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Read the bar heights as frequencies, identify the unique highest bar, and report its horizontal score label. Check that no other bar ties it and that the displayed frequencies agree with the stated total of 71.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The bar for score 5 represents 12 students. Every other bar is lower; the next highest is score 6 with 11 students. Therefore 5 is the unique modal score. The plotted frequencies sum to 3+4+6+7+8+12+11+9+6+3+2=71, consistent with the stated sample size.
domain_case_checks: The task concerns a fixed sample of 71 students, not a freely varying sample size.
The graph displays individual score labels, so the answer is a score rather than a grouped modal interval.
The vertical axis gives numbers of students directly. No frequency-density conversion is required.
All read frequencies are nonnegative integers and sum to 71.
The maximum frequency is attained only at score 5, so there is no tied-mode case.
The requested unit is score, not students. The answer is exact and requires no rounding.

prompt_html:
The diagram shows an equilateral triangle divided into nine smaller equilateral triangles, with two additional lines.

What fraction of the large triangle is shaded?
solution_html:
Each shaded triangle is half of a parallelogram made from 4 of the smallest equilateral triangles.

So each shaded triangle has the area of 2 small triangles.

There are 2 such shaded triangles, so shaded area = area of 4 small triangles.

The large triangle is made of 9 equal small triangles.

Hence the shaded fraction is

\[\frac{4}{9}.\]

Answer: E
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Exact data versus apparent diagram scale Area accounting through geometric dissection Basic planar area formulas Part-to-whole fractions and complements Area scaling for similar figures Similarity, scale and preserved ratios Use geometric reflection or rotational symmetry

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Measure areas in units of one original equilateral cell. Its area is u=bt/2, where b and t are its base and perpendicular height. The upper shaded triangle has base b and height 2t, so its area is 2u. The lower shaded triangle has base 2b and height t, so its area is also 2u. Add their areas and divide by the nine-cell whole: 4u/(9u)=4/9.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Use the point labels in the diagram description. Let one original grid triangle have base b, perpendicular height t and area u=bt/2. The nine cells are congruent: adjoining equilateral cells share complete sides, so equality of side length propagates across the grid. Triangle BPQ has base PQ=b and perpendicular height 2t, hence area 2u. Triangle BVT has base BV=2b and perpendicular height t, hence area 2u. These are the two shaded components and have disjoint interiors. The shaded fraction is therefore (2u+2u)/(9u)=4/9, which is option E.
domain_case_checks: The large triangle and every original cell are nondegenerate, so b>0, t>0 and u>0.
The original nine equilateral cells are congruent by propagation across shared complete sides. Equal areas are therefore justified independently of apparent drawing scale.
The three grid rows have equal perpendicular spacing t. Thus the heights 2t and t used with bases PQ and BV are perpendicular heights, not sloping side lengths.
BPQ and BVT have disjoint interiors and share only B. Both visible shaded components are included, so adding their areas neither omits nor double-counts shading.
For the complement method, APQ, BQT and CVT are exactly the three unshaded components. The corner triangles have positive length scale 1/3, so their area scale is 1/9.
For the reflection method, equilateral-triangle symmetry interchanges A and C while fixing B; the subdivision points then satisfy P↔V and Q↔T.
The clipped bottom outline does not require an estimated length or an assumed drawing scale: the stated subdivision and visible grid determine the base subdivision.
The denominator 9u is positive. The requested ratio is dimensionless and exact; no approximation, rounding or root selection is involved.

skills.definition: Distinguish labelled or logically specified geometric relations from lengths, angles or equalities suggested only by a drawing's appearance.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The solution identifies the shaded boundaries and derives equal cell sizes from the stated equilateral cells and their shared complete edges, rather than measuring the raster.
skills.learning_objective: Extract exact grid relationships and shading boundaries without relying on apparent drawing scale.
skills.name: Exact data versus apparent diagram scale

skills.definition: Justify a finite, non-overlapping partition of a planar region and express the whole area as a sum, or an unknown component as a difference, without omissions or double counting.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 adds the two shaded triangles; M2 subtracts the three unshaded triangles; M3 verifies that reflection pairs the two shaded components.
skills.learning_objective: Account for every shaded or unshaded component exactly once before combining its area.
skills.name: Area accounting through geometric dissection

skills.definition: Calculate the areas of triangles, rectangles and squares from valid dimensions, using perpendicular height for a triangle and squared side length for a square.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The shaded triangles have dimensions (b,2t) and (2b,t), giving 2u each. M2 also compares BQT with ABC using their common perpendicular height to AC.
skills.learning_objective: Compare triangle areas through the correct bases and perpendicular heights.
skills.name: Basic planar area formulas

skills.definition: Express the size of a specified part as a fraction of a positive whole, and obtain the remaining fraction by subtracting from one while retaining the same reference whole.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 divides 4u by 9u. M2 takes the complement of the unshaded fraction. M3 doubles one shaded area before dividing by the whole.
skills.learning_objective: Use the entire large triangle as the reference whole when reporting the shaded fraction.
skills.name: Part-to-whole fractions and complements

skills.definition: For similar plane figures with positive finite areas and positive length scale factor k, use the area ratio k² and recover the length scale from a positive area ratio.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 assigns area K/9 to each corner triangle because its positive length scale relative to ABC is 1/3.
skills.learning_objective: Square a justified length scale when comparing areas of similar triangles.
skills.name: Area scaling for similar figures

skills.definition: Use justified similarity to transfer scale and side ratios between figures.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 identifies APQ and CVT as equilateral triangles similar to ABC, with corresponding side ratio 1/3.
skills.learning_objective: Establish the similarity and corresponding length scale before applying area scaling.
skills.name: Similarity, scale and preserved ratios

skills.definition: Use justified geometric reflection or rotation to preserve distances and reduce equivalent cases.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M3 uses reflection in the angle bisector at B to exchange BPQ with BVT after checking the vertex correspondence.
skills.learning_objective: Verify a reflection of the complete configuration before using it to equate component areas.
skills.name: Use geometric reflection or rotational symmetry

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The unshaded region consists of APQ and CVT, each of area K/9 by similarity, and BQT, of area K/3 by a shared-height comparison with ABC. Subtracting gives shaded fraction 1-(1/9+1/3+1/9)=4/9.
limitations: It accounts for three components rather than the two in M1.
The shared height for BQT must be taken perpendicular to AC.
The corner length ratio must be squared when converted to an area ratio.
useful_alternatives.method: Calculate the unshaded fraction and take its complement.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the three unshaded triangles are easier to identify than the tilted shaded regions, or for practising area scaling and shared-height comparisons.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Reflection in the angle bisector at B exchanges A and C, hence P and V and Q and T. It maps BPQ onto BVT. One shaded triangle has area 2u, so both together have area 4u out of 9u.
limitations: The correct axis and point correspondence must be justified.
This avoids only one elementary area comparison and is not a material shortcut relative to M1.
useful_alternatives.method: Use reflection to equate the two shaded areas, then compute one and double it.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the bottom-left angle-bisector symmetry is recognised and can be checked exactly.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 already measures areas in units of a single original cell.
conditions_checked: The question asks for an area ratio, not a fixed dimensional area.
Dividing every area by the same positive cell area leaves the ratio unchanged.
No vertex or segment endpoint is moved.
limitations: Normalisation does not permit changing the grid or the shaded boundaries.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: SC03 — Choose Your Own Numbers: take one cell's area as one area unit. The shaded areas are then two units each and the whole has nine units.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful normalisation, but it is already the ordinary baseline and earns no additional shortcut badge.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Unnecessary side-length, altitude and square-root calculations.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 obtains both shaded areas through one-line base-height comparisons.
conditions_checked: The justified reflection axis is the angle bisector at B.
Reflection exchanges A with C, P with V and Q with T.
It therefore exchanges shaded triangles BPQ and BVT.
Vertical symmetry about the altitude from A is not being assumed.
limitations: Checking the point correspondence adds work.

shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Valid and pedagogically useful, but not a material saving relative to M1.
