prompt_html:
Consider the following attempt to solve the equation

\[4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5.\]

The steps have been numbered for reference.

I \[4x\sqrt{2x-1}=5(2x-1)\]

II Dividing by \(2x-1\) and then squaring gives a quadratic equation.

III Solving this quadratic gives \(x=\frac58\) or \(x=\frac52\).

IV Hence the solutions of the original equation are \(x=\frac58\) and \(x=\frac52\).

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.html: Only one of \(x=\frac58\) and \(x=\frac52\) is correct, and the error arises as a result of step II.
options.label: B

options.html: Only one of \(x=\frac58\) and \(x=\frac52\) is correct, and the error arises as a result of step III.
options.label: C

options.html: Both \(x=\frac58\) and \(x=\frac52\) are correct, but there is another solution lost as a result of step II.
options.label: D

options.html: There is another solution, but it is lost as a result of step IV.
options.label: E

solution_html: The real domain is \(x\ge\tfrac12\). The endpoint \(x=\tfrac12\) gives \(0=0\), but step II divides by \(2x-1\) and discards it. For \(x>\tfrac12\), the divided equation has positive sides, so squaring is reversible and gives \((8x-5)(2x-5)=0\). Both roots \(\tfrac58\) and \(\tfrac52\) satisfy the original equation. The complete set is \(\{\tfrac12,\tfrac58,\tfrac52\}\), and the missing root was lost in II. Hence D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Domain restrictions and reversible operations Cancellation of common nonzero factors Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Locate the first unsupported implication in a proof Signs of real quantities and squares Factorisation and algebraic expansion Solving quadratics and checking roots Zero-product property and factor roots Substitute or independently check a proposed result Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Audit the given steps rather than restart with an unnecessarily long solution. Establish x ≥ 1/2, check the zero of the divisor 2x−1 in the original equation, and verify the two reported roots. To certify completeness and distinguish division from squaring, inspect the x > 1/2 branch: the divided equation has positive sides and its squared quadratic factors as (8x−5)(2x−5) = 0. The only omitted case is x = 1/2, excluded in II.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The real domain is x ≥ 1/2. At x = 1/2, both sides of the original equation are zero, so this is a solution. Step II divides by 2x−1 and therefore discards it. For x > 1/2, the divided equation is 4x/√(2x−1) = 5. Both sides are positive, so squaring is reversible and gives 16x²−50x+25 = (8x−5)(2x−5) = 0. Its roots are exactly 5/8 and 5/2, both in this branch. Direct substitution into the original equation gives equal sides of 5/4 and 20 respectively. Thus both reported roots are correct, but the additional solution x = 1/2 was lost in step II. Only D is true.
domain_case_checks: For real x, √(2x−1) is defined exactly when x ≥ 1/2. The endpoint is included, and no integer restriction is stated.
The original equation contains no denominator. At x = 1/2 it is defined and reads 0 = 0; this value must not be excluded merely because a later divided equation is undefined there.
The cases x = 1/2 and x > 1/2 are disjoint and exhaust the original real domain. The divisor 2x−1 vanishes only in the first case.
On x > 1/2, both 2x−1 and its square root are positive. Division is valid, and 4x/√(2x−1) and 5 are positive, so squaring introduces no extraneous solutions in this branch.
The quadratic factors as (8x−5)(2x−5). Its two distinct roots, 5/8 and 5/2, both exceed 1/2. Together with the separately retained endpoint, these give all three solutions.

Step I is an exact factorisation, and step III correctly solves the restricted quadratic. Step IV makes an incomplete final claim, but the missing solution had already been excluded by the division in step II.
All results are exact fractions; no approximation or rounding is required. The option audit establishes uniqueness rather than assuming it.

skills.definition: Identify expression domains and conditions under which algebraic transformations preserve equivalence.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The original domain includes x = 1/2; the divided equation instead requires x > 1/2. M1 checks when squaring is reversible, and M2 carries the substitution domain t ≥ 0.
skills.learning_objective: Retain the original radical domain and distinguish it from restrictions introduced by division or a change of variable.
skills.name: Domain restrictions and reversible operations

skills.definition: Cancel or divide by an expression only when it is a common multiplicative factor and is known to be nonzero; retain restrictions from the original expression and do not cancel individual addends across addition or subtraction.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Division by 2x−1 is valid only after retaining x = 1/2 separately. M2 does not divide in its own derivation, but still uses this condition to identify why the supplied step II loses t = 0.
skills.learning_objective: Identify every zero of a proposed divisor and explain why unconditional division can discard a valid root.
skills.name: Cancellation of common nonzero factors

skills.definition: Organize exhaustive and disjoint cases, including equality, degeneracies and exceptional values.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 combines the endpoint x = 1/2 with the branch x > 1/2. M2 retains all three nonnegative factor-zero cases, including t = 0.
skills.learning_objective: Account for the exceptional zero case and combine it with the remaining cases without losing or duplicating solutions.
skills.name: Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases

skills.definition: Locate the first unjustified proof step while retaining valid local statements and checking their dependencies.
skills.evidence_in_solution: I is valid, II first excludes a genuine root, III correctly solves the restricted quadratic, and IV inherits the earlier omission.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish the operation that first changes a solution set from a later incomplete conclusion.
skills.name: Locate the first unsupported implication in a proof

skills.definition: Determine signs of real expressions, squares and products, including zero cases.
skills.evidence_in_solution: For x > 1/2, both sides of 4x/√(2x−1) = 5 are positive. This proves that the squaring in II adds no roots on that branch. M2 avoids squaring an equation.
skills.learning_objective: Use established signs to decide whether squaring preserves equivalence rather than assuming it must introduce roots.
skills.name: Signs of real quantities and squares

skills.definition: Expand, factor and collect algebraic expressions while retaining equality.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The audit checks 10x−5 = 5(2x−1) and 16x²−50x+25 = (8x−5)(2x−5). M2 factors 2t³−5t²+2t as t(2t−1)(t−2).
skills.learning_objective: Verify the relevant factorisations exactly without changing the equation.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

skills.definition: Solve quadratic equations and verify allowed real roots, including repeated roots.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The restricted quadratic has exactly the roots 5/8 and 5/2. In M2, the quadratic factor 2t²−5t+2 gives t = 1/2 and t = 2, both permitted.
skills.learning_objective: Recover and check all roots of a factored quadratic within the current domain.
skills.name: Solving quadratics and checking roots

skills.definition: Over the real numbers, use ab = 0 if and only if a = 0 or b = 0, extending to finite products; apply it only when the complete product is equal to zero.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The factors of (8x−5)(2x−5) = 0 exhaust the nonzero branch. The product t(2t−1)(t−2) = 0 in M2 retains the otherwise omitted zero factor.
skills.learning_objective: Extract every factor-zero solution after setting the complete product equal to zero.
skills.name: Zero-product property and factor roots

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 substitutes x = 1/2, 5/8 and 5/2 into the original equation. M2 instead derives the complete set through reversible substitution and need not repeat those numerical checks.
skills.learning_objective: Check reported and potentially omitted roots in the original equation, not merely in a transformed equation.
skills.name: Substitute or independently check a proposed result

skills.definition: Choose an algebraic replacement, carry its domain and reverse it without losing or adding solutions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 uses t = √(2x−1) ≥ 0 with the inverse x = (t²+1)/2, a bijection between the permitted domains.
skills.learning_objective: Replace a principal radical by a nonnegative variable and reverse the substitution for every permitted root.
skills.name: Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The bijection t = √(2x−1) ≥ 0, x = (t²+1)/2 turns the equation into t(2t−1)(t−2) = 0. Its permitted roots t = 0, 1/2, 2 map to x = 1/2, 5/8, 5/2. Dividing by 2x−1 = t² in the supplied attempt discards the t = 0 root.
limitations: The condition t ≥ 0 is essential because t represents a principal square root.
This is an alternative complete derivation, not a material shortcut over the short ordinary audit.
The original numbered steps must still be inspected to attribute the missing root to II.
useful_alternatives.method: Replace the radical by a nonnegative variable and factor without dividing by that variable.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when a candidate prefers a reversible polynomial reformulation that keeps the endpoint visible and avoids both variable division and squaring an equation.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: test the zero of the divisor and verify the reported roots.
conditions_checked: x is an unknown, not a freely adjustable parameter.
Nevertheless, x = 1/2 is a legal candidate and supplies a witness against the claimed completeness of the reported set.
The candidate satisfies the original domain and equation.
limitations: One additional solution disproves the reported set's completeness but does not by itself prove the full solution set.
The nonzero branch still needs checking.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose Your Own Numbers: test the value forced by 2x−1 = 0 as a legal omitted-root witness, rather than choose an arbitrary convenient x.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This targeted value check is already M1, so it earns no additional shortcut saving.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Avoids an unstructured search for a missing root, but M1 already avoids that search.

prompt_html: On a standard die one of the dots is removed at random with each dot equally likely to be chosen. The die is then rolled. What is the probability that the top face has an odd number of dots?
solution_html: There are \(1+2+3+4+5+6=21\) equally selectable dots. The originally odd faces contain \(1+3+5=9\) dots; removing one leaves two odd faces. The originally even faces contain \(2+4+6=12\) dots; removing one leaves four odd faces. All six physical faces remain equally likely on the roll, including a possible blank face, and zero is even. Thus\[P(\text{odd top})=\frac9{21}\frac26+\frac{12}{21}\frac46=\frac{66}{126}=\frac{11}{21}.\]The answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity Model finite random-experiment events Condition on the correct event and denominator Multiplication rule for sequential probability Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities Exact surd and rational arithmetic

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Group removals by the original parity of the affected face. There are 9 dots on odd faces and 12 on even faces, out of 21. The two cases leave respectively 2 and 4 odd faces out of 6. Apply total probability: (9/21)(2/6)+(12/21)(4/6)=11/21.
audited_reference.concise_proof: There are 1+2+3+4+5+6=21 equally selectable dots. Of these, 1+3+5=9 lie on originally odd faces and 2+4+6=12 lie on originally even faces. Removing a dot from an odd face leaves two odd faces; removing one from an even face leaves four odd faces. Under the standard fair-die model, the requested probability is therefore (9/21)(2/6)+(12/21)(4/6)=66/126=11/21.
domain_case_checks: Use the usual standard-die probability model: six equally likely physical faces originally carrying 1 through 6 dots. Removing a marking changes its displayed count, not the rolling probabilities.
The first selection is uniform over the 21 original dots, not over the six faces. The subsequent roll is uniform over six faces, not over the remaining 20 dots.
Removal from an originally odd face and removal from an originally even face are disjoint and exhaustive cases. Their probabilities are 9/21 and 12/21, which are positive and sum to 1.
Exactly one face changes parity. In particular, removing the sole dot from the one-dot face produces zero, which is even. The blank face remains one of the six possible top faces.
Two faces can have the same displayed count after removal, but they remain distinct equally likely physical faces. Distinct displayed values must not replace physical faces in the sample space.
The requested probability averages over both stages. The rolled physical face is independent of the selected dot, but final oddness depends on which face lost a dot.

The conditional odd-top probabilities are 1/3 and 2/3. Their positively weighted average 11/21 lies strictly between them. The complementary even-top probability is 10/21, and the two probabilities sum to 1.
All denominators are positive sample-space sizes. The result is an exact, dimensionless probability; no rounding is needed.

skills.definition: Count equally likely probabilistic outcomes with the correct order and multiplicity.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 counts 21 individual dots and their 9/12 grouping. S2 retains six physical faces. S5-S6 count distinct removed-dot/top-face pairs without merging equal displayed values.
skills.learning_objective: Identify whether dots or faces are equally likely and retain multiplicities when grouping outcomes.
skills.name: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity

skills.definition: Translate a verbal rule for a finite random experiment into an event or ordered outcome patterns, preserving positional restrictions, conjunctions and alternatives, and determine which outcomes satisfy the rule.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 translates a single deletion into the correct parity change. S6 identifies exactly when an originally odd or even top face ends with an odd count.
skills.learning_objective: Translate one-dot deletion into the correct odd-top event while retaining distinct physical faces.
skills.name: Model finite random-experiment events

skills.definition: Identify the conditioning event and compute conditional probability with a nonzero evidence probability.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 calculates 2/6 and 4/6 conditional on the removal-parity case. M2 instead counts successful elementary pairs without calculating these conditional odd-top probabilities.
skills.learning_objective: Calculate the odd-top probability within a specified removal case using the unchanged six-face denominator.
skills.name: Condition on the correct event and denominator

skills.definition: Compute a sequential joint probability using P(A intersection B)=P(A)P(B given A), extending through further stages when the relevant conditional probabilities are defined and treating zero-probability branches separately.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 multiplies each removal probability by its conditional odd-top probability. S5 verifies that each removed-dot/top-face pair has probability (1/21)(1/6).
skills.learning_objective: Multiply the probabilities for successive requirements to obtain a joint branch probability.
skills.name: Multiplication rule for sequential probability

skills.definition: Partition into disjoint exhaustive cases and sum correctly weighted conditional probabilities.

prompt_html: A traffic light runs repeatedly through the following cycle: green for 30 seconds, then yellow for 3 seconds, and then red for 30 seconds. Leah picks a random three-second time interval to watch the light. What is the probability that the color changes while she is watching?
solution_html:
The traffic light has a 63-second cycle (30 + 3 + 30 = 63). Taking \(t=0\) as the moment it turns green, the color changes at \(t=30,\;33,\;63\).

Leah's 3-second watching interval will include a change exactly when its start time lies in the intervals \([27,30],\;[30,33],\;[60,63]\), which together have total length \(3+3+3=9\) seconds.

Thus the probability is \(\dfrac{9}{63}=\dfrac{1}{7}\), so the correct answer is (D).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Uniform-phase probability for a repeating process Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Decompose a favorable event into disjoint components Interval length and proportion Part-to-whole fractions and complements

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Work with one 63-second cycle. Each of its three colour changes is observed by starts in the three seconds immediately preceding it. Include the red-to-green change, check that these start-time intervals have no positive-length overlap, and divide their total length by 63.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Use the usual continuous-time interpretation of a random interval: its starting phase t is uniform over one complete cycle of length 30+3+30=63 seconds. Taking the start of green as time 0, the next changes occur at 30, 33 and 63 seconds. Apart from endpoint cases, a three-second watch contains a change exactly when t lies in (27,30), (30,33) or (60,63). These intervals are disjoint and have total length 9 seconds. Thus the probability is 9/63=1/7, which is D. Whether changes exactly at the observation endpoints count makes no difference, since those finitely many starting phases have probability zero.
domain_case_checks: Random observation time is interpreted conventionally as a continuous uniform starting phase over the 63-second cycle. This does not require a uniform distribution over an unbounded timeline, and periodicity alone would not justify a different sampling distribution.
The integer durations do not restrict the starting time to whole seconds or to a prescribed grid of three-second slots.
The requested event is at least one colour change. All three transition types must be included: green to yellow, yellow to red, and red to green.
The observation may cross the chosen cycle boundary. Starts between 60 and 63 seconds see the red-to-green transition at 63 seconds; the observation is not truncated there.
Successive changes are separated by 3, 30 and 30 seconds cyclically. Consequently, the three preceding start-time windows of length 3 have no positive-length overlap.

A three-second observation can include both changes bordering yellow only in an endpoint case. Such isolated starting phases have probability zero, so they neither change the answer nor create positive-probability double counting.
The complementary no-change start lengths are 27 seconds in green, zero seconds of positive length in yellow, and 27 seconds in red. Their total 54 plus the favourable length 9 equals 63.
The denominator 63 is positive. Numerator and denominator are both measured in seconds, giving a dimensionless probability strictly between 0 and 1. The result is exact; no rounding is required.

skills.definition: For an observation beginning at a uniformly sampled phase of a deterministic cycle with known period T>0, represent the start by a real variable in [0,T) and calculate event probabilities from favourable phase lengths divided by T. Distinguish the uniform-sampling assumption from periodicity itself.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 represents the start by a uniform real phase in a 63-second cycle. S4 and S5 use that common sample space to turn start-time lengths into probabilities.
skills.learning_objective: Represent a random observation start by a uniform phase in one full cycle and use time lengths, rather than equal weights for colour names, to determine probabilities.
skills.name: Uniform-phase probability for a repeating process

skills.definition: Manipulate and solve inequalities while preserving direction, sign conditions and solution sets.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 converts t<c<t+3 into the equivalent interval c-3<t<c for the observation start.
skills.learning_objective: Translate a transition lying inside a fixed-duration observation into the corresponding interval of starting times.
skills.name: Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets

skills.definition: Express a probability event or measurable favorable region as a disjoint union and add the component probabilities or measures, ensuring completeness and avoiding double counting.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 and S3 include all three transition windows and check their disjointness. S5 instead decomposes the no-change event by its constant-colour run.
skills.learning_objective: Identify every successful start-time component, including the cyclic boundary, and check overlap before adding lengths.
skills.name: Decompose a favorable event into disjoint components

skills.definition: For a finite union of disjoint real intervals inside an interval of positive length, sum the component lengths and divide by the ambient length when a proportion is requested; inclusion or exclusion of finitely many endpoints does not change the length.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 obtains total favourable length 3+3+3=9, S4 forms 9/63, and S5 obtains complementary length 27+0+27=54. Isolated endpoints contribute no length.
skills.learning_objective: Calculate the proportion occupied by a finite union of time intervals while handling isolated endpoints correctly.
skills.name: Interval length and proportion

skills.definition: Express the size of a specified part as a fraction of a positive whole, and obtain the remaining fraction by subtracting from one while retaining the same reference whole.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S5 subtracts the no-change proportion 54/63 from 1, retaining the full cycle as the reference whole.
skills.learning_objective: Find the change probability from its no-change complement without changing the sample-space denominator.
skills.name: Part-to-whole fractions and complements

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: A no-change observation must fit within one constant-colour run. The available start lengths are 30-3=27, 3-3=0 and 30-3=27 seconds. Therefore P(change)=1-(27+0+27)/63=1/7.
limitations: It uses the same uniform continuous-phase model as M1.
For other timings, a run shorter than the observation contributes zero safe-start length, not a negative length.
The constant-colour runs must be identified correctly across the cyclic boundary.
useful_alternatives.method: Count no-change observations and take the complement.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when fitting a fixed-length observation inside each colour run is more intuitive than locating windows before transitions; it also provides a short independent arithmetic check.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 counts three disjoint length-3 start windows in a length-63 cycle.
conditions_checked: The given cycle repeats every 30+3+30=63 seconds.
Shifting the observation start by 63 seconds preserves the event.
The transition into the next cycle must remain included.
limitations: Periodicity does not itself establish uniform sampling.
Reducing the start phase to one cycle must not truncate the observation at the cycle boundary.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Shrink the Giant — Replace the indefinitely repeating timeline by one complete cycle of start phases.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is the natural ordinary model, already used by M1, not an additional shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Avoids redrawing repeated cycles, which the ordinary baseline already avoids.

prompt_html: For each positive integer n, the mean of the first n terms of a sequence is n. What is the 2008th term of the sequence?
solution_html:
Letting \(S_n\) be the nth partial sum of the sequence:

\(\frac{S_n}{n}=n\)

\(S_n=n^2\)

The only possible sequence with this result is the sequence of odd integers.

\(a_n=2n-1\)

\(a_{2008}=2(2008)-1=4015\Rightarrow \mathbf{(B)}\)
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Arithmetic mean and recovery of a total Recover a term from adjacent partial sums Factorisation and algebraic expansion Update an arithmetic mean after membership changes

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Convert each prefix mean into its total, S_n=n×n=n². The requested term is the difference of the totals of the first 2008 and first 2007 terms. Factor 2008²−2007² to obtain 4015 without calculating either large square.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let S_n be the sum of the first n terms. The premise gives S_n/n=n, so S_n=n². Therefore a_2008=S_2008−S_2007=2008²−2007²=(2008−2007)(2008+2007)=4015. Both partial sums are fixed by the premise, so the requested term is uniquely determined. Only option B equals 4015.
domain_case_checks: The condition holds for every positive integer n, so it applies at both n=2007 and n=2008; using the preceding prefix is justified.
Each mean has a positive denominator. For the general term identity, use a_n=S_n−S_(n−1) for n≥2 and handle n=1 directly: a_1=1. No mean at n=0 is assumed.
No arithmetic-progression, positivity or integrality assumption about the individual terms is needed. The derived formula a_n=2n−1, together with a_1=1, forces positive odd integer terms.
Multiplication by the positive count, subtraction of finite sums and the difference-of-squares identity are exact operations. No root extraction or other operation introduces extraneous candidates.
Only finite prefixes are used, so convergence of an infinite series is irrelevant. The stated means are exact, and no rounding or unit conversion is required.
The equations force one value independently of any single-correct-option convention. All five numerical options are distinct, and exactly one equals that value.

skills.definition: For a finite nonempty collection, use mean = total/count and the equivalent relation total = count×mean.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 obtains S_n=n×n=n². M2 uses the old group's count and mean to calculate its aggregate shortfall from the new mean.
skills.learning_objective: Given a nonempty group's size and mean, recover its total and use total divided by count to verify a mean.
skills.name: Arithmetic mean and recovery of a total

skills.definition: For a sequence with partial sums S_n=a_1+...+a_n, recover an individual term using a_n=S_n−S_(n−1) for n≥2 and a_1=S_1, identifying the common prefix and preserving the adjacent indices.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 isolates a_2008 by subtracting S_2007 from S_2008. M2 instead reasons through the change in mean without using partial-sum notation or an explicit prefix-subtraction step.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish a term from a partial sum and recover the term by subtracting the immediately preceding prefix total.
skills.name: Recover a term from adjacent partial sums

skills.definition: Expand, factor and collect algebraic expressions while retaining equality.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 factors n²−(n−1)² as [n−(n−1)][n+(n−1)]=2n−1, avoiding large-square arithmetic.
skills.learning_objective: Apply the difference-of-squares identity with the correct order and sign.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

skills.definition: When observations are added or removed, update both the total and the count before computing or equating the new arithmetic mean; require the resulting collection to be nonempty.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 compares the old group of 2007 terms with the enlarged group of 2008 terms. The added term supplies a surplus of 2007 above the new mean.
skills.learning_objective: Model the new mean correctly when one observation is added to a group.
skills.name: Update an arithmetic mean after membership changes

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The old 2007 terms average 2007, so their total is 2007 below what it would be at average 2008. To make all 2008 terms average 2008, the new term must supply that shortfall in addition to its own share of 2008. It is therefore 2008+2007=4015.
limitations: The shortfall is an aggregate statement; individual old terms need not equal their mean.
The old count is 2007 and the new count is 2008. Confusing these counts changes the result.
This is comparable in length to M1, not a material shortcut.
useful_alternatives.method: Reason by the surplus needed to raise the mean when one term is added.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the change in mean is easy to interpret and the student prefers balancing totals to partial-sum notation and difference-of-squares factorisation.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: derive S_n=n² and use a_2008=S_2008−S_2007.
conditions_checked: The mean condition is valid for every positive integer.
The preceding index is 2007, not 2008 or 2009.
The formula follows algebraically from the premise rather than from a numerical pattern.
limitations: This is already M1, so avoiding term-by-term reconstruction does not earn an additional shortcut badge.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Shrink the Giant: the closed form S_n=n² turns the large-index request into the difference of two adjacent totals, giving a_n=2n−1.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful and decisive, but ordinary here; no saving beyond the best baseline.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Both this method and M1 avoid generating the first 2007 terms.

prompt_html: Bernardo randomly picks 3 distinct numbers from the set \{1,2,3,...,7,8,9\} and arranges them in descending order to form a 3-digit number. Silvia randomly picks 3 distinct numbers from the set \{1,2,3,...,6,7,8\} and also arranges them in descending order to form a 3-digit number. What is the probability that Bernardo's number is larger than Silvia's number?
solution_html:
We can solve this by breaking the problem down into two cases and adding the probabilities.

Case 1: Bernardo picks 9. If Bernardo picks a 9 then his number is necessarily larger than Silvia's. The probability that he picks a 9 is \(\dfrac{1\cdot\binom{8}{2}}{\binom{9}{3}}=\dfrac{1}{3}\).

Case 2: Bernardo does not pick 9. This happens with probability \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).

Condition on both not picking 9 (i.e. consider only numbers 1 to 8). They are then picking from the same set, so the probabilities that Bernardo's number is larger or Silvia's number is larger are equal, except when they pick the same 3 numbers (which results in the same ordered 3-digit number).

The probability that they pick the same 3 numbers (ignoring order) is the number of distinct 3-element subsets relative to ordered picks: there are \(8\cdot7\cdot6\) ordered picks but each unordered 3-set corresponds to \(3!\) orders, so the probability two independent unordered picks coincide is \(\dfrac{3!}{8\cdot7\cdot6}=\dfrac{1}{56}\).

Thus, conditional on neither picking 9, the probability Bernardo's number is larger is \(\dfrac{1-\tfrac{1}{56}}{2}=\dfrac{55}{112}\). Multiplying by the probability \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) of not picking 9 gives \(\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{55}{112}=\dfrac{55}{168}\).

Adding the two cases: \(\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{55}{168}=\dfrac{37}{56}\). Hence the answer is \(\dfrac{37}{56}\) (B).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Count fixed-size unordered subsets Bijective counting and representation multiplicity Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity Independence and multiplication of probabilities Condition on the correct event and denominator Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities Exact surd and rational arithmetic Ranks and population constraints Finite sums of an arithmetic sequence

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Condition on whether Bernardo selects 9. This has probability 1/3 and guarantees a win. Otherwise the players independently choose from the same 56 final numbers. Subtract the conditional tie probability 1/56 before dividing the remaining probability equally between the two strict comparison directions. Combine the branches using total probability.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Use the standard interpretation of separate random choices: independent, uniform three-element subsets. Sorting gives one distinct number per subset. Bernardo has C(9,3)=84 possible numbers; Silvia has C(8,3)=56. Bernardo selects 9 with probability C(8,2)/C(9,3)=28/84=1/3, and then certainly wins. Otherwise, both numbers are independent and uniform on the same 56 possibilities. There are 56 equal pairs among 56² conditional pairs, so the conditional tie probability is 1/56. Swapping the two numbers pairs every strict Bernardo win with a strict Silvia win. Hence P(X>Y | no 9)=(1−1/56)/2=55/112. Therefore P(X>Y)=1/3+(2/3)(55/112)=37/56, which is option B.
domain_case_checks: The usual interpretation is independent uniform selection of three-element subsets from the two stated sets. The question does not describe biased selection, coordination or a shared physical pool.
Distinctness applies within each person's selection. Their selections may overlap, and they may choose the same three digits; ties therefore have positive probability.

Every allowed digit is nonzero. Each three-element subset produces exactly one three-digit number when sorted in descending order. There is no additional random arrangement and no factor of 3! in the number of final outcomes.

Selecting 9 and not selecting 9 are disjoint exhaustive cases with probabilities 1/3 and 2/3. Both conditional probabilities are defined. A number beginning with 9 exceeds every possible Silvia number.

Conditional on Bernardo not selecting 9, his 56 possible numbers have the same uniform distribution as Silvia's. Conditioning on an event determined only by Bernardo's choice leaves Silvia's independent distribution unchanged. This symmetry is not valid before conditioning.
The conditional tie probability is 1/56, while the unconditional tie probability is (2/3)(1/56)=1/84. The strict comparison excludes these ties.
The complete joint sample space has 84×56=4704 equally likely pairs: 3108 Bernardo wins, 1540 Silvia wins and 56 ties. These counts sum to 4704.

In the rank-counting alternative, Silvia's rank ranges inclusively from 1 to 56. The corresponding numbers of strictly larger Bernardo outcomes are 83 and 28 at the endpoints; the equal outcome is excluded throughout.
All divisions are by positive finite counts. The result is exact and lies in [0,1]; no rounding or equation-solving operation that could introduce extraneous roots is needed.

skills.definition: For n distinct objects and an integer r with 0≤r≤n, count unordered r-element selections using C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n−r)!), adjusting the pool and quota for forced or excluded objects and including the endpoint cases r=0 and r=n.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Counts 84 Bernardo subsets, 56 Silvia subsets and 28 Bernardo subsets containing 9.
skills.learning_objective: Count three-element digit subsets and adjust the remaining pool and quota when 9 is required or excluded.
skills.name: Count fixed-size unordered subsets

skills.definition: Count finite configurations through a proved one-to-one correspondence with simpler encodings, checking existence, uniqueness, and the treatment of excluded or multiply represented exceptional configurations.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Both methods use the one-to-one correspondence between digit subsets and descending numbers. M1 additionally swaps unequal conditional outcome pairs and treats the diagonal fixed points separately.
skills.learning_objective: Justify unique subset-to-number encoding and a comparison-swapping bijection while retaining its tie exceptions.
skills.name: Bijective counting and representation multiplicity

skills.definition: Count equally likely probabilistic outcomes with the correct order and multiplicity.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Uses uniform subsets and ordered player-pairs, rather than treating all three-digit integers or all possible leading digits as equally likely.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the equally likely final outcomes and count ties and strict comparisons with consistent multiplicity.
skills.name: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity

skills.definition: Recognise or justify independence of events determined by separate independent random selections, including functions of those selections, and calculate joint probabilities by finite products. Do not infer independence merely from equal marginal probabilities or disjointness.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The standard independent-selection model gives equally likely joint pairs. Conditioning on Bernardo excluding 9 leaves Silvia's distribution unchanged and independent of Bernardo's conditional selection.
skills.learning_objective: Carry independence through deterministic sorting and through conditioning on an event involving only one selection.
skills.name: Independence and multiplication of probabilities

skills.definition: Identify the conditioning event and compute conditional probability with a nonzero evidence probability.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Restricts Bernardo to the 56 outcomes not containing 9 and computes the tie and strict-win probabilities in that conditional experiment.
skills.learning_objective: Use the correct restricted sample space after excluding 9 and distinguish conditional from unconditional tie probabilities.
skills.name: Condition on the correct event and denominator

skills.definition: Partition into disjoint exhaustive cases and sum correctly weighted conditional probabilities.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Combines the certain-win branch and the common-support branch as (1/3)×1+(2/3)×(55/112).
skills.learning_objective: Weight conditional success probabilities by the probabilities of the disjoint cases that produce them.
skills.name: Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities

skills.definition: Perform exact rational and surd arithmetic and comparisons under real-domain restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Simplifies the probability to 37/56 and compares every option exactly using denominator 504; M2 simplifies 3108/4704.
skills.learning_objective: Calculate and compare exact rational probabilities without rounding away the tie correction.
skills.name: Exact surd and rational arithmetic

skills.definition: In a tie-free ranked list of N objects, interpret rank r as having r - 1 objects ahead and N - r behind, enforce 1 ≤ r ≤ N, and translate strict comparisons into rank inequalities using the stated ranking direction.
skills.evidence_in_solution: In ascending order, Silvia's possible value at rank r has exactly 84−r larger Bernardo values.
skills.learning_objective: Count values strictly above an ascending rank while excluding the value at the rank itself.
skills.name: Ranks and population constraints

skills.definition: Derive and apply S_n = n(a_1 + a_n)/2 = n[2a_1 + (n−1)d]/2 for a finite arithmetic sequence with positive-integer n, including consecutive blocks with correctly identified endpoints.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Sums the 56 favourable counts 83,82,...,28 as 56(83+28)/2=3108.
skills.learning_objective: Sum a rank-indexed arithmetic progression with the correct number of terms and included endpoints.
skills.name: Finite sums of an arithmetic sequence

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Place Bernardo's 84 possible numbers in increasing order. Silvia's possible numbers occupy ranks 1 through 56, since the remaining 28 numbers contain 9 and are larger than all of them. For Silvia rank r, exactly 84−r Bernardo outcomes win. Thus the favourable count is Σ from r=1 to 56 of (84−r)=56(83+28)/2=3108, out of 84×56=4704 equally likely pairs, giving 37/56.
limitations: The ranking must be over allowed final numbers, not over all three-digit integers.
Strict comparison requires 84−r rather than 85−r.
This method still uses the subset-to-number bijection and independent uniform selections, and it requires an arithmetic-series sum.
useful_alternatives.method: Rank-counting over the common ordered outcome list.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for a counting-first solution or when a student prefers explicit favourable-pair counts to conditioning and a symmetric probability split.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: condition on selecting 9, use tie-aware symmetry on the common 56-number distribution, then apply total probability.
conditions_checked: M2 proves that the favourable counts are 84−r for every integer r from 1 through 56.
These are exactly 56 arithmetic-progression terms, from 83 down to 28.
limitations: The progression follows from the rank formula, not from guessing a pattern from a few examples.
M1 avoids this rank sum altogether.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Shrink the Giant: in M2, sum the 56 counts using 56(83+28)/2=3108 rather than listing and adding each count.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: A useful ordinary finite-sum calculation within M2, but not a material saving over M1.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: It replaces a literal 56-term summation, which would require 55 additions. Those operations are not part of the best ordinary baseline.

prompt_html: A high school basketball game between the Raiders and Wildcats was tied at the end of the first quarter. The number of points scored by the Raiders in each of the four quarters formed an increasing geometric sequence, and the number of points scored by the Wildcats in each of the four quarters formed an increasing arithmetic sequence. At the end of the fourth quarter, the Raiders had won by one point. Neither team scored more than 100 points. What was the total number of points scored by the two teams in the first half?
solution_html:
Let the common first-quarter score be \(a>0\), and let the Wildcats have positive integer difference \(d\), so their total is \(W=4a+6d\). Write the Raiders ratio as \(p/q>1\) in lowest terms. Integrality of \(a(p/q)^3\) forces \(a=kq^3\) for a positive integer \(k\); their scores are \(kq^3,kpq^2,kp^2q,kp^3\). The cap \(R\le100\) implies \(p\le4\); if \(q\ge3\), then \(R\ge27+36+48+64=175\), impossible. Thus the reduced pairs are \((2,1),(3,1),(3,2),(4,1)\). For the only noninteger ratio \(3/2\), the margin is \(R-W=33k-6d\), a multiple of3, so it cannot equal1. Hence only integer ratios2,3,4 remain. Also \(W\) is even and \(R=W+1\) is odd, so \(R\le100\) indeed implies \(R<100\).

Let the Wildcats' quarterly scores be \(a,a+d,a+2d,a+3d\). Then

\(S_W=4a+6d\), and \(S_R=a(1+r)(1+r^2)\). The Raiders win by one point, so

\[a(1+r)(1+r^2)=4a+6d+1.\]

Since \(S_R<100\), we have \(r<5\), so \(r\in\{2,3,4\}\). Consider each case:

  • \(r=4\): Then \(S_R=85a\), so \(85a=4a+6d+1\) giving \(81a-6d=1\) or \(3(27a-2d)=1\), impossible for integers.
  • \(r=3\): Then \(S_R=40a\), so \(40a=4a+6d+1\) giving \(36a-6d=1\) or \(6(6a-d)=1\), impossible for integers.
  • \(r=2\): Then \(S_R=15a\), so \(15a=4a+6d+1\) which gives \(11a-6d=1\). Reducing mod 6 yields \(a\equiv5\pmod6\). Also \(15a<100\) so \(a<100/15\), hence \(a\le6\), and the congruence forces \(a=5\). Then \(11\cdot5-6d=1\) so \(d=9\).

Thus the Raiders' scores are \(5,10,20,40\) and the Wildcats' scores are \(5,14,23,32\). The Raiders' total is 75 and the Wildcats' total is 74. The total points scored by both teams in the first half (first two quarters) is \(5+10+5+14=34\), corresponding to choice (E).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Geometric progression and constant multipliers Arithmetic progression and constant finite differences Finite arithmetic-series sum Domain restrictions and reversible operations Divisibility, prime and composite factors Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Model the four quarterly scores using the shared first term. Express the geometric ratio in lowest terms and use integrality to write the Raiders' scores as kq³,kq²p,kqp²,kp³. The 100-point cap leaves four reduced ratio pairs. Apply the one-point margin equation and divisibility to eliminate three pairs, then determine the remaining integer scale and arithmetic difference. Verify the resulting scores and add the first two quarters for both teams.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Basketball scores are nonnegative integers. Write the quarterly scores as a, ar, ar², ar³ and a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, where a,d are positive integers and r>1. The Wildcats' total is 4a+6d. Write r=p/q in lowest terms. Since ar³ is an integer, q³ divides a, so the Raiders' scores are kq³, kq²p, kqp², kp³ for a positive integer k. Put T=q³+q²p+qp²+p³. The cap kT≤100 gives p≤4; if q≥3, then p≥4 and T≥175, so q≤2. The only reduced pairs (p,q) are (2,1), (3,1), (3,2), (4,1). The one-point win requires k(T−4q³)−6d=1. For these pairs, T−4q³ is respectively 11, 36, 33, 81. The last three are impossible because the left side would be divisible by 3. Thus r=2, a=k, and 11k−6d=1. Also 15k≤100, so 1≤k≤6. Modulo 6, k≡5, giving k=5 and d=9. The quarterly scores are therefore 5,10,20,40 and 5,14,23,32, with totals 75 and 74. The combined first-half total is 5+10+5+14=34 points.

The common difference d is an integer because it is the difference of two integer scores. The common ratio need only be rational, not integral; r=3/2 must therefore be considered before it is excluded.

The reduced-ratio parametrisation is exhaustive: integrality of ap³/q³ and coprimality give q³ dividing a. Conversely, every positive integer k and reduced pair p>q≥1 produces four increasing integer scores kq³, kq²p, kqp², kp³.

The bound of 100 applies to each team's whole-game total, not to the combined total or merely to an individual quarter. The proof uses R≤100. Since W=4a+6d is even and R=W+1, R is actually odd, so equality R=100 is impossible; using the weaker inclusive bound loses no cases.
The ratio cases are complete: p≥5 makes the fourth-quarter score at least 125, and q≥3 makes the total at least 175. Coprimality and p>q leave exactly the four listed pairs.
For the four ratio cases, the possible scale ranges are respectively k=1,...,6; k=1,2; k=1; and k=1. Integrality of d is enforced rather than rounding a fractional value.

If 'increasing' were read as nondecreasing, no extra solution would arise. A constant Raiders progression cannot beat a nondecreasing Wildcats progression with the same first term. If only the Wildcats were constant, the Raiders' strictly increasing integer scores would total at least 4a+6, not 4a+1.

The surviving scores are positive integers, both progressions increase, the first-quarter scores agree, the totals are at most 100, and 75−74=1. This substitution establishes feasibility in addition to the exhaustive uniqueness argument.

The first half consists of quarters 1 and 2. Its team totals are 15 and 19, not equal merely because the first quarter was tied. The result is an exact integer number of points, so no approximation or rounding is required.

prompt_html: Two integers have a sum of 26. When two more integers are added to the first two, the sum is 41. Finally, when two more integers are added to the sum of the previous 4 integers, the sum is 57. What is the minimum number of even integers among the 6 integers?
solution_html:
Let the first two integers be \(x,y\) with \(x+y=26\). Since 26 is even, this pair can be both odd (for example 15 and 11), so 0 evens are required among the first two.

The next two integers sum to \(41-26=15\), which is odd. To obtain an odd sum from two integers, exactly one of them must be even and the other odd, so at least 1 even is required among this pair.

The final two integers sum to \(57-41=16\), which is even; this pair could be both odd, contributing 0 evens.

Thus the minimum total number of even integers among the six is \(0+1+0=1\). Answer: (A) \(1\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Model verbal linear relationships Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Global extrema from attained bounds Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the final odd total for the lower bound: if none of the six integers were even, all six would be odd and their sum would be even. Hence at least one even integer is necessary. For attainment, the pair-sums must be 26, 41 - 26 = 15, and 57 - 41 = 16. Choose the pairs (1,25), (2,13), and (7,9). Verify all cumulative totals and count the single even entry. The lower bound and the example together prove the minimum is 1.
audited_reference.concise_proof: If all six integers were odd, their sum would be even, contrary to the total 57. Thus at least one integer must be even. The ordered integers 1, 25, 2, 13, 7, 9 have cumulative totals 26, 41 and 57 after two, four and six entries, and only 2 is even. Therefore the minimum number of even integers is 1.
domain_case_checks: The domain is six integers. Positivity and distinctness are not required, although the attaining example uses distinct positive integers.
The newly added pairs have sums 41 - 26 = 15 and 57 - 41 = 16; 41 and 57 are cumulative totals, not the sums of the new pairs.
Two integers with an even sum are either both odd or both even. Two integers with an odd sum consist of one odd and one even integer. These are exhaustive residue cases modulo 2.

Consequently the three pairs contribute respectively 0 or 2, exactly 1, and 0 or 2 even entries. The only possible total even counts are 1, 3 and 5; examples in the option verification attain each count.
The zero-even case is impossible independently of the options: six odd integers cannot have the odd sum 57.
The lower bound is attained by a tuple satisfying every staged equality, so this is an actual minimum rather than merely a bound or a trial value.

prompt_html: The Tigers beat the Sharks 2 out of the 3 times they played. They then played N more times, and the Sharks ended up winning at least 95% of all the games played. What is the minimum possible value for N?
solution_html: After \(N\) extra games the Sharks can have at most \(N+1\) wins out of \(N+3\) games. Therefore reaching at least95% requires \[\frac{N+1}{N+3}\ge\frac{19}{20}.\]Since \(N+3>0\), this gives \(20N+20\ge19N+57\), hence \(N\ge37\). The bound is attainable: the Sharks win the third initial game and all37 additional games, giving \(38/40=95\%\). Thus the minimum is37, optionB.

prompt_html: For every composite positive integer \(n\), define \(r(n)\) to be the sum of the factors in the prime factorization of \(n\). For example, \(r(50)=12\) because the prime factorization of \(50\) is \(2\times 5^2\), and \(2+5+5=12\). What is the range of the function \(r\), \(\{r(n): n \text{ is a composite positive integer}\}\)?

options.html: the set of composite positive integers
options.label: B

options.html: the set of even positive integers
options.label: C

options.html: the set of integers greater than 3
options.label: D

options.html: the set of integers greater than 4
options.label: E

solution_html:
Note that for composite \(n\), \(r(n)\) is the sum of the prime factors of \(n\), counted with multiplicity. Thus \(r(n)\) is a sum of at least two primes. Conversely, given any multiset of primes \(p_1,\dots,p_k\) with \(k\ge 2\), the integer \(n=\prod_{i=1}^k p_i\) is composite and satisfies \(r(n)=\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\). Hence the range of \(r\) is exactly the set of integers that can be written as a sum of at least two primes.

Observe the smallest possible sum of two primes is \(2+2=4\), so no integers \(1,2,3\) occur. For any integer \(m\ge 4\): if \(m\) is even, write it as a sum of \(m/2\) copies of \(2\); if \(m\) is odd (so \(m\ge 5\)), write \(m=3+(m-3)\) and express the even number \(m-3\) as a sum of copies of \(2\). In each case \(m\) is a sum of at least two primes, so \(m\) occurs in the range. Therefore the range is the set of integers greater than 3.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Prove a lower bound and then construct every candidate output. A composite integer has at least two prime-factor occurrences, each at least 2, so r(n)≥4. For an arbitrary even target 2k≥4 use n=2^k; for an arbitrary odd target 2k+3≥5 use n=3·2^k. Their prime-factor sums are exactly the requested targets, and both inputs are composite. This proves both inclusions needed for the range.
audited_reference.concise_proof: A composite positive integer has at least two prime factors counted with multiplicity, each at least 2. Therefore r(n) is an integer at least 4. Conversely, every even integer 2k≥4 is attained by n=2^k, since r(2^k)=2k. Every odd integer 2k+3≥5 is attained by n=3·2^k with k≥1, since r(3·2^k)=3+2k. Both constructions give composite positive integers. Thus the range is exactly {4,5,6,...}, the set of integers greater than 3.
domain_case_checks: The domain contains only composite positive integers. Prime inputs, 1, zero and negative integers are excluded; values such as r(2) cannot be used.
The supplied example r(50)=2+5+5 confirms that repeated prime factors are counted separately. Neither distinctness of the prime factors nor exactly two prime factors is required.
Writing n=p_1···p_t with repeated primes allowed gives t≥2 and every p_i≥2. Hence r(n)≥4. Equality is possible precisely when t=2 and both factors are 2, giving n=4.
For an even target m=2k≥4, k is an integer at least 2, so 2^k is composite. The construction does not accidentally admit the prime input 2.
For an odd target m=2k+3≥5, k is an integer at least 1, so 3·2^k has at least two prime factors and is composite. The first odd output is r(6)=5.
The even and odd target cases are disjoint and exhaust every integer at least 4. The construction works for arbitrary target integers, not just for a finite list of examples.
The endpoint 4 is included, so 'integers greater than 3' is correct and 'integers greater than 4' is not. All calculations are exact integer calculations; no approximation or rounding is involved.

There is no separate exactly-one-true premise in the stem. The range proof and the checks of all five options establish unique correctness independently; finite option elimination alone does not prove the full range.

prompt_html: The number 21!=51,090,942,171,709,440,000 has over 60,000 positive integer divisors. One of them is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is odd?
solution_html: We can consider a factor of 21! to be odd if it does not contain a 2; hence, finding the exponent of 2 in the prime factorization of 21! will help us find our answer. We can start off with all multiples of 2 up to 21, which is 10. Then, we find multiples of 4, which is 5. Next, we look at multiples of 8, of which there are 2. Finally, we know there is only one multiple of 16 in the set of positive integers up to 21. Now, we can add all of these to get 10+5+2+1=18. We know that, in the prime factorization of 21!, we have \(2^{18}\), and the only way to have an odd number is if there is not a 2 in that number's prime factorization. This only happens with \(2^{0}\), which is only one of the 19 different exponents of 2 we could have (of which having each exponent is equally likely). Hence, the probability is \(\dfrac{1}{19}\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Prime exponents in products and factorials Positive divisors from bounded prime exponents Counting integer points in intervals Multiplication principle for finite choices Favourable-over-total probability ratio

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Count only the power of 2 in 21!, obtaining 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18. Write 21! = 2^18 m with m odd. Each divisor is uniquely 2^k u for k = 0, ..., 18 and u | m. Every exponent has the same number of possible odd parts, and only exponent zero gives an odd divisor. Therefore the probability is 1/19. Neither the displayed decimal expansion nor the full divisor count needs to be calculated.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The exponent of 2 in 21! is ⌊21/2⌋ + ⌊21/4⌋ + ⌊21/8⌋ + ⌊21/16⌋ = 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18. Each factor containing r factors of 2 is counted in exactly r of these layers. Write 21! = 2^18 m with m odd. Every positive divisor is uniquely 2^k u, where 0 ≤ k ≤ 18 and u is a positive divisor of m. If m has T positive divisors, there are 19T divisors in total, of which exactly T are odd, corresponding to k = 0. Thus the required probability is T/(19T) = 1/19, which is option B.
domain_case_checks: The sample space consists of distinct positive integer divisors of the fixed number 21!, including 1 and 21! itself. It is not the list of integers from 1 to 21 or a list of prime-factor occurrences.

The standard reading of choosing one divisor at random is uniform selection from this finite divisor set. Equal probabilities for exponent classes follow from their equal sizes; they are not assumed merely because the classes have different labels.
The valuation sum stops after 16 because 32 > 21. Multiples of 4, 8 and 16 supply additional factors of 2 beyond the first factor supplied by every even number.
The exponent k is an integer in the inclusive interval 0 ≤ k ≤ 18, giving 19 choices. Exponent zero is permitted even though the divisor itself must be positive. A divisor is odd exactly when k = 0.
The representation 2^k u is necessary, sufficient and unique: removing all factors of 2 gives its unique odd part, and every permitted pair divides 2^18 m because the quotient is 2^(18-k)(m/u).
T is positive because 1 divides m, so cancelling T in T/(19T) is valid. The result is an exact, dimensionless probability strictly between 0 and 1; no approximation or rounding is required.

As a separate source-consistency check, 21! = 2^18 × 3^9 × 5^4 × 7^3 × 11 × 13 × 17 × 19 = 51,090,942,171,709,440,000. Its divisor count is 19 × 10 × 5 × 4 × 2^4 = 60,800, confirming the stated 'over 60,000'. There are 10 × 5 × 4 × 2^4 = 3,200 odd divisors. This expanded calculation is not needed for M1.

prompt_html: What is the value of \[\log_3 7\cdot\log_5 9\cdot\log_7 11\cdot\log_9 13\cdots\log_{21} 25\cdot\log_{23} 27?\]
solution_html: From the Change of Base Formula, we have \[\frac{\prod_{i=3}^{13} \log(2i+1)}{\prod_{i=1}^{11}\log(2i+1)} = \frac{\log 25 \cdot \log 27}{\log 3 \cdot \log 5} = \frac{(2\log 5)\cdot(3\log 3)}{\log 3 \cdot \log 5} = \boxed{6}.\]

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Take reciprocals to obtain b_n = 2b_{n-1} - b_{n-2}. Rearrange this as equality of consecutive differences, giving an arithmetic progression with first term 1 and difference 4/3. Obtain b_n = (4n-1)/3 and invert. Validate the resulting formula against the original recurrence and its denominators, then evaluate at n = 2019 and check lowest terms before adding p and q.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For nonzero terms, put b_n = 1/a_n. Taking reciprocals gives b_n = 2b_{n-1} - b_{n-2}, so consecutive differences are constant. Since b_1 = 1 and b_2 = 7/3, their common difference is 4/3. Thus b_n = 1 + (n-1)4/3 = (4n-1)/3, suggesting a_n = 3/(4n-1). To validate all divisions, let f_n = 3/(4n-1). It matches both initial values, and for n >= 3, 2f_{n-2} - f_{n-1} = 3(4n-1)/[(4n-9)(4n-5)] > 0. Substitution into the recurrence gives f_n. Induction therefore establishes that the original sequence is defined and equals f_n at every positive integer index. Consequently a_{2019} = 3/8075. Since 8075 = 3(2691) + 2, this fraction is in lowest terms. Hence p + q = 3 + 8075 = 8078, option E.
domain_case_checks: The initial terms have indices 1 and 2, and the recurrence applies at every integer n >= 3. The requested index 2019 is permitted.
The candidate formula 3/(4n-1) is positive and nonzero for every integer n >= 1. It gives exactly a_1 = 1 and a_2 = 3/7.
For n >= 3, the original recurrence denominator equals 3(4n-1)/[(4n-9)(4n-5)], which is strictly positive. Thus the original recurrence never encounters an undefined update.

Checking the candidate against both initial conditions and the deterministic recurrence proves existence and uniqueness throughout the required index range. The reciprocal manipulation is therefore validated, rather than assumed valid indefinitely.
There are 2018 increments from b_1 to b_{2019}, or 2017 increments from b_2 to b_{2019}. Direct evaluation of the original recurrence would require 2017 updates, from n = 3 through n = 2019.

The general representation 3/(4n-1) need not be reduced at every index; for example, a_4 = 3/15 = 1/5. At the requested index, 8075 is not divisible by 3, so p = 3 and q = 8075 are relatively prime positive integers.
No approximation or rounding is required. No root-taking or squaring is used; the relevant equivalence conditions are precisely the nonzero reciprocal and denominator conditions checked above.

prompt_html: Positive real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy\[\sqrt{\log a}+\sqrt{\log b}+\log\sqrt a+\log\sqrt b=100,\]and all four terms on the left are positive integers. Here \(\log\) denotes the base-10 logarithm. What is \(ab\)?
solution_html: Put \(x=\sqrt{\log a}\) and \(y=\sqrt{\log b}\), positive integers. Since \(\log\sqrt a=x^2/2\) and \(\log\sqrt b=y^2/2\) are also integers, \(x\) and \(y\) are even. Write \(x=2m,y=2n\), where \(m,n\) are positive integers. Then\[m(m+1)+n(n+1)=50.\]Each variable is at most6. The possible values of \(t(t+1)\) for \(t=1,\ldots,6\) are \(2,6,12,20,30,42\); only \(20+30=50\). Hence \(\{m,n\}=\{4,5\}\), so\[\log(ab)=4(m^2+n^2)=164,\qquad ab=10^{164}.\]Conversely, \(a=10^{64},b=10^{100}\) gives the four positive integer terms \(8,10,32,50\), summing to100. The answer is D.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Replace the square-root logarithms by positive integers x,y. The logarithm power rule makes the other two terms x²/2,y²/2, forcing x,y to be even. Set x=2m,y=2n to obtain m(m+1)+n(n+1)=50. Order m≤n and bound the larger integer to n=5 or 6. Check those two cases, then calculate log(ab)=4(m²+n²), exponentiate and verify the original four terms.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put x=√(log a) and y=√(log b). These are positive integers, while log(√a)=x²/2 and log(√b)=y²/2 are also integers. Thus x and y are even. Write x=2m and y=2n, where m,n are positive integers. The equation becomes m(m+1)+n(n+1)=50. By interchange symmetry, assume m≤n. If n≤4, the left side is at most 40; if n≥7, its second term alone is at least 56. Hence n is 5 or 6. For n=6, m(m+1)=8, impossible because the consecutive relevant values are 6 and 12. For n=5, m(m+1)=20, so m=4. Therefore {x,y}={8,10}, and log(ab)=x²+y²=164. Conversely, a=10^64 and b=10^100 give the four terms 8,10,32,50, whose sum is 100. Thus ab=10^164, uniquely option D.
domain_case_checks: The fixed logarithm base 10 is positive and different from 1. Although a,b>0 are given, positivity of the square-root logarithms further forces log a>0 and log b>0, hence a,b>1. Values at or below 1 cannot satisfy all four positive-integer conditions.
The square roots are principal roots, so x=√(log a) and y=√(log b) are positive, not arbitrary signed square roots. Recovering a=10^(x²) and b=10^(y²) is unique for each such x,y.

For an integer x, x²/2 is an integer exactly when x is even: an odd integer has an odd square. Therefore x=2m and y=2n with m,n≥1 captures precisely the individual integer conditions; no odd candidate may be retained.

All transformations use valid logarithm identities and division only by the nonzero constant 2. Reversing the positive-integer substitution recovers all original terms without introducing extraneous solutions.

The equation and requested product are unchanged by swapping a and b, so m≤n may be assumed for the search. Equality m=n is not excluded in advance. The bounds n≥5 and n≤6 are exhaustive and include both integer endpoints.

The two ordered parameter pairs are (m,n)=(4,5) and (5,4). They give the same product, and direct substitution verifies existence. Thus uniqueness of the requested product is proved rather than assumed from the MCQ format.
No approximation or rounding is used. The distinct exponents in the five options give distinct values because the base-10 exponential is injective.

subtopic: perfect matchings on a 10-cycle with diameters
prompt_html: There are 10 people standing equally spaced around a circle. Each person knows exactly 3 of the other 9 people: the 2 people standing next to her or him, as well as the person directly across the circle. How many ways are there for the 10 people to split up into 5 pairs so that the members of each pair know each other?
solution_html:
Consider the 10 people to be standing in a circle, where two people opposite of each other form a diameter of the circle.

Let us use casework on the number of pairs that form a diameter of the circle.

Case 1: 0 diameters

There are 2 ways: either 1 pairs with 2, 3 pairs with 4, and so on or 10 pairs with 1, 2 pairs with 3, etc. So \(\boxed{\textbf{2}}\) cases.

Case 2: 1 diameter

There are 5 possible diameters to draw (everyone else pairs with the person next to them). So \(\boxed{\textbf{5}}\) cases.

Exactly two diameters are impossible. After their four endpoints are removed, the remaining adjacent-only paths have lengths \(a,b,a,b\), where \(a,b\ge0\) and \(a+b=3\). At least one of these lengths is odd. Each adjacent pair stays inside one path, so an odd path cannot be fully paired without an additional diameter.

Case 3: 3 diameters

There are 5 possible sets of 3 diameters to draw. Notice we are technically choosing the number of ways to choose a pair of two diameters that are neighbors to each other. This means we can choose the first diameter in the pair, and have only two diameters to choose from for the second in the pair. The two omitted diameter classes must be adjacent among the five classes around a half-circle. Choosing them in order gives \(5 \cdot 2 = 10\) possibilities. However, notice that there are duplicates, so we divide the 10 possibilities by 2 to get \(\boxed{\textbf{5}}\).

Note that there cannot be a case with 4 diameters because then there would have to be 5 diameters for the two remaining people as they have to be connected with a diameter. A contradiction arises.

Case 4: 5 diameters

There is only \(\boxed{\textbf{1}}\) way to do this.

Thus, in total there are \(2+5+5+1=\boxed{\textbf{(C) }13}\) possible ways.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Label the people and classify complete divisions by the number k of opposite pairs used. For k>0, a selected opposite pair separates the remaining neighbouring pairings into two semicircles; each has 5−k people, so k must be odd. Count k=0,1,3,5 using forced pairings along chains and the two representations of a pair of opposite neighbouring edges. Add the contributions 2,5,5,1.
audited_reference.concise_proof:
Label the people 1 to 10 around the circle, and let k be the number of opposite pairs used.
If k>0, cut the circle at one selected opposite pair. Each open semicircle initially contains four people, and each further opposite pair removes one person from each side. Thus each side has 5−k people left. All remaining pairs must be neighbouring pairs within a side, so 5−k must be even. Hence positive k can only be 1, 3 or 5.
For k=0, person 1 can pair with 2 or 10; either choice forces all subsequent neighbouring pairs. This gives 2 divisions.
For k=1, choose one of the 5 opposite pairs. Each remaining four-person chain has a unique neighbouring pairing, giving 5 divisions.
For k=3, the four remaining people form two opposite-position pairs. Once one neighbouring pair is chosen, the other must be its half-turn image. There are 10 choices of the first neighbouring pair, and each complete division is represented twice, once by each of its two neighbouring pairs. This gives 10/2=5 divisions.
For k=5, everyone pairs with their opposite person, giving 1 division.
These cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so the total is 2+5+5+1=13. Therefore C is the unique correct option.
domain_case_checks: The ten people are distinct. A division consists of five disjoint unordered pairs covering every person exactly once; it is not an ordered sequence of pair selections.

The stated friendship rule gives exactly ten neighbouring pairs and five opposite pairs. These relations are symmetric, so every permitted pair satisfies the requirement that its members know each other.
No non-crossing condition is stated. Several opposite pairs may be used even though their connecting diameters would cross in a drawing.
The integer k lies in {0,1,2,3,4,5}. The semicircle parity argument requires k>0, so k=0 is handled separately rather than incorrectly excluded.

For positive k, evenness of 5−k is necessary. It does not say that every selection of three opposite pairs can be completed. The neighbouring-pair construction proves precisely which k=3 configurations work.

Both endpoint cases are permitted: k=0 gives two distinct alternating neighbouring pairings, while k=5 gives one complete opposite pairing. A completed division has one empty-remainder completion, not zero.
The division by 2 in the k=3 count corrects two representations of the same division. It is not a quotient by rotations of the ten distinct people.
This is an exact finite count. The circle's radius, lengths and units do not affect the friendship relation, and no approximation or rounding is needed.

prompt_html: Suppose a is a real number such that the equation \[a\cdot(\sin{x}+\sin{(2x)}) = \sin{(3x)}\] has more than one solution in the interval (0, \pi). The set of all such a can be written in the form \[(p,q) \cup (q,r),\] where p, q, and r are real numbers with p < q < r. What is p+q+r?
solution_html: Start with \[a(\sin x + \sin 2x)=\sin 3x.\] Using \(\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and \(\sin 3x=\sin x(4\cos^2 x-1)\), and noting \(\sin x\neq0\) for \(x\in(0,\pi)\), divide both sides by \(\sin x\) to obtain \[a(1+2\cos x)=4\cos^2 x-1.\] Rearrange to get a quadratic in \(\cos x\): \[4\cos^2 x-2a\cos x-(1+a)=0.\] By the quadratic formula, \[\cos x=\frac{2a\pm\sqrt{4a^2+16a+16}}{8}=\frac{a\pm(a+2)}{4}.\] Hence the two possible values are \[\cos x=-\tfrac{1}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\cos x=\tfrac{a+1}{2}.\] The equation \(\cos x=-\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives the solution \(x=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\in(0,\pi)\) for every \(a\). For there to be more than one solution in \((0,\pi)\), the value \(\cos x=\tfrac{a+1}{2}\) must also give a (distinct) solution in \((0,\pi)\). Thus we require \[-1<\tfrac{a+1}{2}<1\Rightarrow -3<a<1,\] and we must exclude the case where this value equals \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) (which would coincide with the other root and yield only one solution), i.e. exclude \(a=-2\). Therefore the required set is \((-3,-2)\cup(-2,1)\), so \(p=-3,\ q=-2,\ r=1\) and \[p+q+r=-3-2+1=-4.\]

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the double- and triple-angle sine identities, divide by the nonzero factor sin x, and factor the resulting equation in c=cos x. Retain the fixed root c=-1/2. The other root must lie in (-1,1) and differ from the fixed root. Translate those conditions into the two parameter intervals and add their three ordered endpoints.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put c=cos x. On 0<x<π, sin x>0 and cosine is a bijection onto (-1,1). Using sin(2x)=2sin x cos x and sin(3x)=sin x(4cos²x-1), divide only by sin x to obtain a(1+2c)=4c²-1. Thus (2c+1)(2c-1-a)=0. The roots are c=-1/2 and c=(a+1)/2. The first always gives one permitted angle. There is a second distinct angle exactly when -1<(a+1)/2<1 and (a+1)/2≠-1/2, equivalently -3<a<1 and a≠-2. Therefore the parameter set is (-3,-2)∪(-2,1), so p=-3, q=-2, r=1 and p+q+r=-4.
domain_case_checks: The parameter a is any real number before imposing the solution-count condition. The unknown x is real and restricted to the open interval (0,π).
Since sin x>0 throughout the permitted interval, division by sin x is reversible. Division by 1+2cos x would not be valid without a separate zero case: its zero gives a solution for every a.
Cosine is continuous and strictly decreasing from 1 to -1 on (0,π), so c=cos x runs through exactly (-1,1), with exactly one permitted x for each c.

The fixed root c=-1/2 corresponds to x=2π/3 and satisfies the original equation for every real a. The reduced polynomial has leading coefficient 4 for every a, so it never becomes an identity and has at most two distinct cosine roots.
At a=-3, the other cosine root is -1, corresponding to the excluded endpoint x=π. At a=1, it is 1, corresponding to the excluded endpoint x=0. Neither parameter gives a second permitted solution.
At a=-2, the reduced equation is (2c+1)²=0. There is only one distinct cosine root and hence only one permitted angle, despite its algebraic multiplicity.
The complete count is two distinct solutions when -3<a<-2 or -2<a<1, and one distinct solution for every other real a. This proves both necessity and sufficiency, not merely some feasible examples.
The ordered endpoints satisfy -3<-2<1, and the single missing interior parameter is -2. The requested sum is exactly -4; no approximation or rounding is involved.

prompt_html: A triangle in the coordinate plane has vertices A(\(\log_2 1\),\(\log_2 2\)), B(\(\log_2 3\),\(\log_2 4\)), and C(\(\log_2 7\),\(\log_2 8\)). What is the area of \(\triangle ABC\)?
solution_html:
Compute the coordinates: \(A=(\log_2 1,\log_2 2)=(0,1)\), \(B=(\log_2 3,\log_2 4)=(\log_2 3,2)\), \(C=(\log_2 7,\log_2 8)=(\log_2 7,3)\).

By the shoelace formula, the area is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl|2\log_2 3-\log_2 7\bigr|=\tfrac{1}{2}(2\log_2 3-\log_2 7)\). Simplifying gives \(\log_2\frac{3}{\sqrt7}\), which is option (B).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Domain conditions for real logarithms Inverse relationship of logarithms and exponentials Product, quotient and power laws for logarithms Logarithmic order, range and limiting behaviour Choose coordinates and compute planar distances Triangle area from a coordinate determinant Basic planar area formulas Area accounting through geometric dissection

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Evaluate the logarithms of powers of 2, set u=log₂3 and v=log₂7, and use the half-absolute-determinant formula on B−A=(u,1) and C−A=(v,2). Determine the determinant's sign exactly from 9>7, then use the logarithm power and quotient laws to express the area as one logarithm.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put u=log₂3 and v=log₂7. The vertices simplify to A=(0,1), B=(u,2) and C=(v,3), so the side vectors from A are (u,1) and (v,2). Therefore the area is K=½|2u−v|. Since 2u−v=log₂(9/7)>0, the triangle is nondegenerate and K=u−½v=log₂(3/√7), which is option B.
domain_case_checks: All coordinates are real: the logarithm base is 2>0 with 2≠1, and the coordinate arguments 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 are positive.
Every option is defined. Its logarithm argument is positive, and the denominators 7, √7 and √3 are nonzero.
The task asks for the unsigned area of one fixed triangle, not an oriented area or an optimum over variable coordinates.
The determinant is 2log₂3−log₂7=log₂(9/7)>0 because 9>7. Thus the vertices are not collinear. Reversing the vertex order would reverse the determinant's sign but not the area.
The conversion ½log₂7=log₂√7 uses the real-power law with positive argument 7. No negative square-root branch is relevant.
All inputs are fixed constants and all transformations are exact identities. There are no variable endpoints, integer cases, equation-solving branches or rounding decisions to check.

For M2, the point M=(v/2,2) is on the segment AC because it is its midpoint. The segment BM partitions ABC into two triangles with disjoint interiors; their perpendicular heights to the horizontal line BM are both 1.
Exactly one option is established by calculation and comparison; an additional exactly-one-true premise is not used to infer the area.
