subtopic: Stationary points, multiplicity and inflection points
prompt_html:
Let
\[y = a x^7 + b x^6 + c x^5 + d x^4 + e x^3 + f x^2 + g x + h, \qquad a \neq 0,\]
where \(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\) are real numbers. Call a point on the graph an inflection with zero gradient if \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\) there but \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) does not change sign as \(x\) passes through it.

Which one of the following triples (number of local minima, number of local maxima, number of inflections with zero gradient) is possible for some choice of the real coefficients?

You may find it useful to be reminded that at local maxima and minima, \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) changes sign.
solution_html:
Since \(y\) is a polynomial of degree \(7\), its derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is a polynomial of degree \(6\).

At a local maximum or local minimum, \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) changes sign. Therefore each local maximum or minimum corresponds to a root of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) with odd multiplicity, so it uses at least \(1\) root.

At an inflection with zero gradient, \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\) but \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) does not change sign. Therefore it corresponds to a root of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) with even multiplicity, so it uses at least \(2\) roots.

Also, since \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) has degree \(6\), it has the same sign as \(x\to -\infty\) and as \(x\to \infty\). Therefore the number of changes from positive to negative must equal the number of changes from negative to positive. Hence the number of local maxima must equal the number of local minima.

Now check the options.

\((0,0,4)\) requires at least \(2\cdot 4=8\) roots of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), impossible.

\((2,2,2)\) requires at least \(2+2+2\cdot 2=8\) roots of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), impossible.

\((2,3,0)\) has unequal numbers of local minima and local maxima, impossible.

\((3,3,1)\) requires at least \(3+3+2=8\) roots of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), impossible.

\((1,1,3)\) requires at least \(1+1+2\cdot 3=8\) roots of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), impossible.

\((2,1,1)\) has unequal numbers of local minima and local maxima, impossible.

But \((2,2,1)\) requires at least
\[2+2+2=6\]
roots of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), which is possible for a degree \(6\) derivative.

For example, \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) could have four simple roots causing two local minima and two local maxima, and one double root giving one inflection with zero gradient.

So the possible triple is \(\textbf{(2,2,1)}\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Differentiate a polynomial Polynomial root multiplicity and axis-contact patterns Polynomial root factors and degree bounds Polynomial end behaviour Stationary points and local extrema of polynomials Signs of real quantities and squares Existential possibility and admissible witness construction Eliminate choices using a valid necessary condition Rolle's theorem and intervening derivative zeros Polynomial distinct-root bound and identity criterion

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Differentiate only as far as needed to identify a degree-six polynomial. Use multiplicity parity to assign cost at least one to each turning point and at least two to each non-turning stationary point. Use the derivative's matching tail signs to show that minima and maxima occur in equal numbers. Apply these two necessary conditions to the options, then verify the survivor with one factored derivative and an explicit degree-seven polynomial.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let P=y'. Since a≠0, P has degree six. At a real root r, write P(x)=(x-r)^k Q(x), where Q(r)≠0. The sign of Q is constant sufficiently near r, so P changes sign exactly when k is odd. Thus each local extremum uses at least one degree of P, while each inflection with zero gradient uses at least two. If the three counts are m, M and s, then m+M+2s≤6. Also P has the same sign at both far ends because its leading term is 7ax^6. Its sign-changing roots therefore alternate between maxima and minima in equal numbers, giving m=M. Options A, B, D and E each require at least eight degrees; C and F have unequal numbers of minima and maxima. To verify G, take y=x^7/7-x^5+4x^3/3. Then P=x^2(x^2-1)(x^2-4), whose only real zeros are -2,-1,0,1,2. Its signs on the six successive intervals are +,-,+,+,-,+. Hence y has maxima at x=-2 and x=1, minima at x=-1 and x=2, and one inflection with zero gradient at x=0. Its leading coefficient is 1/7≠0, so this is a legal witness. Exactly G is possible.
domain_case_checks: The variable x and all coefficients are real, and x ranges over the whole real line. The condition a≠0 makes y exactly degree seven and y' exactly degree six.

The derivative is a nonzero polynomial, so its real zeros are isolated and finite in number. Every stationary point is either a sign-changing derivative zero or a non-sign-changing derivative zero; there is no interval of zero derivative.

A turning point can have any odd positive derivative-root multiplicity, not necessarily one. A non-sign-changing derivative zero has even positive multiplicity, at least two. Higher multiplicities only strengthen the degree restriction.

Distinct stationary points are counted once in the requested triple. Multiplicities are used only in the degree budget. Nonreal roots can consume remaining degree but cannot increase the allowed real-root budget.
For a>0, y' is positive at both far ends; for a<0, it is negative at both far ends. Either case forces equal numbers of maxima and minima. Even degree does not mean that y' must be an even function.
There are no finite domain endpoints at which additional one-sided extrema could occur. Inflections with nonzero gradient are not included in the third count.

The witness has real coefficients a=1/7, c=-1 and e=4/3, with all other coefficients zero. Its complete derivative zero set and interval signs establish the exact counts, not merely lower bounds on them.
No approximation, rounding or numerical graph inspection is used. The exclusions and the legal witness independently verify the single-correct-option premise.

skills.evidence_in_solution: The leading term ax^7 gives 7ax^6, and differentiating the proposed witness gives the stated factored derivative. M2 also identifies y'' as degree five.

prompt_html:
A point \(P\) lies on the curve
\[y^2=11-8\cos x-4\sin^2 x-x^2.\]
Let \(d\) denote the distance from \(P\) to the origin. As \(P\) varies over the curve, how many integer values of \(c\) are there for which
\[d^3-12d+c=0\]
has exactly two distinct possible values of \(d\)?
solution_html:
Since \(d^2=x^2+y^2\), we have
\[d^2=x^2+11-8\cos x-4\sin^2 x-x^2.\]
So
\[d^2=11-8\cos x-4\sin^2 x.\]
Using \(\sin^2 x=1-\cos^2 x\),
\[d^2=11-8\cos x-4(1-\cos^2 x)=4\cos^2 x-8\cos x+7.\]
Hence
\[d^2=4(\cos x-1)^2+3.\]
Since \(-1\leq \cos x\leq 1\),
\[3\leq d^2\leq 19.\]
Therefore any possible value of \(d\) must satisfy
\[\sqrt{3}\leq d\leq \sqrt{19}.\]

Now consider
\[f(d)=d^3-12d.\]
We need \(f(d)+c=0\), so \(f(d)=-c\). Also
\[f'(d)=3d^2-12=3(d-2)(d+2).\]
On \(\sqrt{3}\leq d\leq \sqrt{19}\), the function decreases up to \(d=2\), then increases after \(d=2\).

At the key points,
\[f(\sqrt{3})=3\sqrt{3}-12\sqrt{3}=-9\sqrt{3},\]
\[f(2)=8-24=-16.\]
For there to be exactly two distinct possible values of \(d\), the value \(-c\) must lie above \(-16\) and at or below \(-9\sqrt{3}\). Hence
\[-16\lt -c\leq -9\sqrt{3}.\]
So
\[9\sqrt{3}\leq c\lt 16.\]
But \(9\sqrt{3}\approx 15.59\), so there are no integer values of \(c\) in this interval.

The answer is A.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Obtain the necessary distance bound d≥√3 by substituting the curve into d²=x²+y², using the trigonometric identity and completing the square. Analyse the two monotone branches of g(d)=12d−d³ on the containing half-line. Two distinct distances require 9√3≤c<16, which contains no integer. Computing the full attainable distance range or solving any cubic explicitly is unnecessary.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For P=(x,y), d²=x²+y²=11−8cos x−4sin²x=7−8cos x+4cos²x=3+4(cos x−1)². Hence every possible distance satisfies d≥√3. Write the equation as c=g(d), where g(d)=12d−d³. On the containing domain [√3,∞), g′(d)=12−3d² is positive before 2 and negative after 2. Thus each branch has at most one root of g(d)=c, and the maximum level g(2)=16 occurs only at d=2. Two distinct admissible distances would therefore require a root in [√3,2), forcing 9√3≤c<16. But 15<9√3<16, since 225<243<256. There is no integer in this required interval. Consequently no integer c can give two distinct distances on the curve, so the answer is 0.
domain_case_checks: The curve is interpreted over real Cartesian coordinates. Its points must have real y, and d=√(x²+y²)≥0. There is no stated positivity restriction on the integer c.

The task counts integer parameters c for which the set of attained distance values satisfying the cubic has cardinality two. It does not count points P, signed cubic roots, or roots with algebraic multiplicity.
The identity d²=3+4(cos x−1)² proves the necessary bound d≥√3. The bound is attained at P=(0,√3), so the original curve is nonempty.

No full attainable distance range is asserted. Real-y feasibility can further restrict the containing half-line [√3,∞), but cannot create additional roots when that half-line already has at most one for each integer c.

The only stationary point of g(d)=12d−d³ in [√3,∞) is d=2. The other derivative zero, −2, is outside the distance domain. The polynomial is continuous, and its strict derivative signs in the two branch interiors establish strict monotonicity including the branch endpoints.
For every integer c≤15, g(d)≥9√3>15 on [√3,2], so no root lies there; strict decrease on (2,∞) allows at most one remaining root. This includes zero and all negative integers.

For c=16, the only possible root on [√3,∞) is d=2, counted once. The factorization d³−12d+16=(d−2)²(d+4) independently confirms that the repeated root does not give two distinct distances and that −4 is inadmissible.
For every integer c≥17, there are no roots on [√3,∞), because g(d)≤16 there. Together with the preceding cases, this exhausts all integers.

The necessary lower parameter endpoint 9√3 is included, whereas 16 is excluded because the two branches meet at one distance. The exact comparison 15<9√3<16 uses positive quantities and requires no approximation or rounding.
The proof uses identities and reversible rearrangement. No equation is squared to generate candidate roots, and no exact solution of the cubic or geometric sketch is required.

prompt_html: Let \(f(x)=2x+1\) and \(g(x)=x+3\). Starting from 0, apply each function exactly twice, in any order. How many distinct final values are possible?
solution_html: The two applications of \(f\) contribute 3 in total. Each \(g\) contributes 3, 6 or 12 according as zero, one or two applications of \(f\) occur later. The six orders \(ffgg,fgfg,fggf,gffg,gfgf,ggff\) give respectively \(9,12,15,18,21,27\) when read chronologically. All are different, so the answer is 6.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Binomial counting of fixed-composition words Evaluate ordered compositions of functions Count attainable values rather than configurations Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Factorisation and algebraic expansion

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Enumerate the six chronological words with two f symbols and two g symbols by choosing the two f positions. Evaluate each word from 0, sharing common prefixes if convenient. The final values are 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 27. Check that none coincide and count the resulting set.
audited_reference.concise_proof: There are exactly C(4,2)=6 legal orders, obtained by choosing the two positions occupied by f. In chronological order, ffgg, fgfg, fggf, gffg, gfgf and ggff give final values 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 27 respectively. These six numbers are pairwise distinct, so exactly 6 distinct final values are possible. Thus A is the unique correct option.
domain_case_checks: Exactly four applications are required: two of f and two of g. Only the value after all four applications is counted.
The affine formulas are defined for every real input. Starting from 0, every intermediate value is a nonnegative integer, so all required applications are defined.
The two occurrences of f are indistinguishable, as are the two occurrences of g. Labelling copies separately would overcount operation orders.
Choosing the positions of f gives the exhaustive list ffgg, fgfg, fggf, gffg, gfgf and ggff. Each legal order appears exactly once.
The number of legal orders is only an upper bound on the number of distinct outputs until collisions have been checked. Here the six calculated outputs are pairwise distinct.
All calculations and comparisons are exact integers; no approximation or rounding is involved.

prompt_html: How many pairs of positive integers \((x,y)\) with \(x\le y\) satisfy \(x+y+xy=71\)?
solution_html:
Adding 1 gives \((x+1)(y+1)=72\). Both factors are at least 2 and the smaller is at most \(\sqrt{72}\). The possible smaller factors are \(2,3,4,6,8\). They give \((x,y)=(1,35),(2,23),(3,17),(5,11),(7,8)\).

Each pair satisfies \(x\le y\) and every factor pair has been included. Thus there are five solutions.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Factorisation and algebraic expansion Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Domain restrictions and reversible operations Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Divisibility, prime and composite factors Count distinct ordered solutions and their contribution multiplicities Symmetric expressions and swapping variables Isolate a variable in linear and reciprocal formulas Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Add 1 to obtain (x+1)(y+1)=72. Count the integer factor pairs of 72 with both factors at least 2 and the smaller factor first. The smaller factor is at most 8, so its complete eligible list is 2,3,4,6,8. Reverse the shift to check that each produces one admissible original pair.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Adding 1 gives (x+1)(y+1)=72. Set u=x+1 and v=y+1, so u and v are integers with 2≤u≤v. Thus u²≤72<81, giving 2≤u≤8. The divisors of 72 in this interval are exactly 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8, giving factor pairs (2,36), (3,24), (4,18), (6,12) and (8,9). Subtracting 1 from each coordinate gives (1,35), (2,23), (3,17), (5,11) and (7,8). The transformation is reversible, so these are all the admissible pairs. There are exactly 5, which is option D.
domain_case_checks: The task is to count all pairs of positive integers satisfying the fixed equation and x≤y. Neither variable is a freely selectable parameter whose convenient value could determine the total count.
The substitution u=x+1, v=y+1 translates positivity and ordering exactly into integer constraints 2≤u≤v. Its inverse is x=u−1, y=v−1.
The factor pair (1,72) is excluded because it would give x=0. Negative factor pairs cannot give positive original variables.
Since u≤v and u>0, u²≤uv=72. Therefore every possible smaller factor is among the integers 2 through 8. This bound is necessary, not sufficient: divisibility must still be checked.
Equality x=y is permitted by the wording but cannot occur here: it would require (x+1)²=72, whereas 8²<72<9².
Each eligible smaller factor determines exactly one larger factor and one original pair. Reversing an unequal pair violates x≤y, so no additional factor of 2 is used.
Adding 1 and shifting integer variables are reversible. All divisions used in enumeration are by positive integers; in M2, x+1≥2. No extraneous solutions are introduced.
The answer is an exact integer count, with no units or rounding required. Uniqueness of the correct option follows from the exhaustive count, not from an assumed exactly-one-correct premise.

prompt_html: What is the value of \(8+7\cdot2+6\cdot2^2+\cdots+1\cdot2^7\)?
solution_html:
Let the sum be \(S\). In \(2S-S\), the powers \(2,2^2,\ldots,2^7\) each have coefficient 1, the constant term is \(-8\), and the final term is \(2^8\). Thus \(S=-8+(2+4+\cdots+128)+256=502\).

Equivalently, each power \(2^j\) appears in \(8-j\) of the sums \(1+2+\cdots+2^m\), for \(0\le m\le7\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Scope of algebraic notation and grouping Laws of real exponentials Factorisation and algebraic expansion Finite geometric sums and quotient identities Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Eliminate choices using a valid necessary condition

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the standard shifted-sum subtraction. Define the given sum as S, multiply by 2, align equal powers and subtract S. The linear coefficient changes leave S=−8+2+2^2+⋯+2^8. Evaluate this finite geometric sum to obtain 502. For only eight terms, direct evaluation is also a reasonable ordinary alternative; the baseline does not assume a needlessly long expansion.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let S=8+7·2+6·2^2+⋯+1·2^7. Multiplying by 2 and subtracting the original sum gives 2S−S=−8+2+2^2+⋯+2^8: each overlapping power has coefficient difference 1. Hence S=−8+2(2^8−1)/(2−1)=−8+510=502. This is option C.
domain_case_checks: The expression has exactly eight terms: (8−k)2^k for integer k from 0 through 7. The initial term is 8·2^0 and the final term is 1·2^7.
The powers apply only to 2. For example, 6·2^2=24, not (6·2)^2.
Multiplying by 2 shifts every exponent up by one. In 2S−S, the unmatched endpoints are −8 and +2^8; both must be retained.
The remaining geometric sum runs from 2^1 through 2^8, inclusive. Its first term is 2, its ratio is 2, and it has eight terms.
The finite geometric identity is valid because 2−1 is nonzero. No convergence condition is needed for this finite sum, despite its ratio exceeding 1.
There are no free parameters, measurement units, rounding requirements or root-selection cases. All calculations are exact integer identities.

The modulo-4 alternative gives only a necessary condition on the value. Its MCQ selection is conditional on an answer being present; the full calculation independently verifies that exactly one original option is correct.

prompt_html: The graph \(y=(x-1)^2\), \(x\ge1\), is reflected in \(y=x\) and then translated upwards by 2. Which equation describes the result?
solution_html: Reflection exchanges the coordinates, so \(x=(y-1)^2\) and \(y\ge1\). The domain condition selects \(y=1+\sqrt x\), with \(x\ge0\). Translating upwards adds 2 to the output, giving \(y=3+\sqrt x\). The negative square-root branch is excluded by the original restriction.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Reflect graph coordinates in y=x Track graph points through affine input and output transformations Absolute values and square roots of squares Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result Eliminate choices using a valid necessary condition

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Swap x and y for the reflection, carrying x≥1 to the reflected ordinate restriction. Solve x=(z−1)² with z≥1 to obtain z=1+√x, x≥0. Then add 2 to the ordinate to obtain y=3+√x, x≥0.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Reflection in y=x swaps the coordinates. Thus the reflected graph satisfies x=(z−1)² with z≥1. Consequently z−1=√x, so z=1+√x for x≥0. Translating upwards by 2 gives y=z+2=3+√x, x≥0. Conversely, every x≥0 arises from the original point (1+√x,x), so this describes the entire transformed graph, not just some of its points. Therefore A is correct.
domain_case_checks: The coordinates are real. The original domain is [1,∞), including the endpoint (1,0). No integer restriction is imposed.
The original range is exactly [0,∞): the square is nonnegative, and every t≥0 is attained at the permitted input 1+√t.
After reflection, the domain is therefore [0,∞), and the ordinate z satisfies z≥1. This restriction selects z=1+√x rather than z=1−√x.
At x=0 the two algebraic square-root branches coincide. For x>0 the negative branch has z<1 and is inadmissible.
The upward translation preserves the reflected domain and changes its range from [1,∞) to [3,∞). The final endpoint (0,3) is included.
The stated order matters. The original endpoint goes (1,0)→(0,1)→(0,3). Translating first and then reflecting would instead send it to (2,1).
All inputs in the proposed final domain are attained, as shown by the original point (1+√x,x). No additional branch or excluded endpoint remains.

prompt_html: How many real solutions does \(\log_{x-1}(x^2-3x+2)=2\) have?
solution_html: The base requires \(x>1\) and \(x\ne2\). The argument \((x-1)(x-2)\) is then positive only when \(x>2\). Exponentiating gives \((x-1)(x-2)=(x-1)^2\). Since \(x-1\ne0\), cancellation would require \(x-2=x-1\), which is impossible. Thus there are no valid solutions.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Domain conditions for real logarithms Logarithm definition and exponential equivalence Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares Cancellation of common nonzero factors Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Logarithmic order, range and limiting behaviour

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Establish the real-logarithm domain by factoring x²−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2), obtaining x>2. Convert the equation to (x−1)(x−2)=(x−1)², divide by the known positive factor x−1, and observe that x−2=x−1 is impossible. This directly gives zero solutions.
audited_reference.concise_proof: A real logarithm requires x−1>0, x−1≠1 and x²−3x+2>0. Since x²−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2), these conditions together give x>2. On this domain the equation is equivalent to (x−1)(x−2)=(x−1)². Dividing by the positive factor x−1 gives x−2=x−1, which is impossible. Thus the solution set is empty and there are 0 real solutions, option C.
domain_case_checks: The exact real-logarithm conditions are x−1>0, x−1≠1 and (x−1)(x−2)>0. Their intersection is precisely x>2.
For x≤1 the logarithm base is nonpositive. For 1<x<2 the base is valid but the argument is negative. At x=2 the base is 1 and the argument is 0. None of these inputs is allowed.
At x=1 both the base and argument are 0. Although expansion of the exponential equality produces this formal algebraic candidate, it is not a solution of the original logarithmic equation.
For every admissible x, x−1>1 and is nonzero. Conversion to exponential form and division by x−1 are therefore reversible on the entire original domain.
The contradiction x−2=x−1 holds throughout (2,∞), so the proof excludes all real solutions rather than merely the tested integer inputs.
In M2, logarithmic monotonicity is applied with the base fixed separately at each admissible x. It is not a claim that the original variable-base function is monotone in x.
The answer is an exact count. There are no units, integer restrictions, approximations or rounding requirements.

skills.definition: Require a positive argument and a positive base different from 1 for every real logarithm, including when the base is a variable or expression.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 imposes the separate base and argument requirements and intersects them to obtain x>2; S4 rejects the formal candidate x=1.
skills.learning_objective: Find and preserve the full real domain of a logarithmic equation whose base and argument both depend on x.
skills.name: Domain conditions for real logarithms

skills.definition: For \(b>0\), \(b\ne1\), and \(a>0\), translate \(\log_b a=x\) equivalently into \(b^x=a\), preserving the roles of base, argument and exponent.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 converts the source equation to an equality with (x−1)²; S6 uses log_b(b²)=2 under a valid base.

skills.learning_objective: Factor the argument to expose its relationship to the variable base while preserving equality.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

solution_html: Let \(S\) be the sum. Replacing \(k\) by \(10-k\) leaves each sine square unchanged, so \(2S=10\sum_{k=1}^9\sin^2(k\pi/10)\). Pair \(k\) with \(5-k\) for \(k=1,2\) to see that the first four sine squares sum to 2. The last four repeat them, and the middle term at \(k=5\) is 1. Thus the unweighted sum is 5 and \(S=25\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Sine equality at supplementary angles Pair reflected indices in a finite weighted sum Evaluate standard-angle sine and cosine values Convert sine of a complementary angle Pythagorean trigonometric identity Allowed sine and cosine values Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Pair indices k and 10−k using sin(π−u)=sin u. Their coefficients add to 10; retain the middle term k=5 separately. In the remaining four squared sine values, pair complementary angles and apply sin²u+cos²u=1. This avoids evaluating any nonstandard individual trigonometric value.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put a_k = sin²(kπ/10). Since sin(π−u)=sin u, we have a_{10−k}=a_k. Pairing indices (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), (4,6), and retaining k=5 separately, gives S=10(a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4)+5, because a_5=1. The angles for indices 1 and 4 are complementary, as are those for indices 2 and 3. Hence a_1+a_4=1 and a_2+a_3=1 by sin²u+cos²u=1. Therefore S=10(1+1)+5=25, so D is the unique correct option.
domain_case_checks: The index k takes exactly the nine integers 1 through 9. There is no free parameter to choose or optimize.
The arguments kπ/10 are fixed real radian angles. Sine and its square are defined at every such angle; the constant denominator 10 is nonzero.
The reflection k↦10−k preserves the index set. Its four two-element pairs are (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), and (4,6); its only fixed index is 5, which must be included once.
At the fixed index, 5sin²(5π/10)=5sin²(π/2)=5.
The secondary complementary pairings cover indices 1 through 4 exactly once: π/10+4π/10=π/2 and 2π/10+3π/10=π/2.
Every regrouping is an equality of finite sums. No limiting argument, convergence assumption, equation-squaring, root selection, or variable-dependent division is used.
The result is exact and dimensionless. No approximation or rounding is requested or needed.

skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 establishes a_{10−k}=a_k, which makes reflected weighted terms combinable.

skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 uses the four pairs (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), and (4,6), adding their coefficients to 10 and retaining index 5 once.

skills.name: Pair reflected indices in a finite weighted sum

skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 evaluates sin²(5π/10)=sin²(π/2)=1, giving the separate contribution 5.

prompt_html: What is the minimum over real x of \(\dfrac{\sin^4x}{1+\cos^2x}+\dfrac{\cos^4x}{1+\sin^2x}\)?
solution_html: Put \(a=\sin^2x\), \(b=\cos^2x\), so \(a+b=1\) and \(a,b\ge0\). On a common denominator the expression is \((a^2+b^2+a^3+b^3)/(1+a+b+ab)\). With \(u=ab\), this becomes \((2-5u)/(2+u)=-5+12/(2+u)\). Also \(0\le u\le1/4\), because \((a-b)^2\ge0\). The reciprocal decreases as \(u\) increases, so the minimum is at \(u=1/4\) and equals \(1/3\). It is attained when \(\sin^2x=\cos^2x=1/2\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Pythagorean trigonometric identity Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Domain restrictions and reversible operations Symmetric expressions and swapping variables Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares Global extrema from attained bounds Exact trigonometric values for special acute angles Two-term Cauchy–Schwarz bound for quadratic quotients

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the Pythagorean identity to set a=sin²x, b=cos²x with a+b=1. Interchange symmetry suggests testing a=b=1/2, giving the candidate 1/3. Certify it by combining fractions to obtain F−1/3=4(a−b)²/[3(1+a)(1+b)]≥0, then verify equality at x=π/4. This is a short elementary algebraic proof; differentiation is unnecessary.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let a = sin²x and b = cos²x. Then a,b ≥ 0, a+b = 1, and both denominators are positive. Writing F for the expression, combination over a common denominator gives F − 1/3 = [3a²(1+a) + 3b²(1+b) − (1+a)(1+b)]/[3(1+a)(1+b)] = 4(a−b)²/[3(1+a)(1+b)] ≥ 0. To check the simplification, use a²+b² = 1−2ab and a³+b³ = 1−3ab. Equality holds exactly when a=b=1/2. At x=π/4, each original fraction is (1/4)/(3/2)=1/6, so F=1/3. Thus the minimum is 1/3, option E.
domain_case_checks: The domain is all real x. Since squared sine and cosine are nonnegative, both original denominators are at least 1. There are no excluded angles or poles.
Every real x gives a,b ≥ 0 with a+b=1, hence 0≤a,b≤1. The substituted variables must not be treated as independent.
The common denominator 3(1+a)(1+b) is strictly positive, so the sign of F−1/3 is determined by the nonnegative square in its numerator.
The boundary cases a=0 or b=0 are permitted and give F=1. Neither can improve the attained value 1/3.
Equality in the lower bound requires a=b=1/2 and is realized by x=π/4. This proves an attained minimum, not merely an infimum or a trial value.
Only squared sine and cosine enter the substituted expression. Equality does not require sin x and cos x to have the same sign; equal squared magnitudes are sufficient.
The argument is uniform over all real x, so no search over periods or stationary points is needed. No equation-squaring, root extraction or division by sine or cosine introduces additional cases.
All calculations are exact. No approximation or rounding is required, and the proof does not assume that one of the listed options must be correct.

subtopic: A cyclic implication with one exception
prompt_html: The statements \(P_1,\ldots,P_8\) are arranged in a cycle, with \(P_9=P_1\). For each \(i=1,\ldots,8\), form the statement “If \(P_i\) is true, then \(P_{i+1}\) is true”. Exactly one of these eight statements is false. How many assignments of true or false to \(P_1,\ldots,P_8\) are possible?
solution_html: A false implication is exactly a transition from true to false around the cycle. Having exactly one such transition means the true positions form one nonempty proper consecutive block. Choose the start of that block in 8 ways and its length from 1 through 7. Each assignment has exactly one start and length, so none is double-counted. The total is \(8\times7=56\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Material implication and disjunctive form Finite-count statements and their complements Bijective counting and representation multiplicity Multiplication principle for finite choices Count fixed-size unordered subsets

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Translate a false implication into a T→F edge. Exactly one such edge means that all true entries form one nonempty proper cyclic block. Choose its first labelled position in eight ways and its length from 1 through 7. Prove that this encoding is exhaustive and unique, then multiply to obtain 56.
audited_reference.concise_proof: An implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. The all-true and all-false assignments therefore have no false implications. In any other cyclic assignment, each maximal consecutive block of true values ends at exactly one T→F edge, and these are precisely the false implications. Thus the condition is equivalent to having one nonempty true block and one nonempty false block. A valid assignment is uniquely specified by the labelled position at which its true block begins and its length k, where 1≤k≤7. Conversely, each of the eight starting positions and seven permitted lengths gives exactly one false implication. Hence there are 8×7=56 assignments.
domain_case_checks: Each of P1,...,P8 has one Boolean truth value. There are eight directed implications, including P8 ⇒ P1.
Exactly one false statement refers to the eight formed implications, not to the underlying statements P1,...,P8.
The all-false and all-true assignments give zero false implications. They correspond to excluded true-block lengths 0 and 8.
Every separate cyclic true block contributes one T→F edge. Consequently multiple true blocks are forbidden, while every single nonempty proper true block is sufficient.
The true-block length is an integer from 1 through 7, with both endpoints allowed. For example, (T,F,F,F,F,F,F,F) has its sole false implication at P1 ⇒ P2.

Blocks crossing from P8 to P1 are included by cyclic indexing. The first true position means the unique true position immediately following a false position, not necessarily the lowest numbered true position.
Assignments are counted at fixed labelled positions. Neither rotations nor complementary assignments are identified.

In M2, the two change edges must be distinct but may be adjacent. Choosing the truth value at P1 then determines a unique consistent assignment because exactly two changes return to the starting truth value.
The answer is an exact integer count. The constructive encodings and their inverses establish completeness and exclude duplicate representations.

prompt_html: A fair coin is tossed six times. Given that exactly three tosses are heads, what is the probability that no two heads are consecutive?
solution_html: Conditional on exactly three heads, all \(\binom63=20\) choices of their positions are equally likely. Arrange the three tails first. They create four gaps: before, between and after the tails. To keep heads separated, put one head in each of three different gaps. There are \(\binom43=4\) choices, so the probability is \(4/20=1/5\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Model finite random-experiment events Condition on the correct event and denominator Independent trials and path probabilities Binomial counting of fixed-composition words Bijective counting and representation multiplicity Favourable-over-total probability ratio Add disjoint counting cases

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Restrict to the C(6,3)=20 equally likely strings containing exactly three heads. Arrange the three tails first, creating four gaps including the two ends. To prevent consecutive heads, place one head in each of three different gaps; equivalently, choose the one unused gap. This gives four favourable strings and probability 4/20=1/5.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let B be the event of exactly three heads and E the event of no consecutive heads. Under the standard independent fair-toss model, every six-toss string has probability 1/64. Thus, conditional on B, the C(6,3)=20 strings are equally likely. The three tails create four gaps: _ T _ T _ T _. A string in E∩B has at most one head in each gap, so its three heads occupy three of the four gaps. Conversely, every such choice gives a valid string, uniquely. There are therefore four favourable strings, giving P(E|B)=4/20=1/5.
domain_case_checks: The experiment consists of six chronological tosses, with exactly three heads and hence exactly three tails after conditioning.

Use the standard model of independent tosses of a fair coin. Independence establishes the original string probabilities; it is not asserted for the tosses after conditioning on their total number of heads.
The conditioning event has probability C(6,3)/64=20/64=5/16>0, so the conditional probability is defined.
Consecutive means adjacent positions among 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5 and 5–6. Positions 1 and 6 are not adjacent.
Only adjacent heads are forbidden. Adjacent tails are allowed, as in HTTHTH and HTHTTH.
Both exterior gaps are included. Choosing three different gaps is necessary and sufficient, and removing the heads recovers a unique gap selection, so there are no missing or duplicated outcomes.
The result is an exact, dimensionless probability in [0,1]. No approximation or rounding is required.
The calculation establishes which option is correct independently of any assumed single-correct-option guarantee.

prompt_html: What are the last two decimal digits of \(7^{222}\)?
solution_html: Since \(7^4=2401\equiv1\pmod{100}\) and \(222=4\cdot55+2\), the required remainder is \(7^2\equiv49\pmod{100}\). The modulus is 100 because two digits are requested; a units-digit cycle alone would not determine the answer.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Laws of real exponentials Prove a recurrence period from a repeated state Index reduction with a correct modular offset Division algorithm and the remainder range Eliminate choices using a valid necessary condition

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Work modulo 100. Calculate 7^2=49 and 7^4=2401≡1. Write 222=4×55+2, then use 7^{222}=(7^4)^{55}7^2≡49. Match the resulting two-digit remainder to the options.
audited_reference.concise_proof: The last two decimal digits are the remainder modulo 100, written with two digits. Since 7^2=49 and 7^4=2401≡1 (mod 100), and 222=4×55+2, we have 7^{222}=(7^4)^{55}7^2≡1^{55}×49=49 (mod 100). Thus the last two digits are 49, uniquely option E.
domain_case_checks: The task concerns the exact final two digits of the positive integer 7^{222}; neither approximation nor rounding is appropriate.
The required remainder is modulo 100, not modulo 10. Its canonical range is 0≤r<100, with leading-zero padding when necessary.
The exponent and base are fixed. Neither may be replaced by a convenient value without a proved relationship.
Exponent reduction is justified by 7^4≡1 (mod 100): for every integer n≥0, 7^{n+4}≡7^n (mod 100). It is not inferred merely from a few observed terms.
The decomposition 222=4×55+2 has canonical remainder 2. If the remainder had been zero, the residual power would have been 7^0=1; that boundary case does not occur here.
No modular division or cancellation is used. The argument relies only on multiplication and nonnegative integer powers of congruent integers.
All five options are distinct two-digit representations of numbers between 0 and 99, and exactly one equals the proved remainder.

subtopic: Root existence from opposite end behaviour
prompt_html: Which fact directly supplies the hypotheses for applying the intermediate value theorem to prove that every real polynomial of odd degree has at least one real zero?

options.html: It has at most as many roots as its degree.
options.label: B

options.html: It is continuous and has opposite signs for sufficiently large positive and negative inputs.
options.label: E

solution_html:
For a real polynomial of odd degree, the leading term has opposite signs at sufficiently large negative and positive inputs, and lower-degree terms do not change those eventual signs. Choose finite inputs \(u<v\) with \(P(u)P(v)<0\). A polynomial is continuous on \([u,v]\), so the intermediate value theorem gives \(c\in(u,v)\) with \(P(c)=0\). Thus E directly supplies the required hypotheses.

Option D can also lead to a proof: an even-degree derivative implies an odd-degree leading term for the original polynomial, from which opposite end signs follow. However, D does not itself state the hypotheses for a direct application of the intermediate value theorem, which is what the revised question asks.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Continuous level attainment by the intermediate value theorem Polynomial end behaviour Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Differentiate polynomials Construct a legal counterexample

audited_reference.ordinary_method: Use continuity and a finite opposite-sign bracket to apply the intermediate value theorem, then match those two hypotheses directly to E.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let p be a real polynomial of odd degree n with leading coefficient a≠0. Leading-term dominance makes p(R) and p(−R) have opposite signs for sufficiently large R>0. Polynomials are continuous on [−R,R]. The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a point c in this interval with p(c)=0. E directly supplies continuity and the sign bracket.
domain_case_checks: Odd degree is positive and its leading coefficient is nonzero.
Choose finite endpoints with opposite signs; infinity is not an IVT endpoint.
The argument works for either sign of the leading coefficient.
The conclusion is existence, not uniqueness or an upper root-count bound.

subtopic: A root count equivalent to a tangent condition
prompt_html:
For real \(k\), let \(f_k(x)=x^3-3x+k\). Consider:

P: \(f_k(x)=0\) has three distinct real solutions.

Q: At some point on the curve, the tangent passes through the origin and has negative gradient.

For Q, condition P is:
solution_html:
The stationary heights are \(f_k(-1)=k+2\) and \(f_k(1)=k-2\). Therefore P holds exactly when \(-2<k<2\).

The tangent at \(x=t\) is \(y=(3t^2-3)x+k-2t^3\). It passes through the origin exactly when \(k=2t^3\), and has negative gradient exactly when \(|t|<1\). Since \(2t^3\) is strictly increasing, such a \(t\) exists exactly when \(-2<k<2\).

Both conditions describe the same parameter interval, so P is necessary and sufficient for Q. At \(k=\pm2\), a repeated root appears and the corresponding tangent has zero gradient; both strict conditions fail.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Differentiate a polynomial with parameters Factorisation and algebraic expansion Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Derivative signs and monotonic intervals Polynomial end behaviour Continuous level attainment by the intermediate value theorem Distinct roots from monotone graph branches Tangent-line equation and intercept Invert real odd powers Distinguish strict, inclusive and degenerate boundaries Separate example checking from a universal proof

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Differentiate once. Use the two stationary values, monotone branches and cubic tails to find the exact k-range for three distinct real zeros. Form the tangent at a general coordinate t, impose zero y-intercept and strictly negative slope, and find the exact k-range for Q using the real cube root. Compare the two ranges. There is no need to solve the cubic's zeros explicitly.
audited_reference.concise_proof:
We have f'_k(x)=3(x²−1). Thus f_k increases on (−∞,−1), decreases on (−1,1), and increases on (1,∞), with f_k(−1)=k+2 and f_k(1)=k−2. Its tails tend to −∞ and +∞ respectively. By continuity and strict monotonicity, there is one zero in each open branch exactly when k+2>0>k−2. At k=±2 there are only two distinct zeros, and outside [−2,2] there is only one. Hence P ⇔ −2<k<2.
At x=t, the tangent is y=f_k(t)+f'_k(t)(x−t)=(3t²−3)x+k−2t³. It passes through the origin with negative gradient exactly when k=2t³ and −1<t<1. These conditions imply −2<k<2. Conversely, for any −2<k<2, take t=∛(k/2); then −1<t<1 and both tangent conditions hold. Thus Q ⇔ −2<k<2, so P is both necessary and sufficient for Q.
domain_case_checks: The parameter k and the variables x and t are real. The cubic is continuous and differentiable everywhere, with finite derivative, so there is no vertical-tangent exception.

Q requires one point whose tangent satisfies both conditions simultaneously. Its tangency coordinate may depend on k. The tangent can pass through the origin without the curve itself passing through the origin.
For −2<k<2, continuity supplies a zero on each of the three open monotone branches, and strict monotonicity makes each zero unique. The branches are disjoint.

At k=2, f_k(x)=(x−1)²(x+2), with distinct roots −2 and 1. At k=−2, f_k(x)=(x+1)²(x−2), with distinct roots −1 and 2. Neither boundary satisfies P. For k>2 only the left branch crosses the axis; for k<−2 only the right branch does.

Negative gradient means 3t²−3<0, not ≤0. At k=2 the unique origin-passing tangent has t=1 and gradient zero; at k=−2 it has t=−1 and gradient zero. These tangents do not satisfy Q. Outside [−2,2], the origin-passing tangent has positive gradient.
At k=0, the admissible tangency coordinate is t=0 and the tangent is y=−3x. Also f_0 has the three distinct roots −√3, 0 and √3. No division by t is used, so this valid case is retained.

The real cube root exists for every real k/2, including negative values. The tangent conditions are transformed reversibly, with division only by nonzero constants; no squaring step introduces extraneous solutions.

Both implications are proved for every real k by complete parameter classifications. Agreement at selected values of k is not being used as a universal proof. No numerical approximation or rounding is required.

subtopic: An equality case does not reverse an inequality
prompt_html:
For positive real \(x\), consider the statement: \(x+1/x\geq2\) only if \(x=1\).

I. The statement is true.

II. Its converse is true.

III. Its contrapositive, “if \(x\ne1\) then \(x+1/x<2\)”, is true.

Which are true?
solution_html:
For every positive \(x\), \(x+1/x-2=(x-1)^2/x\geq0\). The inequality holds for all positive \(x\), not just \(x=1\). At \(x=2\) the inequality is true but the conclusion \(x=1\) is false, so I is false.

The converse says that if \(x=1\) then the inequality holds; substituting gives equality, so II is true. The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original statement and is also false, again witnessed by \(x=2\). Thus II only is true. The familiar equality condition applies to \(x+1/x=2\), not to \(x+1/x\geq2\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Distinguish converse from original statement Negate and reverse to form a contrapositive Construct a legal counterexample Negate simple comparative statements Separate example checking from a universal proof Domain restrictions and reversible operations Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Translate “P only if Q” as P⇒Q, where P is x+1/x≥2 and Q is x=1. Use the legal value x=2 to refute the original. Check the converse directly at its only true-antecedent input, x=1. The contrapositive is equivalent to the original, so it too is false; the same x=2 verifies this directly. Match the resulting truth vector to the options. No general inequality theorem is needed.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let P(x) mean x+1/x≥2 and Q(x) mean x=1. The original statement is P⇒Q. At the permitted value x=2, P is true because 2+1/2=5/2≥2, but Q is false. Thus I is false. The converse is Q⇒P: when x=1, x+1/x=2, so II is true. The contrapositive ¬Q⇒¬P is equivalent to the original and is therefore false; directly, x=2 also contradicts its conclusion 5/2<2. Hence the truth values are (false, true, false), giving C, II only.
domain_case_checks: The statement is understood universally over x>0. The legal value x=2 suffices to refute I and III; testing every positive real is unnecessary for these refutations.
Both x=1 and x=2 are permitted. The restriction x>0 excludes x=0, so the reciprocal is defined at every permitted input.
The original implication is false precisely when its antecedent is true and its conclusion false. At x=2 these conditions are verified exactly, without approximation.
For the converse, its antecedent x=1 restricts the non-vacuous check to one value. At every other permitted value its antecedent is false, so the implication is true.
The exact negation of x+1/x≥2 is x+1/x<2, not x+1/x≤2. Thus the printed statement III is indeed the contrapositive.
Equality is included in ≥2: x=1 gives 2≥2. In the alternative identity proof, equality holds exactly when (x−1)²=0, namely x=1.
For the alternative proof, x>0 ensures that (x−1)²/x is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive when x≠1. No multiplication by an expression of unknown sign is used.
There is no premise that exactly one of I, II and III must be true. Their truth values are established independently of such a premise, and then every offered combination is checked.

skills.learning_objective: Refute a universal implication by checking both its premise and the failure of its conclusion at one permitted input.

skills.definition:
Form the exact logical complement of an atomic real comparison, including \(
eg(x\ge a)\iff x<a\), \(
eg(x>a)\iff x\le a\), \(
eg(x\le a)\iff x>a\), and \(
eg(x<a)\iff x\ge a\), retaining the correct equality boundary.

skills.learning_objective: Negate the displayed non-strict comparison with the correct strict boundary when checking the contrapositive.

skills.definition: Distinguish finite example checking from proof of a universally quantified statement.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 uses a failed instance only for refutation. S3 explains why substitution at x=1 is complete for the converse, whose antecedent fixes x.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish a counterexample to a universal statement from a successful example, and recognise when an antecedent reduces the proof to one possible input.

skills.definition: Identify expression domains and conditions under which algebraic transformations preserve equivalence.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 retains x>0; S2 and S3 use permitted values. S6 relies on the denominator x being positive when determining the sign of the quotient.

skills.definition: Expand, factor and collect algebraic expressions while retaining equality.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S6 rewrites x+1/x−2 as (x²−2x+1)/x=(x−1)²/x.
skills.learning_objective: Rewrite a reciprocal expression's excess above a bound as a square divided by the original variable.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

skills.definition: Determine signs of real expressions, squares and products, including zero cases.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S6 uses (x−1)²≥0 and x>0 to prove nonnegativity, with strict positivity away from x=1.
skills.learning_objective: Separate the zero and positive cases of a square quotient to distinguish a lower bound from its equality condition.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: For x>0, x+1/x−2=(x−1)²/x≥0, with equality exactly at x=1. Hence the antecedent of the original holds even when x≠1, while the conclusion of III is false at every such input. Taking x=2 witnesses both failures. Substitution at x=1 proves the converse.
limitations: This requires more algebra than M1 and is not a material shortcut.
The equality condition must not be substituted for the condition ≥2.
The positivity of x is essential to the sign argument.
useful_alternatives.method: Prove the domain-wide bound and equality condition using a square quotient, then evaluate the three implications directly.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when explaining why the familiar inequality is true but the original “only if” claim is false, or when a student prefers a global algebraic description to immediate numerical testing.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 deliberately chooses x=2 as a legal counterexample and checks the converse at x=1.

The choice x=2 respects x>0 and keeps arithmetic exact.
For the converse, x=1 is forced by its antecedent rather than freely chosen to represent all cases.

No invariance argument or freely adjustable fixed datum is being assumed.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose Your Own Numbers: choose x=2 for refutation, not as a representative proof of all positive inputs.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is the ordinary counterexample method, not an extra shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: No additional work relative to M1.

The remaining combinations A, C and G are distinguished by the actual proof, not by an assumed exactly-one-true premise for I–III.

The source does not assert that exactly one numbered statement is true, so that stronger premise must not be imposed.

subtopic: Two different similarity ratios in one diagram
prompt_html: In triangle \(ABC\), points \(D\) and \(E\) lie on the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\), respectively, with \(DE\parallel BC\). Lines \(BE\) and \(CD\) meet at \(P\). The area of triangle \(PBC\) is 25 times the area of triangle \(PDE\). What is \(AD:DB\)?
solution_html:
Triangles \(PBC\) and \(PED\) are similar: the angle at \(P\) is vertically opposite and the remaining corresponding angles follow from \(DE\parallel BC\). Their area ratio of \(25\) therefore gives \(BC:DE=5:1\).

Triangles \(ADE\) and \(ABC\) are also similar, so \(AD/AB=DE/BC=1/5\). But the question asks for \(AD:DB\), not \(AD:AB\). Since \(DB=AB-AD=4AB/5\), the required ratio is \(1:4\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Similarity, scale and preserved ratios Area scaling for similar figures Part-to-whole fractions and complements Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result Choose coordinates and compute planar distances Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions Basic planar area formulas

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use AA similarity of PBC and PED to convert the area ratio 25:1 into BC:DE = 5:1. Then use ADE ∼ ABC to obtain AB:AD = 5:1. Subtract AD from AB to get DB = 4AD, hence AD:DB = 1:4.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Since DE is parallel to BC, triangles PBC and PED are similar by AA: their angles at P are vertically opposite, and their angles at B and E are equal alternate angles. Hence 25 = [PBC]/[PDE] = (BC/DE)². Lengths are positive, so BC/DE = 5. Also, ADE ∼ ABC, giving AD/AB = DE/BC = 1/5. Therefore DB = AB − AD = 4AB/5, and AD:DB = 1:4.
domain_case_checks: The task concerns nondegenerate Euclidean triangles and unsigned lengths and areas. The multiplier 25 is exact, and the requested ratio is dimensionless; no rounding or integer-length restriction is involved.

The endpoints are inadmissible: D = E = A would collapse DE, while D = B and E = C would make BE and CD the same line and collapse the named shaded triangles. Thus the stated configuration has D and E in the interiors of their sides.
DECB is then a convex trapezoid. Its diagonals BE and CD intersect internally, so P lies between the parallel bases and both shaded triangle areas are positive.
The first similarity has correspondence PBC ∼ PED, not an unverified left-to-left pairing. The second has correspondence ADE ∼ ABC.
BC/DE is positive, so its square being 25 gives 5, not −5. Every area and side length used as a denominator is nonzero.
AD/AB = 1/5 lies strictly between 0 and 1. Subtracting from the same whole gives DB/AB = 4/5, so the requested denominator DB is positive.

For any nondegenerate ABC, choosing D one fifth of the way from A to B and drawing DE parallel to BC produces an admissible E and an internal intersection P. The similarities then give the stated area ratio 25, establishing attainability as well as necessity.
The proof does not require an isosceles, acute or right triangle. The parallel-line angle arguments apply to every admissible shape.

skills.definition: Use justified similarity to transfer scale and side ratios between figures.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 establishes PBC ∼ PED by AA and identifies BC with ED. S3 establishes ADE ∼ ABC and transfers DE/BC to AD/AB.
skills.learning_objective: Establish AA similarity using parallel and intersecting lines, then preserve vertex correspondence when transferring ratios.
skills.name: Similarity, scale and preserved ratios

skills.definition: For similar plane figures with positive finite areas and positive length scale factor k, use the area ratio k² and recover the length scale from a positive area ratio.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 converts area ratio 25 into corresponding length ratio 5. S5 uses the same square law to verify each candidate.
skills.learning_objective: Recover the positive corresponding length ratio from a similar-triangle area ratio rather than applying the area multiplier directly to lengths.
skills.name: Area scaling for similar figures

skills.definition: Express the size of a specified part as a fraction of a positive whole, and obtain the remaining fraction by subtracting from one while retaining the same reference whole.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S4 turns AD/AB = 1/5 into DB/AB = 4/5. S5 and S8 use the general conversion between a part-to-whole fraction and a part-to-remainder ratio.
skills.learning_objective: Convert a known fraction AD/AB into the requested ratio AD:DB by taking the complement with respect to AB.
skills.name: Part-to-whole fractions and complements

skills.definition: Identify expression domains and conditions under which algebraic transformations preserve equivalence.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The setup excludes collapsed endpoints. S2 selects a positive length ratio, and S6–S8 retain 0 < t < 1 and positive denominators.
skills.learning_objective: Exclude degenerate configurations and preserve positivity when dividing or recovering a length ratio from its square.
skills.name: Domain restrictions and reversible operations

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S5 tests all original options against the area relation and verifies an admissible construction. S8 independently recovers and checks the same ratio.
skills.learning_objective: Verify both the original area condition and the exact requested pair of segments before selecting an option.
skills.name: Substitute or independently check a proposed result

skills.definition: Choose planar coordinates and use them to calculate geometric positions or distances.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S6 represents a general triangle by B = (0,0), C = (b,0), A = (u,h) and determines D and E from their common height.
skills.learning_objective: Choose coordinates that simplify parallel bases without imposing an unstated special shape.
skills.name: Choose coordinates and compute planar distances

skills.definition: Solve simultaneous equations while checking consistency and completeness of the solution set.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S7 equates the two parameterizations P = λE and P = C + μ(D − C), obtaining λ = μ = 1/(1+t).
skills.learning_objective: Find a line intersection by equating coordinate representations and checking that the solution is admissible.
skills.name: Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions

skills.definition: Calculate the areas of triangles, rectangles and squares from valid dimensions, using perpendicular height for a triangle and squared side length for a square.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S8 uses horizontal bases BC and DE and their vertical perpendicular distances from P to derive the two areas directly.
skills.learning_objective: Use each triangle's own perpendicular height when comparing areas with different parallel bases.
skills.name: Basic planar area formulas

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Take B = (0,0), C = (b,0), A = (u,h), with b,h > 0, and t = AD/AB in (0,1). Parallelism gives D and E height H = (1−t)h and DE = tb. Solving the two line equations gives P height H/(1+t). The two areas are therefore bH/(2(1+t)) and bt²H/(2(1+t)), whose ratio is 1/t². Setting this equal to 25 gives t = 1/5 and AD:DB = 1:4.
limitations: It is longer than the two-AA-similarity method.
The general vertex coordinates must be retained; choosing a special shape without justification is not a general proof.
The heights from P to the two bases are different and must not be treated as equal.
useful_alternatives.method: General-coordinate intersection and direct base-height areas
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful as an independent algebraic check or for a candidate who prefers coordinates. It derives the area-ratio equation directly without invoking AA similarity or the similar-figure area-scaling theorem.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: two AA similarities, a positive square root and a part-to-remainder conversion.
conditions_checked: BC is positive and no absolute length scale is fixed.
Under a common positive rescaling by s, both lengths in a length ratio gain a factor s and both areas gain a factor s², so the two ratios are unchanged.
A general vertex A = (u,h), with h > 0, must be retained; a right angle or isosceles shape cannot be assumed.
limitations: A convenient shape alone would be only an example unless invariance were proved.
The coordinate calculation remains longer than M1.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose Your Own Numbers — a coordinate variant may normalize BC to 1. M2 keeps BC = b to display the same scale independence explicitly.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Safe ordinary normalization, but no material saving over M1.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: At most one common base-length factor in the longer coordinate method; nothing beyond the work already avoided by M1.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: two AA similarities, a positive square root and a part-to-remainder conversion.
conditions_checked: Parallel bases and vertically opposite angles justify the correspondence PBC ∼ PED.
A dilation centred at P maps E to B and D to C with a negative signed factor because the rays are opposite.
The second similarity is centred at A and has positive scale.
No reflection symmetry of ABC is given.
limitations: The apparent mirror symmetry does not justify equal sides or a centroid claim.
Rephrasing AA similarity as a dilation does not remove a step from M1.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Mirror, Move, Match — match the opposite triangles by AA, or equivalently by a dilation centred at P, then transfer the scale through the triangles sharing A.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is the ordinary similarity solution, not an additional shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Explicit lengths and altitudes are unnecessary, but M1 already avoids them.

prompt_html:
Let \(b>4\), and define

\[F(x)=\int_0^x t(t-2)(t-4)\,dt\qquad(0\leq x\leq b).\]

For which value of \(b\) is the global maximum value of \(F\) attained at exactly two distinct values of \(x\)?
solution_html:
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(F'(x)=x(x-2)(x-4)\). Its signs show that \(F\) increases on \((0,2)\), decreases on \((2,4)\), and increases on \((4,b)\). Consequently only \(x=2\) and \(x=b\) can give global maxima.

Integration gives \[F(x)=x^4/4-2x^3+4x^2=\frac{x^2(x-4)^2}{4},\qquad F(2)=4.\]

The two candidate heights tie when \(b^2(b-4)^2=16\). Since \(b>4\), this means \(b(b-4)=4\), giving \(b=2+2\sqrt2\). Strict monotonicity between the stationary points and endpoints ensures exactly two maximising points.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Derivative of a variable-upper-limit integral Signs of real quantities and squares Derivative signs and monotonic intervals Distinct roots from monotone graph branches Establish an attained global extremum Split and combine definite integrals Translate the variable and integral limits Integrate powers and evaluate endpoints Factorisation and algebraic expansion Solving quadratics and checking roots Domain restrictions and reversible operations Exact surd and rational arithmetic Complete the square and locate a quadratic vertex

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Read F' from the continuous integrand and use its +,−,+ sign pattern to identify x=2 and x=b as the only possible global maximum locations. A tie is necessary and sufficient. Evaluate only their signed height difference: cancel the common integral from 0 to 2, translate t by 2, integrate the two resulting power terms, and solve the zero condition subject to b>4.
audited_reference.concise_proof:
The integrand is continuous, so F'(x)=x(x−2)(x−4) in the interior of the domain. Its signs are +, −, + on (0,2), (2,4), (4,b). Thus F attains its maximum on [0,4] only at x=2, and its maximum on [4,b] only at x=b. Exactly two global maximizers therefore occur if and only if F(b)=F(2).
Put d=b−2>2. Cancelling the common part of the integrals and setting u=t−2 gives
F(b)−F(2)=∫₂ᵇ t(t−2)(t−4)dt=∫₀ᵈ(u³−4u)du=d⁴/4−2d²=d²(d²−8)/4.
Since d>2, this vanishes exactly when d=2√2. Hence b=2+2√2, which satisfies b>4. The strict monotonicity on the three branches ensures that the only maximizers are x=2 and x=b.
domain_case_checks: The task concerns real b>4 and every real x in the closed interval [0,b]. No physical units or integer restriction are specified. The polynomial integrand is continuous, so F is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable in its interior.

The derivative sign pattern is strict on each of (0,2), (2,4) and (4,b). Consequently x=0 and x=4 cannot be global maximizers, and there is no constant interval that could produce infinitely many maximizers.

The endpoint x=b is included. It can be a global maximizer even though F is strictly increasing immediately to its left; the stationary-point condition for an interior extremum does not exclude endpoint extrema.
The cancellation F(b)−F(2)=∫₂ᵇ t(t−2)(t−4)dt preserves signed contributions. The contribution on (2,4) is negative, whereas that on (4,b) is positive.
Under u=t−2, the bounds become 0 and d=b−2>2, and dt=du. Dividing d²(d²−8)=0 by d² is valid because d>2. The discarded possibility d=0 would give b=2, outside the stated domain.
The equation d²=8 has roots ±2√2, but d>2 permits only the positive root. Its corresponding b=2+2√2 is greater than 4 because √2>1.
Writing c=2+2√2 gives a complete classification: for 4<b<c the sole maximizer is x=2; for b=c the maximizers are exactly x=2 and x=b; for b>c the sole maximizer is x=b.
The value b=4 is excluded by the strict parameter restriction. Even at that boundary the height difference F(4)−F(2) is −4, not zero.
All calculations are exact. There are no variable denominators beyond the explicitly checked positive factor d², and no rounding or approximation is required.

skills.definition: For a real continuous function g on [a,c], differentiate the accumulation function H(x)=∫_a^x g(t)dt at interior points a<x<c to obtain H'(x)=g(x), keeping the integrand distinct from its derivative.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 reads F'(x)=x(x−2)(x−4) directly from the integral definition. M2 instead evaluates F explicitly and uses algebraic bounds.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the derivative of a continuous accumulation integral directly from its integrand.
skills.name: Derivative of a variable-upper-limit integral

skills.definition: Determine signs of real expressions, squares and products, including zero cases.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 determines the signs of the three linear factors on successive intervals. S8 uses nonnegative inner factors before comparing their squares.
skills.learning_objective: Determine product signs on root-separated intervals and check nonnegativity before squaring a bound.
skills.name: Signs of real quantities and squares

skills.definition: Use a known derivative's sign on intervals to establish strict increase or decrease and classify stationary turning points, checking both sides rather than assuming every derivative zero is an extremum.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 and S2 use the +,−,+ pattern to establish strict branches, a peak at x=2, and the endpoint maximum on [4,b].
skills.learning_objective: Translate derivative signs into strict monotonicity and correctly classified turning points.
skills.name: Derivative signs and monotonic intervals

skills.definition: Count distinct solutions of f(x)=k on a stated real domain using continuous strictly monotone branches and their finite or infinite endpoint values. Use continuity for existence, monotonicity for uniqueness, and count shared endpoints only once.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 excludes every maximum-level contact except x=2 and x=b. S5 and S6 distinguish a tie from a unique maximizer and do not count x=2 twice merely because two branches meet there.
skills.learning_objective: Count distinct maximum-level contacts using strict branches and included endpoints.
skills.name: Distinct roots from monotone graph branches

skills.definition: Prove a universal upper or lower bound over a feasible set and exhibit a feasible point attaining it, identifying equality conditions when needed. Distinguish an attained extremum from an unproved trial value or an unattained bound.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 bounds every value by one of the two candidate heights. S5 verifies the equality case. S8 and S9 provide the corresponding algebraic bound and equality locations in M2.
skills.learning_objective: Prove that candidate heights bound the whole domain and identify every point attaining the bound.
skills.name: Establish an attained global extremum

skills.definition: Split, combine and reverse definite integrals with correct coefficients and oriented bounds.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 cancels the shared integral on [0,2]. S4 and S7 integrate finite polynomial sums with their coefficients retained.
skills.learning_objective: Cancel overlapping accumulated integrals and preserve the orientation and coefficients of the remaining integral.
skills.name: Split and combine definite integrals

skills.definition: Translate an integration variable and update every bound and term consistently; general nonlinear substitutions may need a separate skill.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 uses u=t−2, changes the limits from 2,b to 0,b−2, and transforms the integrand to u(u²−4).
skills.learning_objective: Translate an integration variable while updating its bounds, factors and differential consistently.
skills.name: Translate the variable and integral limits

skills.definition: Integrate power expressions under the rule's domain and exponent conditions, then evaluate bounds.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S4 evaluates ∫₀ᵈ(u³−4u)du. S7 evaluates the expanded polynomial integral from 0 to x.
skills.learning_objective: Integrate polynomial powers accurately and evaluate both limits of a definite integral.
skills.name: Integrate powers and evaluate endpoints

skills.definition: Expand, factor and collect algebraic expressions while retaining equality.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 rewrites the shifted product; S4 factors d⁴/4−2d²; S7 factors the explicit primitive; S8 factors a difference to prove strict increase algebraically.
skills.learning_objective: Expose useful product structure without changing coefficients, signs or equality conditions.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

skills.definition: Solve quadratic equations and verify allowed real roots, including repeated roots.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S5 solves (b−2)²=8. S9 solves b²−4b−4=0 and checks the permitted root.
skills.learning_objective: Find all quadratic roots before filtering them against the parameter restriction.
skills.name: Solving quadratics and checking roots

skills.definition: Identify expression domains and conditions under which algebraic transformations preserve equivalence.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 carries b>4 to d>2. S5 validates division by d² and selects the permitted root. S6 rejects b=4. S9 selects the positive square-root branch using b(b−4)>0.
skills.learning_objective: Carry b>4 through substitutions, division and root extraction without losing or adding solutions.
skills.name: Domain restrictions and reversible operations

skills.definition: Perform exact rational and surd arithmetic and comparisons under real-domain restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S5 simplifies √8=2√2 and checks the strict domain. S6 computes exact option differences. S9 obtains the same exact surd through the quadratic formula.
skills.learning_objective: Keep the parameter and option comparisons exact rather than relying on decimal approximations.
skills.name: Exact surd and rational arithmetic

skills.definition: Rewrite a real quadratic with nonzero leading coefficient as a(x−h)²+k, preserving equality, and use this form to identify its vertex, reflection axis and bounds with the appropriate sign of a.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S8 uses x(4−x)=4−(x−2)² to prove that the inner quadratic has its unique maximum 4 at x=2 on [0,4].
skills.learning_objective: Use a completed square to bound an inner quadratic before applying a nonnegative square.
skills.name: Complete the square and locate a quadratic vertex

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Direct integration gives F(x)=x²(x−4)²/4. On [0,4], 0≤x(4−x)=4−(x−2)²≤4, so F≤4 with equality only at x=2. On [4,b], x(x−4) is nonnegative and strictly increasing, as its difference at y>x is (y−x)(x+y−4)>0. Therefore exactly two maximizers require F(b)=4. Since b>4, this is equivalent to b(b−4)=4, giving the unique admissible root b=2+2√2.
limitations: The quadratic vertex argument applies to the inner factor, not directly to the quartic F.
Nonnegativity must be established before squaring the bound on [0,4].
The interval [4,b] still needs a separate comparison; symmetry on [0,4] does not cover the whole domain.
useful_alternatives.method: Integrate first, factor the resulting quartic as a square, and use algebraic bounds instead of derivative signs.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for a solver who prefers explicit polynomial structure or wishes to avoid differentiating a variable-upper-limit integral. Its work is comparable to M1 rather than materially shorter.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: identify x=2 and x=b as the only maximum candidates, evaluate their signed height difference using u=t−2, and solve its zero condition for b>4.
conditions_checked: The exact translation t=2+u gives t(t−2)(t−4)=u(u²−4).
The translated integration interval is [0,b−2], not a symmetric interval.
In M2, x(4−x)=4−(x−2)² proves the inner quadratic's bound on [0,4].
limitations: The full domain [0,b] is not symmetric about 2 when b>4.
Symmetric factor locations alone do not prove that two equal-height points are global maximizers.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Use the actual vertex and reflection axis of the inner quadratic x(4-x)=4-(x-2)^2 in M2 to establish its bound and equality point; centering the integration variable is separately ordinary substitution.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is standard structure exploitation already included in M1, or a comparably short alternative, rather than an additional material shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Centering avoids a three-term expansion in the height-difference integral, but that saving is already part of the ordinary baseline.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: identify x=2 and x=b as the only maximum candidates, evaluate their signed height difference using u=t−2, and solve its zero condition for b>4.
conditions_checked: The two candidate heights bound the full domain.
Strict monotonicity excludes extra maximizers.
The signed height difference changes sign exactly once for b>4, at c.
limitations: Rejecting A does not distinguish B, C, D and E.
Finding two equal function values without the global branch comparison would not prove a tied maximum.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Prove the complete parameter transition: for4<b<c only2 maximizes, at c=2+2sqrt2 exactly2 andb maximize, and for b>c onlyb maximizes.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Valid ordinary SC06 boundary classification, with no material shortcut badge.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: No additional work beyond the best ordinary exact parameter classification.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: identify x=2 and x=b as the only maximum candidates, evaluate their signed height difference using u=t−2, and solve its zero condition for b>4.
conditions_checked: Both integrals have the same continuous integrand and lower limit 0.
Since b>4>2, subtracting them leaves the correctly oriented integral from 2 to b.
The remaining integral is signed; its negative part is not replaced by an unsigned area.
The centered integrand is odd, but its interval [0,b−2] is not symmetric, so oddness does not make the integral vanish automatically.
limitations: Only the common interval cancels without calculation.
The remaining zero condition and the global-maximum argument are still required.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Cancel Before Calculating — use F(b)−F(2)=∫₂ᵇt(t−2)(t−4)dt instead of computing two separate accumulated values.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This legitimate cancellation is already the best ordinary method, so it earns no additional shortcut badge.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Separate evaluation of F(b) and F(2), and irrelevant accumulation on [0,2]; all of this is already avoided by M1.

subtopic: Restricted substitutions and parameter root counts
prompt_html:
For which real values of \(a\) does the equation

\[4^x+4^{-x}-a(2^x+2^{-x})+3a-4=0\]

have exactly two distinct real solutions?
solution_html:
Let \(t=2^x+2^{-x}\ge2\). Then \(4^x+4^{-x}=t^2-2\), so

\[q(t)=t^2-at+3a-6=0,\qquad q(2)=a-2.\]

Each root \(t>2\) gives two real values of \(x\); \(t=2\) gives only \(x=0\).

If \(a<2\): \(q(2)<0\), so the monic quadratic has exactly one root above \(2\). This gives two values of \(x\). At \(a=2\), the roots are \(0,2\), giving only one value of \(x\).

If \(a>2\): \(q(2)>0\). A root above \(2\) requires the vertex to lie to the right of \(2\), so \(a>4\). The discriminant is \((a-6)^2-12\). With \(a>4\), it is non-negative exactly when \(a\ge6+2\sqrt3\).

At equality there is one repeated root \(t>2\), giving two values of \(x\). Above it there are two distinct roots above \(2\), giving four. Thus \(\boxed{a<2\text{ or }a=6+2\sqrt3}\).
