subtopic: Counting roots after a symmetric exponential substitution
prompt_html: How many distinct real solutions does \(4^x+4^{-x}-5(2^x+2^{-x})+8=0\) have?
solution_html: Put \(t=2^x>0\) and \(u=t+1/t\ge2\), since \((t-1)^2\ge0\). As \(t^2+t^{-2}=u^2-2\), the equation becomes \(u^2-5u+6=0\). For \(u=2\), \(t=1\), giving only \(x=0\). For \(u=3\), the quadratic \(t^2-3t+1=0\) has two distinct positive roots, each giving one real \(x\). The two cases are disjoint, so there are three solutions.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Laws of real exponentials Reciprocal exponential substitution Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Domain restrictions and reversible operations Signs of real quantities and squares Factorisation and algebraic expansion Solving quadratics and checking roots Clear denominators in equations Logarithms as inverses of exponentials Solve composite equations by intermediate level sets Count distinct real roots across branches Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use the reciprocal-sum substitution s=2^x+2^(-x). The identity 4^x+4^(-x)=s²−2 reduces the equation to (s−2)(s−3)=0. Reverse each level using u=2^x>0: s=2 gives the single root u=1, while s=3 gives two distinct positive roots of u²−3u+1=0. Each positive u gives one real x, so the total is 1+2=3. This avoids expanding a quartic and does not require numerical logarithms.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put u=2^x>0 and s=u+1/u. Then 4^x+4^(-x)=s²−2, so the equation becomes s²−5s+6=(s−2)(s−3)=0. For s=2, multiplication by u gives (u−1)²=0, hence u=1 and x=0. For s=3, it gives u²−3u+1=0, hence u=(3±√5)/2. These two roots are positive, distinct and different from 1: 0<(3−√5)/2<1<(3+√5)/2. Each positive u corresponds to exactly one real x=log₂u. Thus there are exactly three distinct real solutions, so E is correct.
domain_case_checks: The requested domain is all real x, not just integer or nonnegative x. Positive bases 2 and 4 make every original exponential term defined and positive throughout this domain.
For u=2^x>0, s−2=u+1/u−2=(u−1)²/u≥0. Equality is permitted and occurs exactly at u=1, hence x=0. The boundary s=2 must not be discarded.
The expansion s²=u²+2+u^(-2) is an identity, not an operation of squaring the original equation. Multiplication by u in M1, and by u² in M2, preserves equivalence because u>0.

The level s=2 gives the repeated algebraic root u=1 but only one distinct x. The level s=3 gives two distinct positive u-values because 1<√5<3. Neither equals 1, so the two level cases have no overlap.

The inverse logarithms introduced in the solution have valid base 2 and positive arguments. The exponential–logarithm correspondence gives exactly one real x for every retained positive u. The resulting x-values are negative, zero and positive.

The factorisation and inverse substitutions exhaust all real x, so no search at large positive or negative x is needed. The answer is an exact count; no approximation, rounding or measurement units are involved.

prompt_html: For which real \(a\) does \(\sin^2x-a\sin x+a-1=0\) have exactly three distinct solutions in \(0\le x<2\pi\)?
solution_html: The polynomial factors as \((\sin x-1)(\sin x-(a-1))\). The first factor always gives just \(x=\pi/2\). For exactly two additional angles, the second sine value must be strictly between \(-1\) and 1 and different from 1. This is exactly \(0<a<2\). At \(a=0\) it adds only one angle; at \(a=2\) the two factors coincide.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Factorisation and algebraic expansion Zero-product property and factor roots Solving quadratics and checking roots Allowed sine and cosine values Recover all angles and signs in an interval Periodicity and endpoint inclusion Solve composite equations by intermediate level sets Count distinct real roots across branches Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Construct a legal counterexample Absolute values and square roots of squares

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Set s = sin x, retain s ∈ [−1, 1], and factor the quadratic as (s − 1)(s + 1 − a). Count the x-preimages of the fixed level 1 and the moving level a − 1 on one half-open turn, treating extremal levels and coincident branches separately.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Factor the equation as (sin x − 1)(sin x + 1 − a) = 0. The level sin x = 1 always contributes exactly x = π/2. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, a sine level c has two preimages when −1 < c < 1, one when c = ±1, and none when |c| > 1. These counts follow from horizontal-line intersections with the unit circle; in particular, c = 0 gives x = 0 and π. Thus, if 0 < a < 2, the second level c = a − 1 contributes two angles distinct from π/2, giving exactly three. At a = 0, the levels are 1 and −1, giving only two angles. At a = 2, both factors describe the same level 1, giving only one angle. For a < 0 or a > 2, the second level is unattainable, again leaving one angle. Therefore the complete parameter set is 0 < a < 2, option C.
domain_case_checks: The task is to find every real a for which there are exactly three distinct real x-values in the half-open interval [0, 2π). No integer restriction on a is present.
Sine is defined throughout the interval and attains exactly the range [−1, 1]. The quadratic in s = sin x has leading coefficient 1 for every a, so it never becomes an identity or changes degree.
The factorisation and zero-product step are equivalences. They involve no division by sin x − 1, so the permanent solution x = π/2 is not lost.

For 0 < c < 1, the two angles lie in quadrants I and II. For −1 < c < 0, they lie in quadrants III and IV. At c = 0, the two angles are 0 and π; 2π is excluded. At c = 1 and c = −1, there is only one angle each.
At a = 0, the solution set is {π/2, 3π/2}. At a = 2, the equation is (sin x − 1)² = 0, whose distinct solution set is {π/2}. Algebraic multiplicity does not add another x-value.
At a = 1, the three solutions are 0, π/2 and π. Thus the change of sign of a − 1 at this parameter creates no exception to the three-solution interval.
The exhaustive count is one solution for a < 0, two for a = 0, three for 0 < a < 2, and one for a ≥ 2. This proves both necessity and sufficiency of the stated range.
In alternative M2, the quadratic formula is valid because the leading coefficient is nonzero, and √((a − 2)²) must be written as |a − 2|. No approximation or rounding is required.

limitations: Longer than direct factorisation in this question.
The square root must be an absolute value unless sign cases are made explicit.
The discriminant counts algebraic roots, not angles; sine-range and branch-overlap checks remain essential.
useful_alternatives.method: Solve the quadratic in s = sin x with the quadratic formula, then count the preimages of its distinct attainable roots.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: A reliable fallback if the parameterised factorisation is not spotted, or an algebraic cross-check of the two sine levels.

a = 3/2 has three solutions and refutes the word only in D.
a = 0 and a = 2 refute candidate sets that include those nonsolutions.
limitations: Choosing a convenient value does not preserve the solution count for every a.
Sample testing is not a proof of the full parameter interval.

Within that open interval it is different from the fixed level 1, establishing sufficiency.
The two boundary parameters and all outside values are checked separately.

prompt_html: For which real x is exactly one of the statements \(x>1\), \(x<3\), \(x^2\ge4\) true?
solution_html: If \(x\le-2\), the second and third statements are true. For \(-2<x\le1\), only \(x<3\) is true. For \(1<x<2\), the first two are true; for \(2\le x<3\), all three are true; and for \(x\ge3\), the first and third are true. Hence precisely the interval \((-2,1]\) gives exactly one true statement.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Finite-count statements and their complements Negate simple comparative statements Absolute values and square roots of squares Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets Construct a legal counterexample Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use logical forcing before making a full table. The first two statements cannot both be false, so the third must be false if the total number of true statements is one. Solve x²<4 as -2<x<2. The statement x<3 is then true throughout, so x>1 must be false, giving x≤1. Intersect the bounds and verify the converse and endpoints.
audited_reference.concise_proof: For every real x, at least one of x>1 and x<3 is true: their simultaneous falsity would require x≤1 and x≥3. Therefore exactly one true statement forces x²≥4 to be false. Thus x²<4, equivalently |x|<2, so -2<x<2. Throughout this interval x<3 is true, so x>1 must be false, giving x≤1. Hence -2<x≤1 is necessary. Conversely, every x in this range makes the three statements false, true and false respectively. The complete solution set is therefore -2<x≤1, option E.
domain_case_checks: The domain is all real x, including negative and nonintegral values. All three expressions are defined throughout this domain; no additional exclusions or approximations are needed.
Exactly one applies to the three original statements at a common x. It does not assert that exactly one of the option inequalities holds pointwise.
The first two statements cannot both be false. Consequently a true third statement would always produce at least two true statements.
The equivalence x²<4 ⇔ |x|<2 ⇔ -2<x<2 retains both signs of x. Taking √(x²) as x without a sign restriction would be invalid.
At x=-2 the truth pattern is (F,T,T), so -2 is excluded. At x=1 it is (F,T,F), so 1 is included.
The other transition values are also excluded: x=2 gives (T,T,T), and x=3 gives (T,F,T).

The alternative table partitions the entire real line into five disjoint regions with constant truth patterns. Its rows are justified by inequalities throughout each region, not merely by sample values.
Necessity and sufficiency are both proved. Numerical endpoint checks verify the boundary conventions but are not used as a substitute for the complete-range proof.

skills.definition: Translate truth or falsity of 'at least', 'at most' and 'exactly' claims about a finite collection into equivalent integer constraints, retaining equality cases and using complementary-category totals where appropriate.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The first two statements contribute at least one true statement, so a total of exactly one forces the third false. M2 explicitly counts 2, 1, 2, 3 and 2 true statements across its regions.
skills.learning_objective: Require exactly one true statement among three, rather than accepting one true statement without checking the others.
skills.name: Finite-count statements and their complements

skills.definition:
Form the exact logical complement of an atomic real comparison, including \(

eg(x\le a)\iff x>a\), and \(
eg(x<a)\iff x\ge a\), retaining the correct equality boundary.

skills.definition: Manipulate and solve inequalities while preserving direction, sign conditions and solution sets.

skills.definition: Refute a universal claim using an example satisfying every premise and violating the conclusion.
skills.evidence_in_solution: In M1's option verification, x=1 refutes ranges omitting a genuine solution, while x=-2 refutes ranges including a nonsolution. M2 can compare the complete classified set with the options instead.

skills.definition: Organize exhaustive and disjoint cases, including equality, degeneracies and exceptional values.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 uses the ordered transition values -2, 1, 2 and 3 to construct five disjoint regions covering every real input, assigning each endpoint to the correct row.

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The final range is checked against all three original statements; -2 and 1 are evaluated explicitly, and every option is compared with the complete range.
skills.learning_objective: Check both the sufficiency of a proposed range and its endpoint conventions in the original statements.

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Solve the original square comparison as x≤-2 or x≥2, then tabulate the three statements over the five regions determined by -2, 1, 2 and 3. Their true counts are respectively 2, 1, 2, 3 and 2, so only -2<x≤1 qualifies.
limitations: The table is longer than M1.
Each row must represent a whole interval justified by the inequalities, not merely one tested point.
The transition values must be assigned explicitly to avoid endpoint errors.
useful_alternatives.method: Construct a complete number-line truth-count table for the original statements.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when a transparent exhaustive classification is preferred, or when the logical forcing in M1 is not immediately apparent. It avoids the need to explicitly rewrite the false statements as negated inequalities.

A chosen input is not representative of every real input.

shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful checking, not a material shortcut over M1.

subtopic: Parity of a random subset sum
tags: MAT 2016 Q6; MAT 2013 Q5; TMUA probability extension
prompt_html: Three distinct numbers are chosen uniformly from \(\{1,2,\ldots,8\}\). What is the probability that their sum is odd?
solution_html: There are four odd and four even numbers. An odd sum needs one odd and two even numbers, or three odd numbers. The favourable count is \(\binom41\binom42+\binom43=24+4=28\). There are \(\binom83=56\) equally likely subsets, so the probability is \(28/56=1/2\).
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor Bijective counting and representation multiplicity Favourable-over-total probability ratio Count fixed-size unordered subsets Sum and product rules for finite counting

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Pair complete selections using the permutation x ↦ 9−x. It preserves the set of permitted three-element selections and is its own inverse. A sum s becomes 27−s, reversing parity. Therefore odd-sum and even-sum selections have equal cardinality and, by uniformity, equal probability.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Pair each three-element selection {a,b,c} with {9−a,9−b,9−c}. This is a permitted selection of three distinct numbers, and applying the transformation again recovers the original selection. If the original sum is s, the transformed sum is 27−s, which has the opposite parity. Thus the transformation pairs odd-sum selections bijectively with even-sum selections. All selections are equally likely, so the probability of an odd sum is exactly 1/2.
domain_case_checks: The sample consists of three distinct members of {1,2,…,8}; repetitions are forbidden and order does not affect the sum.

Uniform unordered selection gives equally likely three-element subsets. Uniform sequential sampling without replacement gives the same answer, since each subset has exactly 3! = 6 ordered representations.
The map x ↦ 9−x permutes {1,2,…,8} and is injective, so applying it to every selected number preserves distinctness and the number of selected members.
Applying the map twice returns every number to itself. It is therefore a bijection on the complete sample space, not merely a construction of some opposite-parity examples.
Every sum is an integer and is either odd or even, exclusively. Since 27 is odd, s and 27−s have opposite parity; no selection can be fixed by this parity-reversing transformation.
For direct counting, an odd sum requires exactly one or exactly three odd selected numbers. Both cases are feasible, disjoint and exhaustive.
The sample space has C(8,3) = 56 > 0 outcomes. Direct counting gives 28 favourable outcomes; equivalently, ordered counting gives 168 favourable outcomes out of 336.
The draws need not be independent, and no independence assumption is used. There are no continuous endpoints, units, logarithms or variable denominators requiring additional checks.

skills.definition: Count equally likely probabilistic outcomes with the correct order and multiplicity.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1 models equally likely three-element subsets and explains their common sixfold ordered representation. A2 uses the same unordered sample space for direct counting.
skills.learning_objective: Choose a consistent equally likely representation of distinct selections and retain its multiplicities.
skills.name: Count equally likely outcomes with correct multiplicity

skills.definition: Reduce sums, products or powers modulo a divisor while distinguishing residue representatives from canonical remainders.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 proves that s and 27−s have opposite parity. A1 classifies an odd sum by whether one or three selected members are odd.
skills.learning_objective: Use reduction modulo 2 to determine sum parity and establish that a transformation reverses it.
skills.name: Reduce products and expressions modulo a divisor

skills.definition: Count finite configurations through a proved one-to-one correspondence with simpler encodings, checking existence, uniqueness, and the treatment of excluded or multiply represented exceptional configurations.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S2 checks that applying x ↦ 9−x to all selected members preserves legality and is its own inverse. S3 uses its restriction to obtain equal odd-sum and even-sum cardinalities.
skills.learning_objective: Prove a correspondence preserves the sample constraints and has an inverse before using it to equate event counts.
skills.name: Bijective counting and representation multiplicity

skills.definition: For a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes with positive total size, compute an event probability as its number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S3 converts equal complementary event cardinalities into probability 1/2. A4 computes 28/56 directly.
skills.learning_objective: Convert a proved favourable-outcome count or proportion into a probability under uniform sampling.
skills.name: Favourable-over-total probability ratio

skills.definition: For n distinct objects and an integer r with 0≤r≤n, count unordered r-element selections using C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n−r)!), adjusting the pool and quota for forced or excluded objects and including the endpoint cases r=0 and r=n.
skills.evidence_in_solution: A2 evaluates C(8,3). A3 uses C(4,1)C(4,2) and C(4,3) to count the two favourable compositions.
skills.learning_objective: Count distinct unordered selections from the complete pool and from its odd and even subpools.
skills.name: Count fixed-size unordered subsets

skills.definition: Count finite objects by adding the sizes of pairwise disjoint exhaustive cases and multiplying sequential choice counts when every partial choice has the claimed number of compatible continuations.
skills.evidence_in_solution: A3 multiplies the independent component choice counts within the one-odd composition and adds the disjoint three-odd composition.
skills.learning_objective: Multiply compatible choices within each composition and add the disjoint complete cases without omissions or duplication.
skills.name: Sum and product rules for finite counting

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Exactly one odd member contributes C(4,1)C(4,2)=24 selections, and exactly three odd members contribute C(4,3)=4. Dividing their sum by C(8,3)=56 gives 1/2.
limitations: Both favourable parity compositions must be included.
Numerator and denominator must use the same ordered or unordered convention.
The calculation uses distinct selections, not sampling with replacement.
useful_alternatives.method: Count unordered selections by their numbers of odd and even members.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the pairing is not apparent, when checking the symmetry solution numerically, or when adapting the counting approach to different odd and even pool sizes.

audited_reference.diagnostic_safeguard: Use actual working and a confirming probe; stored candidates and skill hypotheses do not establish student mastery.

tags: MAT 2014 Q7; MAT 2019 Q7; TMUA probability extension
prompt_html: A fair coin is tossed until either HTH or HHT appears as three consecutive tosses. What is the probability that HTH appears first?
solution_html: Let p be the success probability with no useful suffix, h with suffix H, and t with suffix HT. With suffix HH, HTH cannot win before HHT: further heads retain HH and the next tail completes HHT. Thus its success probability is 0. The transitions give \(p=(p+h)/2\), \(h=t/2\), and \(t=(1+p)/2\). Consequently \(p=h=t/2=(1+p)/4\), so p=1/3. The stopping time is almost surely finite since disjoint blocks have a fixed positive chance of containing either pattern.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: First-step and restart probability equations Independent trials and path probabilities Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities Equivalence-preserving solution of a linear equation Convergent geometric series and tails Substitute or independently check a proposed result

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Wait for the first H, which occurs almost surely. From there, partition continuations into H (HTH can no longer win), TH (HTH wins immediately) and TT (a genuine restart). Their probabilities are 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4. If p is the required eventual probability, write p = 1/4 + p/4 and solve the single linear equation.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Ignore leading tails: the first H occurs with probability 1, and neither target can occur before it. Let p be the required probability, which is therefore also the winning probability after this first H. If the next toss is H, the ending is HH: any further heads preserve HH, and the first subsequent T completes HHT, so HTH cannot win. This branch has probability 1/2. If the next two tosses are TH, HTH wins immediately, with probability 1/4. If they are TT, the ending HTT retains no partial target and the experiment restarts, with probability 1/4. Hence p = 1/4 + p/4, giving p = 1/3. Nontermination has probability zero: no winner after 3n tosses implies that none of the n disjoint three-toss blocks equals either target, an event of probability (3/4)^n. The two distinct targets cannot finish simultaneously. Thus the required exact probability is 1/3, option E.
domain_case_checks: Use the conventional model of independent repeated tosses of a fair coin: after any finite history, the next H and T each have probability 1/2. The requested probability is dimensionless.
The stopping rule checks every consecutive three-toss window, not merely disjoint triples. Stopping cannot occur before toss 3, and there is no deterministic finite upper bound on the stopping time.
Leading tails cannot begin either target. The probability that the first n tosses are all tails is 2^(-n), tending to zero, so waiting for the first H introduces no extra probability factor.
After the first H, the continuations H, TH and TT are disjoint and exhaustive, with probabilities 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4. They describe unequal-length branches, not three equally likely outcomes.
HH is not a restart: the first subsequent T completes HHT before HTH can occur. By contrast, HTT ends in TT, so no suffix is a nonempty prefix of either target; this is a genuine restart.

Distinct words of the same length cannot first finish on the same toss. Also P(no winner after 3n tosses) is at most (3/4)^n, which tends to zero. Disjoint blocks are used only for this termination bound, not as replacements for the sliding-window stopping rule.
The equation has coefficient 1 - 1/4 = 3/4, which is nonzero, so its rearrangement gives a unique solution. The result 1/3 lies strictly between 0 and 1.
All calculations are exact. No rounding or approximation is requested.

skills.definition: Identify a state containing the information relevant to future evolution, then condition on the next trial or a regenerative block to set up linear equations for eventual-event probabilities, with absorbing outcomes and possible nontermination accounted for.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S1–S3 distinguish leading tails, HH, immediate HTH and the HTT restart, producing p = 1/4 + p/4. M2 uses this same restart model and relation before expanding by repeated attempts.
skills.learning_objective: Retain the relevant ending of a toss history and identify a genuine restart before writing an eventual-winning equation.
skills.name: First-step and restart probability equations

skills.definition: For independent trials with specified outcome probabilities, calculate the probability of a prescribed finite outcome path by multiplication, and justify that past outcomes do not change the distribution of future trials.
skills.evidence_in_solution: TH and TT after the first H each have probability (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4. Independent future tosses justify the restart, the termination bound and the repeated-attempt products.
skills.learning_objective: Multiply probabilities along specified toss continuations and justify why a finite past history does not change future fair-toss probabilities.
skills.name: Independent trials and path probabilities

skills.definition: Partition into disjoint exhaustive cases and sum correctly weighted conditional probabilities.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The branches H, TH and TT after the first H have weights 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4, contributing 0, 1 and p respectively. M2 partitions successful histories by their number of restarts.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish branch probabilities from conditional eventual probabilities and add their correctly weighted contributions.
skills.name: Partition into disjoint cases and sum weighted probabilities

skills.definition: Solve a single linear equation in one unknown by collecting terms and applying reversible operations, distinguishing a unique solution from an identity or inconsistency when the unknown's coefficient may vanish.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S4 rearranges p = 1/4 + p/4 to (3/4)p = 1/4 and divides by the nonzero coefficient 3/4. M2 instead sums the repeated-attempt probabilities.
skills.learning_objective: Solve a self-referential linear probability equation by equivalence-preserving rearrangement.
skills.name: Equivalence-preserving solution of a linear equation

skills.definition: Evaluate an infinite geometric series b + br + br² + … as b/(1 − r) when |r| < 1, including tails whose first term must be recovered from a stated starting index.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S7 sums 1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + … with first term and ratio both 1/4. M1 does not evaluate an infinite series, although it uses elementary geometric decay to check termination.
skills.learning_objective: Identify the first-attempt winning probability and restart ratio before summing the convergent series of eventual-winning contributions.
skills.name: Convergent geometric series and tails

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S5 checks termination, absence of ties and every original option. S7 checks the alternative result against the restart equation and requested event.
skills.learning_objective: Check the derived probability against the stopping rule, event label, recurrence and original options.
skills.name: Substitute or independently check a proposed result

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: The restart model has immediate-success probability s = 1/4 and restart probability q = 1/4. Expanding by the number k of restarts gives disjoint winning contributions s q^k for k >= 0. Their sum is s/(1 - q) = 1/3 because |q| < 1.
limitations: The genuine restart and all success/loss branches must still be justified.
The ratio is 1/4, and waiting for the first H does not contribute an extra factor 1/2.
This is not shorter than the ordinary one-variable equation.
useful_alternatives.method: Expand the restart model as a geometric series of winning attempts instead of solving its linear equation by collecting terms.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful for connecting eventual probabilities to repeated opportunities, or for a learner who prefers summing a geometric series to rearranging a self-referential equation.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1: identify the three branches after the first H and solve p = (1 + p)/4.
conditions_checked: Leading tails do not change the relevant state.
HTT retains no target prefix and genuinely restarts the experiment.
Independent future tosses have the same law after each finite restart.
The restart probability is 1/4, not 1/2.
limitations: A failed partial match is not automatically a restart; HH must be treated separately.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: SC02 — Shrink the Giant. Replace the unbounded toss-history tree by a proved three-branch restart model.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is the shortest clear ordinary method itself, not an additional shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: The model avoids indefinite history enumeration, but that reduction is already included in M1.

subtopic: Minimum operations to build a target pair
prompt_html: Start at \((1,1)\). Each move replaces either coordinate by the sum of the two coordinates. What is the minimum number of moves needed to reach \((13,8)\)?
solution_html: For any unequal positive target, the last changed coordinate must be the larger one. Hence reverse the process uniquely by subtracting the smaller coordinate from the larger. Starting from (13,8) gives (5,8),(5,3),(2,3),(2,1),(1,1), exactly five reverse moves. Reversing this list constructs a valid five-move route, and uniqueness of each predecessor proves no shorter route exists.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Reverse additive coordinate moves using positivity Global extrema from attained bounds Substitute or independently check a proposed result Translate and evaluate a recurrence Symmetric expressions and swapping variables

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Work backwards using positivity. The coordinate updated last must be the larger coordinate, so subtract the smaller from it to obtain the unique positive predecessor. This gives (13,8) → (5,8) → (5,3) → (2,3) → (2,1) → (1,1). Count five transitions and reverse the chain to verify attainability. Uniqueness of each predecessor proves minimality, not merely the existence of a five-move route.
audited_reference.concise_proof: All coordinates remain positive integers. A move from (a,b) produces either (a+b,b) or (a,a+b), so the coordinate just changed is strictly larger than the unchanged coordinate. Therefore every reachable noninitial state has a unique positive predecessor, found by subtracting the smaller coordinate from the larger. The forced reverse chain is (13,8) → (5,8) → (5,3) → (2,3) → (2,1) → (1,1), containing five transitions. Reversing it gives the legal route (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,3) → (5,3) → (5,8) → (13,8). Every predecessor was forced, and (1,1) has no positive predecessor, so no shorter route is possible. The minimum is exactly 5 moves, option C.
domain_case_checks: Starting from (1,1), addition preserves positive integer coordinates. Thus zero and negative coordinates cannot occur in any legal history, even though the prompt does not separately state a coordinate domain.
The permitted operations are exactly (x,y) → (x+y,y) and (x,y) → (x,x+y). Simultaneously updating both coordinates, swapping coordinates as a move, and forward subtraction are not permitted.

For a current pair (X,Y) with X>Y, only the first coordinate could have changed last, giving predecessor (X-Y,Y). For Y>X, the unique positive predecessor is (X,Y-X). These two cases cover every reachable noninitial state.

Equal positive coordinates cannot be the output of a legal move because the new sum strictly exceeds the unchanged coordinate. The reverse calculation stops at the specified initial pair (1,1); continuing to a zero coordinate would be invalid.
Every forward move increases the changed coordinate and the total coordinate sum. There are no waiting moves or cycles that could be inserted into the route.
The reverse chain contains six displayed states but five moves. The initial state is reached after zero moves.

In the forward-bound alternative, both possible coordinate updates are covered by the same bound. Sorting coordinates is used only to bound their magnitudes; the ordered target is checked using the explicit route.
All calculations are exact integer additions or subtractions. No approximation, rounding, or geometric distance measurement is involved.

skills.definition: Reverse the updates (x,y)→(x+y,y) and (x,y)→(x,x+y) on positive integer pairs by subtracting the smaller coordinate from the larger. Prove the predecessor is unique for unequal coordinates and that equal-coordinate states have no positive predecessor; use the forced chain to determine reachability and the move count from a specified initial pair.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 identifies the last updated coordinate as the larger one, reconstructs five unique predecessors and stops at (1,1).
skills.learning_objective: Recover the unique legal predecessor of an additive coordinate move and use the forced reverse chain to justify the move count.
skills.name: Reverse additive coordinate moves using positivity

skills.definition: For a real-valued function on a specified nonempty domain, establish a global minimum or maximum by proving a universal lower or upper bound and exhibiting an admissible point attaining it. Distinguish this from a merely feasible value or an unattained bound.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The objective is the length of a legal route to the target. M1 proves that every such route must follow the five-step reverse chain; M2 excludes all routes of at most four moves. Both exhibit a legal five-move route.
skills.learning_objective: Certify a global minimum by proving a lower bound on the entire domain and exhibiting a legal equality point.
skills.name: Global extrema from attained bounds

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The solution checks that each arrow changes exactly one coordinate, counts five transitions rather than six states, and verifies the ordered endpoint (13,8).
skills.learning_objective: Audit the final answer against the exact requested quantity and its representation conditions.
skills.name: Substitute or independently check a proposed result

skills.definition: Translate and evaluate a recurrence with the correct initial state and valid indices.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 starts comparison bounds at (U_0,V_0)=(1,1) and applies (U_(n+1),V_(n+1))=(V_n,U_n+V_n) four times to obtain (5,8).
skills.learning_objective: Evaluate a proved coordinate-bound recurrence from the zero-move state with the correct number of updates.
skills.name: Translate and evaluate a recurrence

skills.definition: Use interchange symmetry of variables or symmetric expressions without losing multiplicity.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 treats the smaller and larger coordinates together because interchanging the coordinates interchanges the move rules. It does not identify the two ordered target states as the same outcome.
skills.learning_objective: Use coordinate-interchange symmetry for a magnitude bound while retaining the order of the required endpoint.

subtopic: Finding the first error in a derivative proof
prompt_html:
A student attempts to prove that a polynomial strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\) must have \(f'(x)>0\) for every real \(x\).

1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(f'(c)\leq0\) for some real \(c\).

2. If \(f'(c)<0\), then \(f\) decreases on some interval containing \(c\).

3. If \(f'(c)=0\), then \(f\) has a local maximum or minimum at \(c\).

4. Either case contradicts strict increase, so \(f'(x)>0\) everywhere.

Which line contains the first error?
solution_html:
Line 1 correctly negates the proposed conclusion. Line 2 is valid for a polynomial: its derivative is continuous, so a negative derivative at \(c\) remains negative on a small interval around \(c\).

Line 3 is the first error. A zero derivative may indicate a stationary point of inflection. For example, \(f(x)=x^3\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\), has \(f'(0)=0\), and has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum there. Thus the proposed theorem is false, and the proof first fails at line 3.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Locate the first unsupported implication in a proof Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Preserve a nonzero sign locally by continuity Derivative sign tests for monotonicity Stationary and turning points via derivatives Power rule for polynomial differentiation Construct a legal counterexample Definitions of interval monotonicity Factorisation and algebraic expansion Signs of real quantities and squares

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Audit the proof in order. Accept the exact negation in line 1. Validate line 2 using continuity of the polynomial derivative and the derivative sign test. Refute line 3 with f(x)=x³ at c=0, checking both the absence of an extremum and strict increase on R. The direct ordered-pair check uses b³−a³=(b−a)[(a−b)²+3(a+b)²]/4>0 for a<b. Stop at line 3; line 4 cannot be the first error.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Line 1 correctly negates the proposed conclusion. Line 2 is valid because a polynomial has a continuous derivative: if f'(c)<0, then f'<0 throughout a neighbourhood of c, so f is strictly decreasing there. Line 3 is false. Take f(x)=x³ and c=0. Then f'(0)=0, but f(-h)<f(0)<f(h) for every h>0, so 0 is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. This polynomial is strictly increasing on all of R: for a<b, b³−a³=(b−a)[(a−b)²+3(a+b)²]/4>0. Thus the counterexample satisfies the original premise, and the first error is line 3.
domain_case_checks: The premise concerns a polynomial strictly increasing on the whole real line. A counterexample must satisfy that global premise, not merely increase near one point.
Every polynomial and its derivative are defined and continuous on R. Thus there are no finite domain endpoints or singularities to exclude.
The negation of 'f'(x)>0 for every real x' is 'f'(c)≤0 for some real c'. In particular, equality must be included in line 1.
The cases f'(c)<0 and f'(c)=0 exhaust the assumption in line 1. The problem is not a missing case; it is the unsupported conclusion within the equality case.

Line 2 uses continuity of the polynomial derivative to pass from negativity at one point to negativity on an interval. Negativity at one point alone would not justify that neighbourhood claim without additional regularity.

For f(x)=x³, strict increase is verified for every ordered pair a<b. The positive factor (a−b)² makes the displayed factorisation strictly positive, including when a and b have opposite signs or one equals zero.

The point c=0 is an interior point of the domain. Arbitrarily close points on its left have smaller function values, and points on its right have larger values, excluding both kinds of local extremum.
Line 4 would correctly combine the claimed case contradictions if the preceding case arguments were valid. It inherits the error in line 3 and is not the first erroneous line.

subtopic: Positivity of a quartic on the whole real line
prompt_html: Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Which condition is equivalent to \(x^4-2ax^2+b>0\) for every real \(x\)?
solution_html:
Put \(u=x^2\), so \(u\geq0\). We need the minimum of \(u^2-2au+b=(u-a)^2+b-a^2\) on this restricted domain.

If \(a\leq0\), the vertex \(u=a\) is outside the positive part of the domain (or at its endpoint), and the minimum is at \(u=0\), with value \(b\). The condition is \(b>0\). If \(a>0\), the vertex is allowed, and the minimum is \(b-a^2\), requiring \(b>a^2\).

These conditions are also sufficient because they make the appropriate global minimum strictly positive. Replacing the strict signs by non-strict signs would allow a real zero.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Choose and reverse an algebraic substitution Quadratic extrema by completing the square Signs of real quantities and squares Exhaustive cases, degeneracies and equality cases Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Distinguish strict, inclusive and degenerate boundaries Separate example checking from a universal proof Construct a legal counterexample Differentiate a polynomial with parameters Derivative sign tests for monotonicity

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Treat the expression as a quadratic in t=x² on t≥0. Its minimum is at the boundary t=0 when a≤0, and at the feasible vertex t=a when a>0. Require the corresponding attained minimum, b or b−a², to be strictly positive.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Put t=x². As x ranges over R, t ranges over exactly [0,∞), so consider q(t)=t²−2at+b on that domain. If a≤0, then q(t)−b=t(t−2a)≥0, with equality at t=0; hence the minimum is b. If a>0, then q(t)=(t−a)²+b−a², whose minimum b−a² is attained at the permitted point t=a. Thus the original polynomial is strictly positive for every real x exactly when either a≤0 and b>0, or a>0 and b>a². This is C.
domain_case_checks: The task asks for an equivalence valid for all real parameter pairs (a,b), with those parameters held fixed inside the statement quantified over x.
The substitution t=x² has image [0,∞), not R. Every t≥0 is attained by a real x, so the transformed universal statement is equivalent to the original one.
The quadratic in t has leading coefficient 1 for every parameter pair. Its vertex t=a is inadmissible when a<0, lies on the boundary when a=0, and is interior when a>0.
The cases a≤0 and a>0 are disjoint and exhaustive. At a=0, the polynomial is x⁴+b and its attained minimum is b.
For a≤0, b=0 fails strict positivity at x=0. For a>0, b=a² fails at x=±√a. A smaller b gives a negative value at the corresponding minimizer.
Equality b=a² is not always forbidden: when a<0, it gives (x²−a)²>0 for every real x. The feasibility of x²=a determines whether that square can vanish.
The minimum is attained in every case. Therefore strict positivity everywhere is equivalent here to a strictly positive minimum; no unattained-infimum issue arises.
The polynomial is defined on all real inputs. No denominator or logarithm restrictions arise, and square roots used for minimizers are taken only when their arguments are nonnegative.
In the derivative alternative, a=0 is handled explicitly: f'(x)=4x³ changes from negative to positive at zero, despite f''(0)=0.

subtopic: The missing discriminant in a proposed converse
prompt_html:
For real \(b,c\), consider the statement: “If \(x^2+bx+c=0\) has two distinct positive roots, then \(b<0\) and \(c>0\).”

I. The statement is true.

II. Its converse is true.

III. Its contrapositive is true.

Which are true?
solution_html:
If the roots are positive, their sum \(-b\) and product \(c\) are both positive. Thus \(b<0\) and \(c>0\), proving I. Its contrapositive is logically equivalent, so III is true.

The converse is false: \(b=-1\) and \(c=1\) satisfy the signs, but \(x^2-x+1\) has discriminant \(1-4=-3\) and no real roots. Even positive roots must first exist and be distinct. The converse would need the additional discriminant condition \(b^2-4c>0\). Hence exactly I and III are true.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Interpret implication and necessary/sufficient conditions Sum and product of polynomial roots Signs of real quantities and squares Distinguish converse from original statement Construct a legal counterexample Solving quadratics and checking roots Negate and reverse to form a contrapositive Negate conjunctions and disjunctions correctly Negate simple comparative statements Real and repeated quadratic roots via discriminant Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Prove the forward implication using the sum and product of two positive roots. Refute the converse with the legal repeated-root example x²−2x+1=(x−1)². Use equivalence of an implication and its contrapositive, checking the full negation b≥0 or c≤0. This gives I and III only without solving a general quadratic or classifying all coefficient pairs.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let P mean that the quadratic has two distinct positive roots, and let Q mean b<0 and c>0. If its roots are r,s>0, then Vieta's identities give −b=r+s>0 and c=rs>0. Thus P⇒Q is true, so I is true. The converse is false: b=−2 and c=1 satisfy Q, but x²−2x+1=(x−1)² has only one distinct root. An implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, so III is true. Explicitly, the contrapositive says that if b≥0 or c≤0, the quadratic does not have two distinct positive roots. Therefore I and III only are true.
domain_case_checks: The implications are evaluated over all real coefficient pairs (b,c). Choosing one legal pair can refute a universal implication, but successful examples alone cannot prove one.
The leading coefficient is fixed at 1, so the equation is genuinely quadratic for every permitted b and c.
The antecedent requires two different real root values, both strictly positive. Distinctness is not needed to derive the necessary coefficient signs, but it is essential when testing the converse.
The counterexample b=−2, c=1 meets both strict coefficient inequalities. Its only root value is 1, with multiplicity two, so it genuinely violates the converse's conclusion.

The coefficient signs do not even guarantee real roots: b=−1, c=1 gives discriminant −3. Under b<0 and c>0, a positive discriminant gives two distinct positive roots, a zero discriminant gives one repeated positive root, and a negative discriminant gives no real roots.

The exact negation of b<0 and c>0 is b≥0 or c≤0. Equality cases must be included. If c=0, zero is a root and is not positive; if b=0, two positive roots are impossible because their sum would have to be zero.
The negation of 'has two distinct positive roots' does not mean 'has two negative roots'. It includes repeated roots, nonreal roots and failures of positivity.
In M2, the quadratic-formula denominator is the fixed nonzero number 2. Squaring the comparison −b>√Δ is used only after requiring Δ>0 and −b>0, so the equivalence introduces no extraneous cases.
There is no premise that exactly one of I, II and III is true. The uniquely correct answer option is established from the proved truth profile (true, false, true), rather than assumed.

skills.learning_objective: Recognise that the original implication and its contrapositive have the same truth value, unlike the converse.
skills.name: Negate and reverse to form a contrapositive

skills.definition: Negate conjunctions and disjunctions using De Morgan's laws without changing logical scope.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S4 expands the negation of the whole coefficient conclusion using 'or', not 'and'. M2 uses abstract contrapositive equivalence without expanding this conjunction.
skills.learning_objective: Negate b<0 and c>0 by allowing either component to fail.
skills.name: Negate conjunctions and disjunctions correctly

skills.definition:
Form the exact logical complement of an atomic real comparison, including \(
eg(x\ge a)\iff x<a\), \(
eg(x>a)\iff x\le a\), \(
eg(x\le a)\iff x>a\), and \(
eg(x<a)\iff x\ge a\), retaining the correct equality boundary.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S4 replaces ¬(b<0) by b≥0 and ¬(c>0) by c≤0. M2 does not need these expanded comparisons.
skills.learning_objective: Retain equality when negating the strict coefficient inequalities.
skills.name: Negate simple comparative statements

skills.definition: Use the discriminant to classify real, repeated or absent quadratic roots, checking the quadratic coefficient is nonzero.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S6 requires Δ=b²−4c>0 for two distinct real roots. S8 identifies Δ=0 in the counterexample.
skills.learning_objective: Separate two distinct real roots, a repeated root and no real roots before testing positivity.
skills.name: Real and repeated quadratic roots via discriminant

skills.definition: Manipulate and solve inequalities while preserving direction, sign conditions and solution sets.
skills.evidence_in_solution: S7 proves −b>√Δ equivalent to b<0 and b²>Δ under Δ>0, explicitly retaining the sign condition before squaring.
skills.learning_objective: Use a reversible squared comparison only after both compared quantities have the required signs.
skills.name: Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Let Δ=b²−4c. For Δ>0 the smaller root is (−b−√Δ)/2. Both roots are positive exactly when −b>√Δ, which, after retaining b<0, is equivalent to b²>Δ and hence c>0. Therefore two distinct positive roots occur exactly when b<0, c>0 and Δ>0. This proves I, shows why b=−2,c=1 refutes II, and gives III by contrapositive equivalence.
limitations: It performs more algebra than the Vieta-and-counterexample method.
It must distinguish Δ<0, Δ=0 and Δ>0.
The inequality involving the square root must not be squared before its sign conditions are retained.
useful_alternatives.method: Quadratic formula and the smaller-root criterion
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when a student prefers the quadratic formula to Vieta or wants to identify the exact additional condition missing from the converse.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 already chooses a legal counterexample to test the converse.
conditions_checked: The converse is a universal claim over real coefficient pairs.
Choosing b=−2 and c=1 is legitimate for a counterexample.
No invariance assumption is needed: one true-premise, false-conclusion pair is sufficient for refutation.
limitations: The special pair does not establish what happens for every coefficient pair.
The roots in the forward proof cannot be replaced by a convenient example when proving I.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose Your Own Numbers — choose coefficients giving the exact square (x−1)².
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is ordinary counterexample construction, already included in M1.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: No work beyond M1 is avoided.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 already uses the equivalence of an implication and its contrapositive.
conditions_checked: I and III concern the original implication and its contrapositive over exactly the same coefficient domain.
The complete options B, D and F require I and III to have different truth values and are therefore impossible.
A, C, E and G remain compatible with that equivalence alone.
Unique correctness of E is checked mathematically; there is no premise that exactly one numbered statement is true.
limitations: Equivalence of I and III does not show that either is true.
The full answer options are distinct truth profiles; their wording cannot replace the forward proof or the counterexample to II.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Make the Answers Fight — use contraposition to reject complete answer profiles that separate I from III, while retaining the full meaning of 'only'.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: A useful logical consistency check, but it saves no work beyond M1's existing use of contraposition.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: Three inconsistent profiles can be discarded early, but both substantive truth tests in M1 are still required.

subtopic: Sector perimeter contains more than arc length
prompt_html: Two sectors are similar, with radii \(r\) and \(r+3\). The smaller has arc length \(8\), and the difference between their areas is \(30\). What is the positive difference between their perimeters?
solution_html:
Let the common angle be \(\theta\) radians. The arc length gives \(r\theta=8\). The area difference is \(\tfrac12\theta[(r+3)^2-r^2]=3r\theta+\tfrac92\theta=24+\tfrac92\theta\). Equating this to \(30\) gives \(\theta=4/3\) and \(r=6\).

A sector perimeter is \(r\theta+2r\). Increasing the radius by \(3\) changes it by \(3\theta+6=4+6=10\). The arc-length difference alone would give only \(4\), omitting the two straight radii.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Similarity, scale and preserved ratios Arc length from a sector's central angle Area of a circular sector Sector perimeter from arc and radial edges Factorisation and algebraic expansion Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions Solve one-variable linear equations Domain restrictions and reversible operations Substitute or independently check a proposed result Area scaling for similar figures

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Use one common radian angle θ. Form rθ = 8 and 30 = θ[(r + 3)² − r²]/2. Expanding only the area difference and replacing rθ by 8 leaves the linear equation 24 + 9θ/2 = 30. Finally calculate the perimeter difference directly as 6 + 3θ. Finding either complete perimeter or the radius is unnecessary until verification.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Let the common central angle be θ radians. The smaller arc gives rθ = 8. The area difference is 30 = θ[(r + 3)² − r²]/2 = 3rθ + 9θ/2 = 24 + 9θ/2, so θ = 4/3. A sector's perimeter is its arc plus two radii, hence the required difference is 3θ + 2·3 = 4 + 6 = 10. For verification, r = 8/θ = 6 and the larger radius is 9. Their areas are 24 and 54, their arcs are 8 and 12, and their perimeters are 20 and 30. Thus D is the unique correct option.
domain_case_checks: The radii are positive real lengths: r > 0 and r + 3 > r. No integrality condition is imposed.
The positive arc length gives θ > 0. The solution θ = 4/3 lies strictly between 0 and π, so it is a valid nondegenerate sector angle without relying on the drawing's apparent angle.

There is no omitted major-sector solution: the area equation 24 + 9θ/2 = 30 has exactly one solution. Even if a full-circle limiting case were admitted, θ = 2π would give area difference 24 + 9π, not 30.
For the common positive angle, P(R) = R(θ + 2) increases with R. Therefore larger minus smaller is the requested positive perimeter difference.
Division by 9/2 and, when recovering r, by θ = 4/3 is valid. No equation is squared and no root branches are introduced.
In M2, k = (r + 3)/r > 1, so the scale is positive and k − 1 is nonzero. Factoring k² − 1 and using r(k − 1) = 3 preserve the original constraints.
The recovered configuration satisfies every given exactly: radius difference 3, smaller arc 8 and area difference 30. No approximation or rounding is required.

skills.definition: Use justified similarity to transfer scale and side ratios between figures.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The given similarity supplies a common angle in M1 and one positive linear scale for radii and arcs in M2.
skills.learning_objective: Use stated sector similarity to identify a common angle and corresponding length scale.
skills.name: Similarity, scale and preserved ratios

skills.definition: For a circle of positive radius R and a simple sector angle 0 < θ < 2π measured in radians, use s = Rθ for the arc length. If the numerical angle is given in degrees, convert it to radians before using this formula.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The smaller arc is represented by rθ = 8.
skills.learning_objective: Form and use an arc-length equation with a consistent angle unit.
skills.name: Arc length from a sector's central angle

skills.definition: For a circular sector of positive radius R and angle 0 < θ < 2π measured in radians, compute its area as A = R²θ/2; equivalently, if its boundary arc length is s, use A = Rs/2. Retain square units.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 forms θ[(r + 3)² − r²]/2 = 30; M2 uses the smaller area A_small = r·8/2 = 4r.
skills.learning_objective: Express sector areas in terms of a common angle or a known arc length and compare them exactly.
skills.name: Area of a circular sector

skills.definition: For a nondegenerate simple circular sector of positive radius R and angle strictly between 0 and 2π, add its boundary arc length s and its two radial sides to obtain P = s + 2R. Include both straight sides when comparing sector perimeters.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The perimeter difference is the arc increase plus 2·3, giving 3θ + 6 in M1 and 8(k − 1) + 6 in M2.
skills.learning_objective: Calculate a sector perimeter or perimeter difference by accounting for its arc and both radii.
skills.name: Sector perimeter from arc and radial edges

skills.definition: Expand, factor and collect algebraic expressions while retaining equality.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 uses (r + 3)² − r² = 6r + 9; M2 uses k² − 1 = (k − 1)(k + 1).
skills.learning_objective: Simplify a difference of squares without losing its cross term or sum factor.
skills.name: Factorisation and algebraic expansion

skills.definition: Solve simultaneous equations while checking consistency and completeness of the solution set.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M1 replaces the product rθ in the area equation by 8. M2 replaces r(k − 1) by 3. Each reduces linked constraints to one unknown.
skills.learning_objective: Substitute a known product into a second equation rather than unnecessarily solving for every variable first.
skills.name: Solve simultaneous equations without losing solutions

skills.definition: Solve equations linear in a designated unknown by applying reversible operations to both sides, distributing operations over whole expressions, and retaining any domain restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The remaining equations are 24 + 9θ/2 = 30 in M1 and 12(k + 1) = 30 in M2.
skills.learning_objective: Isolate the remaining unknown using reversible subtraction and division.
skills.name: Solve one-variable linear equations

skills.definition: Identify expression domains and conditions under which algebraic transformations preserve equivalence.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The solution retains r > 0, θ > 0 and k > 1, checks the sector-angle range, and divides only by known nonzero quantities.
skills.learning_objective: Keep geometric positivity and nonzero conditions through the algebra and verify the recovered configuration.
skills.name: Domain restrictions and reversible operations

skills.definition: Substitute or independently verify a proposed result against the original problem and restrictions.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The reconstructed radii 6 and 9 give arcs 8 and 12, areas 24 and 54 and perimeters 20 and 30.
skills.learning_objective: Check every given and ensure the selected number represents the requested perimeter difference.
skills.name: Substitute or independently check a proposed result

skills.definition: For similar plane figures with positive finite areas and positive length scale factor k, use the area ratio k² and recover the length scale from a positive area ratio.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 writes the larger area as k² times the smaller area, producing 4r(k² − 1) = 30.
skills.learning_objective: Distinguish the area factor k² from the arc-length and radius factor k.
skills.name: Area scaling for similar figures

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Let k = (r + 3)/r > 1. Then r(k − 1) = 3, the larger arc is 8k and the smaller area is 4r. Area scaling gives 30 = 4r(k² − 1) = 12(k + 1), so k = 3/2. The perimeter increase is 2·3 + 8(k − 1) = 10.
limitations: Requires the sector-area identity A = Rs/2 and the square law for similar areas.
The scale factor must be derived rather than chosen.
It is not materially shorter than M1.
useful_alternatives.method: Angle-free similarity and area scaling
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when the student prefers corresponding-length ratios or wishes to avoid introducing an angle. It bypasses explicit use of the radian arc-length formula.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 uses s = Rθ, A = R²θ/2 and P = Rθ + 2R.
conditions_checked: The sectors have a common angle and radii r and r + 3.
The smaller curved length is 8.
Both radial boundary edges must be included.
The task compares individual areas and perimeters, not overlapping regions.
limitations: A circular boundary does not force a surviving π term.
The numerical angle is not supplied and cannot be measured from the image.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Follow the π: use exact sector formulas with θ in radians, and retain the straight contribution 2·3 to the perimeter difference.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is the ordinary sector method itself, not an additional shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: No extra saving beyond M1; radian formulas already incorporate the full-circle factors.

subtopic: Polynomial sign changes and exact root bounds
prompt_html:
Let \(p>0\) and \(0<a<2<b<4<c<6\). Define

\[F(x)=x^2(x-2)^2(x-4)^2(x-6),\qquad G(x)=-p(x-a)^2(x-b)^2(x-c)^2.\]

For every permitted choice of \(p,a,b,c\), how many distinct intersections do \(y=F(x)\) and \(y=G(x)\) have?
solution_html: Let \(H=F-G\). It has degree 7 with positive leading coefficient, so it is negative for sufficiently large negative \(x\). At \(0,2,4,6\), \(F=0\) and \(G<0\), so \(H>0\). At \(a,b,c\), \(G=0\) and \(F<0\), so \(H<0\). Thus \(H\) changes sign in each of \(( -\infty,0),(0,a),(a,2),(2,b),(b,4),(4,c),(c,6)\). A polynomial graph is continuous, so each interval contains a root. There are at least seven roots, but a nonzero degree-7 polynomial has at most seven. Hence there are exactly seven distinct intersections.
answer_verification_basis: Completed held-question review with source-bound proof and full teaching profile
skill_search: Degree arithmetic for polynomial combinations Signs of real quantities and squares Polynomial end behaviour Continuous level attainment by the intermediate value theorem Polynomial distinct-root bound and identity criterion Count distinct real roots across branches Separate example checking from a universal proof Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets

audited_reference.ordinary_method: M1: Form H=F−G, which is monic of degree 7. Read its alternating signs at the interlaced zeros 0,a,2,b,4,c,6, and use its negative left tail to obtain one further sign-change bracket. Continuity gives seven distinct real roots. The degree bound then proves there are no others. No expansion, differentiation, numerical plotting, or explicit root calculation is needed.
audited_reference.concise_proof: Fix any permitted p,a,b,c and put H=F−G. This is a monic polynomial of degree 7. At x=0,2,4,6, F(x)=0 and G(x)<0, so H(x)>0. At x=a,b,c, G(x)=0 and F(x)<0, so H(x)<0. Continuity therefore gives a zero in each of (0,a), (a,2), (2,b), (b,4), (4,c), (c,6). Also H(x)→−∞ as x→−∞, while H(0)>0, giving a further zero in (−∞,0). These seven zeros are distinct because their intervals are disjoint. A nonzero degree-7 polynomial has at most seven distinct real zeros, so these are all its zeros and there is exactly one in each interval. Each zero gives one intersection of the two graphs. The argument uses only the stated restrictions, so every permitted choice gives exactly 7 intersections.
domain_case_checks: The graphs are real polynomial graphs, defined and continuous for every real x. In particular, negative x-values must not be excluded by the positive parameter ordering.
The strict ordering makes a,b,c distinct and prevents them from coinciding with 0,2,4,6. Together with p>0, this makes every sign used in the proof strict.
F has degree 7 and leading coefficient 1; G has degree 6 and leading coefficient −p. Thus F−G has degree exactly 7 and cannot be the zero polynomial.
None of 0,a,2,b,4,c,6 is an intersection abscissa: at each such point exactly one of F and G is zero, while the other is strictly negative.

For the leftmost bracket, the limit at −∞ is used to choose a finite L<0 with H(L)<0. The intermediate value theorem is then applied on [L,0], not with infinity as an endpoint. L may depend on the fixed parameter choice.
The seven open brackets are nonempty and disjoint. Continuity initially gives at least one root in each; uniqueness within each bracket follows only after applying the global degree bound.
There are no intersections for x≥6: at x=6, F=0>G, and for x>6, F>0>G. The degree bound also excludes any additional roots elsewhere.
Distinct roots of H give distinct points (x,F(x)), even if some ordinates happen to agree. Repeated factors in F or G do not count as additional intersections between the two graphs.
The proof leaves all parameters arbitrary. Excluded boundary cases such as p=0 or a=0 are not silently included, and no numerical sampling or assumed stability of a sketch is used.

In M2, T=p+6>0. All compared factors T+a,T+b,T+c,T+2,T+4,T+6 are positive, so the product inequalities retain their direction. The chosen input −T is a negative-value witness for H, not a claimed root.

The transformation F(x)=G(x) ⇔ H(x)=0 is reversible for every real x. No division or squaring of an equation introduces exclusions or extraneous roots. The requested count is exact; no approximation is needed.

skills.definition: Bound the degree of polynomial sums and differences by the maximum input degree, allowing cancellation or the zero polynomial, and use degree addition for products of nonzero polynomials.
skills.evidence_in_solution: F has degree 2+2+2+1=7 and G has degree 2+2+2=6. Their difference therefore retains F's leading x⁷ term.
skills.learning_objective: Determine the exact degree and leading coefficient of a polynomial difference when its two inputs have unequal degrees.
skills.name: Degree arithmetic for polynomial combinations

skills.definition: Determine signs of real expressions, squares and products, including zero cases.
skills.evidence_in_solution: H is positive at the zeros of F and negative at the zeros of G. Strictness follows from nonzero squares, p>0 and a,b,c<6.
skills.learning_objective: Evaluate strict signs at interlaced zeros while retaining the outside negative coefficient and the unsquared factor x−6.
skills.name: Signs of real quantities and squares

skills.definition: Determine the limits of a nonconstant real polynomial as x→±∞ from its leading term, using the degree's parity and the leading coefficient's sign.
skills.evidence_in_solution: The monic degree-7 polynomial H tends to −∞ on the left, supplying a finite negative-value endpoint before x=0.
skills.learning_objective: Use odd degree and a positive leading coefficient to obtain a negative value sufficiently far to the left.
skills.name: Polynomial end behaviour

skills.definition: For a real continuous function, prove that every level between two attained endpoint values is attained between those endpoints. On an unbounded interval, first use a justified limit to obtain a finite bracket. Uniqueness requires an additional argument such as strict monotonicity.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Continuity of H and opposite strict endpoint signs produce a root in each of seven disjoint finite brackets.
skills.learning_objective: Turn sign brackets into root-existence statements without claiming uniqueness from continuity alone.
skills.name: Continuous level attainment by the intermediate value theorem

skills.definition: Use that a nonzero real polynomial of degree d has at most d distinct real roots; consequently, two polynomials of degree at most d that agree at d+1 distinct real inputs are identical.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Once seven distinct real zeros of H are established, its degree-7 upper bound excludes any extra zero and forces one distinct root per bracket.
skills.learning_objective: Combine a proved lower bound on distinct real roots with the polynomial degree cap to obtain an exact count.
skills.name: Polynomial distinct-root bound and identity criterion

skills.definition: Count distinct solutions of a real equation using exhaustive branches or a proved solution correspondence, filtering against domain and case restrictions, identifying overlaps and counting repeated roots only once.
skills.evidence_in_solution: A real zero x of H corresponds to exactly one common point (x,F(x)). Roots in the seven disjoint open brackets are distinct and exhaust the possible common points.
skills.learning_objective: Count graph intersections through a proved root correspondence and avoid counting separate graph zeros or multiplicities as extra points.
skills.name: Count distinct real roots across branches

skills.definition: Distinguish finite example checking from proof of a universally quantified statement.
skills.evidence_in_solution: Both methods fix an arbitrary permitted tuple and derive the count solely from p>0 and the strict ordering, rather than choosing sample parameter values.
skills.learning_objective: Prove a parameter-independent count using assumptions valid for every permitted tuple.
skills.name: Separate example checking from a universal proof

skills.definition: Manipulate and solve inequalities while preserving direction, sign conditions and solution sets.
skills.evidence_in_solution: M2 compares positive factors using a<2,b<4,c<6 and multiplies the inequalities to prove H(−(p+6))<0.
skills.learning_objective: Use positive-factor comparisons to construct a finite sign witness while retaining strictness.
skills.name: Inequality direction, multiplication and solution sets

useful_alternatives.concise_justification: Let T=p+6>0. Positive-factor comparisons give H(−T)<(T+2)²(T+4)²(T+6)[p(T+6)−T²]=−36(T+2)²(T+4)²(T+6)<0. Together with H(0)>0, this gives a finite negative-root bracket. The six interior brackets and the degree-7 cap then finish the proof exactly as before.
limitations: This is longer than the leading-term argument in M1.
The chosen point is only a negative-value witness, not an intersection.
It still requires the landmark signs, continuity and the degree bound.
Its factor comparisons depend on the stated strict parameter bounds.
useful_alternatives.method: Construct an explicit finite left bracket instead of appealing to polynomial end behaviour.
useful_alternatives.when_useful: Useful when an explicit finite witness is desired, or when a solution should avoid invoking a limit at infinity. It illustrates that the bracketing point may depend on p while the final count remains universal.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 obtains a finite negative left-hand value from the monic odd-degree tail.
conditions_checked: The evaluation input x is unrestricted, while p,a,b,c remain arbitrary fixed parameters.
With T=p+6>0, the factor comparisons in M2 give H(−T)<−36(T+2)²(T+4)²(T+6)<0.
The chosen input is a sign witness, not a root or a special parameter assignment.
limitations: The rest of the continuity and degree-bound proof is still required.
Specialising p,a,b,c to convenient values would not replace a universal proof.
The explicit finite bound requires more algebra than leading-term end behaviour.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Choose Your Own Numbers — M2 legally chooses the evaluation point x=−(p+6) to construct an explicit finite left bracket.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: Useful when a finite witness is preferred, but not a material shortcut relative to M1.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: It avoids the limiting argument for the left tail, replacing it with several positive-factor inequalities rather than reducing total work.

shortcut_assessments.best_ordinary_baseline: M1 already evaluates H at the supplied factor roots instead of expanding.
conditions_checked: F has axis zeros 0,2,4,6 and G has axis zeros a,b,c.
The given inequalities strictly interlace these landmarks.
At each landmark the other graph has a strictly negative ordinate.
No reflection symmetry or tangency between the two graphs is assumed.
limitations: Repeated roots of the individual polynomials are not common points.
The landmark sign pattern alone supplies existence, not local uniqueness.
shortcut_assessments.method_here: Mirror, Move, Match — Use the known axis intersections as exact landmarks to obtain alternating signs of F−G.
shortcut_assessments.saving_judgment: This is part of the best ordinary method, not an additional shortcut.
shortcut_assessments.work_avoided: It avoids expanding and sketching detailed curve shapes, but M1 already takes this approach.
